News.title: Female exec sacked by AI firm after falling asleep in sauna on boozy work trip could win record £76MILLION payout
News.content:
BOILING POINT Female exec sacked by AI firm after falling asleep in sauna on boozy work trip could win record £76MILLION payout







Next

A FEMALE exec sacked by an AI firm after falling asleep in a sauna on a boozy work trip is in line for a record £76million payout.

Senior tech engineer Shannon Burns won a disability discrimination case against Gitpod, which is now owned by ChatGPT developers OpenAI.



She had been dismissed by the “tech bro” company after she had to resort to kipping in the hot room when she lost her hotel room key.

Shannon, who earned £220,000 a year, was fired over three years ago but is still fighting to receive compensation.



The former VP of Engineering has developed PTSD after her sacking and has had to leave a career in tech for good.

She is seeking £76million based off “forensic” calculations of what she could have earned in the highly-lucrative industry.



Gitpod attempted to restrict the amount she could seek to £1million using a legal application described as “oppressive” by her lawyers.

But now, Birmingham Employment Tribunal has dismissed their application, meaning she can formally seek £76,071,992 compensation.

Gitpod has also been ordered to disclose to Shannon what the recent sale of the company to OpenAI was worth.

The firm did not tell her how much it was sold for even though she has shares in the firm, which are thought to be worth £2.6million alone and could rise to £21million after four years.



Currently, the biggest known award in UK Employment Tribunal history is £4.58million.

The tribunal previously heard Shannon was seen as a “trailblazer” in the tech industry who had worked for Silicon Valley firms including Slack and Lyft.

She was headhunted by Gitpod in late 2022 and appointed to the key leadership role of Vice President of Engineering, on a £220,000 salary with a £78,000 bonus per year.

Shannon who has ADHD – went on an off-site team building event in Lofer, Austria, in April 2023.

CEO Johannes Landgraf and other staff drank alcohol during the trip and one evening Shannon, who had also been drinking, could not access her room as she forgot her key.



Her ADHD caused her to have a “great deal of forgetfulness” and she would “persistently” lose items, the tribunal heard.

That night, she ended up having to sleep in a sauna – causing CEO Mr Landgraf to say he was concerned about her “lack of professional accountability”.

Shannon was sacked in June 2023 and later told the hearing: “My male colleagues were drinking alcohol/drunk at the offsite but I was the only one who was dismissed.”

Last year, Birmingham Employment Tribunal found she was dismissed as a result of her disabilities and she won a disability discrimination case.

She is seeking £76million, which relies on calculations made in her “schedule of loss” that examines what she could have gone on to earn.



As she earned such a huge salary and the tech industry is so lucrative, it is estimated that her total future losses are over £59million.

The remainder of the £76million is made up of sums to cover injury to feelings and what is known as an ACAS Uplift.

At the latest Birmingham hearing, Gitpod applied to have her £76million schedule of loss capped at £1million.

The company argued that Shannon’s claim for over £76million was “extraordinary”, adding: “The arguments set out in the [schedule of loss] are palpable nonsense.”

Employment Judge Rachel Wedderspoon dismissed the application.



She: “The Tribunal finds that an award in the sum claimed by [Shannon] is highly unusual and the sort of award that may be more commonplace awarded in the US jurisdiction.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“However, the Tribunal cannot say at a summary assessment in the absence of an employment renumeration expert report or an expert medical information that [her] valuation has little reasonable prospect of success.”

A full compensation hearing will be held at a later date, pending Gitpod’s appeal of the previous tribunal ruling.

News.title: Could Baby April murder finally be solved? Four ‘promising’ new leads after mystery woman visited tot’s grave, cop says
News.content:
TRAGIC TOT Could Baby April murder finally be solved? Four ‘promising’ new leads after mystery woman visited tot’s grave, cop says







Next

A MURDERED newborn who was strangled and dumped may finally get justice 30 years later thanks to four “promising” leads.

Baby April, thought to be just a week old, was strangled by a pair of tights and found wrapped in a plastic toilet roll Kleenex bag on April 3, 1995.



After 30 years, even the advancement in DNA could not solve the mysterious death, and no parents or relatives could be found.

However, new leads have set new hope after detectives released an e-fit of a woman found at the grave of the murdered child earlier this month.



Detective Chief Inspector Neil Kimber, who is leading the probe, said the appeal had prompted four “promising” lines of inquiry.

He said: “The answers to this investigation are overdue but I am optimistic about the enquiries that we have got from that last appeal.



“I didn’t expect to get as much as we did. The public are fantastic; they are all so willing to help.

“As a direct result of the e-fit we quite quickly got a lot of information that started to come into the incident room.



“That led to us having probably in excess of 25 lines of enquiry to follow up on. Three or four of them I would say look reasonably promising.”

The woman was said to have visited the grave between 2pm and 3pm on June 21, 2025 and appeared to be distressed, according to police.

She is described as white, in her 40s, no taller than 5ft 7in, medium to slim build and with a pale complexion.

She had grey shoulder-length hair, wearing a grey short cardigan, trainers, and black leggings, carrying two bags.

One was a small shoulder bag, and the second, worn across her body, was a women’s floral fabric holdall bag, and appeared quite full.



DCI Kimber continued: “It has been really frustrating, but what we have is a team of investigators that are absolutely determined to get the answers. We are not going to let it go.

“There has been a huge amount of work done on this. There are over 180 statements that have been taken in this inquiry and in excess of 80 DNA samples.”

Police estimated Baby April was born between March 25 and April 3, 1995 – the week before she was found dead.



Nameless, police called the helpless tot after the month she was born.

They said the 7lb baby was not born with medical intervention as the umbilical cord was roughly severed.

She was found by a teen couple in Singleton Lake, wrapped up in a Kleenex toilet roll bag before being placed inside another plastic bag.

DCI Kimber, who joined the investigation last year, says the public have really banded together to help solve the mystery, and he is appealing for even more to come forward with information.

He said: “We are still really desperate for the answers in relation to Baby April. No one is really looking out for her, so it is our job to do that.



“The public really need the answers to this as well because there is a lot of interest in it in the community in Ashford and in the wider country.

“This is quite an emotional case and people are really coming forward to help us with it which I am so grateful for.

“We have a number of lines of inquiry and they could be really key or it could be back to the drawing board.”

Anyone who recognises the woman pictured, or who has information which could assist the investigation is urged to call Kent Police on 01622 652006.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

People can also contact Crimestoppers on 0800 555111 or complete their online form.



Information can also be submitted via their online portal: https://mipp.police.uk/operation/4601020100X37-PO1.

News.title: Two men, 44 and 27, arrested after woman’s body found and town centre pub cordoned off
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

'MURDER' PROBE Two men, 44 and 27, arrested after woman’s body found and town centre pub cordoned off







Next

TWO men have been arrested after a woman’s body was found as a town centre pub remains cordoned off.

Emergency services responded to an address in Parkgate, County Durham, yesterday evening.



Tragically, despite the best efforts of medics, a woman was pronounced dead at the scene.

Formal identification is yet to take place however police believe the woman to be in her 40s.



An investigation was launched and police arrested two men, 44 and 27.

The older man was taken into custody on suspicion of murder while the younger was arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender.

Both have been taken to a police station where they both remain at this time.

Specialist investigators remain at the scene today as a probe into the tragedy continues.

Officers will be carrying out inquiries in the area, Durham Constabulary said.

The force added: “Anyone with any information is asked to call Durham Constabulary on 101, quoting incident number 521 of September 23.



“Information can also be passed on to Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111.”

News.title: Desperate family of Brit, 43, missing in Colombia for seven weeks fear for his life as Marcus Rashford joins appeal
News.content:
WHERE IS ANTON? Desperate family of Brit, 43, missing in Colombia for seven weeks fear for his life as Marcus Rashford joins appeal







Next

THE family of a Brit who vanished seven weeks ago in Colombia are terrified for his safety.

Anton Green, 43, moved out to the South American country to work remotely after falling in love with its language and culture.



He usually calls “at least weekly, if not more often”, and his family is “extremely worried” for his safety, they told The Sun.

Anton’s family have launched a desperate plea for help finding him and have urged anyone with information about his whereabouts to come forwards.





Footballer Marcus Rashford has joined the search for Anton, calling him “a family friend”.

Anton’s mum Nyla Green, 64, said Rashford had played with her youngest son, ex-Manchester United youth team defender Ro-shaun Williams, both at the academy and at junior football club Fletcher Moss.

She told The Sun it was “very nice of him” to share the appeal for Anton, adding: “We’ve known Marcus since they were six, seven years old.

“So he’s like a son to us.



“We’re really hoping that people can reach out if they know something.”

Anton, originally from Whalley Range, Manchester, settled near Colombia‘s capital Bogotá, three years ago.



He was staying around the Fontibón and Mesitas del Colegio areas before he vanished and may have been planning a trip to neighbouring Ecuador.

His loved ones have had radio silence from the Brit since August 6.

Nyla, a teaching assistant, said when she last spoke to Anton they ended the call saying: “We’ll speak next week.”

Anton’s dad last spoke to him on August 5 and a friend in Colombia reportedly heard from him the next day.



Neither reported anything unusual at the time.

But his family said his phone has been off since August 8.

And his friends in Colombia have not heard from him either.

Anton’s sister, Sian Tuohey, 40, told The Sun her worst fear would be him “not being alive”.

Sian described her older brother as a “great uncle” with a “love of learning languages”.



He speaks Spanish and Dutch fluently, and had moved out to Colombia three years ago, where he works remotely.

Sian told The Sun: “He decided to just try Colombia and ended up feeling like he really likes the culture there.

“He likes the fact that he knows the language, the cost of living is good.”

Mum Nyla said Anton grew up as a “typical young boy, really mischievous, funny, really bright”.

He travelled around Europe before moving to South America.



She said: “He was keen on learning languages. He liked to know about the world and loved animals as well.

“You want your children to be happy and to be free and do things that, let’s say, maybe you didn’t do.

“I didn’t do a lot of travelling when I was younger. I encourage them to do that, to get to know other places.”

The family said this time last year he started struggling with his mental health, and had been suffering with low mood.

Nyla said it was difficult to see her son suffer from far away, adding: “I continued to talk to him and reassure him that he’s loved and that we’re here for him.”



Anton’s sister said it was particularly hard that he was missing more than 5,000miles away from family.

She said “Even if he was lost in Manchester, it would be problematic.

“But to be on the opposite side of the world and be suffering with really low moods, it’s obviously really worrying for anyone.

“He’s on a completely different continent in a country where we don’t speak the language and we don’t know anyone”.

“And, you know, he doesn’t have a partner and a family and people he’s there with. He’s there alone.”



Sian said the whole family are “extremely worried” about him.

She urged Anton to get in contact if he could, “just to let us know that he’s safe and that he’s okay”.

Sian said: “I would want him to know that he’s loved and he’s missed.”

“He’s missed here and there’s a lot of people, a lot of friends, probably more than he knows, are really worried.”

The family said the UK police were limited in what they could do to search for her brother abroad, but that working with Colombian cops had been difficult, and that they hadn’t received enough updates.



Nyla said the whole search process had been “extremely slow”.

They are considering flying out to Colombia to search for him, but Sian said: “It’s a long shot in general, because we don’t know what we’d be going out to do.”

Anton’s mum added: “If anyone knows anything, contact the police.

“And obviously for Anton, if he is able to see this, we love him and we just want him to come home.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

An Foreign Office spokesperson told The Sun: “We are supporting the family of a British man reported missing in Colombia and are in touch with local authorities.”



The Sun contacted the Interpol, the NCA and the Colombian national police for comment.

News.title: We live in shadow of 20ft ‘mega dump’ – we’ve been moaning for months… it’s filled with rats, kids’ bikes & wheelie bins
News.content:
ABSOLUTE STATE We live in shadow of 20ft ‘mega dump’ – we’ve been moaning for months… it’s filled with rats, kids’ bikes & wheelie bins







Next

A 20FT mountain of rubbish dubbed the “mega-dump” is causing misery and an “unpleasant odour” for residents in a UK town.

Dubbed the “mega dump” by residents, the pile towers over buildings nearby, visible from streets away – blocking residential properties and shops on the other side of the road.



The mountain consists of children’s bicycles, broken plastic chairs, mattresses and even a wheelie bin.

Household items were also perched on the stinking heap of waste – with a skip precariously perched at the top.



The council has issued a “temporary stop notice” to the firm, who were found to have no planning permission for waste transfer activity.

The pile was first noticed by next-door Chartist Garage in March, and reported to the Environment Agency shortly after – yet it still towers over the M67 today.

A garage worker told Manchester Evening News: “I’m concerned about potential vermin in there.

“It is an absolute state. A sad, sad state of affairs.”



While neighbors are outraged at the lack of action over the months – Tameside Council has now informed locals they have 56 days to investigate before the cleaning process can start.

One local said: “It’s got to be worth almost half a million to remove all of that. I’m not looking forward to when that time comes.

“Yes, I want it gone, but I’m worried about the process because that is not an easy job.”

While another voiced “I can’t understand the mentality, to actually think they can get away with doing something like this. Particularly with everything that’s on the news about people fly- tipping.

“It’s an increasing problem and I just can’t believe it’s got to this stage before intervention.”



A Tameside council spokesperson said: “We’re working with the Environment Agency, supported by Greater Manchester Police, on the matter and we’ve served a temporary stop notice at MD Waste Management Ltd, Edward Street, requiring the unauthorised use of the site – which does not have planning permission for waste transfer activity – to cease while investigations continue.

“We’re working with the landowner to ensure compliance with the notice and removal of the waste from the land.”

MD Waste Management have been approached for comment.

News.title: Fears small boat migrants evading capture with smugglers using ‘scatter gun’ tactics – after 2 dinghies avoid detection
News.content:
BORDER CHAOS Fears small boat migrants evading capture with smugglers using ‘scatter gun’ tactics – after 2 dinghies avoid detection







Next

OFFICIALS fear small boat migrants will evade capture and be at large in the UK with smugglers having to use new “scatter gun” tactics.

Two packed dinghies arrived on the shores of Kent in the space of 48 hours this week without being intercepted by UK Border Force officers.



On Wednesday alone, 10 boats made the Channel crossing carrying a record 781 migrants in total.

Some 21 people have been detained and taken to a Home Office facility where they will be processed ahead of making asylum claims.



As many as 30 migrants landed on Samphire Hoe, near Dover, before cops could get to the scene on Tuesday.

It is feared as many as 10 migrants evaded capture after their arrival, which came hours after five migrants landed in Folkestone on Monday.



The Government claimed it was an “isolated and rare” case, but Border Officials believe the landings show smuggling gangs using new tactics.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has since ordered an “urgent review” of the two unescorted landings.



Tony Smith, a ex-director general of Border Force, described the recent undetected arrivals as a “much greater security risk”.

He told The Telegraph: “To avoid our controls altogether does worry me as it poses a much greater security risk than the ones we are picking up in the Channel.

“If they were picked up on a small boat as normal, they would likely be detained or prosecuted if they were returnees or wanted.

“They may be people previously deported from the UK…. It is definitely a different business model to the one we are used to.”

The Home Secretary yesterday said the arrivals were “unacceptable”.



But critics have fumed that Ms Mahmood has “lost control” of Britain’s borders.

She said: “This was not acceptable. Our improved monitoring has led to uncontrolled crossings becoming incredibly rare. But even one is one too many.

“That is why I have ordered an urgent review by the Border Security Command into how this happened, and what must be done to ensure it doesn’t happen again.

“The new tactics adopted by the smugglers, like launches from much further west in France, are a reminder of two things.

“Firstly, these gangs have no regard for human life. They are putting people on increasingly long and dangerous crossings.



“Secondly, our efforts are having an impact. We are making it much harder for gangs to launch vessels, forcing them to change their approach.

“As a result we are significantly reducing the numbers coming here by small boat.”

However, Chris Philp, the Shadow Home Secretary, said: “This is a day of despair for the Labour Government.

“Our border security has descended into chaos, with illegal immigrants crossing at will over ever larger distances and in ever larger boats.

“What’s more, there have been two uncontrolled illegal migrant landings in just 48 hours.



“It is a free for all – the Labour Government has no idea who is coming into the country.

“The only way to stop Channel crossings is to deport anyone who arrives illegally to their home country or a safe third country.”

It comes after 10 boats arrived on these shores on Wednesday alone, having crossed the Channel.

They carried a record 781 migrants in total.

The cumulative number of arrivals by small boats in 2026 now stands at 18,565, according to provisional figures from the Home Office.



This is down 42 percent on the equivalent point last year, when the total stood at 32,188.

It is also 26 percent below the figure at this stage in 2024, when the total was 25,165.

It means there have been 6,096 arrivals in 83 dinghies since Andy Burnham became Prime Minister on July 20.

And six people were arrested on Tuesday night after a packed mega-dinghy crossed the Channel from France.

Riot cops and masked men were seen facing off against each other in tense scenes after police closed off the access road to Haslar Marina in Gosport, Hampshire.



Some protesters were seen standing over-looking the harbour to see if the packed boat was approaching.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A few groups of men dressed all in black were spotted wearing masks and hoods as they argued with police as darkness fell.

The dinghy had set off from near Bayeux — home to the famous tapestry depicting the 1066 Norman invasion — on Monday morning to make the 70-mile trip.

News.title: Dangerous amounts of cancer-causing ‘forever chemicals’ found in blood of residents living next to UK industrial plant
News.content:
Next

DOZENS of people living near an ex-chemical plant have tested positive for high levels of cancer-causing toxins in their bloodstream.

In April, families in Thornton-Clevelys, Lancashire, were warned they could be at risk from dangerous “forever chemicals” coming from nearby former industrial site, Imperial Chemical Industries (ICI).



Now, blood tests have confirmed “really high levels” of the toxins in dozens of residents – with one local even found to have the highest level of synthetic substances ever recorded in the UK.

A groundbreaking investigation revealed the resident had PFOA levels 100 times higher than the average in the general population.



The village has been under investigation for years by the Environment Agency after fears of contamination of soils and locally grown food.

Tests revealed that PFOA (Perfluorooctanoic Acid) – chemicals often used to coat non-stick pans – had contaminated soil surrounding the plant.

The “forever chemical” can accumulate in blood and cause cancer, immune system disorders and high levels of bad cholesterol.

Forever chemicals are human-made substances that are resistant to water and oil – found in many everyday products like waterproof clothing.



Residents were warned to take a “precautionary approach” to eating homegrown produce grown from gardens or allotments within half a mile of the site.

Two allotments next to the AGC Chemicals Europe factory – which manufactured the coating for frying pans until 2012 – were immediately shut down.

However, an investigation has now revealed 70 per cent of local residents are at risk of serious health conditions linked to PFOA.

The alarming results came after Manchester Metropolitan University, Watershed and Law for Change conducted blood tests on 49 volunteers living next to the the former plant.

Possible effects include a higher risk of reduced thyroid function, kidney cancer, testicular cancer, elevated cholesterol, pre-eclampsia and ulcerative colitis.



One woman called Sam said her and her husband’s results had been “off the scale”.

She said: “When we opened the results … it was like, my God, that is ridiculously off the scale.

“I feel guilty because I’ve introduced [my children] to that way of life. I know it isn’t my fault, but the guilt is horrific.

“Knowing that I’ve offloaded what levels I probably had over the years into those children when I breastfed them – that’s heartbreaking.”



Meanwhile, Andrew Molloy – whose home was built on land that used to be part of the factory – found out he was in the highest-risk category.

He said: “I was half expecting it to be just normal.



“Because the investigation here has all been focused on – you’re only really being at risk if you eat fruit and veg from the garden or grow your own eggs – which I don’t.”

“One of the first things I’m going to do is take [the results] to my GP and at least get it on my record.

“They seem to refuse to do anything related to this, but now I have hard information and data.”

Andrew said that he underwent the tests because he was worried about persistent health problems in his family.

Mario Pantel – whose results were also among the highest – said it was “quite emotional, a shock” and that he would have to stop his children from playing in the garden.



He told the BBC: “I bought a property, assuming that this is our forever home.

“I’m going to have to stop my children from going in the garden, front and back. I feel constricted, like I’m in a cage now.”

More than 100 residents are now plotting a group legal action against AGC Chemicals to claim damages for the contamination.

PFOA was banned in the UK in 2020 after the World Health Organisation (WHO) classed it as a Group 1 carcinogen – which means there is clear scientific evidence it can increase the risk of cancer.



Sarah Moore, partner at Leigh Day – the law firm representing some of the residents – said compensation could be sought for financial losses on the value of their homes and the impact it had had on their use and enjoyment of the land.

Sarah Moore, partner at law firm Leigh Day – which is representing some residents – said compensation could be sought for financial losses on residents’ homes and the impact it has had on their use and enjoyment of the land.



She told the BBC damages could also be sought “in relation to the health risks, which we now consider to be a significant issue as a result of the testing we’ve been doing locally”.

The case would mark the first time a community had brought a legal claim over contamination from forever chemicals in the UK.

Sarah added: “My worry is that it’s the tip of the iceberg, it’s just the beginning.”

A spokesperson for AGC Chemicals Europe, Ltd. told The Sun: “We are aware of the recent blood testing initiative, and we understand the concerns this may have caused amongst local residents.

“Whilst the parties conducting these tests have chosen not to share their findings and data with us, we would emphasise that the UK Government’s position is clear: PFAS blood testing does not predict future health problems and can sometimes create unnecessary concern.



“For these reasons PFAS biomonitoring is not currently recommended through the NHS or private blood tests.

“The Hillhouse site and surrounding area has been dedicated to industrial chemical manufacturing for well over a century – long before AGC Chemicals Europe, Ltd. was established – and a wide variety of historical users have operated on the site.

“Since the wider multi-agency investigation is still ongoing and no formal determination of land contamination has been made under Part 2A of the Environmental Protection Act, we cannot speculate on future outcomes or next steps.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“AGC Chemicals Europe, Ltd. has been part of the Thornton Cleveleys’ community since 1999.

“The health, wellbeing and safety of our employees and the local community remain our priority.”

News.title: Brit vanishes in Benidorm with ‘lost passport and no money’ after missing flight home as desperate wife pleads for help
News.content:
FIND HIM Brit vanishes in Benidorm with ‘lost passport and no money’ after missing flight home as desperate wife pleads for help







Next

A BRIT has vanished in Benidorm without his passport or any money, his distraught wife said in an appeal for help.

Geoff Cumiskey disappeared after allegedly missing his flight home and being left by himself in the popular resort town.



The holidaymaker, from Workington, Cumbria, has left his family worried sick after being unable to get hold of him.

Geoff’s wife, Nikki Jane, reported him missing on September 23.



She revealed that her husband has lost his passport and has no luggage or money with him.

Nikki said that Geoff was not in “the best frame of mind”, which is adding to the family’s stress.



Geoff’s phone has also died, leaving his loved ones and friends unable to contact him.

The Brit allegedly went back to the holiday apartment he was staying in to retrieve his passport.

Since then, there has been no update from Benidorm – with Nikki now involving the police.

She claimed that local authorities are now liaising with Interpol to try and find him.



Nikki is urging expats and Brits abroad to come forward with any information they may have about Geoff.

She said: “Reaching out to anyone who may be in Benidorm at the minute, or who knows someone who is there.

“My husband Geoff Cumiskey is alone in Benidorm, has lost his passport, has no luggage, and no money.

“He isn’t in the best frame of mind, his phone has died, and we are all worried about him and can’t get in touch with him.

“This has been reported to the police, who are liaising with Interpol to try and locate him.



“In the meantime, I am hoping that there is someone I know in Benidorm at the moment who may be able to help locate him.

“If you can help please get in touch.”

The Sun has contacted the Foreign Office and Interpol for comment.

It comes as a Brit expat went missing in Colombia, prompting his family to make a desperate appeal for help.

Anton Green, 43, from Manchester, moved to South America three years ago.



But his terrified family have been tortured by weeks of radio silence from the Brit and are concerned for his safety.

They last heard from Anton on August 5.

His family said his lack of contact was deeply out of character.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Marcus Rashford has joined the appeal, with Anton being the brother of a former Manchester United youth teammate.

The England winger described Anton as a “family friend” on his social media as he posted an appeal for information.

News.title: Crashed RAF jet steered to 'avoid built-up areas' before pilots ejected, commander says
News.content:
An RAF jet was steered to "avoid built-up areas" before two pilots ejected out of the aircraft, an RAF commander has said.

Gp Capt Gez Currie, Station Commander, said: "The aircraft would have been aimed in a direction that the pilot believed was open field, in order to avoid built-up areas and anybody on the ground."

The Hawk T2 aircraft had been flying out of the RAF Valley station on Anglesey on Wednesday when it plummeted to the ground in the nearby Pencarnisiog area.

The trainee and an experienced professional, who parachuted out of their plane moments before it crashed, are expected to make a full recovery after they were treated for minor injuries.

Hawk operations have been paused by the RAF as a "precautionary measure" while investigations into the crash are ongoing - the Red Arrows are included in the pause as the aerobatics display team use the T1.

News.title: Anti-migrant activist arrested after dinghy slashed in Channel
News.content:
Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been arrested after a video appeared to show him slashing at a boat in the English Channel with a knife.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary said a 37-year-old man of no fixed abode had been arrested after a "boat that had an emergency responder on board" was damaged in the Channel.

He was arrested on suspicion of criminal damage with intent to endanger life, "destroying ships" under the Aviation and Maritime Security Act 1990 and "conduct endangering ships" under the Merchant Shipping Act 1995. He remains in custody.

The force previously said it was examining the video which Thomas, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, had live-streamed on Tuesday.

A French coastguard official was on board when Thomas appeared to slash at the vessel. Some 50 migrants who had travelled in the boat from Normandy had already been taken to Dover for processing.

Far-right activist Tommy Robinson shared a video of Thomas's arrest on social media late on Wednesday, claiming it was in relation to an attempt to "stop the invasion of our country".

Thomas organised anti-migrant protests in Dover and Portsmouth in early September which saw roads blocked by hundreds of demonstrators, including groups of men in black balaclavas.

He has been rallying support for "mass resistance" to "take our country back" through his venture Patriot Platform, which he founded earlier this year.

News.title: NHS trust to review 4,500 breast cancer cases after unnecessary surgeries found
News.content:
Hospital chiefs in County Durham have agreed to review up to a further 4,500 breast cancer cases after failings including delayed diagnoses and unnecessary surgeries were found.

Hundreds of patients suffered harm under County Durham and Darlington NHS Foundation Trust, according to a review of cases dating back to 2023.

The BBC previously investigated the failings and has spoken to multiple women affected, including one who said she felt "mutilated" and the trust's mistakes were "absolutely unforgivable".

Ahead of agreeing to expand the review to cases dating back to 2015, members of the trust's board offered "sincere" apologies for the failings and harm caused.

At an extraordinary meeting of the board held in Durham, board chair Alison Marshall said: "I would like to offer a sincere apology to all the women and their families who have been affected by the failings in our breast services.

"I can't imagine the impact that has had."

She said they could "not turn back the clock" but would be "open, honest and transparent" about the failings.

Chief nurse Gill Hunt told the board concerns were first raised in 2015 after a "service reconfiguration" and loss of breast surgical trainee posts.

Over the following years patients and bodies such as the Northern Cancer Alliance, Care Quality Commission and NHS England raised multiple issues, she said.

The key "themes" included treatment "not aligned to best practice", excessive surgery and delayed diagnosis, she said.

The trust's breast surgery lookback review began in April 2025 by examining cases between January 2023 and February 2025.

Hunt said 538 cases had been reviewed so far with 321 having experienced some form of harm, including one death.

News.title: Watch: What you need to know about the OpenAI Australian government hack
News.content:
A rogue OpenAI agent has hacked an Australian government website, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said. The agent hacked a statistics portal containing private data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme, Medicare.

The BBCâs North America technology correspondent Lily Jamali explains what you need to know about the breach, and why it matters.

More on this story.

News.title: Ex-England striker Andy Carroll reveals he was sexually assaulted in 2021
News.content:
Former England striker Andy Carroll has revealed he was sexually assaulted by a man in 2021.

The 37-year-old, who was automatically granted anonymity as a victim of sexual assault, has made the details public in an autobiography titled 'Owning it'.

The incident took place at Carroll's home, during his second spell with his hometown club Newcastle and led to the perpetrator being jailed for three years.

Carroll, now a player/co-owner of non-league club Dagenham & Redbridge, says he decided to include the incident in his book "at the very last minute" after discussing it with his girlfriend Lou Teasdale.

A friend of his former partner, who was away at the time, was set to stay over after coming to his home to watch a boxing match.

Carroll says the incident occurred while he was sleeping and he then threw the man out of the house, before knocking him unconscious as he tried to return.

Carroll, who also played in the Premier League for Liverpool and West Ham, called the police and was "sobbing" in the arms of his children's nanny.

The unnamed attacker was found guilty of sexual offences and placed on the sex offender register. Carroll testified in court, a process he says was "humiliating and embarrassing and absolutely horrendous".

Carroll wrote: "I was sexually assaulted, there I said it. Scary to even think about and only a few people knew about it before now.

"Me and Lou spent a lot of time discussing whether to mention it in this book or not. I avoided my publisher for so long that they probably suspected I got cold feet.

"Scary to talk about but it's made [me] the person I am today as much as any of the good stuff. And if me talking about it helps just one person then good, it will have been worth it."

Carroll, who won nine England caps, added: "What happened to me affected every facet of my life. I'd think about it every day, making it difficult to focus on anything else, including footballâ¦ The trauma of what happened to me hasn't gone away."

Carroll joined Dagenham in July 2025 and has made six appearances in the National League South this season.

If you have been affected by any of the issues in this article, you can find information and support at BBC Action Line

News.title: Elephants use medicinal plants to treat themselves, researchers find
News.content:
The scientists collaborated with the conservation charity the Mount Elgon Foundation, external. They interviewed local people, including wildlife scouts and community elders.

Accounts described elephants selecting particular plants when they seemed unwell, and mothers reportedly giving medicinal plant material to their calves.

From this, the researchers concluded that the elephants use 35 different plant species, and that 25 of those are known locally to have medicinal uses.

The study, published in the journal Scientific Reports, external, did not name the interviewees - keeping participants anonymous so they felt free to share their stories.

Their accounts reveal some intriguing details. In one testimony, a wildlife scout described seeing elephants using a plant known as Angurweet "as medicine to give to babies".

Angurweet is used as a remedy for ailments including stomach ache. The scout, who described elephant mothers mixing it in their mouths - "removing the leaves and chewing it until smooth, along with the roots of some other trees".

He also recounted that he had seen mothers mix this plant material with their own milk. "They give it to the babies, who chew on it themselves and spit out the solids".

Professor Michael Huffman, a primatologist based in Japan, currently at Nagasaki University, said this particular account was "tantalising", but more evidence would be needed to prove that elephants provided bespoke medical treatment for their calves.

The scientists have already embarked on gathering that evidence - giving the local wildlife experts they worked with cameras to record the behaviour they witness.

They are also analysing plants that the elephants use - looking for new medicines that the elephants themselves may have discovered.

Another lead reearcher on the project, Dr Fabien Schultz from the Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine in Hamburg, told BBC News: "Local knowledge has given us a map".

"We [now] want to follow the elephants and investigate whether they select particular plants in particular health contexts, and whether those plants have relevant biological activity."

News.title: Cardiff to host long-awaited Fury v Joshua fight
News.content:
Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury will contest their long-awaited all-British heavyweight fight at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on 11 December.

The bout, more than a decade in the making, will be broadcast globally on Netflix.

BBC Sport understands the main event could take place in the early hours of Saturday morning in the UK, with organisers considering a late start to cater for audiences in the United States.

Joshua and Fury will come face-to-face at a news conference in London on Wednesday, 30 September, as the build-up begins to one of the most anticipated fights in British boxing history.

"I am inspiring a generation," Joshua, 36, posted on Instagram. Fury, 38, is yet to comment on the announcement.

The event is being promoted as a collaboration between Saudi boxing powerbroker Turki Alalshikh's The Ring and UFC chief Dana White.

"Two of the best heavyweights of this generation, finally in the ring together," Alalshikh said.

"This will be one of the biggest fights in boxing history. I am very happy to make this fight happen for the fans."

The former two-time world champions had already signed contracts for the bout earlier this year, but the date and venue had yet to be confirmed.

London's Wembley Stadium and New York's Madison Square Garden were the frontrunners to stage the fight, but both presented issues before Cardiff recently emerged as an alternative.

The Principality Stadium has hosted late-night boxing before, including Joe Calzaghe's fight with Mikkel Kessler in November 2007, which began at 01:00 GMT.

Welsh Rugby Union and Cardiff Council officials welcomed the fight, saying it would reinforce the city's reputation for staging major events and could bring a significant economic boost, although some operational details still need to be finalised.

Joshua had been pushing for the fight to take place in the UK and has got his wish.

"Forever indebted to the UK public for their support of Anthony Joshua. We couldn't have got this over the line without you," his promoter Eddie Hearn said.

It is notable that White, who fronts Zuffa Boxing, is involved in the promotion.

"For more than a decade, boxing fans have been clamouring for the heavyweight showdown between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua. Together, they bring 66 wins, 52 knockouts and multiple heavyweight world titles into the ring," White said.

"On December 11, two of the biggest heavyweights of this generation finally collide - and the winner will take a significant place in heavyweight history."

There was no official statement from Hearn or Fury's promoter Frank Warren in the official news release sent by Netflix. Hearn had previously said he did not want White to be involved in promoting the fight.

News.title: Blood tests find high level of cancer-causing forever chemical in residents near factory
News.content:
Blood tests have found "really high levels" of a cancer-causing forever chemical in dozens of people living near a major chemical factory in the UK.

The residents, from Thornton-Cleveleys, Lancashire, have been told they could be at elevated risk of serious health conditions from the substance, known as PFOA.

The village has been under investigation for years by the Environment Agency over contamination of soils and locally grown food from the substance, which is a type of forever chemical - so-called because they do not easily break down.

That investigation said high levels likely came from the nearby AGC Chemicals factory, which used it in their manufacturing processes until 2012.

Sam Hammond and her husband, both from the village, have been told they were at increased risk of health impacts from PFOA. However, she told the BBC was more shocked by her son's result.

"When we opened the results...it was like, my God, that is ridiculously off the scale.

"I feel guilty because I've introduced [my children] to that way of life. I know it isn't my fault, but the guilt is horrific. Knowing that I've offloaded what levels I probably had over the years into those children when I breastfed them - that's heartbreaking," she said.

News.title: Teenagers to be offered new vocational GCSE subjects in school
News.content:
New vocational GCSEs will be introduced from 2029 for 14-year-olds alongside existing core academic subjects in England.

The new subjects could include building and construction, business management and finance, and child development.

A new national target for employers to help create 200,000 work experience opportunities for under 16s is also being set by Prime Minister Andy Burnham, as part of reforms to shake-up the education system to better prepare young people for the world of work.

Education unions said the ideas were welcome but a clear strategy was needed to make them happen. The Conservatives said the plans risked "throwing away" progress made in recent years.

Standards for the new qualifications will be set nationally by the regulator Ofqual to ensure grades are in line with other GCSEs, and will gradually replace other qualifications at this level such as BTec tech awards.

The vocational GCSEs will be designed to allow teenagers to progress at 16 to studying similar courses at college, including the new V-levels, which schools and colleges are teaching from autumn 2027, and T-levels.

The idea is to create a clear pathway for teenagers into different types of work through a ladder of qualifications.

News.title: No 'switch' to stop small boats, Lucy Powell tells BBC
News.content:
There is no "switch" to stop small boat crossings, and not every migrant boat can be intercepted, Labour's deputy leader has told the BBC.

Lucy Powell's comments came after two uncontrolled landings from the Channel in two days, at Folkestone and Samphire Hoe in Kent.

The Home Secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has ordered an urgent review by Border Security Command, calling the failure to intercept the two boats "not acceptable".

But the Conservatives say Labour has lost control of Britain's borders, and a "radically different" approach is needed.

A total of 781 people were recorded as arriving in 10 boats on Wednesday, the highest in a single day for far this year.

In a round of interviews with BBC local radio ahead of Labour's annual conference, Powell told BBC Solent: "We are taking all steps we can to really bear down on and eradicate the small boat crossings altogether.

"This has been a mammoth task across a whole range of different policy areas over the last couple of years, which is now starting to bear fruit, in that small boat crossings are significantly down this year - in fact significantly lower than at any time in the last six years.

"Obviously as we close down some avenues and we close down routes criminal gangs look to find new ways to deliver their terrible business model."

The thousands of migrants crossing the Channel are usually brought to shore by Border Security Command or RNLI boats.

Before Monday, no small boat arrivals to the UK coast without an escort had been officially recorded since September 6, 2025.

Uncontrolled landings are so rare that last year's incident was the only other one recorded since the Home Office began keeping data in 2023.

News.title: Burnham describes ban on alcohol in football stands as 'discrimination'
News.content:
Andy Burnham has branded a ban on fans being allowed to drink alcohol in the stands during men's football matches as "discrimination".

The prime minister told reporters that "I don't think it's fair for football fans to be singled out", as he suggested a change could be trialled.

Laws are in place which prevent drinking in view of the pitch at stadiums for clubs in the top five tiers of men's football in England. Other sports do not face such a restriction.

The Football Supporters' Association (FSA) said the "outdated" legislation should be reviewed, but police chiefs have warned against relaxing the law and would like to meet the PM to "explain the challenges".

The legislation was introduced in 1985 by Margaret Thatcher's government for English and Welsh football grounds. At the time, then-Home Secretary Leon Brittan said that alcohol was a "major contributory factor in violent and disorderly behaviour" in football grounds.

Burnham is a keen football fan and a season-ticket holder at Premier League team Everton.

Shortly before he became prime minister, he criticised the restriction on football fans as he attended a rugby league game at Everton's Hill Dickinson Stadium where it was possible for supporters to have a drink in the stands.

Speaking to reporters on his trip to the United Nations in New York, Burnham was asked if it was still his view now he is in Downing Street.

Burnham replied: "I think that legislation dates to an era where football was very different.

"And I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination. There are different ways it could be done. It could happen on a trial basis.

"But I'm not going to back away from what's been a long held view of mine. I don't see how it can be fair that some supporters of one sport can be treated differently."

Government sources have stressed that Burnham was restating an opinion that he has long held, rather than making any sort of policy announcement.

The prime minister's comments are not being seen inside government as an indication that he is looking to change the law in the area.

A trial or pilot scheme to look at whether a change would be possible is not being ruled out but any wider move would require extensive consultation involving football clubs, fans and the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport - none of which is currently planned.

News.title: Police in Scotland arrest 36 in raids on Vietnamese crime gangs linked to human trafficking
News.content:
One of Scotland's biggest police operations has targeted a Vietnamese organised crime group linked to human trafficking and cannabis farms.

About 300 officers took part in simultaneous early-morning raids, leading to the arrest of 36 people and the discovery of 14 cannabis-growing operations.

In total, police searched or checked 47 addresses in Aberdeen, Dundee, Falkirk, Edinburgh, Glasgow, Ayrshire, Lanarkshire, Midlothian and the Scottish Borders.

Police Scotland allege the gang is involved in "poly-criminality," including human trafficking, drug production, fraud, money laundering and organised immigration crime.

The force says the activities first came to light after Vietnamese criminals were connected to 150 cannabis farms discovered in Scotland last year.

Around 120 people had been arrested - so-called "gardeners"- and drugs worth Â£26m were seized.

News.title: Tories would prevent long-term jobless spending benefits on alcohol and cigarettes
News.content:
The Tories estimate the proposed changes would move about 350,000 claimants onto the lower rate of Universal Credit, saving around Â£538m a year.

Under the proposals, anyone fit to work would get six months on full benefits to find a job.

Every two years a claimant has previously worked would buy an extra year on the full rate of Universal Credit - but those who have not contributed enough would drop to a new "subsistence allowance", worth 70% of the full rate.

The party said this would protect "those with a strong employment record".

For example, a 58-year-old who has worked since leaving school but has been made redundant would keep the full allowance up to state pension age.

Claimants who are sick, disabled or already in work would also be exempt, with only those judged capable of work affected.

The Tories said the reduced subsistence allowance would be loaded onto pre-paid card that would not allow cash withdrawals, and would "prevent spending" on alcohol, cigarettes, or gambling.

The party is yet to detail how its proposal would work, but shadow welfare secretary Helen Whately said it would be "a version" of the pre-paid Aspen card issued to asylum seekers living in government-funded accommodation.

These cards cannot be used to make contactless, telephone or internet payments, whilst asylum seekers whose applications have failed cannot withdraw cash.

The Home Office confirmed last year it had tightened the list of permitted retailers where the cards can be used, after reports that some asylum seekers had used the cards to gamble in sites such as slot machine arcades.

Whately said the party would also look to learn from Australia, where certain claimants are issued with debit cards that restrict purchases, external at shops selling alcohol, tobacco products or pornography.

News.title: NHS staff investigated over access to dead teenager's medical records
News.content:
The mother of a teenage boy who died in hospital has said she is "deeply concerned and hurt" after learning his medical records may have been accessed inappropriately for years after his death.

Paula McGowan, whose 18-year-old autistic son Oliver died in 2016, was told that at least five members of staff at Bristol Foundation NHS Trust may have accessed his records without permission as recently as this year.

Three nursing staff are under formal investigation, while a doctor who no longer works for the trust has self-referred to the General Medical Council. Another member of staff is having their case reviewed separately.

The trust said it was "deeply sorry" for any stress and anxiety caused.

It said it had voluntarily referred itself to the Information Commissioner's Office.

It is the latest case involving concerns that NHS staff may have accessed patient records without a legitimate professional reason. In July the head of NHS England, Sir Jim Mackey, issued a "stark warning" that staff could face the sack or even prison for doing so.

Recent high-profile examples include the victims of the Nottingham and Southport attacks and a child who was injured in a crocodile enclosure in Cambridgeshire.

This month an investigation for the Health Services Journal found that at least 214 NHS staff have lost their jobs and around 2,000 been sanctioned for snooping on sensitive patient data over the past five years.

Oliver, who had a mild learning disability and epilepsy, died in 2016 at Southmead Hospital in Bristol after being given anti-psychotic medication that his family had repeatedly warned he should not receive.

After requesting information about his medical records, his mother was told that 38 people had accessed the data since his death, with 637 items viewed and 67 printed off.

News.title: Choirs pull out of Principality Stadium gig over 'cheeky' individual singer fees
News.content:
Wales is the land of song, but there may be distinct lack of voices at a festival in the Principality Stadium next year, because choirs are being charged thousands of pounds to take part.

The event, billed as the The Land of Song Festival, will feature world-renowned Italian Tenor Andrea Bocelli, but choirs are pulling out because of steep costs that include fees for individual singers.

Huw Watkins, who has performed in the Royal Albert Hall and at Wales rugby matches with Glynneath Male Voice Choir, said: "We couldn't get over it - we've never paid anything before to participate."

The event organisers, The Land of Song Festival and the Principality Stadium, have been asked to comment.

The festival next May is being marketed as "one of the world's largest shared singing events", with tenor Bocelli appearing on the Saturday, and up to 20,000 choristers appearing on the Sunday.

But choristers believe the event would be fortunate to get a fraction of those numbers, given the costs involved.

The festival's own website outlines the costs, with each choir paying a "choir subscription" of Â£150.

Then each individual choir member has to pay an additional Â£42, which means some choirs having to pay thousands of pounds to attend.

News.title: I had no heating or electricity for more than two years - now I have a new island home
News.content:
For the past-two-and-a-half years, some basic home comforts have been hard to come by for Ruari Morgan.

A fire in the backup generator of his old stone cottage on Rathlin Island left him without electricity, heating or hot water.

Now he's enjoying the simple pleasures of being able to come home and put the kettle on or have a shower after he moved in to a new social home two weeks ago.

The development of 10 social houses is the first on the island for more than a decade and it is hoped it will allow the unique community to sustain its population and provide a boost to its economy.

Rathlin is a small island off the north east coast of Northern Ireland, between Northern Ireland and Scotland, with a population of about 150 people.

Morgan, who was born and bred on the island and returned 15 years ago after living and working abroad, said social housing created more opportunities for islanders to come home.

"Obviously the more accommodation and the more affordable accommodation on the island is a good thing," he said.

"It's not always about encouraging new people to come to the island - which we do of course - but it's about making life here sustainable for the people who live here and have a connection to the island."

Morgan had been on the waiting list for four years before being allocated the property.

"I travel quite a lot and I volunteer abroad, but Rathlin's my base, this is my home," he said.

"We have a really good community here and it's not only people who have a lifelong connection...it's a nice mix."

A British tourist is facing backlash after complaining about prices at the Auschwitz cafe in a video posted to social media.

The woman, called Lynne but who posts under the name FreeSpirit666 on TikTok, bemoaned the price and quality of drinks at the restaurant adjoining the museum on the site of the former concentration camp in Poland.

In the video, which has been seen more than four million times, she said she and her daughter had paid £9 (10 euros) for a strawberry smoothie and a small bottle of lemonade, which they claimed tasted “a bit like” the disinfectant Dettol.

“Very expensive,” she assessed. “But the taxi from the station to here, which saved us a 25 minute walk, was £1.20. That was a bargain. So when you come to Auschwitz, bring some food and drink.”

open image in gallery Lynne took to TikTok to bemoan the prices of the drinks in the restaurant near the museum at Auschwitz ( TikTok / @freespirit666 )

The content creator also criticised the café’s lack of alternative milks, saying: “We fancied a coffee because we were early but they don’t do decaf or any milk other than real milk, so we gave that a miss.”

The camp at Auschwitz was set up in occupied Poland during the Second World War, with more than 1.1 million people, mostly Jews, dying in gas chambers or from starvation, cold and disease.

Commenters on the cafe video accused the poster of insensitivity, given the setting the tragic history of the location.

“Let’s not forget where we are,” one wrote. “This is a concentration camp where thousands died, not a 5 star restaurant experience.”

Another wrote: “I went to Auschwitz, I didn't take food and drink, and quite honestly, I didn't feel like eating and drinking, It wasn't entertainment for me. The last thing on my mind, was my comfort.”

In later videos, Lynne pushed back on mocking comments left on her post she said were “terribly disrespectful for the camp and the people that died there”.

open image in gallery The camp at Auschwitz was set up in occupied Poland during the Second World War to murder European Jews on a huge scale ( PA Media )

She responded: “No-one died in the cafe. No-one died there. No-one was gassed there. I just had a drink there which is nowhere near the park... the camp entrance.”

“People are saying I shouldn’t moan about the price of the food and drink but why are they selling it?” she said in another video. “People have got to have drinks, haven’t they - some of those tours take ages.”

A spokesperson for the Auschwitz-Birkenau museum said the restaurant was operated by an external provider with prices clearly displayed.

“For us, the essential point remains that people come to the Auschwitz Memorial to learn about the history of the German Nazi concentration and extermination camp, to confront the fate of its victims and to commemorate them,” they told The Times.

open image in gallery The video was seen more than four million times and received backlash for perceived insensitivity ( TikTok / Freespirit666 )

TripAdvisor was forced to remove an insensitive review of the museum itself in 2021 after initially saying it complied with submission guidelines.

The writer was eventually banned for saying they went to Auschwitz to “test the chamber” and describing the site as “fun for the family”.

And in 2023, the museum issued a warning after a visitor posted a “disrespectful” photo of themselves smiling next to the railway tracks into the camp.

“Pictures can hold immense emotional & documentation value for visitors. Images help us remember,” the museum’s social media page wrote.

“When coming to Auschwitz Museum visitors should bear in mind that they enter the authentic site of the former camp where over 1 million people were murdered. Respect their memory.”

Donald Trump’s administration has blocked reporters and staff from three news outlets from the White House and stripped them of their credentials despite a federal judge’s court order overturning the president’s media ban hours earlier.

Reporters from Politico and MS NOW said they were denied entry on Thursday morning after U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly issued a temporary restraining order that requires the White House to immediately return reporters’ press passes.

Some CNN staff were also unable to gain access to the White House. CNN reporter Betsy Klein and a photojournalist were denied entry at roughly 6 a.m., though one producer was able to enter the area by using their pass, the network reported.

In an order that arrived around 1 a.m., hours before a busy day in Washington, D.C., as the Trump administration welcomes Chinese leader Xi Jinping, Judge Kelly rejected the government’s arguments that the president’s ban was motivated by national security concerns. The ban appeared to be motivated by the president’s attempts to restrain negative press, according to Kelly.

“The record lacks factual support for defendants’ contention that the revocation of plaintiffs’ hard passes will in fact protect national security or that national security will be endangered if the court orders their passes reinstated while this litigation proceeds,” he wrote.

Several journalists from CNN, MS NOW and POLITICO, including Akayla Gardner (pictured), had their access to the White House revoked on Saturday morning ( Reuters )

Laura Barrón-López, who covers the White House for MS NOW, told the network that she showed her pass to Secret Service agents to get past a barricade and then entered a press area where she was denied entry.

After scanning her pass and entering her PIN, the machine began flashing red, she said.

A Secret Service agent told her “it’s still being disabled,” she told the network.

Her badge was then confiscated, she said.

She said it remains unclear whether the administration is explicitly defying Kelly’s court order or whether there is a “lag” in the system.

The White House did not immediately return The Independent’s request for comment.

Trump and the Department of Justice have accused the outlets of endangering national security by reporting sensitive and classified information that the president has also called “fake news” that is “negative, wrong and, in many cases, DANGEROUS for our Country.”

“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” he wrote on Truth Social September 18. “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.”

A federal lawsuit filed by lawyers representing the outlets accuses the Trump administration of “brazenly” violating their First Amendment rights and due process requirements under the Fifth Amendment by discriminating against them based solely on their editorial viewpoint.

This is a developing story

Bob Chapek, who was fired as Disney’s CEO in 2022, stands by his controversial decision to aggressively raise prices at the parks, he writes in his upcoming memoir.

Chapek’s less-than-three-year tenure at Disney was mired in issues like COVID, but also in controversies of his own making, including steep park price hikes and a botched response to Florida’s “Don’t Say Gay” law.

But in his upcoming memoir, Behind the Castle Walls: My Thirty Years at the Happiest Place on Earth, Chapek, 66, showed no remorse for the steep price hikes he implemented during his tenure, The New York Times reported after receiving an advance copy.

Under his reign, Disney introduced an airline-style dynamic pricing and monetized previously free perks.

Some of those formerly free perks include Disney’s once-complimentary FastPass system, which allowed for shorter lines at attractions. The perk was replaced by Disney Genie+ and Lightning Lane, which involve an added cost for guests.

open image in gallery Bob Chapek, the former CEO of Disney who was fired in 2022, is releasing a memoir next Tuesday ( Getty Images )

Guests must also pay for parking at Disney hotels in Florida, and Disney’s long-running complimentary airport shuttle service was discontinued.

Outside of the parks, Chapek also raised prices for Disney’s streaming service, Disney+, and ESPN, which jumped up from $7.99 to $10.99 and $6.99 to $9.99 a month, respectively.

Chapek proudly recounts these changes, and argues that the higher prices helped reduce crowding and bolster guests’ experiences.

“We’d been, at a minimum, leaving revenue opportunities on the table to avoid stirring the hornet’s nest,” he wrote, referring to growth seen under his tenure as chairman of Disney’s theme park division.

In the upcoming memoir, Chapek blames his firing on a “relentless” sabotage campaign allegedly carried out by the man who picked him as his replacement: Bob Iger.

“My abrupt dismissal hurt my reputation, leaving those close to me, outsiders and some within the kingdom trying to figure out what I did wrong,” Chapek wrote. “The answer, again, is nothing.”

open image in gallery Chapek blames Bob Iger (pictured) for his ouster, claiming he carried out a ‘relentless’ sabotage campaign in order to get him removed as CEO ( Getty )

Iger attempted to retire in 2021 and chose Chapek as his replacement, but soon after, the board of directors fired Chapek and brought Iger back, extending his contract through March of this year.

The feud between Iger and Chapek — including Chapek’s belief that Iger was undermining him — has long been reported. In the memoir, Chapek writes that Iger played “an intentional and preconceived role in abruptly ending my ride as Disney CEO.”

“I didn’t get a chance to finish what I started,” Chapek wrote. “In truth, it pisses me off.”

Disney recently named Josh D’Amaro as its new chief executive officer. In his memoir, Chapek says he was instrumental in helping the current CEO rise the corporate ladder.

“I consistently suggested the idea of promoting him,” Chapek wrote. “He had been a relative unknown in the corporate hierarchy before I singled him out.”

Disney declined to comment.

Macklemore has set his concert return with a solo show after being dropped from Ed Sheeran’s tour.

Earlier this month, Macklemore announced he had been fired from the British singer-songwriter’s Loop tour over his pro-Palestine comments at an earlier gig. Macklemore claimed that Robert Kraft — the CEO of Kraft Group who owns Gillette Stadium — personally called Sheeran to say he would not be allowed to perform at the venue, while Sheeran later responded by stating he would not be drawn into a public debate about the Gaza war and that it was “the promoter’s decision” to remove Macklemore.

The fallout continued when Sheeran’s other opening acts withdrew, while protesters gathered outside his first concert without Macklemore last week.

Now, the “Thrift Shop” rapper will perform a solo show at Colorado’s iconic Red Rocks amphitheater on October 22 for a one-off performance.

While the show was originally announced in March, demand for tickets has surged following the controversy. Only resale tickets — now starting at $220 for general admission — remain available for purchase on Ticketmaster.

That price is significantly higher than the $68 tickets available for Sheeran’s solo show in Philadelphia in the wake of the controversy. Some fans who were unhappy with how the situation was handled tried to resell their tickets to Sheeran’s concert, with prices falling sharply as last Saturday’s show approached.

The Princess of Wales has met with people recovering from addiction during a solo public appearance north-east of London.

Kate, who is patron of the Forward Trust, a charity that supports recovering addicts, visited its Forward Growing initiative at Garon Park in Southend, Essex, to mark Addiction Awareness Week, which runs from Saturday until Friday.

At the greenspace, people on the Forward Trust’s treatment and recovery service in the area are encouraged to engage with the natural world.

The princess was shown the Forward Trust’s garden, where service users have a go at gardening to help them in their recovery.

Liam King, who leads conservation at the park, told Kate about the plants being grown.

open image in gallery Kate was shown the garden, where service users can try their hand at gardening to support their recovery ( PA )

Kate then revealed: “I should have my husband here; he knows a lot (about gardening), he’s really passionate.”

She described the planting area at Garon Park as a “fantastic space” as she chatted with people in recovery.

When asked by Mr King if she does any gardening, the princess said “a little bit”.

Last November, ahead of the 2026 Addiction Awareness Week, Kate called for the “stigma” faced by those with addictions to end and for society to show “compassion and love” to those dependent on drugs, alcohol or gambling.

open image in gallery Kate praised her husband’s gardening knowledge, describing the Prince of Wales as ‘really passionate’ ( PA )

Kate said society’s experience of addiction was “shaped by fear, shame and judgement” and urged people to have open conversations and bring the issue “out of the shadows,”.

“Addiction is not a choice, or a personal failing, but a complex mental health condition that should be met with empathy and support. But still, even now in 2025, people’s experience of addiction is shaped by fear, shame and judgement. This needs to change,” she said.

“The stigma surrounding those who face addiction allows it to thrive behind closed doors, impacting families and communities, and ultimately ruining lives. Many of us will know someone who is struggling with an addiction.

“Now is the moment to show our compassion and love to help them, or their friends and family, to reach out to organisations like The Forward Trust for support.”

Kate launched the first Addiction Awareness Week in 2021 on behalf of the trust.

Nine more prisoners trapped on indefinite jail terms have had their sentences referred to the Court of Appeal by the miscarriages of justice watchdog.

The Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) is currently reviewing more than 250 cases involving people serving Imprisonment for Public Protection (IPP) and the youth equivalent, Detention for Public Protection (DPP) jail terms.

So far the watchdog has referred 25 cases to the appeal courts this year after a string of sentences were overturned by top judges.

The latest cases include Carl Lamb, who cut off his own ear with a razor blade in front of a prison officer in protest at his sentence.

He was jailed with a tariff of one year, seven months and 25 days in 2006 for grievous bodily harm with intent following a road rage incident when he was 26. Now 46, he has never been released.

open image in gallery Shaun Lloyd and his mother Shirley Debono ( Supplied )

Shaun Lloyd, 38, has been hauled back to prison five times and served almost 14 years under his indefinite jail term for the street robbery of a mobile phone he committed 20 years ago.

Chair of the CCRC, Dame Vera Baird KC, has said the referrals represent a “fraction” of those who remain “caught up in this abolished sentencing regime”.

The open-ended punishments were scrapped in 2012, but not retrospectively, leaving thousands languishing in prison without a release date.

The Independent has repeatedly called for all remaining IPP and DPP prisoners to have their sentences reviewed, highlighting shocking cases including Mr Lloyd’s and Mr Lamb’s.

Andy Burnham has now pledged to bring legislation to end the “long-running” injustice of IPP sentences before the end of this parliament. Details of how the scandal will be addressed are to be decided by a cross-party oversight group.

open image in gallery Carl Lamb, pictured as a child, has never been released from his IPP jail term ( Supplied )

Dame Vera, a former victims commissioner, said public protection must remain paramount but “so too must fairness” as she offered to support the government in their efforts to bring the sentence to an end.

"These nine referrals bring to 25 the number of IPP and DPP cases that the CCRC has referred to the Court of Appeal so far this year,” she said.

"But while 25 referrals are a significant number, this represents only a fraction of the people who remain caught up in this abolished sentencing regime.

"The latest figures show that 856 people who were given IPP sentences have never been released from prison. Around eight in ten of those who have passed their minimum tariff have already spent at least ten years beyond the point at which the Court originally said they should become eligible to seek release. A further 1,415 people are in custody following recall.

"These are extraordinary figures for sentences which were abolished more than a decade ago.”

Recent Court of Appeal judgments have seen indefinite sentences overturned because the original judge had not fully considered the defendant’s age or maturity when handing out the punishment.

open image in gallery Dame Vera Baird KC says an ‘extraordinary’ number are still locked up under the abolished jail term ( CCRC )

Dame Vera said the CCRC will continue reviewing applications, adding: "The Commission will continue to examine these cases carefully and independently. Where we identify a real possibility that a sentence would now not be upheld, we will refer the case to the appropriate court. It will then be for the court to decide what should happen.

"There is no simple solution to the legacy of IPP and DPP sentences. Public protection must remain paramount, but so too must fairness and the principle that people should not remain imprisoned indefinitely because of a sentencing regime that has already caused so much damage and which Parliament abolished more than a decade ago.”

The nine latest referrals include:

Abdiwali Hassan, convicted at Isleworth Crown Court in 2011 and sentenced aged 19 to an IPP with a tariff of three years

Carl Lamb, convicted at Cardiff Crown Court in 2006 and sentenced aged 26 to an IPP with a tariff of 21 months

Ben Nye, convicted at Leeds Crown Court in 2007 and sentenced aged 21 to an IPP with a tariff of three years

Scott Prince, convicted at Derby Crown Court in 2008 and sentenced aged 19 to an IPP with a tariff of three years and six months

Liam Osborne, convicted at Wolverhampton Crown Court in 2006 and sentenced aged 21 to an IPP with a tariff of two years and three months

Jerome Barrett, convicted at York Crown Court in 2005 and sentenced aged 19 to a DPP with a tariff of two years

Victoria Hathaway, convicted at Ipswich Crown Court in 2009 and sentenced aged 19 to a DYPP with a tariff of six years (varied on appeal to four years)

Shaun Lloyd, convicted at Cardiff Crown Court in 2005 and sentenced aged 18 to a DYPP with a tariff of two years and nine months

Jason Ritchie, convicted at Teeside Crown Court in 2008 and sentenced aged 38 to an IPP with a tariff of three years

Eddie Hearn continues to reject Dana White’s involvement in Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua despite the fight being made official.

The two legendary British heavyweights finally clash in Cardiff on 11 December, with the mega fight diverted away from New York after lengthy negotiations, fronted by Saudi boxing chief Turki Alalshikh.

Ahead of the announcement, much of the debate swirled around who would be the face of the promotion, with Matchroom’s Eddie Hearn maintaining Zuffa Boxing’s Dana White would not be involved due to the contracts signed.

Despite Netflix’s announcement detailing how White will be the promoter of the show alongside Alalshikh: “HE Turki Alalshikh’s The Ring and Dana White will collaborate to promote this historic showdown that will stream live on Netflix globally to its 325+ million members at no additional cost.

Dana White speaks during a press conference for Ryan Garcia vs Conor Benn ( AP )

“The event will also feature a star-studded undercard with marquee fighters from around the world, further underscoring the global scale of the event. Undercard bouts will be announced at a later date.

Yet Hearn insists that is explicitly not the case and has been given the word of Sela and Alalshikh that the UFC chief will not be involved and told the Independent: “We expect the contracts to be honoured and unless we decide otherwise, Dana White cannot be involved in the fight.”

In addition to Hearn, promoter Frank Warren has also claimed White cannot be involved in the fight: "He's not [promoting Joshua vs Fury] because the contract with Tyson says that Zuffa will not be able to promote that fight. I don't know [where he has got that from]. Ask him. I mean, it is just b******."

The pair will come face to face at a press conference next Wednesday, 30 September, at British Airways Arc in London.

While Dana White responded to the fight being made in a statement: “For more than a decade, boxing fans have been clamoring for the heavyweight showdown between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua. Together, they bring 66 wins, 52 knockouts and multiple heavyweight world titles into the ring.

“On December 11, two of the biggest heavyweights of this generation finally collide– and the winner will take a significant place in heavyweight history.”
