A senior technology executive who suffered disability discrimination after sleeping in a sauna has won the right to pursue £76m in compensation, in what could prove to be the largest payout ever awarded by a British employment tribunal.

Shannon Burns could be in line for the landmark payout after winning a disability discrimination case against Gitpod, a company now owned by ChatGPT developer OpenAI.

Ms Burns was dismissed from her £220,000-a-year role as vice-president of engineering ver three years ago, after she resorted to sleeping in a sauna during a boozy work trip.

She is still fighting to receive compensation, alleging that Gitpod has been using “aggressive litigation tactics to drag out the process and wear her down”.

Ms Burns developed PTSD during her sacking and has now left the tech industry for good. She is seeking £76 million in compensation, based on “forensic” calculations of her lost potential earnings.

Gitpod attempted to restrict the compensation that she could seek to £1m, using a legal application described as “oppressive” by her lawyers.

open image in gallery Shannon Burns was dismissed after losing her room key and sleeping in a sauna while on a work trip ( Solent News )

The Birmingham Employment Tribunal has now dismissed the company’s application, meaning she can formally pursue £76,071,992 in compensation.

Gitpod has also been ordered to disclose to Ms Burns what the recent sale of the business to OpenAI was worth.

Currently, the biggest known award in UK employment tribunal history is £4.58m.

Ms Burns also has shares in Gitpod, which are thought to be worth about £2.6m and could rise to £21m after four years.

Before working for the company, Ms Burns had roles at Silicon Valley firms including Slack and Lyft.

She was headhunted by Gitpod in late 2022 and appointed to the key leadership role of vice-president of engineering, commanding a £220,000 salary with a £78,000 bonus per year.

Ms Burns – who has ADHD – went on an off-site team building event in Lofer, Austria, in April 2023.

CEO Johannes Landgraf and other staff drank alcohol during the trip, and one evening Ms Burns, who had also been drinking, could not access her room as she forgot her key.

Her ADHD caused her to have a “great deal of forgetfulness” and she would “persistently” lose items, the employment tribunal heard.

She had to sleep in a sauna that night, and after the trip, Mr Landgraf said that he was concerned about her “lack of professional accountability”.

She was sacked in June 2023.

“My male colleagues were drinking alcohol/drunk at the offsite but I was the only one who was dismissed,” Ms Burns said.

In 2025, the Birmingham Employment Tribunal found that Ms Burns was dismissed as a result of her disabilities and she won a disability discrimination case.

She is seeking £76 million, relying on calculations made in her “schedule of loss”, which examines what she could have gone on to earn.

As she earned such a huge salary and the tech industry is so lucrative, it is estimated that her total future losses are over £59 million.

The remainder of the £76 million is made up of sums to cover injury to feelings and what is known as an ACAS Uplift, a percentage adjustment of up to 25 per cent that an employment tribunal can add to an award.

open image in gallery Shannon Burns developed PTSD during her sacking and has since left the tech industry ( Georgia Bates/Solent News )

At the latest Birmingham hearing, Gitpod applied to have her £76 million schedule of loss capped at £1 million.

The company applied for the judge to enforce a “deposit order” of £1,000, and as part of the order find that any claim worth more than £1 million has “little reasonable prospect of success”.

In its application, Gitpod argued that Ms Burns' claim for over £76 million was “extraordinary”, adding: “The arguments set out in the [schedule of loss] are palpable nonsense.”

The company added: “[Gitpod] seeks an order that [Ms Burns] be ordered to pay a deposit of £1,000 to continue her claim for losses in excess of £1 million.”

Employment Judge Rachel Wedderspoon dismissed the application.

Judge Wedderspoon said: “[Ms Burns] has an exceptionally high pay history... Her case is that but for the treatment she suffered at the hands of [Gitpod] she would have continued to have a highly lucrative career.

“[Her] schedule of loss is based on past and future predicted loss and she has included the amount for loss of salary but also loss of equity because if she had continued her career in this sector part of remuneration would have consisted of equity.”

Judge Wedderspoon said that OpenAI has acquired Gitpod for a sum believed to be $400 million (£302 million).

The judge said that since Ms Burns had 0.85 per cent shares in Gitpod, her shares could be worth $3.4 million (£2.6 million) now and $27.85 million (£21 million) in four years if the $400 million acquisition fee is true.

Judge Wedderspoon concluded: “The Tribunal finds that an award in the sum claimed by [Ms Burns] is highly unusual and the sort of award that may be more commonplace awarded in the US jurisdiction.

“However, the Tribunal cannot say at a summary assessment in the absence of an employment renumeration expert report or an expert medical information that [her] valuation has little reasonable prospect of success.”

Tara Grossman, an employment lawyer assisting Ms Burns, said after the hearing: “The outcome of this hearing was a resounding success for Shannon and I am over the moon for her.

“Shannon’s £76 million schedule of loss is a forensic calculation of what she could very well have earned if she had not been dismissed by Gitpod due to her disabilities.

“She was working in tech which is probably the most lucrative career of our time.

“She had already earned well over £1 million in junior roles and when she joined Gitpod she was given a £220,000 annual salary and told her shares could be worth anywhere from $1.06 million to $27.85 million.

“This was from one job in tech over a four-year period.

“She is now in a position where she can never work in tech again and is retraining to be a therapist with nowhere near the same earning potential.

“Gitpod made an application at this hearing to try and prevent Shannon from claiming more than £1 million.

“Gitpod were trying to get Shannon’s schedule of loss reduced from £76 million to £1 mmillion by using a draconian application called a 'deposit order'.

“In my opinion this application was oppressive.

“Shannon was working in a career where the top generative AI companies are fighting for tech talent and in some cases offering stock packages worth hundreds of millions of dollars.

“It is particularly oppressive given that Gitpod now know what Shannon’s shares in Gitpod would have been worth (as it is being acquired by OpenAI) but won’t disclose this information to Shannon.

“My view is that Gitpod are attempting to use aggressive litigation tactics to drag out the process and wear her down."

A full compensation hearing will be held at a later date, pending Gitpod's appeal of the previous tribunal ruling.

News.title: Zelensky lashes out at EU
News.content:
Volodymyr Zelensky lashed out at the European Union over its moves to weaken sanctions on Russian oligarchs.

In his address to the UN General Assembly, the Ukrainian leader warned that beyond making life “more comfortable” for Russians, “it also gives the war more time for Putin to send poor people into the kill zone. So Russia’s revenues must remain a target.”

His criticism came after France and Luxembourg successfully pushed for sanctions exemptions for Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, Russian oligarchs, on Tuesday.

Kyiv branded the decision “shameful and unjustifiable”. The men are known to share close ties to Vladimir Putin and have net worths of $14bn and $16bn, respectively.

In his fourth address to the UN as a wartime leader, Mr Zelensky said it was paramount that the international community increased pressure on the Kremlin to stop “the madness” of the war spreading.

Under pressure from Donald Trump to halt attacks on Russian energy targets, Mr Zelensky defended his country’s aerial offensive for successfully depriving Putin of revenue for his war.

“When someone gives Russia more money through trade, they give this war more time. And that is exactly why we insist on limiting trade with the aggressor, and why we are burning Russia’s revenues ourselves,” he said.

‘End the war before winter’

Washington has recently attempted to revive the long-stalled negotiations between Ukraine and Russia. On Tuesday, Mr Zelensky implored Mr Trump to help Kyiv end the war “before winter”.

Mr Trump appeared optimistic, suggesting an agreement would happen “more quickly than people understand”.

Sergei Lavrov, the Russian foreign minister, told the UN Security Council on Wednesday that Russia was prepared to negotiate for a lasting peace but would not “pause the war”.

Mr Zelensky sought to remind world leaders that the conflict was not constrained within Ukraine’s borders at a time when the global community was distracted by a myriad of conflicts and crises.

Citing the support of Iran and North Korea for Russia, he warned that Putin’s war kept “spreading further”.

“Putin is always looking for someone who can help him kill more, kill more people for every kilometre of land, take more territory and take another country instead of simply stopping and running his own country,” Mr Zelensky said at the UN.

He noted that fighters from at least 47 countries were helping to prosecute Moscow’s war against Ukraine and urged leaders to prevent their citizens from being dragged into the conflict.

After Mr Zelensky’s address, reports emerged that Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s envoy, was on his way to the US where he would meet Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the Trump administration representatives.

Sources told Reuters that the meeting would take place in New ‌York on the sidelines of the UN summit.

Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, also confirmed Mr Trump had invited his Russian counterpart to attend the G20 summit of world leaders in Miami in December.

News.title: Male contraceptives could hit pharmacies in ‘three to five years’, says WHO
News.content:
Game-changing contraceptives for men could be on pharmacy shelves as soon as 2029, according to the World Health Organization.

Speaking to the Telegraph, Dr James Kiarie, head of the UN agency’s contraception and fertility care unit, said he expects male birth control to be available in just a few years, in a major expansion of contraceptive options for men.

“In three to five years, we will actually have a method available, [so] men can be more than supporters of their female partners in using contraception – men can actually be users,” he said.

On Tuesday, the WHO released its first Target Product Profiles (TPPs) for these products, setting out guidelines for the desired and minimum standards any male contraceptive product must meet.

“[The TPPs] signals that this is a priority issue for the WHO,” said Dr Kiarie.

“Currently men do not have much option in terms of their contraceptive methods. They have to either use condoms… [or] they have to use withdrawal, which has a high failure rate, or they have to use vasectomy, which is a permanent method.”

At the moment, the most advanced new product is called NES/T. It is a daily hormonal gel that is applied to the shoulders and upper arms, and suppresses sperm production without affecting testosterone levels.

Other candidates include injectable hydrogels that block sperm travel, an approach that has been described as a “reversible vasectomy”. ADAM, developed by Contraline, is in phase 1 trials while Next Life Sciences is set to trial a similar product called Plan A.

A third option is YCT-529 – the first non-hormonal, daily male birth control pill. It is currently in phase 1b and 2a clinical trials.

Dr Kiarie said it was important to have multiple options as “there’s no one size fits all” approach, but warned development could take longer than five years if clinical trials face unexpected hurdles.

News.title: England learn more in scrappy Sri Lanka win than in summer of white-ball walkovers
News.content:
You do not expect spinners to dominate at Chester-le-Street, but this hot summer has produced strange events, none more so than Jacks recording the second-best figures by an England spinner in one-day international cricket having previously only taken three wickets in 16 games at home.

Sachindu Colombage, Sri Lanka’s debutant leggie who was playing club cricket in East Anglia a year ago, laid down a marker as he impressed with three for 44 starting with the wicket of Root, his first dismissal in one-day international cricket since February.

England’s 89-run win was completed by Jacks taking three for none in four balls as Sri Lanka were bowled out for 176, their run chase a timid effort when they had a sniff of victory after restricting England to 265 and preventing them from hitting a six for the first time in an innings since 2019.

Vice-captain Jacks has evolved under Harry Brook’s leadership from an opening batsman to middle-order finisher who can chip in with the ball. “He is just a good leader with bat ball and in the field. He is buying into everything we want to do,” Brook said. “We are always talking about adapting to conditions and he has done it really well since coming back in. He could have moaned and groaned about batting in the middle order and playing as an all-rounder but has accepted that will be his place for a long time.”

Brook thought England made “just about par” on a very dry pitch and was reluctant to shower too much praise on batting consultant Kevin Pietersen, whose spin class the day before concentrated on making runs on a slow surface. “It will take time, more than one day. He’s not a miracle worker but it helps the more opportunity we get,” Brook said.

England were stretched and Pietersen will be happy. He told them to think about their approach, that in this type of game “rotation of strike is incredibly important”. He was right, they ran well, apart from Rehan Ahmed, and did not hit a six in an innings for the first time in seven years.

When England batsmen tried to force the pace they perished. Ben Duckett, Root and Brook all had opportunities to build an innings without seeing it through and it required Jacks to tip the total to more than 250. He batted within himself at first, but hit four fours in a row in the 47th over in a late burst that took England to a winning score.

News.title: Africa faces new threat as chronic disease rate leaps
News.content:
Chronic ailments like heart disease, cancers and diabetes now account for almost half of deaths in Africa and will soon overtake the continent’s infectious disease toll, new research has found.

Between 1990 and 2023 the proportion of deaths caused by non-communicable diseases (NCDs) almost doubled, from 25 per cent to 45 per cent, with heart disease and strokes now the leading killers.

The shift is not unexpected: public health experts have long warned that although African countries are making huge strides cutting infectious disease deaths through vaccinations, better sanitation and improved healthcare, lifestyle changes pose a new threat.

But the continent is not necessarily ready to tackle this “epidemiological transition”, researchers warned, in a study published in the Lancet Global Health journal on Tuesday.

“Although the epidemiological transition is well recognised, the speed and scale of NCD growth in Africa is particularly concerning,” they wrote.

“Health systems face increasing demands for chronic disease management, yet low-resource settings remain poorly equipped, underfunded, and unable to provide adequate preventive or treatment services.”

News.title: Zika mosquitoes still breeding in London
News.content:
Dr Medlock said there is still “no conclusive” evidence about how the insects arrived, but it’s possible that someone brought them back from holiday in their luggage, or that mosquito eggs were hidden on a tropical plant.

The mosquitoes are very temperature sensitive – they typically survive and multiply between 25C and 30C – and the UK has historically been too cold. But the species are gradually making their way north through Europe, after successive summers of record heat.

As temperatures drop in the coming weeks, the UKHSA hopes London’s invasive mosquitoes will die off naturally – though an unprecedented El Niño has made the predicament more challenging.

“This is a tropical mosquito, so the model has convinced me this won’t survive the winter,” Dr Medlock said. “Although we’ve got El Niño, [so] it’s very mild – it’s certainly warm enough still in East London [for the insects to survive].”

Diseases such as dengue and Zika virus do not typically circulate in Britain, but an infected traveller returning from a country where the diseases are present could carry the virus back with them.

If an invasive mosquito then bit an infected person, it could potentially catch and spread on the disease to others.

Several countries in Europe, including France, Italy and Spain, have started to see local transmission of mosquito-borne viruses, including dengue fever and West Nile virus, in recent years as the climate becomes more suitable for mosquitoes to survive and multiply.

Just last week, a third person died in Frankfurt, Germany, from malaria despite having no travel history, after mosquitoes infected with the disease were imported into the country on an aeroplane and subsequently infected eight people over the summer.

“We [already] see imported cases of malaria, dengue and chikungunya each year, with significant associated mortality and morbidity,” Dr Phillip Veal, a consultant in public health at the UKHSA, said.

“But if we [in Britain] follow the pattern of Europe, and all models suggest we will, Aedes albopictus and other Aedes species may become established. We’ve got a window of opportunity to do something, to prepare, to be ready, to fulfil our mission of protecting the public,” Dr Veal said.

News.title: Tax rises ‘virtually inevitable’ after £8bn borrowing blow
News.content:
Tax rises are “virtually inevitable” after official figures showed the Treasury has borrowed £8bn more than expected so far this year.

Economists said the Chancellor faced an “uncomfortable” Budget after the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said spending outstripped tax receipts by £18.3bn in August, £3.5bn more than expected.

It means John Healey, the Chancellor, has borrowed £77.3bn so far this financial year, which is £8.1bn more than forecast.

Reacting to the figures, Emma Reynolds, the Chief Secretary to the Treasury, warned of “tough decisions” in Mr Healey’s Budget.

Thomas Pugh, chief economist at RSM UK, said: “The jump in borrowing in August compared to last year sets the stage for what is likely to be a much trickier Budget than Andy Burnham or Healey anticipated when they came to power.

“Another round of tax rises in October now looks inevitable.”

Philip Shaw, an economist at Investec, added: “We suspect that some tax increases are virtually inevitable.”

Ruth Gregory, deputy chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said the Chancellor would need to raise up to £14bn to restore the £24bn of fiscal headroom left by his predecessor Rachel Reeves to balance the books.

The Government’s debt interest bill soared to £8.8bn last month, according to the ONS, the biggest August figure since records began in 1997.

So far this year, the Treasury has spent £50bn on debt interest – £2bn more than forecast in March.

Nick Ridpath, an economist at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said: “Debt interest spending is a worryingly large share of overall government spending.

“Both higher borrowing costs and higher inflation make life harder for a Chancellor who is looking to bring down borrowing and to spend more on government priorities.”

Higher prices caused by the Iran war mean the Chancellor must pay more interest on the country’s huge stock of inflation-linked debt.

Inflation is also pushing up the welfare bill. The Government spent almost £30bn in August on benefits, 7pc more than a year ago.

Despite this, the Treasury continued to see substantial tax receipts. Income tax, capital gains, and National Insurance receipts stood at £231bn in the financial year to August.

That is £16.6bn higher than the same period a year ago.

Inheritance tax receipts also grew. They have risen to £3.8bn so far this financial year, a £100m increase compared with a year ago.

Ms Reynolds, the Treasury minister, said: “At a time when debt interest costs billions of pounds that could otherwise be spent on improving lives, we must always know where the money is coming from to pay for public services.

“That is why we are committed to meeting our fiscal rules with a buffer against uncertainty.”

The figures also showed total debt rose to £2.985tn in August, taking the level just shy of £3tn.

Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, said: “Labour has lost control of the public finances.

“It takes a rare fiscal incontinence to have both the highest tax take in history and see borrowing still shoot up.”

News.title: France releases infertile Asian tiger mosquitoes to fight dengue threat
News.content:
French cities are fighting the growing threat of diseases like dengue, chikungunya and Zika in mainland Europe by releasing millions of sterile male Asian tiger mosquitoes.

Terratis, a new company in the southern city of Montpellier, is breeding infertile males on an industrial scale as a long-term solution to the rapid spread of the disease-carrying insects.

The sterile males are bred at a factory in the southern city of Montpellier and then released in urban hot zones where the mosquitoes are most prevalent. After they have mated, females reproduce only empty eggs for the remainder of their lives.

“By using this technique, the mosquitoes will have no descendants and then, in theory, we can reduce the population with each generation,” said Clelia Oliva, the founder of Terratis.

“We are confident of being able to achieve a reduction of between 70 and 90 per cent in the towns in which we are releasing the sterile mosquitoes.”

The company, which started only two years ago, has experienced a dramatic surge in demand in the last few years as France tries to deal with the invasive species.

Sports.title: Thierno Barry leads five best Dream Team surprise packages so far this season
Sports.content:
Next

THIS lengthy international break allows us time to reflect on the Dream Team season so far.

Here we have selected the five best surprise packages who have punched well above their weight across the first five Gameweeks.

Thierno Barry (£2.5m)

Only Erling Haaland (£8.8m) has racked up more points than Everton’s No11 among Dream Team strikers.



Barry scored eight goals in 41 appearances last season but has raced to five in his first seven outings this term.



Granted, his tally includes a hat-trick against Preston in the Carabao Cup but his 29-point haul at Deepdale served as a reminder of what’s possible when top-flight clubs take on lower-league opposition in the domestic cups.

Barry ranks joint-fifth in the Premier League for total shots and was unlucky to have a second goal against Ipswich ruled out by VAR last weekend.

The 23-year-old has provided incredible value for money for his backers having notched 59 points from the first five Gameweeks.



Whether he’ll be able to keep pace with the top forwards remains to be seen but he deserves full credit for his performances so far.

Maxim De Cuyper (£3.8m)

Injuries to Kaoru Mitoma (£4m) and Yankuba Minteh (£4m) have resulted in the Belgium wing-back being deployed as Brighton’s starting left winger.

And he’s contributed two goals and three assists to the Seagulls’ bright start.



Since De Cuyper is categorised as a defender, he’s also benefited from three clean sheets, hence his impressive overall total of 51 points.

His out-of-position privilege is a huge bonus but it may be temporary.

Mitoma is expected to be available from Gameweek 6 onwards and the Japan international will be pushing to reclaim his place on the left flank in Fabian Hurzeler’s 4-2-3-1 formation.

De Cuyper has been a gift for gaffers so far this season but his owners should monitor his minutes closely once the action resumes.

Pascal Gross (£3.7m)



While we’re on the subject of Brighton, their 35-year-old midfielder has been immense.

We almost didn’t include Gross in this list because he has been an occasionally popular selection in previous seasons and therefore isn’t a true surprise package.

But not even his most ardent admirers would have predicted that he would rank second among all midfielders after five Gameweeks with 60 points to his name.

Gross has scored four goals and provided four assists from his first six outings, a remarkable return for a player who only scored more than seven goals once in seven seasons during his first stint at the Amex.

Long may his success continue!



Konstantinos Tzolakis (£2.7m)

Before the season got underway, fans and pundits alike were almost unanimous in predicting Hull to finish 20th.

The Tigers were labelled the Premier League’s whipping boys before a ball was kicked only for them to beat Manchester United on the opening weekend.

Sergej Jakirovic’s side marked their return to the top flight with three consecutive clean sheets, thanks in no small part to Tzolakis’s efforts between the sticks.

The Greek goalkeeper ranks joint-first in his position for bonus points with four and has made 17 saves in five games.



He even saved a penalty in his most recent appearance.

A cheap keeper who performs well above expectations at the start of the campaign is a hugely valuable asset in the world of Dream Team and Tzolakis has fulfilled the role perfectly this time around.

Marcus Tavernier (£3.5m)

The top ten midfielders in Dream Team right now is populated by many big names: Cole Palmer, Morgan Rogers, Rayan Cherki, Bruno Fernandes, Dominik Szoboszlai, Bukayo Saka, Bryan Mbeumo.

The aforementioned Gross stands out in such company, as does Tavernier.



The Bournemouth winger has earned 47 points via three goals and has posed a constant threat.

Palmer and Saka are the only midfielders to have registered more shots on target than Tavernier at this stage.

The 27-year-old seems likely to provide plenty more points after the break as the Cherries are scheduled to fulfil eight fixtures across the next four Gameweeks.

A YOUTH footballer has died in a tragic motorcross accident as tributes pour in for a player “loved by everyone”.

Richie “RJ” Anderson played for Margate Youth FC in Kent with the club confirming he had “tragically lost his life” earlier this week.



A fundraiser set up following his passing revealed Anderson died in a “tragic motorcross accident”.

“RJ loved riding his bike, and was at the track every weekend and was loved by everyone on and off the track and will be deeply missed by many,” it said.





Margate FC also released a statement confirming the heartbreaking news, saying “RJ was, and always will be, part of the Margate FC family.”

“He grew up wearing the Margate shirt, representing our youth section throughout the age groups,” the statement read.



“For many of our coaches, players and families, RJ will be remembered as much more than a footballer, a kind, hardworking person.

“Football clubs are about so much more than what happens on the pitch. They are communities and families, and losing someone who has been part of that journey is incredibly difficult.

“Everyone connected with Margate FC sends their love, thoughts and deepest condolences to RJ’s family, friends, former teammates and everyone who had the privilege of knowing him.”

They added there would be a minute’s applause at their next game on Saturday to remember the youngster.



Grassroots Football UK also paid tribute following the “heartbreaking news”

They said: “Our thoughts and condolences are with RJ’s family, friends, teammates, coaches and everyone at the club at this incredibly difficult time.”

A GoFundMe has been set up to contribute toward his funeral costs and support his family and partner – it has so far raised more than £6,000.

The football club is based in the seaside resort of Margate, Kent and plays in the eight tier of English football.

Sports.title: F1 teams expect mid-October decision on Qatar, Abu Dhabi GPs
Sports.content:
F1's teams understand they will learn in mid-October whether the season-ending races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi will take place as scheduled.

​The 2026's season is due to finish with a back-to-back races in Qatar (November 27-29) and Abu Dhabi (December 4-6) but those events have appeared uncertain for a number of months owing to the conflict this year in the Middle East, which started in February.

The two events remain on the calendar, with currently runs to 23 races, with Sky Sports News understanding that the intention remains for them to take place. Italy's Imola circuit is thought to be the contingency option to close the season if it is deemed that the Middle Eastern rounds cannot go ahead, with F1 able to wait longer before a final decision is taken.

An F1 Commission meeting took pace on Monday and, speaking in Thursday's press conference at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, team chiefs said they had been given clarity on when a decision would be taken by.

Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu said: "I believe that Stefano [Domenicali, F1's president] is targeting to tell us in mid-October so we all know what the situation is.

"I believe that Imola is getting ready in case we have to do it [there].

"But hopefully things can stay as a baseline and we can go to Qatar and Abu Dhabi. That'd be really good."

Audi counterpart Mattia Binotto added: "We discussed it during the F1 Commission last Monday. Mid-October is the last call for such a decision."

What's the latest on Qatar and Abu Dhabi GPs?

Sky Sports' F1 correspondent Craig Slater:

"The latest information I have from leadership sources at Formula 1 itself is that they are both on the calendar, the intention is to go.

"I have been informed that, as things stand in terms of the level of stability in the region, should those events have been happening in the next couple of weeks, it would be stable enough for them to go ahead. The situation would be that unless there is a deterioration again then those races would be going ahead.

"There is a contingency of Imola but they do not have to commit to that to the exclusion of those last two races. So Imola will be a contingency situation if they can't run the last two races, but they will compensate Imola for any financial loss they make in getting ready for that.

"Mid-October is the teams' understanding that they will get some kind of clarification on that matter, so we will have to watch this space to a degree."

'I do hope that we get to go there' - Hamilton keen on Middle East return

Speaking in Baku on Wednesday, Ferrari driver Lewis Hamilton said he hoped the sport was able to return to the Middle East as scheduled at the end of November,

"I personally want to go. I love going to the Middle East," said Hamilton.

"From what I've read, I think things seem OK out there. But I don't have all the information so I don't know what the risk levels are. But I trust in Stefano to make the right decision for the sport, but I do hope that we get to go there.

"Finishing in winter in Imola might not be the best weather-wise, and also it's a beautiful track, but it's not a track that we're going to be doing any overtaking in and the more races, the better."

"I can now confirm that Fury ss Joshua will be coming to the UK, as I promised British boxing fans. The time for talking is over."

Both Fury and Joshua swiftly reposted the promotional image for the fight to their social media channels.

Joshua shared a cryptic post shortly before Alalshikh's announcement, hinting at his own influence on the protracted negotiations.

"The quietest ones often pull the strings," Joshua wrote on Instagram alongside a photo of himself in front of a Union Jack. "Those who appear least involved may hold the greatest control. Let them shout first, the wisest wait until the final move. Yours truly, Anthony Joshua."

White said: "For more than a decade, boxing fans have been clamouring for the heavyweight showdown between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua.

"Together, they bring 66 wins, 52 knockouts and multiple heavyweight world titles into the ring. On December 11, two of the biggest heavyweights of this generation finally collide - and the winner will take a significant place in heavyweight history."

Finally: How Fury vs AJ was agreed

Joshua and Fury, both former heavyweight world champions, have had a long-running rivalry that's stretched over years, punctuated by callouts and trash talk but marred by the difficulty of finalising a deal.

Earlier this year the British boxing stars did sign to fight one another but months passed without a date or a venue being set. The wrangling intensified as taking the contest to New York's Madison Square Garden became a genuine possibility.

The fight appeared to be on the edge of collapse once again, with Fury threatening to seek alternative options.

But the all-British showdown has been salvaged and has now set a date for a UK stadium.

The Principality Stadium is no stranger to major UK boxing events. Joshua has fought there twice before, against Carlos Takam and in a unification with Joseph Parker. Historically, the all-British heavyweight super-fight between Lennox Lewis and Frank Bruno took place at the National Stadium in Cardiff, which preceded the Principality.

The main event is expected to start late at night due to international broadcasting considerations. But there is a precedent for that. Joe Calzaghe's 2007 fight with Mikkel Kessler took place at the stadium in the early hours of the morning.

As tortuous as negotiations for this super-fight have been, events in the ring also threatened to derail it.

Joshua's tune-up bout in July almost ended in disaster when little-known Kristian Prenga knocked him down twice in the first round. Joshua rallied to dispatch Prenga in the second round.

Fury's road to the fight has also been unusual. He announced his retirement after losing a rematch to Oleksandr Usyk and, after a year out of the sport, began training in Thailand. In April he came back at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London when he soundly outpointed Aslanbek Makhmudov.

He decided he wanted his own additional warm-up in July and boxed Mariusz Wach in Thailand in a non-TV bout, eventually stopping the veteran after seven rounds.

But the long journey towards Fury vs Joshua is now in its final stretch, set to end finally on December 11 in Cardiff.

Sports.title: Fox signs new Arsenal deal
Sports.content:
Arsenal defender Emily Fox has signed a new contract at the club.

The 28-year-old joined the Gunners from North Carolina Courage in January 2024 and has made 93 appearances, scoring three goals.

She was nominated for the Ballon d'Or in 2025.

Speaking in an exclusive interview with Sky Sports, USA international Fox said: "It was easy - I love the club.

"I'm being challenged in a competitive environment and it's my second home. A very easy decision to want to stay.

"I've got a mindset to get better and more to prove. I'm always hungry as a player and leaning towards perfection. When I'm playing with the best players in the world, there are so many things I can learn.

"I want to push myself and in an environment where I'm challenged, there's consistency every day and matching it. I want to be even more consistent to prove myself."

Fox the perfect blend of modern and old-school full-back

Image: The 28-year-old has played 93 times for the Gunners

Sky Sports' Laura Hunter:

Tying Emily Fox down to a new contract was something Arsenal have been wanting to do for a while. It's easy to see why. The American has been one of the most consistent full-backs in the league since joining in 2024.

She is a modern-day full-back, but in the most traditional sense. By that I mean she runs the channels with intelligence, a constant source of energy and offensive threat, but does not shirk her defensive duties. The picture of reliability in both directions.

What I is especially like is how progressive she is in possession, always looking to pass forwards and someone who rarely gives the ball away. As Arsenal attempt to establish some rhythm in the early knockings of this season, the 28-year-old is an important stabilising figure to keep around. Her consistency is something Renee Slegers can depend on.

Sports.title: Russell fastest as Antonelli suffers reliability issues in Baku first practice
Sports.content:
George Russell was fastest in first practice at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix as championship leader Kimi Antonelli stopped on track with a hydraulics issue.

Russell is 81 points behind Antonelli in the Drivers' Championship and must start gaining ground on his team-mate soon to avoid an early conclusion to the Formula 1 title race and he's started the event in Baku strongly.

The Mercedes driver was helped by a big slipstream from Fernando Alonso on his best lap to outpace Red Bull's Max Verstappen and both Ferraris by four tenths but showed great speed earlier in the session too.

Antonelli lost 35 minutes of track time after a hydraulics issue forced him to stop, so he will be on the back foot heading into second practice later on Thursday at 1pm, live on Sky Sports F1.

The Italian has won the last two races but Baku is one of the toughest tracks on the calendar and often throws up drama, so Antonelli is wary of how his 81-point lead over Russell and 100+ points advantage to Lewis Hamilton and Lando Norris could quickly be cut.

"In terms of Kimi's session, FP1 is the least representative session, so that's a blessing," said Sky Sports F1's Jamie Chadwick.

"The bigger concern is why they had the issue. We knew reliability was a big talking point for Mercedes earlier in the session; it seems to have been in a much better place the last few races especially, but that's going to be the biggest concern."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Craig Slater breaks down the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, including why the race takes place on a Saturday, while doing his best Craig David impression!

Hamilton and Charles Leclerc set their best times on the mediums, so will be hoping to be in contention for pole in Qualifying on Friday and the win in the race itself on Saturday afternoon.

Red Bull have brought some new parts to Baku including a revised floor, sidepod and mirrors and Verstappen looked very quick on the hard tyres early in the session.

Take away Russell's slipstream on his best lap and Red Bull appear to be in the fight at the front with Mercedes and Ferrari.

McLaren's Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris were sixth and 14th, over one second behind Russell despite having upgrades on their car.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Lewis Hamilton says he believes the team can make improvements as he strives for 'cleaner' weekends

McLaren's developments are mainly aerodynamic changes which will be more beneficial on high-speed non-street tracks and they have lots of time to find in the remaining two practice sessions.

At one point, Piastri thought he had damage on the car but the team told him there was nothing they could see, while Norris is yet to show his true pace.

Isack Hadjar, who was announced to stay at Red Bull for 2027, is back for the first time since July after missing the last three race weekends due to a wrist injury but lost 30 minutes of running due to an engine problem.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Williams' Carlos Sainz was forced to enter pits after a fire on his brakes during practice at Azerbaijan GP

That means Liam Lawson returns to Racing Bulls and he has flown out of the blocks in seventh with team-mate Arvid Lindblad in eighth.

Esteban Ocon, who is set to be left without an F1 seat next year as Haas are expected to drop him, was ninth and Audi's Gabriel Bortoleto was 10th.

Williams' Carlos Sainz suffered a minor brakes fire early on, but it cost him little track time on a weekend the team have brought a significant upgrade package.

Sports.title: Essex cricketer Das charged with two counts of rape
Sports.content:
Robin Das was arrested in August 2025 following reports of a women being raped in Brixton in March 2024; the 24-year-old has been suspended by Essex after being charged by police in July; Das is due to appear at a London court on October 9

Essex cricketer Robin Das has been charged with two counts of rape.

The 24-year-old was arrested in August last year following reports of a women being raped in Brixton in March 2024.

Das is due to appear at Inner London Crown Court on October 9.

Essex have confirmed that he has been suspended since he was charged.

The Metropolitan Police said in a statement: "The 24-year-old was arrested in August last year following reports of a women being raped in Brixton in March 2024."

Das, a top order batter, made his Essex debut in the Vitality Blast as an 18-year-old in September 2020.

The most recent of his 60 appearances for the county came in a One-Day Cup match against Middlesex on July 21, two days after which he was charged.

Essex said in a statement: "Essex County Cricket Club can confirm that a male member of the playing staff, currently under contract with the club, recently appeared in court in relation to an incident that took place outside club activities.

"Throughout, the club has remained in contact with the ECB, PCA, The Cricket Regulator and the player with regard to the matter, which included an immediate and ongoing suspension. The club will continue to follow all appropriate legal processes and guidance.

"As a club we have strict safeguarding and HR procedures in place, and all employees of Essex County Cricket Club are required to meet the highest standards of professional conduct at all times.

"As legal proceedings are in progress, the club are unable to make any further comment at this time."

Sports.title: How Barry Hearn is helping shape the future of his local non-league club
Sports.content:
Barry Hearn is best known for transforming snooker, darts and boxing into major television sports.

Even at 78, the Matchroom founder remains one of the world's most recognisable sporting promoters.

His involvement in football is perhaps lesser known - but every bit as intriguing.

In March 1995, Hearn saved Leyton Orient - who he first watched at the age of 11 - from bankruptcy by buying the club for just £2.43.

By 2007, three sides of Brisbane Road had been rebuilt. By 2012, he had wiped out any debt and reportedly invested around £8m.

In 2013/14, Orient reached the League One play-off final and had a rare chance to reach the second tier - but they lost 4-3 on penalties to Rotherham at Wembley. Within two months he had sold the club to Italian businessman Francesco Becchetti.

For nine years, Hearn was away from football. There was no shortage of work for him to be getting on with elsewhere.

Then, in July 2023, Matchroom sponsored the home shirt of Brentwood Town, the Isthmian League North Division side based three miles up the road from their headquarters.

"The reason Barry came over initially was we were doing something for Saint Francis Hospice, which he is a patron of, and he sat next to me for a game," says chairman Jez Dickinson.

"It was an entertaining game and Barry said afterwards, 'I'm never going to sit next to you again, Jez! Every time the ball went into the box, you were going up for a header and elbowing me in the side!' Barry is very much about passion and wearing his heart on his sleeve, so that's probably where we connected.

"We had some lunches and, after about the third one, he asked me what I wanted. I said obviously I wanted him to get involved, but I wanted him to get involved because he wanted to get involved, not because I was asking him - and he said he'd do it."

Hearn's name is, naturally, the one that catches the eye, but Dickinson has been the driving force since taking over as chairman in May 2019.

Before his appointment, he says there was "no pathway for the youth into the first team", "the bar was like a 1970s pub", and "the ambition was just to stay in the league".

They installed a brand new 3G pitch in the summer of 2024, won the Isthmian North Division in 2024/25 and last season lost the play-off final, where a place in the National League South was on the line.

Brentwood now have a Centre of Excellence, with 250 boys and girls between the ages of six to 12 in it. "It's hollow if that isn't there," he says.

Dickinson has spent seven years building the foundations so far - and Hearn's involvement provides the chance to take the club to another level.

So how does the partnership work?

"I speak to him probably once a week, maybe twice. It depends what's happening," says Dickinson.

Image: Hearn was Leyton Orient owner between 1995 and 2014

"He's hands-on in as much as he's available for anything we talk about. We'll sit down every couple of months, look at the financials, how we're getting on. He loves his numbers!

"Though he's a minority shareholder and he owns some of the club, he doesn't want to run it. He says: 'I look at you, Jez and you're stressed enough, I don't want any of that!'

"What he does is actually raise the bar, subconsciously, for what I want to achieve. We'll have a catch-up at Matchroom and it is quite inspiring and you come away thinking, 'let's go for it'.

"I don't underestimate that. It's probably 10 times as important as the financial stuff he does - not that I don't want the financial support as that's really important!

"He's a fantastic ambassador for the club as well as a sponsor and partner. I was speaking to a potential partner recently and they said they were interested because if he's committing to five years, he doesn't do things by halves and won't give up easily. It creates confidence with us and people looking to be partners."

There are plans for a 1,000-seater stand in place, but their purchase of the Brentwood Centre Arena needs to be completed before any progression can be made on that front.

Where does Dickinson think the partnership with Hearn and Matchroom will take Brentwood over these next five years?

Sports.title: Has the time come to separate home and away fans at WSL games?
Sports.content:
With interest in the Women’s Super League on the rise and more clubs playing at their main stadiums, there are questions over whether to separate supporters into stricter home and away sections, as in the men’s game, or to continue with mixed seating and optional away ends.

From the 2023-24 season, new league regulations required clubs to include an away-ticketing policy in their licensing agreements, a move backed by the Football Supporters’ Association (FSA).

The issue became a bigger talking point following the expedited growth of women’s football after Euro 2022. The SheGulls supporters’ club for Brighton Women said: “Now there are bigger and more passionate crowds with louder voices commanding more respect and attention. Put two sets of them together, and you can expect issues as we see on occasions at the moment.”

Under the policy, travelling fans wishing to sit with their own supporters can do so in a designated area, while others retain the choice of where they want to sit. Some supporters believe separation is a foregone conclusion. SheGulls added: “It would be nice to live in a world where it isn’t required, but the truth is it can be hard enough to generate an atmosphere at home from within our own fan base, never mind if they’re interspersed with Arsenal or Chelsea fans, for example. It feels inevitable.”

Dedicated away seating has been welcomed by, among others, Manchester City Women Official Supporters Club (MCWFC OSC), who cite an “increase in Manchester City supporters at away matches” as having “given a real boost to the atmosphere in stadiums”.

The FSA has taken a keen interest in developments and a spokesperson said: “The FSA and its members helped advocate for dedicated away sections, to help create community, atmosphere and allow travelling fans to connect, and to have a visible travelling fan section for away players to look towards.”

The infrastructure is already in place to segregate fan bases in most stadiums, where it is established for men’s games, but there is no stipulated away-ticket allocation owing to varying stadium sizes. Manchester United Women’s Supporters Club (MUWSC) feels supporter segregation could be a good move. “This doesn’t feel like a bad thing; segregation often results in an increased atmosphere which players regularly comment on as a positive thing,” it said.

Some experiments have taken place, with the WSL-run League Cup final using “club ends” behind the goals with mixed seating in the other stands, a model also used at FA Cup finals and at the 2025 Euros.

View image in fullscreen Brighton fans at St Andrew’s watch their team take on Birmingham in the WSL earlier this month. Photograph: Natalie Mincher/SPP/Shutterstock

The FSA added: “It is important now to look at whether home-only sections might be helpful for the same reasons: visibility, community and atmosphere. For us, this is about fan choice rather than ‘segregation’, and that choice is really important to an enjoyable matchday experience for all. It is important to consider general and neutral fans in the conversation, too, and there may not be a one-size-fits-all answer for every club.”

The current policies used in the league were developed through dialogue among the league, its member clubs and fans, through the FSA. This collaboration has enabled initiatives such as the Fan Choice trial and the Stadium Design Guidance. The belief is that the women’s game requires a distinct approach as its fanbase grows.

Tottenham, for example, have embraced the mixed home and away seating format. The club is understood to view its flexibility and family-friendly environment as a way to maintain atmosphere. It is felt an inclusive environment does not diminish the passion or noise levels of home supporters. However, it is also understood that the club may consider trialling a more segregated model if it is proven to improve the overall product and help the game grow.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

There are potential pitfalls with segregated stadiums. MCWFC OSC said separating fans often is not practical: “Even when matches are held at the main stadia, the men’s away end isn’t always used due to lower attendances. Clubs often keep fans together in just one or two stands to reduce operational costs so that traditional segregation can be impractical or simply unnecessary.”

SheGulls said: “There are some minor concerns about the way the game is going in terms of the need for segregation, but equally many think if we were segregated, or had the option of say a mixed zone, it would alleviate the angst that is sometimes caused by the current system.”

Creating a good atmosphere is key and many of the fan groups point out that supporters can still sing if they are in a mixed area. MUWSC has chants adapted for all ages, as well as a songbook where fans can look up the lyrics and join in. “There are so many positives about the environment that has been created in the women’s game, but remembering that welcoming atmospheres don’t mean you have to be quiet, and that being inclusive doesn’t mean never saying anything negative about the opposition.”

View image in fullscreen Crystal Palace fans applaud the players after their goalless draw against Arsenal at the Emirates Stadium. Photograph: COLORSPORT/Ashley Western/Shutterstock

Arsenal, meanwhile, have a separate away section for all WSL home fixtures at the Emirates, with the infrastructure already in place from men’s matches. It is felt this helps create a more competitive atmosphere and gives opposition fans a dedicated space. While Arsenal have a dedicated away end, away fans are still able to sit in “home” sections, especially families or groups with mixed loyalties.

Chelsea are staging all 13 of their home WSL matches at Stamford Bridge, which has a designated away end, this season, following consultation with players and supporter groups. The club are launching a new fan engagement project, The Blueprint, to help shape matchday culture and atmosphere. That is similar to Arsenal’s Block by Block initiative, introduced when they began playing all their WSL matches at the Emirates.

Chelsea host Arsenal in the WSL on Sunday, with the visitors selling out their allocated away tickets for the second consecutive time. Last season, Arsenal fans who missed out on away-end tickets sat in home sections alongside Chelsea supporters, raising questions around segregation.

The FSA has praised the clubs’ approach to collaborating with their fans: “We believe clubs should consult with their own fans to come up with local solutions that allow passion and vibrant support, but that keep the game welcoming and inclusive for all.”

As the league grows, so do the needs of different, growing fan bases, making it a key point of discussion among clubs, supporters and the league for the foreseeable future.

Sports.title: Infantino under pressure to include abandoned World Cup sell-off plan in external Fifa review
Sports.content:
Fifa council members will demand that Gianni Infantino include the abandoned World Cup sell-off plan and the Folarin Balogun affair in his proposed external review of Fifa’s governance.

In a letter sent to all 211 of Fifa’s member associations on Monday, Infantino said he would ask the council to commission a review of “Fifa’s current governance framework for major strategic initiatives” at its next meeting, in Zurich on 15 October, but he faces an internal battle over its terms of reference.

The Football Association’s chair, Debbie Hewitt, wrote to Infantino last week demanding the release of all documents relating to the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme that was abandoned last month, as well as the background to the global governing body’s decision to lift Balogun’s suspension during the World Cup, a request that has the support of many fellow council members.

One told the Guardian that without a retrospective analysis of FFE and Balogun, any governance review would lack credibility. Another suggested Infantino was seeking to avoid personal scrutiny by offering to look at Fifa’s governance structures moving forward rather than past controversies.

The council is made up of 28 representatives of the six confederations, eight vice-presidents, Infantino and Fifa’s secretary general, Mattias Grafström.

In the immediate aftermath of the Balogun affair, when the US striker’s suspension from the World Cup last-32 tie against Belgium was lifted after a phone call to Infantino from Donald Trump, a group of council members attempted to call an extraordinary general meeting but were unable to get the 19 votes required.

The European, Asian and North and Central American and Caribbean confederations campaigning against Infantino have 21 of the 38 council seats between them, but that includes delegates from Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Malaysia, who have issued public statements of support for the president.

The German football federation president, Bernd Neuendorf, expressed the European view clearly this week by describing Infantino’s offer of a governance review as cynical electioneering, but any vote on the matter at the council is likely to be tight.

“I regard Gianni Infantino’s letter as a transparent ploy to secure ⁠his re-election next year,” Neuendorf said. “Fundamentally, Fifa now seems to have recognised that changes are essential. However, Gianni Infantino ⁠is definitely not the right person to lead a reform ⁠process.”

Infantino said on Wednesday his letter had been well received. He was speaking while attending the opening night of the Arabian Gulf Cup in Jeddah, from where he will fly to New York for meetings at the United Nations general assembly.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“I am looking forward to receiving feedback from everyone, following my letter,” he said. “I have received positive messages about it from different parts of the world, and it is important that we keep listening to each other, here in Saudi Arabia, in any one of Fifa’s 211 member associations.

“We have a council meeting next month, so we will continue to have dialogue on these important matters. There must be a culture of dialogue, of listening to each other and respecting each other.

“This is not about generating positive headlines, it is about doing what is right for the game. And I have never been more determined and committed in doing that. Fifa is always engaged. I am always engaged and want to hear how we can continue to grow football for the benefit of everybody, everywhere.”

Sports.title: Andy Burnham signals he may lift ban on alcohol in football stands
Sports.content:
Andy Burnham has signalled he may lift the ban on drinking alcohol in the stands at football matches, suggesting it is “unfair” for fans to be singled out when it is permitted for other sports.

The prime minister, a committed Everton fan who still attends matches, said there was a case for trialling an end to the ban to bring football in line with rugby and cricket.

The move was welcomed by the Football Supporters’ Association and the English Football League, but police warned it would be “incredibly rash” to make changes without considering their impact on safety.

Burnham has long opposed the ban, saying it is discriminatory and out of date, harking back to an era when football violence was fuelled by drinking within view of the pitch.

Asked by reporters on the plane to New York about lifting a ban, Burnham said: “I don’t think it’s fair for football fans to be singled out in that way and I made that point. I think that legislation dates to an era where football was very different. And I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination.

“There are different ways it could be done, perhaps on a trial basis. But I’m not going to back away from what’s been a long-held view of mine. I don’t see how it can be fair that some supporters of one sport can be treated differently.”

The Sporting Events (Control of Alcohol etc) Act 1985 prohibits drinking in sight of the pitch in England and Wales.

The fan-led review of football governance in 2021 called for the ban to be re-examined and suggested piloting the sale of alcohol within sight of the pitch in lower-tier English football.

A spokesperson for the UK Football Policing Unit, which coordinates football policing policy in England and Wales, said: “The UKFPU would welcome a meeting with the prime minister to discuss his views and explain the challenges these proposed changes would bring to policing and the safety of staff and fans at football games.

“Other sports simply don’t see the violence and criminal behaviour from their supporters that football does, albeit a minority, with alcohol often playing a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour. It would be irresponsible to fuel this by allowing greater alcohol consumption during games.

“Following a number of football-related tragedies, changes in legislation were implemented after the Taylor report [of 1990 into the causes of the 1989 Hillsborough disaster] for good reason and we are currently in the longest ever period without a significant football-related disaster. It would be incredibly rash to make fundamental changes without a full examination of the evidence and meaningful consultation with police practitioners who have the expertise in this area.”

A spokesperson for the English Football League said it would be “receptive” to a review of legislation that “was introduced more than 40 years ago and has not kept pace with significant developments in stadium management, safety and stewarding”.

Tom Greatrex, the chair of the Football Supporters’ Association, said: “The FSA has always argued that it’s unfair to criminalise football fans for having a pint while watching the match – especially since you can sit in the same seat drinking alcohol whilst watching an Oasis gig or rugby league. We welcome the prime minister’s comments and totally agree that the legislation is outdated and deserves to be reviewed. We look forward to being part of that consultation.”

Supporters at Women’s Super League and WSL2 matches have been permitted to drink alcohol in view of the pitch since the start of this season, after a successful 18-month trial period led to a change to the WSL’s regulations this summer, allowing clubs – but not obliging them – to give fans that option.

Since that rule change, 25 of the 26 clubs across the two divisions of English women’s football have decided to take up the option at all of their home games. The only exception is Brighton & Hove Albion’s home matches at Crawley’s Broadfield Stadium, but Brighton have permitted fans to drink in view of the pitch when the team play their home matches at the Amex Stadium, such as last Sunday when they hosted Aston Villa. Women’s matches have typically seen fewer incidents of crowd trouble.

Sports.title: ‘It’s not in us’: Anthony Gordon backs Tuchel over England’s possession problem
Sports.content:
Anthony Gordon has sided with Thomas Tuchel’s assertion that controlling games through possession is not part of English football’s DNA. Although Gordon revealed surprise at being substituted when England were 1-0 up in their World Cup semi-final against Argentina, the winger refused to blame the defeat on Tuchel’s decisions and argued that wider cultural issues influenced the side’s collapse.

England’s perennial struggle to keep the ball when under pressure flared when a place in the final was within touching distance in July, allowing Argentina to fight back and go through with two late goals. The pain has not gone away and there has been intense scrutiny of Tuchel’s role in Atlanta. The head coach’s tactical choices were criticised and he faced a backlash after saying “ball possession” was not in his team’s DNA.

But Gordon, who thinks he will always be scarred by losing against Argentina, sided with Tuchel’s observations about England’s style as he looked towards the Nations League game against Spain on Saturday. The 25-year-old admitted the side had an ingrained inability to control games but argued they should stop trying to copy other nations.

Gordon has gained an insight into the Spanish understanding of how to use the ball since his move to Barcelona. His view is that England should lean more into their physical strengths.

“Culturally it’s not just that tournament or that game where we couldn’t control a game,” Gordon said. “As a nation we don’t have that strength like the Spanish, where we control games like they do. It’s not in us. I’m not sure it’s something that can be taught. Playing in Spain I can speak with an educated view on the way they keep the ball.

“It’s much different than I’ve ever experienced in this country, so I’m not sure we can ever get that. We can definitely get better – or maybe go the other way and really play to our strengths, which is play physical, play direct football and on the counterattack.”

Tuchel, who has talked about embracing the chaos of English football, is unsure whether his side can play with more control. “It’s not in the English DNA,” Gordon said. “We as English players are educated the same way as the Spanish players, we know how to keep possession, but it’s the decision-making of certain players in Spain. I look at some of the decisions they take on the ball sometimes and think: ‘I’m not sure how you’ve seen that.’”

Gordon opened the scoring against Argentina and was surprised to be replaced by Ezri Konsa when Tuchel made the first of two defensive moves and switched to a back five after the hydration break in the second half.

View image in fullscreen Thomas Tuchel tries to get his ideas across in a drinks break during the semi final against Argentina. Photograph: Simon M Bruty/Getty Images

“I’d just scored,” Gordon said. “I’m really good when I play off adrenaline. When I score, I normally don’t have many bad games, because I get into an untouchable mode of confidence.

“But as a winger I come off most games. It’s normal, it’s usually the position that’s targeted first for substitutions, because the player on the bench in your position is usually quick, and usually really good.”

Gordon defended Tuchel and said England’s performances did not match their level in training. “It makes a lot of sense to me why the manager would then go more safe and more defensive [against Argentina],” he said.

“As players we could have done more to take the initiative, to control the game. We had the best team, we had the best players in that semi-final, and in the last 20 minutes we didn’t play the best football. That’s something the manager can’t really affect.”

Gordon said his Barça teammates had told him England would have given Spain a tougher game than Argentina in the final. Spain dominated in New Jersey, winning 1-0 in extra time.

Sports.title: Anger at Tuchel over World Cup exit exposes biggest obstacle to England success | Barney Ronay
Sports.content:
In the end, Steve, Brian, Gaz or similar, he’s just not done the job he was hired to do. The job? The one he was hired to do? He’s not done it. How can I put this? There are three things here. The job. The being hired. The doing it. And him. Four things. And if you put those things together, there is no clear equation of … no linear semiotic cluster, he’s not, he’s just not, what I’m saying is …

How many times have you heard variations on this statement in the few short, tender weeks since England’s World Cup campaign? Perhaps you strayed too close to a sport-themed radio show, or accidentally ingested a celebrity football pundit podcast. Either way the verdict is pretty much universal, and delivered always with an air of finality, a sad shake of the head.

The non-winning of a World Cup. The failure to make substitutions to nullify big-game full-bore Lionel Messi. The non-doing of a job you were, apparently, hired for. Even if that job, in isolation, was also a pretty stupid idea in the first place.

Tuchel made a decent effort last week at steering attention to the more favourable aspects of England’s World Cup, but it’s clear he’s fighting a losing battle here. Nobody cares about his all-time highest managerial win ratio, or a best-ever England World Cup performance overseas.

Instead the key note is failure. And not just everyday failure, but failure so profound it amounts to outright wage-theft. As England arrive at a vital 20-month period in the national team’s history, Tuchel’s capacities in the job will be defined, until proved otherwise, by those final 20 minutes against Argentina, during which he failed to control the endless variables of a World Cup semi-final and was reduced to looking on helplessly, whirling his arms around like a scurvy-ridden Prussian general on his way to an executive golf weekend, out there not doing the thing he was hired for. Even if – and it is quite an important point – that thing made little actual sense.

This isn’t surprising. All political careers end in failure. All England managerial careers start in failure, continue in failure and implode in failure. One of the most interesting parts of any managerial reign is detecting early on the exact nature of the rage that will inevitably define the job.

Gareth Southgate took England from total dysfunction to the most successful sustained six-year period in their history, but still spent most of his time in the job dismissed as a yes-man, traitor, and basically the sole obstacle to all-consuming world domination on a scale never before seen.

It is hard to remember exactly why now. Not producing a team that played as if haring about the pitch on a jetski. Trying hard to be sensitive about politics. Exuding at all times that beaky, priestly sense of virtue, the suspicion that he may at any moment start talking about cheddar cheese, Spitfires and the traditional family unit.

View image in fullscreen Thomas Tuchel got the best out of Jude Bellingham at the World Cup but Harry Kane faded. Photograph: Dave Shopland/Shutterstock

With Tuchel the cycle was always likely to complete itself more quickly given the transactional nature of his appointment. Plus, the fact he is, and there is no other way of putting this, German. Tuchel has accelerated this with his inability to appear sufficiently penitent when the inevitable fine-margins defeats arrive. Arrogance, hubris, tactical robotism, failing to understand our native-tongued Premier League culture. This was always likely to be the narrative here.

It is also the biggest current obstacle to progress. As England prepare to set off on a run of four pretty decent games, it is the right moment to go back to this once again, if only because the next two years present such an obvious opportunity,

The next European Championship is the best chance England are going to get any time soon to win something. Home advantage. Good players. Plus, of course, a very good manager, or at least the best one they’re going to get at this point. Put it all together and the biggest obstacle to making this work is not the team or the manager, but the energy around them, a reaction to Tuchel that is, in itself, the biggest example of why England fail.

First, nobody really knows where the idea Tuchel was appointed solely to win tournaments came from. But it is clearly absurd. Winning a World Cup is the hardest thing in football, a grail, a history quest, never mind winning it with a nation that comes pre-cooked with hangups and uncertainties.

Winning it as foreign manager of a national team? History suggests this may even be impossible. Here’s a stat. There have been 22 World Cup-winning managers. All 22, from 1930 to 2026, have been the same nationality as their players. But here you go, Thomas. Win or bust.

In the event England lost in the way they always lose these late-stage knockout games, by failing to control the ball and the rhythm in the key period when things become stretched and desperate, when what matters above all is your midfield, when the base-level technique and game intelligence of your footballers are left pinned and wriggling on the wall, when it turns out Luka Modric, Messi and Andrea Pirlo are simply better adapted to this level.

The key misunderstanding is that Tuchel somehow caused this to happen, rather than failing to reverse it once it had begun. To appreciate this properly it is worth breaking down that sorrowful 18-minute spell in Miami, if only because this wasn’t actually an 18-minute spell, but a 40-minute spell.

The standard analysis asks: why didn’t England go forward, unleash, get on the front foot from about the 72nd minute, when Tuchel instead began to make defensive substitutions? The key point is that this was already happening. England had played well right up until the point Anthony Gordon scored the opening goal on 55 minutes. At which point the players just stopped. Watch it back and it’s startling. Suddenly the entire method is hacked clearances, deep defence, desperation measures.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

double quotation mark A World Cup is an examination of an entire sporting culture. You win by creating one, not by bolting it on

Tuchel reacts the right way to this. In the stadium you could see him jump up and urge his players forward, saying: “Wait, why are you doing this?” skinny arms whirling, like a man very angrily shepherding an elderly swarm of bees towards a distant hive.

For 17 minutes England’s players didn’t do what Tuchel wanted, trapped instead in their own vertigo, swamped by opponents playing “surge football” and backed by the conviction of having a genius in their ranks. At which point Tuchel had a choice to make. “We’re 18 minutes from the World Cup final. These blokes are in bits. Do we try to rewire this on the hoof, say: ‘Hey, everyone, we really need to change our outlook, run forward, reboot the mainframe?’ Or just take a breath and lean into what you have?”

In that moment Tuchel chose the latter, probably based on winning that way in the previous two games. Football reasoning is always outcome-based. Hold out and this is an act of icy Germanic cool. Lose and it’s downright fraudery. But there was at least logic in the process.

England got to within five normal-time minutes of a World Cup final in a game where they had long since begun to panic. And the failure was one of omission. Tuchel didn’t cause it. He also didn’t stop it happening. And this is a vital point not just in judging his choices, but in understanding what international football is for.

View image in fullscreen Cole Palmer was in Thomas Tuchel’s squad for the four Nations League games but withdrew with injury. Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PA

A World Cup is an examination of an entire sporting culture. Victory rewards decisions made at structural and economic levels. This is how we understand what works, which style of development succeeds. You win by creating a functioning culture, not by bolting one on. There has to be patience, intellectual weight, judgment calls made years in advance. This is why nations with coaching cultures win things. This is why England being able to shortcut this, to game the system, to buy a world-class coach and therefore win would be contrary to the basic beauty of the whole, but of no real use to the national sporting culture.

The real issue here is not Tuchel’s choices, but the fact elite English football can’t produce a Tuchel of its own with which to bend a little more and to learn as it goes along. Sack Tuchel, go English, and you’re basically looking at Graham Potter, Eddie Howe, Gary O’Neil, Frank Lampard, Michael Carrick, Liam Rosenior and Will Still.

There is no identifiable English way of playing, no English coaching school. It’s no good saying “Premier League”. What is that? A portmanteau culture of borrowed influences. Tuchel was polite and evasive when he was asked why he didn’t just make the players better at keeping and passing the ball. What he wants to say is: “You don’t understand how football works. Give me a Vinícius, a Rodri, an Antoine Griezmann, and then we’ll talk.”

There are other elements to the summer that have been quietly packed away in the past few weeks. Why didn’t he pick a squad that could have played in a more adaptive fashion, you might ask? Why didn’t he take Cole Palmer? Well, where’s Cole Palmer now? How’s the load management going? How about Phil Foden, now up to 37 games without a goal? Perhaps Adam Wharton of Crystal Palace might have changed everything. Maybe. Does it seem as if anyone else in elite football thinks this could be the case?

In the end England were good in parts. They showed spirit to get to that semi. They beat the hosts in Mexico City with 10 men, because the manager reorganised on the hoof. They got the best out of Jude Bellingham, Harry Kane faded, as he does, but his most likely replacement is now playing in Saudi Arabia.

They got to five minutes from beating the holders and reaching a first final outside England. This is something to learn from, for Tuchel as much as anyone else. To see it as an act of managerial fraudulism is to lean into the reasons why England fail, not to progress any further towards success.

Tuchel has no space to breathe from here, no real margin for error. But England do have a pretty good chance of winning something two years from now. As ever, the task will be to separate the job from its expectations, something that shows no signs of becoming any easier with time.

Sports.title: Netherlands v Germany: Klopp and Xavi begin revival projects with derby
Sports.content:
Before the latest instalment of a time-honoured international rivalry gearing up for two distinct new beginnings, Jürgen Klopp could not resist sprinkling a little of the old mischief. “The good thing is that we both have the exact same situation,” he said of Xavi Hernández, his counterpart when Germany visit the Netherlands on Thursday night. “We met on Monday and play on Thursday. And the coach knows the players from television. I actually know more of the Dutch players personally than Xavi does. Whether that’s an advantage, I don’t know, but it’s still a fact.”

In his public appearances Klopp has been on irrepressible form since taking the role in July. The task of whipping Germany back into shape has visibly and audibly topped up the energy levels that had drained by the time he departed Liverpool. Klopp, his wit sharp and appetite piqued, looks a far cry from the character who, to most trained eyes, was going through the motions upon his unveiling as Red Bull’s head of global soccer early last year.

Securing Klopp was a coup for the German football federation even if it came with a caveat, issued within seconds of his introduction to the media, that he would not be seen for dust if his family were hounded by the media. Xavi’s arrival in Amsterdam is no less fascinating even if, in the Dutch way, no bones were made by his employers about the fact Pep Guardiola and Arne Slot had been higher in their sights after Ronald Koeman’s departure. He is the Netherlands’ first foreign manager since Ernst Happel’s 10-month stint ended in 1978 but the fit is instinctively pleasing. Even if Guardiola was out of reach, they could land upon another product of the Johan Cruyff school that created modern-day Barcelona.

View image in fullscreen Xavi’s captain is Virgil van Dijk, who considered international retirement after the World Cup. Photograph: Koen van Weel/ANP/AFP/Getty Images

If Xavi is to take the Netherlands, occasionally exciting but frequently unstable during a World Cup run that shuddered to a halt in the last 32, back to their roots it will require a measure of patience. The pool of players does not allow much else; the recall of Borussia Dortmund’s Joey Veerman, who has not played international football for more than two years, speaks of the need for a technically adept midfield fulcrum but otherwise Xavi has scant scope for surprises. Virgil van Dijk will continue as captain despite considering international retirement during the summer; the head coach’s options may feel more complete when Frenkie de Jong and Donyell Malen have returned from injury.
