Xavi has resisted any temptation to engage in analysis of the Netherlands’ performance in the United States. “I don’t talk about the past,” is the standard line, ironically an easier one to roll out if the Nations League opener in Amsterdam brings a performance redolent of headier times. The revolution may have to be conducted with minimal effusive pronouncements from the coach. It is certainly a less dramatic shake-up than the one Klopp, acting like a man licensed to break a few moulds, has enacted before the next fortnight’s four-game baptism.

It raised eyebrows when Klopp named a squad of 44 players for the matches against the Netherlands, Serbia and, home and away, Greece. The expanded unit will be split into two: half will play on Thursday and in Germany’s next game, at home against the Greeks, and the remainder will be involved in the second two games. Only Finn Dahmen, the Augsburg goalkeeper, will be required across the set.

“I want to get to know as many players as possible,” Klopp said. “There is no A or B team. The squads are put together in a way that makes sense on the pitch and in terms of character and experience.”

View image in fullscreen The goalkeeper Finn Dahmen (centre) is the only player on call for all four Germany matches. Photograph: Federico Gambarini/DPA/AP

Club managers feeling squeamish at their players’ workloads during this expanded break will immediately have warmed to Klopp’s split selection. But the priority is to discover who best fits his vision for an intensely committed, front-footed, enthusiastic Nationalmannschaft that places round pegs, even unexpected ones, in round holes. Four players from Freiburg have made his sprawling selection; so has Felix Keidel from promoted Elversberg. Mika Baur of Celtic and the Hoffenheim winger Bambasé Conté were both stunned to receive first call-ups. The Brentford midfielder Vitaly Janelt joins his teammate Kevin Schade in the fray. Sixteen are uncapped.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Last weekend Klopp and his coaching staff convened at their headquarters in Herzogenaurach to watch as many of their charges’ domestic games as possible in one go. Freiburg’s Max Rosenfelder, one of the new brood, acknowledged the aura surrounding Klopp and described him as “a very, very special person”. Even if the mixed lineups prove to lack experience and cohesion, Klopp hopes his charges’ sheer thirst for the task will lift Germany from the doldrums of their most recent World Cup flop.

If he can unite 44 players, why not a whole country? Among Klopp’s many recent pronouncements was the timely intervention in favour of “positive patriotism” that followed an election victory by the anti‑immigration Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party in Saxony‑Anhalt. If it is some time since Germany’s football team have been at their best, perhaps the same may be said for the nation too.

In the Dutch capital, two big‑name managers will take their first steps towards bringing the good times back. “It could be a bit wild, but I accept that, it just has to be lively,” Klopp said. That comes with something approaching a cast‑iron guarantee.

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo vows to play on for Portugal and targets 1,000 career goals
Sports.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo said he considered quitting international football after the World Cup, but confirmed he plans to play on for Portugal and hopes to reach 1,000 goals for club and country. Ronaldo, who is 21 goals shy of the milestone, accepted some critics are trying to “kill” him but is determined to carry on.

Ronaldo, who has won 233 caps for his country, captained Portugal in the summer at the World Cup, where they exited to Spain in the last 16. Asked if he considered walking away from international duty, he replied: “Yes, I did. Of course, I’m always thinking about my decisions, my future, the present also. I’m a thinker; you have to think. This is why you see me here now, it means I will continue.

“I had a conversation with our president [Pedro Proença], with our coach. I still believe that I’m able to help the national team to reach what they want. I think I can give the national team my support, not only through the goals, but also outside of football. There is a new young generation, but for me the basic point is to be able on the pitch to score the goals and to help the team win games.

“Whenever they say they don’t want me in the national team, I will be the first one to go. When I think I am not adding anything to the team, or that I create an atmosphere, I will be the first to go. I will take my suitcase and leave. The Portuguese count on me. That’s why I’m still here … Just look at the numbers, I’m sure you can make some calculations, I’m still doing well. The day they don’t count on me, no problemo, I will leave. I will always be the No 1 fan of this federation.”

Jorge Jesus, the Portugal head coach who managed Ronaldo at Al-Nassr, said the 41-year-old would start in his first game in charge, against Wales in the Nations League on Thursday. Jesus, who has succeeded Roberto Martínez, also launched a passionate defence of Ronaldo, drawing applause from many in attendance at Portugal’s City of Football complex in Lisbon.

Quick Guide Bellamy remembers 'president' Ronaldo's arrival Show Craig Bellamy said Wales must enjoy facing “heavyweight” opposition in Portugal on Thursday and colourfully recalled being stuck at Lisbon airport because it was on lockdown to ensure Cristiano Ronaldo a “president-like” arrival. Bellamy (pictured) twice visited the city on pre-season camps with Burnley, where he worked as assistant to Vincent Kompany for two years. “He is beyond a superstar,” the Wales manager said of the Portugal captain, whom he shared a pitch with in the Premier League almost 18 years ago, when Ronaldo, who turns 42 in February, scored twice in a 2-0 win for Manchester United at home to West Ham. “There were rows of police cars everywhere,” Bellamy said of the moment he realised the airport was on lockdown. “We were like: ‘Something’s happened. We thought it was a security breach. We were stuck on the coach for about 10, 15 minutes. ‘When are we going to get off the coach?’ Suddenly this car turns up – I’ll be doing it a disservice but it was a Bentley or something like that – and parks in this parking slot, this guy walks out the front, goes to the boot, grabs this rucksack, and this other kid comes out the front, puts the rucksack on. Who is it? Ronaldo. “Even the police are like [trying to look at Ronaldo] but no one could bother him. It was the coolest walk I’ve ever watched. For a minute, we were on the coach just jaws dropped. ‘Everyone who is moaning? Shut up.’ We don’t mind. We’re watching this … it was like president stuff. How can you lock off a whole airport? I won’t even be able to get my computer through customs at Cardiff. What have I just seen?” Bellamy was effusive in his praise for Portugal’s all-time record goalscorer, who is closing on 1,000 goals for club and country. “Who gets 1,000 goals?” the 47-year-old said. “Seriously? It’s just silly, eh? I hope he gets it – but I hope he gets nothing on Thursday. We’re talking about one of the greatest players of all generations – his name will go down in history for hundreds and hundreds of years.” Ben Fisher Photograph: José Sena Goulão/LUSA Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

“Cristiano is a symbol of Portugal and the national team,” said Jesus, sitting alongside Ronaldo at the Portugal federation’s campus. “If he will play the games, he is not entitled to that, it is up to the manager to decide.”

Ronaldo cut a relaxed figure on stage alongside Jesus. “For me the most important thing is I know what I am,” he said. “I know what I do to be here, I know what I have done to have the success that I have had. I know why young kids love Cristiano, because they see me as an example, and I will continue to do that. Even when I am retired … in 10 years.

“I’m happy with myself. It doesn’t matter if I play tomorrow, if I’m rested for the next game, for me the most important thing is that I feel good. The people around me, they trust in my work. Focus on the people who love Cristiano, not the people who criticise me, so I am a happy person.”

Asked directly about the criticism, Ronaldo triggered laughter from many in the room by replying: “I cannot be 100% honest, sometimes I have to be politically correct.” He added: “I do understand that some TV channels like to criticise me, they’ve tried to kill me – with a shotgun – but I can still move away from it. Anyway, I am used to it. I have been doing this for more than 20 years, I’m quite used to it. What I can control, I will. What I can’t, I won’t.”

View image in fullscreen Cristiano Ronaldo attends a training session before the Nations League group stage match against Wales. Photograph: Rodrigo Antunes/EPA

On Thursday Ronaldo will return to the Estadio José Alvalade, where he began his career with Sporting, before joining Manchester United in 2003. It is Portugal’s first game in Lisbon since beating the Republic of Ireland in a World Cup qualifier last October.

“It’s a special feeling because it was there where my beautiful history started,” Ronaldo said. “I’m very proud about that, to play for the national team after so many years, playing where I practically was opened to the world … It was a beautiful moment.

“It is always a pleasure to play for the national team, to wear the colours of Portugal. After so many years, it is [still always] like the first time. I will step on to the pitch with passion, emotion. I hope we can get off on the right foot. Because it’s at Sporting, it does feel a bit more special.

“It would be the cherry on the top of the cake to score my 1,000th goal with the national team. It would be the culmination of a beautiful story. I said I wanted to reach that target and I will reach that target. But I don’t have an obsession. If you are obsessed with something, you won’t get it … Just enjoy. Carpe diem, enjoy the day.”

Sports.title: Christian Eriksen leaves Wolfsburg by mutual consent after on-pitch collapse in June
Sports.content:
Christian Eriksen and the German side VfL Wolfsburg have agreed to terminate ⁠his contract by mutual consent, the club announced on Wednesday.

The 34-year-old collapsed during a Denmark friendly ⁠against Ukraine in June. Eriksen said in July he would ​return to his homeland to undergo a ‌rehabilitation programme. He previously suffered a cardiac arrest during Denmark’s opening Euro 2020 group match ⁠against Finland in Copenhagen in 2021.

The decision brings ⁠an early end ⁠to ​Eriksen’s contract, which was set to run until June 2027. The midfielder joined Wolfsburg as a free agent a year ago, making 34 appearances across all competitions. Eriksen scored three goals and provided 10 assists for the Wolves, but could not prevent their relegation from the Bundesliga.

“At the moment, it is important for me to ‌be close to my family in Denmark. I’m pleased that we were able to find a solution together,” Eriksen said in a statement. “My time in Wolfsburg was marked by many highs and lows,” he added. “I know that the club is now ‌in good hands as it aims to make its way back to the Bundesliga, and I am convinced ​that a successful future lies ahead for VfL.”

The Wolfsburg ⁠managing director of sport, Dieter Hecking, said the second-tier club granted ​Eriksen’s request to ​cancel the agreement. His last appearance for the team came in May’s promotion/relegation playoff defeat by Paderborn.

“He has already ​experienced and achieved a great deal during his ​extraordinary career,” ‌Hecking said. “Despite his ​short time ​here, he has left a lasting impression on his teammates, our staff and the fans.”

Eriksen played for Ajax, Tottenham and Inter before his on-pitch collapse in 2021. He was fitted with an implantable cardioverter-­defibrillator (ICD) device, but had to leave Inter because Serie A rules prohibit playing with a pacemaker.

View image in fullscreen Denmark and Ukraine players gather around Christian Eriksen after his collapse in June. Photograph: Bo Amstrup/Ritzau Scanpix Foto/AP

After joining Brentford in 2022, Eriksen spent three years at Manchester United before joining Wolfsburg last summer. He said in June that his ICD device “did what it was designed to do” after he collapsed on the pitch for a second time.

“Receiving a shock from my ICD has had a major impact on both me and my family, but I want to reassure everyone that this was a different situation from what happened in 2021,” Eriksen posted on social media.

“I am feeling good, and my recovery has already started. I am incredibly grateful to the doctors who have cared for me and my heart over the years. Thanks to their expertise, my ICD did exactly what it was designed to do: protect me when I needed it.”

Sports.title: Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua £150m fight is finally CONFIRMED - in Cardiff at 2am on a Friday night in December - after years of waiting
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua £150m fight is finally CONFIRMED - in Cardiff at 2am on a Friday night in December - after years of waiting

Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury will finally fight on December 11, with the long-awaited all-British £150million ($200m) heavyweight blockbuster confirmed to take place in Cardiff.

Boxing supremo Turki Alalshikh confirmed today that Britain's biggest fight will be held in the United Kingdom after weeks of fraught talks. Netflix will show the showdown live and a start time of around 2am UK is expected for the ring walks.

'For 15 years no one has been able to make this fight,' Alalshikh said. 'Back in April, I said that any announcement would come from me. I can now confirm that Fury Vs Joshua will be coming to the UK, as I promised British boxing fans.

'The time for talking is over. Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua. Years in the making. One night to settle it. December 11th. LIVE on Netflix.'

Netflix today confirmed the fight would be available 'at no additional cost' to subscribers. Their general membership pricing starts at £7.99 in the UK.

Bookmakers Betfair make Fury the early favourite to win, pricing him at 8/15. Joshua is priced at 13/8.

Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua has been announced for Friday, December 11

The roots of Joshua-Fury stretch back more than a decade, to when both men were emerging as Britain's leading heavyweight prospects

Joshua tweeted: 'I am inspiring a generation' alongside an emoji of the British flag.

His promoter Eddie Hearn, who fought relentless to keep the fight in the UK, wrote: 'WE DID IT. Forever indebted to the U.K. public for their support of Anthony Joshua. We couldn’t have got this over the line without you.'

Fury's name appearing first on the card for the Battle of Britain will be an early win for the Gypsy King in his constant PR war with Joshua.

The pair had originally been pencilled in for November 20 at Madison Square Garden in New York, but a determined push from Joshua and Hearn saw the contracts re-negotiated to bring the fight back to British soil.

Hearn had been adamant that British fans deserved the opportunity to watch two of the country's biggest sporting stars go head-to-head at home and fought hard to make that happen.

Fury, too, wanted the fight in the UK, but had been prepared to accept a move to America because of his concerns that the bout could once again slip away.

Now those fears, after 10 years old heartbreak, have been put to bed. The fight will take place in Cardiff, with the later-than-usual start time expected to mean ring walks at around 2am UK time as organisers attempt to satisfy the American audience watching on Netflix.

Wembley had been the preferred venue for the showdown, but the major stumbling block was securing the necessary late-night permit.

With Netflix and Turki Alalshikh keen for the event to cater to viewers in the United States, organisers required a start time significantly later than would normally be permitted at Wembley.

Cardiff, however, was able to secure the required permit - clearing the final obstacle to bringing the fight back to Britain.

Cardiff's Principality Stadium has come out on top to host the fight after weeks of negotiations

The scale of the occasion is already being felt in the Welsh capital, with hotels in Cardiff now understood to be sold out as supporters scramble to secure accommodation for one of the biggest fights in British boxing.

For Joshua, the move represents the culmination of a push to ensure the fight was staged in the UK.

The former two-time world champion and Hearn had been clear that, after years of watching British heavyweight stars travel overseas for major fights, Joshua-Fury belonged in front of their home crowd.

Fury was willing to compromise on the location if necessary, however, with his priority being to finally get the fight over the line.

The roots of Joshua-Fury stretch back more than a decade, to when both men were emerging as Britain's leading heavyweight prospects.

Joshua won Olympic gold at London 2012 before turning professional, while Fury had already made his professional debut in 2008 and was building an unbeaten record of his own.

For years, the prospect of the two eventually sharing a ring became one of British boxing's great hypothetical match-ups.

Fury's stunning victory over Wladimir Klitschko in 2015 elevated him to the summit of the heavyweight division, while Joshua was rapidly closing in on world-title status himself.

FURY VS JOSHUA - BIG FIGHT ODDS Fury to win - 8/15 Draw - 16/1 Joshua to win- 13/8 Victory method: Tyson Fury by Points or Decision - 16/5 Fury by TKO/KO/DQ - 13/10 Anthony Joshua by Dec/Tech Dec - 15/2 Joshua TKO/KO/DQ - 13/5 Fight to go the distance: Yes - 13/8 No - 4/9 Odds courtesy of Betfair

Joshua claimed the IBF heavyweight title by stopping Charles Martin in 2016 before adding the WBA and IBO belts to his collection. By 2017, Joshua-Fury had evolved from a fantasy fight into a genuine target. But the negotiations repeatedly broke down.

The closest it came to fruition was in 2021, when the two camps appeared to be on the brink of agreeing a two-fight deal.

The proposed showdown was publicly discussed and appeared to be edging towards reality, only for Fury to become contractually obligated to face Deontay Wilder after an arbitration ruling.

That fight ultimately took place, with Fury beating Wilder for a third time, while Joshua embarked on his own defining chapter against Oleksandr Usyk.

Joshua lost his WBA, IBF and WBO titles to Usyk in 2021 before suffering a second defeat to the Ukrainian in their 2022 rematch. Once again, Joshua-Fury seemed to drift further away. Then came another tantalising opportunity.

Negotiations accelerated in late 2022, with both camps discussing a potential December showdown, but the fight again failed to materialise. Fury moved on to other opponents while Joshua began rebuilding his career following the two defeats by Usyk.

The emergence of Alalshikh and the rapid expansion of Saudi Arabia's influence over boxing created a fresh route to making the fight. And this time, the years of disappointment are finally over. The contracts have been signed. Joshua-Fury is no longer a fight being negotiated, teased or promised. It will take place in Cardiff on December 11.

Sports.title: How Premier League clubs are exploiting their most loyal fans - the season ticket tricks used by Chelsea and Man United, the subtle ways 'old-school' supporters are being swapped out for tourists, 'hospitality' rip-offs and why the worst is yet to come
Sports.content:
The railing that once hoisted the Holmesdale Fanatics flag at Selhurst Park has gone. The distinctive and raucous Crystal Palace ultras group? Disbanded.

The flagpole remained in place for the first home game of the season, just 24 hours after the group announced their dissolution, but had vanished by the following match.

Selhurst has felt a little lifeless ever since. The ceaseless noise from the 400-man section behind the goal in the Holmesdale Road End is no more.

When Daily Mail Sport asked the Holmesdale Fanatics for an explanation, they declined and redirected us to their initial statement, where they criticise the ‘draconian restrictions’ imposed on supporters.

Those restrictions extend well beyond Selhurst Park. Across the country, the football fan experience is changing, replaced by a game that is increasingly commercialised and gentrified.

Daily Mail Sport has spoken to insiders across the Premier League and beyond, industry experts and, most importantly, loyal supporters themselves to uncover just how the modern-day fan is being exploited – and why the worst may yet be to come...

Crystal Palace's distinctive and raucous Holmesdale Fanatics group has disbanded, leaving Selhurst Park a little lifeless

It is a sign of the wider exploitation and disenfrachisement of old-school, matchgoing supporters

Times are tough for football fans of all stripes, but season-ticket holders are feeling the pinch more than anyone. Premier League regulations now restrict those fans from sharing their season tickets with fellow supporters, family and friends.

At the start of the season, digital tickets became mandatory, supposedly to improve stadium security, prevent ticket touting and streamline entry into stadiums.

Manchester United have used digital ticket enforcement to identify what they describe as ‘suspicious activity’ and curb ticket touting, banning 685 season ticket holders as a result. However, fears remain that innocent fans using the ticket sharing system have been caught up in the clean-up operation.

A cynic would argue the new policy presented a fresh opportunity for clubs to squeeze supporters and monetise them sharing their season ticket.

Rather than the trusty plastic card which supporters could hand over to friends if they were not attending a match or wanted to split the cost of a season ticket, fans must now resell their tickets through official club channels – which clubs can make a profit from – or share them using the club’s ticketing platform, with access often commanding a membership fee.

At Chelsea, for example, to share a ticket the recipient must be a member, with prices beginning at £15. Meanwhile, Crystal Palace allow season-ticket holders to share their match ticket with non-members but charge a one-off £50 fee for the privilege.

Manchester United offer a ‘ticket sharing’ membership which allows supporters to receive forwarded tickets from season-ticket holders – charging £30 per person.

There are, in fairness, valid safety concerns behind this development. The Premier League partly introduced the scheme to ensure match attendees can be identified, which helps the enforcement of banning orders and detection of high-risk supporters.

But the self-serving, avaricious clubs have opportunistically commercialised supporters' autonomy over their own tickets.

At Manchester City, season tickets must be used for 16 Premier League home games, ten of which must be attended by the named individual, or the ticket will be cancelled

Across town, United have used digital ticket enforcement to identify what they describe as ‘suspicious activity’ but fears remain that innocent fans have been caught up in the clean-up

Things are unlikely to get better anytime soon. One senior football executive told Daily Mail Sport that clubs view season tickets as a ‘discounted rate’, blocking a conveyor belt of high-spending corporate and tourist spectators attending one-off games that would generate more revenue. They added that clubs could look to reduce the number of their season tickets.

That perspective was echoed by football finance expert and host of The Price of Football Podcast Kieran Maguire, who told Daily Mail Sport: ‘The bigger brands see season-ticket holders as bed blockers because tickets can be sold at a higher price to international fans and those desperate to see their club but who can only manage it once a year due to logistical challenges.

‘If we take the case of Liverpool, Anfield has gone from 44,000 to 61,000 capacity, but there was hardly any increase in season-ticket sales. It is far more lucrative to target the corporate market or the day-fan market as opposed to someone who is a local Red and unlikely to go to the megastore and drink in the ground beforehand because they go to the pub with their mates, sit at the same table and have the same chats.

‘These people, of course, are the bedrock of football fans. For political reasons, clubs won’t want to be seen to be reducing season tickets. But I don’t think we will see an increase going forward unless they are for corporate seats.

‘In some of the more desirable areas of the stadium, the clubs might not convert season tickets that haven’t been renewed into new season tickets despite long waiting lists.'

That shift has already begun, with United relocating around 500 fans sat behind the dugout at Old Trafford to the top of the North Stand to increase hospitality tickets in what United describe as a ‘high value area of the stadium’.

At Manchester City, meanwhile, season tickets must be used for 16 Premier League home games, ten of which must be attended by the named individual, or the ticket will be cancelled. Some fans argued the move breaches the Equality Act as pregnant women, mothers or disabled people could struggle to attend for prolonged periods.

To make matters worse, season-ticket waiting lists are becoming increasingly exploitative. Arsenal’s exceeds 110,000 people, meaning the club would need to turn over every season ticket three times before reaching the bottom. With the current wait time estimated at around 20 years and a £50 deposit required to join, it is difficult to envisage many supporters ever securing one.

There is therefore logic in closing the waiting list – as Liverpool have done – rather than asking supporters to part with their hard-earned cash for a ticket they may never receive. However, clubs' passive income would take a hit. Arsenal say they regularly review the waiting list and would consult supporters on any proposed changes.

Liverpool supporters recently successfully protested ticket price hikes of 3 per cent for three consecutive seasons

English football is shifting towards a matchday experience built around tourists rather than hardcore supporters. Americans fans used to taking in entertainment that goes beyond the game itself

Aside from their wallets being raided, the fan experience is also declining as English football culture shifts towards a matchday experience built around tourists rather than hardcore supporters. American fans, in particular, are accustomed to taking in entertainment that goes beyond the game itself.

Tourism dilutes the home support. At Selhurst Park, people were spotted wearing Erling Haaland Norway shirts in the home end during Manchester City’s 4-1 win over Palace in August.

And when Palace travelled to Craven Cottage earlier this month, Daily Mail Sport observed Chicago Fire and Brazil shirts in Fulham's newly redeveloped Riverside Stand, with some spectators even whipping out their phones to record themselves when the visitors scored. A similar picture is painted weekly across Premier League stadiums.

Fan experience has played a significant role in the breakdown in relations between Palace and the Holmesdale Fanatics. The fan group want an organic atmosphere inside the stadium, while the club have veered towards an artificial one.

Before kick-off, the HF had found themselves competing with Natasha Bedingfield’s Unwritten - among other pop songs - blared over the recently upgraded PA system.

There is an internal directive to ensure the stadium looks attractive on television; hence the introduction of fireworks and pyrotechnics when the players enter the pitch. But manufacturing a look is precisely what the HF stand against.

Perhaps the pomp and circumstance makes football clubs more marketable to international audiences.

The Premier League’s own economic and social impact report from July 2026 boasts that the top flight drew over a million international fans to matches in the 2023-24 season, with a trip-related spend of £903million. Those numbers are projected to rise continuously.

The Premier League say the top flight drew over a million international fans to matches in the 2023-24 season, with a trip-related spend of £903million

Palace's Holmesdale Fanatics want an organic atmosphere inside the stadium, while the club have veered towards an artificial one

Daily Mail Sport spoke to one US-based neutral who regularly flies over to attend Premier League games. Among the thousands he has spent on tickets already this season, he paid £350 for a general admission ticket to watch Ipswich take on Liverpool at Portman Road, purchased through a third-party reseller.

Clubs discourage buying third-party tickets as they do not receive the benefits besides the money spent in the stadium on merchandise, food and drink – although it does indicate the extravagant prices international fans are willing to pay for a £38 ticket, splashing nine times over the odds.

It has not gone unnoticed at Premier League clubs that World Cup stadiums in the United States were 99.7 per cent full despite extortionate general admission prices. That spells danger for domestic supporters.

Sites like Seat Unique and Sportsworld have partnerships with Premier League clubs including Manchester City, Manchester United and Everton and market padded seat packages suitable for tourists. For Manchester City’s Champions League match against Paris Saint-Germain next month, Sportsworld are selling a £279 padded seat package which non-members can purchase – the only requirement is they are not in away colours.

'Westview' at Stamford Bridge is similar. The package ranges from £225 to £625 per game depending on the prestige of the fixture for a padded seat and a market hall style concourse with no food or drink included.

It is barely a hospitality package, besides sitting in a swankier area of the stadium. Simply put, Westview allows Chelsea to sell extortionately priced tickets to non-members, enabling the club to benefit directly from the tourist trade. These visitors are also likely to spend money on food and drink and visit the megastore.

Some Premier League clubs have even been spotted bringing the megastore to fans, with merchandise staff now carrying trays of baseball caps and scarves around the pitch and concourses to cater to the tourist market.

The Premier League needs to captivate an international audience but it should not come at the expense of ordinary fans.

Last year, the Football Supporters' Association said: ‘Football is becoming a luxury good for some, pricing out working-class communities, young supporters and families who represent the future heartbeat of the game. Record broadcast revenues – the 2025-28 deal is worth £12.25billion – and packed corporate hospitality sections tell us that financial sustainability does not depend on pricing out traditional supporters.’

Yet the cheapest ticket for a Category A game in nine of the 20 Premier League grounds exceeds £50, while general admission season tickets range from £380 to £3,192. Newcastle offer the cheapest season ticket, and Fulham’s is the most expensive.

Coventry City are one of the few clubs that have looked out for their supporters in recent years

‘Football is becoming a luxury good for some, pricing out working-class communities, young supporters and families who represent the future heartbeat of the game,' say the FSA

Although the outlook for fans appears bleak, there are rays of positivity to cling on to. Coventry City deserve praise for rewarding loyalty. In 2023, the club committed to giving supporters who bought a season ticket a free one should they reach the Premier League. This season, some 5,000 fans are benefiting from that scheme.

The £30 price cap for away fans has been extended until the end of the 2027-28 season – providing good value for the most loyal supporters.

Five clubs that were in the Premier League last season froze their season ticket prices for 2026-27. Attendances remain very strong across the top flight and concession prices are reasonable at many clubs, in line with the League's guidance.

And despite the wider rip-off, fans can still fight back. Liverpool supporters had success at the end of last season after the club announced season ticket price hikes of 3 per cent for three consecutive seasons. But a protest at Anfield – where supporters raised yellow cards – prompted the club to reconsider, raising prices for this season and freezing them for next year.

In light of the European Super League debacle, Premier League clubs created fan advisory boards to ensure that supporters' concerns were heard. Now, however, those bodies must stop being symbolic – and ensure English football remembers its most loyal fans represent the heart of the game.

Sports.title: Liverpool outcast Harvey Elliott accused of being overweight by brutal Spanish press as he fights for fitness at Valencia after a nightmare year
Sports.content:
Harvey Elliott has been accused of being 'well overweight for his physique' by the Spanish press after enduring a difficult start to his loan spell at Valencia.

Elliott, 23, joined the Spanish club on a season-long loan from Liverpool at the start of the month and is fighting to regain fitness after suffering from a lack of playing in the last year.

The midfielder was handed a second chance at the Reds by new boss Andoni Iraola during pre-season, after a campaign of struggle on loan at Aston Villa last season. But the England U21 international star failed to impress and he was shipped over to Valencia as he sought game time.

Elliott is yet to start a LaLiga game for Valencia and his three substitute appearances for the club have left a lot to be desired.

And now Spanish media outlet Marca has hit out at the Reds loanee for arriving at the Mestalla 'out of shape'.

In a damning report, they claim that an 'atypical pre-season' at Liverpool has led to Elliott's fitness levels being suboptimal and that he is 'paying the price' by getting fewer minutes on the pitch than expected.

On loan Valencia midfielder Harvey Elliott is being accused of being 'overweight' by the media in Spain

Media outlet Marca say that Elliott (pictured during pre-season) arrived from Liverpool 'out of shape'

Club football has now halted for three weeks for an extended international break, and with Elliott not involved in the England set-up currently, he is being encouraged to use his time to get up to scratch in the fitness department.

He also has the chance to impress a new manager, with Javier Aguirre, the manager of Mexico when England beat them at the Azteca in that titanic World Cup clash, arriving at the club.

His second loan spell away from Liverpool, where he is just one shy of 150 appearances and won a Premier League title, is proving to be as difficult as his previous one at Aston Villa last season.

During his miserable spell at Villa Park, Unai Emery chose not to select Elliott after a handful of games and admitted that it affected the midfielder.

He made just nine appearances and scored one goal last season, though he still finished with a Europa League winners' medal, albeit as an unused substitute.

And, speaking during Liverpool's pre-season tour of the US, Elliott revealed how much of a toll that period had on him.

‘Mentally, it was a very tough one,’ he said. ‘(Going to Villa) was a learning curve. It was an opportunity for me to experience something new.

‘I don't wish (the situation) upon any other player, because it's not nice at all, but I have no hard feelings. I wish them all the very best.

'I did really have a lot of love for them. They treated me as one of their own, and for that I respect them highly.

‘But it was tough, mentally and physically. I'm on the other side of it now. I was able to get through it and achieve something at the end of the season as well (winning a Europa League medal).’

Sports.title: Ivan Toney's assault court case adjourned: England World Cup striker to appear in court next week over incident in upmarket London nightclub
Sports.content:
England footballer Ivan Toney will appear in Westminster Magistrates' Court next Thursday after his assault case was delayed by a week.

The 30-year-old, who plays for Saudi Pro League club Al-Ahli, was charged with assault causing actual bodily harm on July 31 following an incident in a Soho nightclub on December 6.

He was due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Thursday to face the allegation for the first time.

But a court official said the hearing is now set to take place on October 1, after a request for a delay was received on Wednesday night.

At the time of his charge, a spokesperson for Toney said: ‘Ivan acknowledges the charge and although he is naturally shocked, he looks forward to being given the opportunity to clear his name in court.’

Ivan Toney will appear in Westminster Magistrates' Court next Thursday after his assault case was adjourned

Toney was a surprise selection in Thomas Tuchel's England World Cup squad in the summer.

He appeared in the semi-final against Argentina as a late substitute and then started the third-place play-off win over France.

The 30-year-old joined Al-Ahli in August 2024 from Brentford for £40million, having scored 72 goals in 141 games for the Bees.

Toney missed the first half of the 2023-24 season due to a gambling ban but went on to feature in England's run to the Euro 2024 final.

Sports.title: Andy Carroll's Liverpool hell: Former star wanted to FAIL his Anfield medical and 'almost cried' at his unveiling - before his life spiralled out of control with boozy strip club and casino nights out
Sports.content:
Andy Carroll has claimed that Newcastle held him 'over a barrel' in order to push through his mega-money move to Liverpool, as he opens up on his miserable spell on Merseyside.

Carroll, 37, became the Reds' record signing when he joined for £35million in January 2011 from Newcastle, making 58 appearances and scoring 11 goals for the club across two seasons.

However, the striker, who currently plays for Dagenham and Redbridge in the National League South – a club he co-owns with YouTuber KSI – has detailed how he never wanted to leave his boyhood club for Anfield in his new book, Owning It.

'After landing in Liverpool, we went straight to Anfield, where I had my medical,' he wrote. 'I kept thinking, "Please just fail this and you can go home." But I passed with flying colours.'

Carroll then detailed how the Magpies forced him to hand in a transfer request, otherwise he 'wouldn't play' for his beloved Geordies again.

The forward continued: 'Newcastle had me over a barrel, and I later learned that me putting in a transfer request meant that Newcastle got to keep 10% of the £35 million fee that otherwise would have gone to me.

Andy Carroll played for Liverpool between 2011 and 2013 and made 58 appearances

'The first thing I did after signing was phone my mom and dad. They were less upset that I'd left Newcastle for Liverpool than the fact I hadn't discussed it with them. "You need to pick up the cat," I said. And that was that.'

Carroll went on to describe how he 'looked like I wanted to cry' when being unveiled as a Liverpool player alongside Luis Suarez, despite forcing himself to explain that he was happy to be at the club.

Back in 2011, the story was that Carroll had forced a move away from Newcastle in order to be Liverpool's new main man after the departure of Fernando Torres to Chelsea.

But Carroll claims the rhetoric from St. James' Park was 'so far from the truth as to be almost laughable' and that then boss Alan Pardew was former owner Mike Ashley's 'puppet'.

He added: 'I was desperate to tell everyone what had really gone on in all its gory detail, but I thought it best to keep a lid on it.

Carroll opened up on how he was hoping to fail his medical at Liverpool and wanted to 'go home'

During his unveiling he describes how he looked like he 'wanted to cry' alongside fellow new signing Luis Suarez (right)

'I didn't want Liverpool and their fans to think I hated the idea of being there, especially as they'd shelled out so much for me and handed me the number 9 shirt as worn by Ian Rush, Robbie Fowler, and Torres.'

In his book, the striker also tackled his persistent problems with alcohol, which arose after he got his first big salary bump up.

'Before my weekly wage jumped to £2,500 a week, I was quite sensible,' said Carroll. 'But soon enough I was spending time in bars, strip joints and casinos. If everyone wanted a tray of shots, I'd buy a tray of shots.

'And while alcohol didn't turn me into some violent loon, a well-known footballer spending time in local establishments was bound to attract trouble.'

Carroll went on to play for a further seven clubs after leaving Liverpool, including the likes of West Ham, West Brom, Reading and even a return to Newcastle. His career also saw him take to the lower leagues of France with Bordeaux.

He continued: 'I'm not saying I could have had a career like Harry Kane but he is a great example of what kind of career you can have when you live a clean and disciplined life.

Carroll has releases a new book called Owning It where he has opened up about his career in depth

'Don't drink alcohol, eat the right things and spend hours each week in the gym and recover properly.

'Contrast, I wanted to live an everyday life. Go out at weekends with friends and go on holiday with friends in the international break. Go to music festivals and have a few too many drinks and a kebab now and again. Make mistakes without appearing in the papers.

'You could argue trying to live a normal life is incompatible with being a majorly successful sports person. But there is no point spending the rest of my days wishing I had a different mindset. I'm sure I've had more fun than your average player.'

Elsewhere in the book, the former England international also made the bombshell admission that he was sexually assaulted 'a few years ago' by a 'celebrity mate' who was later jailed for three years.

In a deeply candid passage in his new book, Carroll has told how he went through the 'traumatic' assault, which he has been unable to forget after a 'humiliating and horrendous' court case.

Carroll explained that the incident occurred one evening after he had played a game for Newcastle United when a 'celebrity mate' of his former partner invited himself round to watch a boxing match.

The striker wrote that after feeling uncomfortable during their interactions, he went to bed early and remembers feeling 'light-headed' after a 'few drinks'. He then claims he awoke to him sexually assaulting him.

Andy said he threw him out the house and 'smack[ed] him as hard as [he could]' and knocked him unconscious when he tried to re-enter. The star then called the police before sobbing in [his children's] nanny's arms.

Sports.title: The young star about to break out at your PREM club: From the rapid Zimbabwean signed via Instagram and an 18-year-old flying Gloucester wing, to a Scottish farmer, the 23-stone Italian and Exeter's 'physical monster'
Sports.content:
The young star about to break out at your PREM club: From the rapid Zimbabwean signed via Instagram and an 18-year-old flying Gloucester wing, to a Scottish farmer, the 23-stone Italian and Exeter's 'physical monster'

The new PREM Rugby season kicks off on Friday, and with it comes a chance to shine for a host of talented youngsters.

When defending champions Northampton Saints host Newcastle Red Bulls and Harlequins meet Bath tomorrow night, the usual stars from Henry Pollock to Ollie Lawrence will be front and centre. But there will also be a number of new faces who could catch the eye of rugby fans.

Here, Daily Mail Sport’s Nik Simon and Alex Bywater pick 10 potential PREM stars – one from each club – to watch out for this term…

EDWARD SIGAUKE

Age: 22, Club: Harlequins, Position: Wing

The young Zimbabwean could be one of the feelgood stories of the season. He was playing university rugby in Johannesburg last year and signed for Harlequins after the club’s head of recruitment sent him a message on Instagram.

A quick look through his highlights reel showcases the winger’s raw ability to turn defenders inside out with his speed and footwork.

Idolising Cheslin Kolbe and Darcy Graham, the 22-year-old scored with his first touch in pre-season.

The electric Edward Sigauke of Harlequins scores in pre-season against Edinburgh

SIONE VA'ENUKU

Age: 26, Club: Saracens, Position: Centre

Ever since Manu Tuilagi moved over to France in 2023, English rugby has been on the lookout for powerful centres.

Va'enuku played rugby league for the Sydney Roosters before moving to the UK in 2024. He is English qualified and joined Saracens through the club’s partnership programme with Ampthill.

Following the departure of Alex Lozowski to Sale, the hard-running Tongan, 26, should get his fair share of game time in the PREM.

The hard-running Tongan centre Sione Va'enuku should get plenty of game-time for Sarries this season

ALLAN FERRIE

Age: 26, Club: Newcastle Red Bulls, Position: Flanker

Ferrie is primed to make his top-flight debut at the age of 26 after signing a two-year contract at Newcastle over the summer.

He hails from Scottish farming stock and is a late bloomer in the professional game. Ferrie spent a year playing amateur Shute Shield rugby in Australia before signing for Coventry, scoring 14 tries in 24 appearances.

He is a wildcard recruit for the big-spending Red Bulls but he has already impressed with his powerful, athletic ball carrying.

Newcastle's Allan Ferrie hails from Scottish farming stock and is a late bloomer in the professional game

JAMES PATER

Age: 19, Club: Northampton, Position: Full-back

The emergence of Pater at full-back is one of the reasons Northampton allowed George Furbank to join Harlequins.

Phil Dowson has not spoken so glowingly about a young player since Henry Pollock broke through.

Last season, Dowson said of Pater: ‘James always looks like he has time on the ball. He reads space exceptionally well, he’s strong under the high ball, his passing is top quality, he’s not afraid to carry the ball into contact or take defenders on and he finds gaps you don’t think are there.

'He’s brave defensively, too. He’s calm, unfazed and remarkably composed for someone so young. His ceiling is incredibly high.’

The emergence of James Pater (centre) at full-back is one of the reasons Northampton allowed George Furbank to join Harlequins

FINN CARNDUFF

Age: 22, Club: Leicester Tigers, Position: Flanker

There is a rich history of abrasive forwards coming through the Tigers academy and Carnduff could be the next cab off the rank.

He captained England Under 20s to their World Cup triumph in 2024 but his development has been stalled by injuries.

The 22-year-old is a lineout-jumping flanker who could step up as Leicester’s pack adapts to life without George Martin and Hanro Liebenberg.

Leicester's Finn Carnduff scores against Quins in the PREM Rugby Cup this month. He captained England Under 20s to their World Cup triumph in 2024

ENOCH OPOKU-GYAMFI

Age: 20, Club: Bath, Position: Lock/No 8

This time last year another young Italian in Edoardo Todaro emerged from nowhere to star on the wing for Northampton. Opoku-Gyamfi, 20, is another Azzurri man who could do likewise.

Despite still being a fringe player for his club, Opoku-Gyamfi has already worn the blue shirt of his country at senior Test level.

A sports performance student, he also helped the University of Bath to silverware last season but is set for bigger things now.

Bath’s pack is ageing so head of rugby Johann van Graan needs to bring through fresh blood. At more than 23 stone and 6ft 5in, you can't miss Opoku-Gyamfi!

At more than 23 stone and 6ft 5in, Bath's Enoch Opoku-Gyamfi is hard to miss!

ZACK WIMBUSH

Age: 22, Club: Exeter Chiefs, Position: Centre

At 22, Wimbush has been around the Exeter set-up for a few years now without ever really cutting the mustard.

When he was loaned to spend time with Cornish Pirates, it looked like his time as a Chief might be up. But Rob Baxter has seemingly kept the faith and the way Wimbush set up a try for Immanuel Feyi-Waboso in a pre-season clash with Cardiff showed exactly what he is about.

Wimbush has pace and power. He’s a monster physically.

With Australian superstar Len Ikitau now departed, Exeter need someone to step up in midfield and Wimbush could be that man.

Zack Wimbush has pace and power and is a monster physically. This could be his time

DOM HANSON

Age: 20, Club: Sale Sharks, Position: Scrum-half

Alex Sanderson’s Sharks have signed a plethora of exceptional new talent, mainly up front in the likes of Courtney Lawes, Nicky Smith and Tomas Francis. Centre Joe Marchant is a big arrival, too.

Highly-rated former Chiefs and New Zealand scrum-half Xavier Roe is likely to start at No 9, but in that position Hanson, 20, could well emerge as a surprise package.

He’s been tipped by experienced Sale and England playmaker George Ford to have a big season and Ford is a man who knows his stuff.

Hanson suits a fast-paced game and there might be pressure on Sanderson to deliver exactly that after a turgid, underwhelming campaign last time out.

Dom Hanson could emerge as a surprise package at No9 for Sale this season

JUNIOR DENNY

Age: 18, Club: Gloucester, Position: Wing

The Cherry and Whites have recruited well with the likes of Jac Morgan, Dewi Lake and Jean Kleyn.

But there is real excitement at Kingsholm about the development of 18-year-old wing Denny. He was a stand-out performer for Gloucester at age-grade level last season and in the build-up to the new PREM season, he scored a try on his PREM Cup debut against Bristol.

Anyone who was at that game went home raving about his performance and so too did George Skivington. ‘

Junior did really well,’ said the Gloucester boss. ‘He’s a real one for the future. We’ve got a lot of hope for him. He’s a really good lad, really humble, and wants to work hard and make an impact.’

There is real excitement at Kingsholm about the development of 18-year-old wing Junior Denny

AIDAN BOSHOFF

Age: 20, Club: Bristol Bears, Position: Wing

If it hadn’t been for injury, it is likely Boshoff would have been selected for senior Wales involvement last season by their head coach Steve Tandy.

Louis Rees-Zammit is the Welsh winger at Bristol who gets all the headlines. But Boshoff, 20, is a coming force in the same position.

The mullet-haired Aidan Boshoff, 20, plays on the wing for Bristol and is a coming force

Boshoff got a taste of the PREM last term after impressing for Wales Under 20s and will only get better for that experience.

He has an interesting background, too, having spent much of his childhood in Cape Town and later attending the prestigious Clifton College.

He's hard to miss with his mullet haircut!

Sports.title: Andy Carroll reveals he was sexually assaulted in a 'traumatic' attack by a 'celebrity mate' who was later jailed for three years after 'humiliating and horrendous' court case
Sports.content:
Andy Carroll reveals he was sexually assaulted in a 'traumatic' attack by a 'celebrity mate' who was later jailed for three years after 'humiliating and horrendous' court case

Andy Carroll was sexually assaulted by a 'celebrity mate' who was later jailed for three years after a 'humiliating and horrendous' court case, the former England footballer has revealed.

In a deeply candid passage in his new book, Owning It, the striker, 37, said he went through the 'traumatic' assault a few years ago, and only decided to detail the incident 'at the last minute' following lengthy discussions with his publisher.

Andy, who played for England from 2010 to 2012, wrote: 'Other things I'd quite like to forget but can't, something happened to me a few years ago that was so traumatic I only decided to include it in this book at the very last minute.'

'I was sexually assaulted, there I said it. Scary to even think about and only a few people knew about it before now.'

The attacker was found guilty of sexual offences and sentenced to three years in prison.

Andy explained he was assaulted the evening after a Newcastle United game when a 'celebrity mate' of his former partner invited himself round to watch a boxing match.

Andy Carroll has revealed he was sexually assaulted in a 'traumatic' attack by a 'celebrity mate' who was later jailed for three years after 'humiliating and horrendous' court case

Andy, who played for England between 2010-2012, said he only decided to detail the incident 'at the last minute' following lengthy discussions with his publisher

Describing their relationship, he wrote: 'He was always asking me and my ex to go out with him and even buys me clothes. He is divorced with kids but I can't shift the feeling he likes me more than a platonic way.

'Whenever I bump into him at parties he is always with young boys.'

He continued: 'I was playing down south somewhere and on my way home this guy texts to ask what I am up to.

'When he texts again to ask if he can come round to watch the boxing with me, my partner tells me to stop pieing him off [putting him off].

'He takes over the kitchen, mixing drinks. I start to feel lightheaded and think has he slipped me something. "Right, time for bed," I say to him, "I'll order you a taxi."

'"Oh no," he says, "I'll stay in the spare room."

He then claims he awoke to the friend sexually assaulting him.

'I sleep naked and when I wake up this guy is under the duvet trying to give me a blowjob.'

Andy went on to 'smack' him as he ordered him out the house. 'I smack him as hard as I can and he hits the deck,' he writes.

'I grab hold of his feet and drag him out on the driveway. I go back inside, lock the door and call the police and the nanny. And then it suddenly occurs to me, what if I killed him?

'He regains consciousness just as the police turn up and immediately starts telling the policed I hit him for no reason. As it is the police arrest him and I have to go to the station as well.'

The attacker was later found guilty of sexual offences and sentenced to three years in prison. He was placed on the Sex Offender Register and banned from entering the village where Andy lived.

Andy described the court case as 'humiliating and embarrassing and absolutely horrendous', while the attacker denied the allegations.

'The case dragged on for two years. Nobody else knew about it other than my partner and her family and they gave me no support whatsoever.

'The police called me to say he had been found guilty and I started uncontrollably crying.'

He added: 'What happened to me affected every facet of my life. I’d think about it every day, making it difficult to focus on anything else, including football…The trauma of what happened to me hasn’t gone away.'

After speaking with girlfriend Lou Teasdale, 42, he decided opening up about being assaulted would be 'worth it' if it helped others.

'Me and Lou spent a lot of time discussing whether to mention it in this book or not. I avoided my publisher for so long that they probably suspected I got cold feet.

'Scary to talk about but it's made the person I am today as much as any of the good stuff. And if me talking about it helps just one person then good it will have been worth it.

Andy had reportedly vowed to cut down on alcohol in a bid to save his relationship with Lou Teasdale (pictured), as he confirmed the pair were trying 'to work through their difficulties'

The ex-Newcastle and Liverpool striker, who now plays for National League South club Dagenham & Redbridge and serves as assistant manager, goes on to talk about his relationship with Lou.

The on-and-off couple, who appear to currently be on, have broken up many times due to alcohol, according to sources.

Andy had reportedly vowed to cut down on alcohol in a bid to save his relationship with Lou, as he confirmed the pair were trying 'to work through their difficulties'.

'Lou couldn't believe how normal I was when she first met me,' he wrote.

'I'm not saying I could have had a career like Harry Kane but he is a great example of what kind of career you can have when you live a clean and disciplined life.

'Don't drink alcohol, eat the right things and spend hours each week in the gym and recover properly.

'Contrast, I wanted to live an everyday life. Go out at weekends with friends and go on holiday with friends in the international break.

'Go to music festivals and have a few too many drinks and a kebab now and again. Make mistakes without appearing in the papers.

'You could argue trying to live a normal life is incompatible with being a majorly successful sports person.

'But there is no point spending the rest of my days wishing I had a different mindset. I'm sure I've had more fun than your average player.'

'I tell young players, if you want to party all the time, go for it. But you won't be as successful in football as you could be but you're an adult, it's up to you.'

He added: 'Strip clubs are very much part of football culture and only when I grew up did I realise how wrong it was to sit around ogling over naked women.

'It's incredibly disrespectful and not who I am. But as a young teenager in Belarus I was excited as anyone.'

Reflecting on how his huge salary rise affected his behaviour, he added: 'Before my weekly wage jumped to £2,500 a week, I was quite sensible.

'But soon enough I was spending time in bars, strip joints and casinos. If everyone wanted a tray of shots, I'd buy a tray of shots.

'And while alcohol didn't turn me into some violent loon, a well known footballer spending time in local establishments was bound to attract trouble.'

The ex-Premier League footballer recently pleaded not guilty to breaching a non-molestation order after being accused of repeatedly calling his reality TV star ex-wife Billi Mucklow.

Andy has formally entered a plea of not guilty to the charge and is due to stand trial next January.

Andy and TOWIE star Billi, 37, were together for 11 years but confirmed their split in September 2024 after secretly separating earlier in the year.

Billi and Andy got engaged in 2014 before marrying in 2022 and share three children. Billi also cares for Andy's two other children who he had from a previous relationship.

Sports.title: The making of Joe Root: From watching Sachin Tendulkar's India as a teenager at Headingley to quitting Nottingham Forest's academy - how Yorkshire's favourite son became the 'grandfather' of the England team
Sports.content:
The making of Joe Root: From watching Sachin Tendulkar's India as a teenager at Headingley to quitting Nottingham Forest's academy - how Yorkshire's favourite son became the 'grandfather' of the England team

Joe Root’s second tenure as England Test captain began in the most fitting surroundings at Headingley last month - the home of Yorkshire’s favourite son. By his own admission, Root could not have chosen a more appropriate venue for his return as captain.

‘Absolutely no pressure at all,’ Root told Daily Mail Sport at Headingley when England turned to him as a quick fix for a leadership crisis, off-field scandals and the underperformance of a side that should, at the very least, have contested one World Test Championship final.

Wearing the famous No66 jersey in his 66th Test as captain, Root made 66 against Pakistan and, with his routine fifty at Headingley, he drew level with Sachin Tendulkar on a record 68 half-centuries.

Root shattered Tendulkar’s record in the third Test against Pakistan and now returns to Leeds for the second ODI against Sri Lanka on Thursday.

His first trip to Headingley came in 2002, when the Sheffield-born teenager watched the third Test against India with his young cricketing team-mates. It was the same Test in which Yorkshire’s first overseas signing returned as the Master Blaster, scoring a memorable 193.

‘India won the toss and batted first, and I watched one wicket all day,’ said Root, chuckling. ‘It was Rahul Dravid (148) and Sourav Ganguly (128) who got a boatload of runs, and that’s one where Sachin got, I don’t know how much.

Joe Root’s second tenure as England Test captain began in the most fitting surroundings at Headingley last month (above) - the home of Yorkshire’s favourite son

Root's first trip to Headingley came in 2002, when the Sheffield-born teenager watched Sachin Tendulkar blast 193 for India

‘It was a tough toil for the England bowlers, but that was my first experience of coming here with a local cricket club. It was with Rotherham Town, actually. And they took the Under 11s out to watch the game, and it was a great experience.’

Ten years later, a 21-year-old Root made his Test debut against an India side still built around Tendulkar. On Tuesday, Root eclipsed Tendulkar when he completed 23,000 international runs during the 1st ODI against Sri Lanka at Durham.

The Yorkshire batter unlocked the milestone in his 521st international innings, while Tendulkar took 522 innings to achieve the same feat in his decorated career. Root is also the first Englishman to pass 23,000 runs in international cricket.

From 12 to 21, Root was forged in Yorkshire, where former county batting coach Kevin Sharp proved instrumental in the making of England’s greatest batter from Sheffield.

‘Huge role (Sharp played),’ said Root. ‘He got hold of me when I was about 12 years old until 21, and very impressionable years of your playing career and of your life in general and having good people, good mentors, is so important.

‘He was excellent for me. Very good technical coach, but also had a really good way in understanding of me as a person. He would be very patient at times. He understood the challenges that I was going to face. I was always very small for my age, and him being very aware of that, and at some point I grew up, my body would catch up with where I wanted to be as a player.

‘I can't thank him enough for the input that he had just managing me as, you know, not getting too emotional, understanding what was gonna be really important further down the line, just looking ahead at how can we get ahead of other players at a young age so that when physically you catch up with everyone else, you're in a really good position.’

Raised by a cricket-loving family and coming from a county where leadership is earned, not given, Root has always led by example - making Sharp prouder than ever. When Ben Stokes dropped the retirement bombshell, Root was happy to call himself the ‘grandfather’ of the England side.

Root said that when he first learned of Brydon Carse's (right) recent nightclub incident, his main concern for the under-fire player was personal

With England hit by another nightclub scandal in the build-up to the second Test against Pakistan, Root spoke to pace bowler Brydon Carse, who was dropped for the Lord’s decider.

Root said that when he first learned of the incident, his main concern for the under-fire Carse was personal. Like his mentor Sharp, who coached the likes of Michael Vaughan and Jonny Bairstow at Yorkshire, Root has become England’s elder statesman, looking after the players on and off the field.

‘I love him,’ he says of Sharp. ‘He's mad. But, you know, he's just a great man who did a lot, a lot for a number of players throughout that era, if you like. He is someone who was very impressionable on me.’

At Lord’s, Root became the highest run scorer on home soil during England’s comfortable 194-run win over Pakistan. The England captain holds the record for smashing the most runs and centuries at the famous venue.

Lord’s is also home to one of Root’s favourite personal memories, shared with his grandfather Don (known as ‘Sir Don’ to those around him), named after the great Don Bradman.

Root’s grandad watched the 1948 Bramall Lane match between the Australians and Yorkshire in which Bradman played a stroke-filled knock of 54.

‘One thing that I'll always hold very dear to me was when I felt the moment at Lord's, where we were holding the World Cup trophy in 2019 together. Just having a moment to reminisce about what it looked like to get to that point from there - from being a kid and him being instrumental in that, something I'm very fond of,’ Root said.

Root had a brief spell at Nottingham Forest’s academy at 11, but he quit because football was getting in the way of batting nets. Root polished his batting with Sharp at Yorkshire, but it was his grandfather who played a quieter, and perhaps most formative, role for the proud product of Sheffield Collegiate.

Root polished his batting with Sharp at Yorkshire, but it was his grandfather who played a quieter, and perhaps most formative, role for the proud product of Sheffield Collegiate

‘My local cricket club, Sheffield Collegiate, didn't have an Under 11 team when I was growing up, so he was involved with Rotherham Town, and that's where I played my Under 11s cricket. I started at that age group and played Under 13s, Under 15s, and Under 17s for Sheffield Collegiate and Rotherham Town.

‘Many great Monday nights there at Clifton Lane. Unfortunately, the club's no longer around, but that was very special, going and playing in a different team, different squad of players and just learning the game in a different setting.’

Don captained the Rotherham side during his playing days, and his father George also came from the same town. ‘I remember going up and down the country playing for Yorkshire as my parents were both working, so Don would take me to the games,’ he said.

‘And, you know, we often stopped to try to find a decent fish and chip shop, everywhere in the world. He would ferry me here, there and everywhere, and I remember listening to Frank Sinatra and all sorts of different things over the years, up and down Yorkshire and away games and stuff,’ Root added.

Yes, Root repaid his grandfather in some style. The Frank Sinatra singalongs stayed, but the destinations changed, as he took Don to exotic cricket grounds and made him a globetrotter.

‘It's been nice, throughout my professional career, to be able to take him around as well and give him opportunities to watch some brilliant Test cricket and experience different things in life.’

Only Tendulkar (200) and James Anderson (188) have played more Tests than Root (169). It was at Headingley, ahead of a busy home summer this year, that the third-most capped player set himself a simple goal on his Yorkshire return: win all six home Test matches for England.

Root was chasing multiple records while gearing up for a busy English summer. However, he insisted he is ‘not one for the numbers’. A lot has changed since then. Root has succeeded the retired Stokes as captain, and England have replaced Brendon McCullum with Stephen Fleming as head coach. After a massive win by an innings and 103 runs in Leeds, Root and Co. completed the 3-0 whitewash of Pakistan at Edgbaston.

When asked about his favourite memory at Headingley, for Root, there was only one answer: ‘As a player in 2019, Stokesey winning that Test match (against Australia)'

Now the 35-year-old will not be able to return to Headingley for Test action until 2029, with his home ground overlooked for next year’s Ashes. ‘Hopefully we can create some more special memories and moments at this brilliant ground. It's one that's steeped in amazing Test matches, brilliant things and rich history. I think it produces the best Test match cricket, the pitch, the outfield, and it's a very knowledgeable crowd,’ he said.

However, Root will receive a hero's welcome again against Sri Lanka on Thursday. The famous ‘Roooooot’ chant always rings out loud whenever the Sheffield-born gets a boundary in Leeds.

‘The Yorkshire supporters, they love their game; they understand it,’ he says. ‘They're very passionate about it. And they let you know what they think as well. So, for those reasons combined, I think it makes for brilliant Test match cricket, and it's always a joy when it's your home ground to get the chance to represent England here.’

When asked about his favourite memory at Headingley, for Root, there was only one answer.

‘As a player in 2019, Stokesey winning that Test match (against Australia), just being there, having the chance to be out there in the middle, but also sitting in that dressing room watching that all unfold, was pretty magical. And the atmosphere that the crowd created that day was really special.’

Sports.title: Why have the Republic of Ireland's two games against Israel become so controversial?
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland will face Israel in a men’s football fixture for the first time since 2005 in this international break, but there have been calls for the two UEFA Nations League games not to be played at all.

Both meetings - the first played in Debrecen, Hungary on Sunday and the second scheduled for the Serbian town of Backa Topola on October 4 - have been overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

Uncertainty over the games going ahead might have subsided, but the tensions between the two nations have not.

Heimir Hallgrimsson, the Republic of Ireland head coach, has been accused of "stupidity and hypocrisy" by the Israel Football Association after last week suggesting his team would be "playing against genocide" when facing Israel, while his players are not ruling out their own protests ahead of the games.

The Athletic examines the key issues ahead of the first meeting this weekend.

Why have these games caused controversy?

This has been a contentious issue rolling down the tracks ever since the 2026-27 Nations League draw was made in February. Group B3 saw the Republic of Ireland pitted against Kosovo, their opening opponents this evening, and Austria, but it was the prospect of facing Israel which created immediate unease.

The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) had overwhelmingly approved a motion that called on UEFA to ban Israel from its competitions just four months earlier due to violations of the governing body's statutes, including "the organisation of clubs in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank without the consent of the Palestinian Football Association".

The Nations League draw duly reignited the row. Irish politicians, including the FAI member Joanna Byrne, were quick to call for a boycott of the Israel games in the following days and protests ensued when Qatar visited Dublin's Aviva Stadium for a friendly in May. Tennis balls featuring the Palestine flag were thrown on the pitch by supporters, twice causing brief interruptions.

Image: Tennis balls with a Palestinian flag on were thrown onto the pitch in Dublin during protests in May 2026

The FAI had already confirmed its plans to go ahead with the Israel games by then, and that decision was formally approved at an EGM in July.

That saw only 32 votes in favour of a boycott, with 75 members voting for the games to be played. The FAI had argued that boycotting games would cause "significant and lasting harm to Irish football" due to the likely disciplinary sanctions from UEFA.

A measure of the opposition to the Republic of Ireland facing Israel also came with the acceptance that the "home" fixture would not be played in Dublin. The FAI cited "operational challenges (that) could impact the delivery of the game on home soil" and the decision was eventually made in late June, with the support of UEFA, to move the game to Backa Topola, a small town in northern Serbia, on Sunday week.

No tickets for the game will be made available to Ireland fans.

The FAI has subsequently revealed that a request to see the two nations kept apart in future competition draws has been rejected by UEFA.

"The answer I got was very clear," FAI chief executive David Courell told reporters on September 18. "That would not be possible because Ireland and Israel have never been in direct conflict."

What is the political backdrop?

The Republic of Ireland has consistently outlined its backing for the Palestinian people since the conflict with Israel began almost three years ago, joining Norway and Spain when officially recognising a Palestinian state in 2024. Taoiseach Micheal Martin has also made his stance clear, accusing Israel of committing "genocide" last year in comments reported by the Irish Mirror.

The conflict in Gaza began after Israel responded to attacks by Hamas militants on October 7, 2023, which saw around 1,200 people, mostly civilians, killed in Israel and 250 taken hostage. The war has subsequently seen 73,000 people killed, according to figures from the Gaza Health Ministry and used by the UN.

Strained relations between the Republic of Ireland and Israel have continued this year. Two Israeli government ministers were the subject of travel bans in June, while foreign minister Helen McEntee also confirmed Ireland's intent to limit goods trading with settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank this summer.

Image: Taoiseach Micheal Martin

A meeting between the Republic of Ireland and Israel on a football field this weekend has subsequently taken on enormous significance against such a backdrop.

There are similarities in Ireland's political stance with those of Norway, who faced similar calls for a boycott when Israel travelled to Oslo last October. The Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) had aligned itself with its government and said in a statement leading up to Israel's visit that the "tragic humanitarian suffering in Gaza" had made the fixture challenging.

That World Cup qualifier, won 5-0 by Norway, saw thousands take part in a protest march to the stadium.

Who has opposed the games taking place?

Moving a home game 1,500 miles away has not stopped the objections building ahead of the two teams meeting on Sunday. More than 160 Irish sportspeople signed an open letter asking their national team to boycott the Israel games under the banner of the Irish Sport for Palestine Group, who have also run the "Stop the Game" campaign that protested outside of the Irish team hotel in Dublin on Monday.

"This is a significant moment and with this moment you have an opportunity to do the right thing," the letter said.

Kevin Kilbane, the former Republic of Ireland international who holds 110 caps, has also been unequivocal in his views. "The Republic of Ireland should not be playing Israel… not while Israeli forces are committing genocide," he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.">he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.

Amnesty International also issued a fresh statement on Tuesday that said UEFA risked letting football "rubber-stamp apartheid" by allowing Israel's continued participation in its club and international competitions. A spokesperson for the Israeli FA responded to that by saying: "Their obsession with the idea of Israel as a state is incurable, as is their need of attention."

The Irish media, meanwhile, has faced its own dilemmas in the coverage of the Israel games. RTE, the public broadcaster behind Ireland's boycott of the Eurovision Song Contest in the last two years due to Israel's continued involvement, has stripped back its coverage. Contractual obligations will be met, RTE confirmed in a statement, but there would be no studio coverage or commentators sent to either fixture.

Image: Kevin Kilbane, former Ireland international, has spoken out

What have the key stakeholders said ahead of this weekend?

Relations between the two nations have grown increasingly hostile in the last week. Hallgrimsson appeared in front of the media to announce his squad for the upcoming friendlies and made pointed remarks when asked how his players would focus on football.

"We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," the former Iceland head coach told reporters. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."

The reaction to those words, in a social media post from the Israel FA account, raised temperatures further still. "We have contributed to the world and humanity in countless fields, earning an impressive number of Nobel Prizes along the way," it read. "Unfortunately, we have not yet found a cure for stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy displayed by @IrelandFootball team coach. We're not playing with ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity, we're playing against the coach who embodies them."

Martin, who was among the world leaders attending the UN General Assembly in New York, was then drawn back into debate on Tuesday. "I think those are unacceptable remarks. They should be withdrawn. Israel can't keep denying what the world knows and what the world understands."

The FAI has not addressed Hallgrimsson's comments publicly, but the Republic of Ireland's head coach said on Wednesday that he had been "grateful for the support" he had received.

"Maybe from a leadership point of view, it was not clever from me to take the attention (away) like this. It's a tricky time for us," Hallgrimsson said in his pre-match press conference ahead of facing Kosovo.

The same extends to his players, too. Dara O'Shea, the Ipswich Town defender, said, according to the BBC, that he and the rest of the players would come together on Friday to "openly discuss" the prospect of a protest ahead of the first Israel game in Debrecen on Sunday.

Image: Dara O’Shea, left, and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson during Wednesday’s press conference

Why are the games being played in Hungary and Serbia?

Hungary has acted as an adopted home for Israel since the start of the conflict. They first played there in November 2023, when resuming their attempts to qualify for Euro 2024 when hosting Switzerland at the Pancho Arena in Felcsut, a small village 26 miles west of Budapest.

Victor Orban, who lost his position as Hungary's prime minister this year, had been a long-standing ally of Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and claimed Hungary to be the "safest country in Europe" for Jews.

The World Cup 2026 qualifiers against Estonia, Norway and Italy were all held in Debrecen, which has also previously hosted European games for Israeli sides Maccabi Haifa and Maccabi Tel Aviv.

The Republic of Ireland's choice of Backa Topola, Serbia, is less clear. Dublin ceased to become an option, even behind closed doors, as the opposition to Israel visiting became clear, which left limited options for relocation.

It needed to be a nation sympathetic to Israel to avoid further protests and Serbia, neighbouring Hungary to the south, has forged strong diplomatic relations. According to the Associated Press, Serbia's president Aleksandar Vucic inaugurated an assembly factory for Israel-made drones last week, with plans for three more production sites.

A switch to Serbia was reliant on UEFA approval and it will be Backa Topola's home of the TSC Arena where this story ends on October 4.
