But once a judgment exists, current officials have a responsibility to explain what actions were taken to address it. That is where Azango’s role becomes relevant. As NOCAL’s Vice President for Finance and Investment, he occupies a senior position within the corporation’s financial management structure.

His explanation that the Ministry of Finance should take responsibility raises another concern about what formal steps did NOCAL took to secure payment from the Government, and when those steps were taken.

The 25-Percent Question

Azango says the court required 25 percent of the debt to be paid. But the September 23 closure order supplied to FrontPageAfrica does not state the exact monetary amount represented by that 25 percent. Nor does the document itself establish whether the payment was made.

That leaves several questions unanswered, as to what exact amount of twenty-five per cent was actually made and if the US$764,762 award was the amount against which the 25 percent was calculated?

A US$764,762 Case Now Threatens Government Operations

An employment or severance dispute that reportedly began at approximately US$170,000 in combined claims has evolved into a court award of US$764,762 and is now threatening the physical operations of two government institutions.

The Commercial Court’s action means that a dispute originating from NOCAL’s troubled 2015 period is now confronting the Boakai administration more than a decade later. And Azango, who was not part of the NOCAL leadership involved in the original dispute, is now one of the officials being called upon to explain how the corporation responded to the judgment.

The Bigger Accountability Issue

The case exposes a recurring problem in Liberia’s public sectorororor, where old liabilities can survive changes in government, management and policy, but eventually return with financial and legal consequences.

The present controversy is therefore not simply about Azango, it is about how NOCAL and the Government of Liberia manage inherited liabilities and whether court judgments against public corporations are promptly incorporated into government financial planning.

For now, the Commercial Court has taken the strongest possible step. NOCAL have been ordered closed, Azango has been held in contempt, a 25-percent payment has reportedly been demanded and a debt dispute that began roughly a decade ago, reportedly at approximately US$85,000 for each of two former NOCAL executives, has grown into a reported US$764,762 court award.

Whether Liberia’s public financial system will resolve the liability, or whether the old NOCAL dispute will continue generating new costs, new contempt proceedings and new answers for the country’s debts, remains a concern.

World.title: Karishma Pelham-Raad Mentorship Program Targets New Generation of Liberian Leaders
World.content:
PAYNESVILLE, Liberia — For 500 young Liberians gathered at the Paynesville City Hall, Wednesday was more than the launch of another youth program.

By Patience M. Jones

It was presented as the beginning of a journey one that organizers hope will help young people discover their purpose, build confidence, develop leadership skills and create pathways toward careers in diplomacy, entrepreneurship, public service and other professions.

The occasion marked the launch of the first cohort of the Karishma Pelham-Raad Mentorship Program, a two-day initiative held under the theme “Empowering Minds, Inspiring Future.”

The program brought together young people from different academic and professional backgrounds, alongside mentors, government officials, professionals and other guests.

For many of the young women and men in the room, the presence and story of the program’s founder, Karishma Pelham-Raad, appeared to offer a practical example of what mentorship can mean.

Pelham-Raad, a diplomat and public servant, told participants that the initiative was born from her own experiences of hardship, uncertainty and the people who helped her along the way.

“I came here as a woman who has lived through adversity,” she said, reflecting on her journey.

“I know what it means to dream while life is difficult. I know what it means to experience loss, and still have the strength to wake up the next morning and continue.”

She said her journey from telecommunications and technology into international relations, diplomacy, public service and international development taught her the importance of having people who believe in others.

“People believe in me. People open doors. People share knowledge. People correct me. People encourage me,” Pelham-Raad said.

“And sometimes someone simply says, ‘Keep going, Karishma. Do not stop.’ These two words can change your life.”

That experience, she said, inspired the creation of the mentorship program.

‘I Am Not Looking for Followers’

Pelham-Raad said the program is not designed to create followers but to prepare young people for leadership.

“Mentorship is not about creating followers. I am not looking for followers. I am looking to build leaders,” she said.

She challenged participants to use the two-day program to learn, ask questions, build relationships and develop themselves.

The program’s objectives include personal development, leadership development, career development, mentorship and networking.

Pelham-Raad said young people need more than encouragement to succeed.

“Telling young people to work hard is not enough,” she said. “We must also give them tools, information, network and exposure.”

She urged the participants to develop confidence while maintaining character, emphasizing that leadership should be rooted in integrity, accountability and service.

“Leadership is not about having a title,” she said. “Leadership begins with how you treat people when no one is watching.”

Her message also focused on resilience.

She told participants that rejection, disappointment and failure are part of life, but should not become definitions of who they are.

“When you fail, and you will fail sometimes, do not allow failure to convince you that you are a failure,” she said. “Failure is just an event. It is not your identity.”

Findley: ‘Set Your Goal and Work Towards It’

Delivering the keynote address, Senator Gbehzohngar Milton Findley of Grand Bassa County drew from his own life experiences to encourage the young participants to pursue their ambitions regardless of their circumstances.

Findley recalled deciding at an early age that he wanted to become a senator.

He said that ambition remained with him through school, college and his time abroad, even though his parents wanted him to pursue engineering.

“I was good in physics, mathematics and chemistry,” he recalled. “My parents decided, ‘You’re going to be the engineer in the family.’ But I always wanted to be what? A senator.”

He eventually earned an engineering degree and later pursued graduate studies, while his professional journey took him through business and public service before he entered the Liberian Senate.

His story, he said, was intended to demonstrate that young people should have goals but must also remain open to opportunities and lessons along the way.

“Set a goal, work towards it, and you will be able to achieve your goals,” Findley told the participants.

He urged them not to allow family expectations or societal pressure to dictate their careers.

“Don’t be pressured to become a doctor. Don’t be pressured to become a lawyer,” he said.

Findley said his own experience of following his parents’ wishes to become an engineer taught him that being successful in a profession is different from being passionate about it.

“There’s nothing wrong with being a bus driver,” he said. “There’s nothing wrong with being a doctor. Whatever goal you set for yourself, make sure that you do it well.”

“Be passionate about it,” he added.

From a Young Assistant to a Public Servant

One of Findley’s stories focused on a young man he encountered after becoming a senator.

He recalled meeting a young student who had performed well academically but had limited his own ambitions because of his circumstances.

The young man initially told Findley that he wanted to become a nurse’s assistant.

Findley encouraged him to aim higher and apply to universities.

According to Findley, the young man subsequently passed entrance examinations at several universities and pursued his education.

Findley later described how the young man became a development superintendent and eventually moved into government service.

The senator said the young man demonstrated an important lesson when he stopped a project he believed was not being properly implemented, despite the fact that Findley had helped him with his education and career.

“That was the right thing to do,” Findley said, stressing that mentorship should not mean creating people who simply follow their mentors.

“It is your duty and responsibility to correct it,” he added.

For Findley, the story demonstrated the kind of independence and integrity that young people should develop.

‘Do Not Be Afraid to Ask for Help’

Findley encouraged the participants to use the mentorship program to identify people who can guide them toward their goals.

“Do not be afraid to ask for help,” he said. “Do not be afraid to ask questions that you need answers.”

He also urged young people to prepare themselves for emerging opportunities, particularly in technology and artificial intelligence.

“We have to be prepared for that,” he said, noting the growing importance of artificial intelligence and the need for young Liberians to develop skills that can enable them to compete in a changing global environment.

Macdonald M. Metzger, Deputy Chief of Staff for Administration in the Office of the Vice President, who delivered a message on behalf of the Vice President, also encouraged the young people to take the mentorship experience seriously.

He challenged participants to build relationships beyond names and titles.

“When you sit with people, get to know them beyond their titles,” Metzger said. “See what you guys have in common and how you can leverage that for the rest of your life.”

Drawing from his own experience growing up during Liberia’s civil war, Metzger recalled participating in youth development and skills-training programs while living in a displaced camp.

He said those early experiences, and the people he met throughout his journey, contributed to shaping his career.

He reminded the participants that mentors can provide direction, but the responsibility for pursuing their goals ultimately rests with them.

“A mentor can help you find a path, but you yourself must be willing to walk it,” he said.

‘Reach Back’

As the two-day program gets underway, Pelham-Raad challenged the participants to think beyond their individual success.

She urged them to remember others when they eventually achieve their goals.

“When you become a professional, reach back,” she said. “When you become an entrepreneur, create opportunities. When you become a leader, develop other people.”

Her vision, she said, is for young people who benefit from the program today to eventually become mentors themselves.

She imagined a young woman entering the program uncertain about her future, becoming an engineer five years later, leading a company years after that, and eventually meeting another young girl who reminds her of herself.

“And she says, ‘Let me help you,’” Pelham-Raad said.

“That is how a woman grows. One person, one opportunity, one conversation. One open door, one lifetime at a time.”

For the 500 young participants gathered at Paynesville City Hall, the challenge now extends beyond listening to inspirational speeches.

The program calls on them to ask questions, build relationships, acquire skills, discover their purpose and begin walking the paths they envision for themselves.

As Findley put it: “Set your goal. Set your future. And anything you want to do within that bound is achievable.”

World.title: Zambia surpasses 95-95-95 HIV targets
World.content:
Vice President, Mutale Nalumango says Zambia has surpassed its 95-95-95 HIV treatment and viral suppression target, achieving 98-98-97.

This means that 98 percent of all people living with HIV in the country know their status, 98 percent of those diagnosed receive sustained Antiretroviral Therapy (Art) and 97 percent of people on treatment have achieved viral load suppression.

Mrs Nalumango has attributed the achievement to Zambia’s leadership and investment in the health sector as well as support from the United States of America government through its Peace Corps and other initiatives.

The Vice President said this in Lusaka last evening in a speech read for her by Permanent Secretary for Resettlement Division, Mavis Nkomeshya, during the launch of a documentary to mark 30 years of Peace Corps in Zambia.

“Through the Peace Corps, PEPFAR, and Zambia’s own leadership, the country has surpassed global HIV targets, achieving 98-98-97 among the general population. These achievements represent transformed lives and families preserved. We shall not forget those who stood with us in this fight,” Mrs Nalumango stressed.

She thanked Peace Corps volunteers for their contributions across health, education, agriculture, and community development, highlighting their impact in public health, especially Zambia’s fight against HIV.

The Vice President further reaffirmed Zambia’s commitment to sustaining the gains in HIV treatment and welcomed continued collaboration with partners.

Speaking at the same event, US Embassy in Zambia Charge d’Affaires, Mich Coker noted that over 1.3 million lives have been saved through joint efforts between the Zambian government and the US government under the Peace Corps and other programmes.

Mr Coker added that Zambia’s average life expectancy has also been increased by about 20 years, following the continued collaborative efforts.

“This achievement belongs first and foremost to Zambia, to its national leadership, to its health professionals, to community health workers, to civil society organizations, to families and to people living with HIV,” he stressed.

Mr Coker welcomed the ongoing dialogue between the Peace Corps and the Ministries of Health, Education, and Green Economy and Environment, stressing that such engagement will strengthen relationships and guide the next chapter of collaboration.

Meanwhile, Peace Corps Zambia Country Director, Natalie Gill-Mensah, disclosed that 2,666 volunteers had served under Peace Corps in Zambia since it started in the year 1994.

World.title: Govt tips farmers to grow early maturing crops
World.content:
Government has advised farmers in areas expected to receive reduced rainfall in the country to grow early maturing and drought-resistant crops.

Zambia Meteorology Department Principal Meteorologist Rodgers Manjomba says farmers should select crop varieties according to the expected rainfall patterns in their respective areas.

Mr Manjomba says farmers in the central parts of the country could consider growing medium-maturing crops, while those in the northern parts, where normal to above-normal rainfall is expected, have a wider choice of crop varieties.

He says farmers in areas with adequate rainfall can grow late-maturing crops because the rains are expected to sustain the crops through the growing season.

Mr Manjomba was speaking in an interview with the media in Lusaka today.

He revealed that the Ministry of Green Economy and Environment, working with the Ministry of Agriculture, has trained 100 Agricultural Camp Extension Officers to help farmers interpret weather information, package and disseminate meteorological information directly to farmers and also help them to adopt appropriate best farming practices.

Mr Manjomba said the initiative is aimed at moving beyond simply providing weather forecasts to explaining the likely impact of weather conditions on crops.

He said the two ministries are working with experts to produce agro-meteorological bulletins which combine weather forecasts with agricultural advice to help farmers make informed decisions.

He said the initiative will help farmers prepare for climate-related shocks and make informed decisions instead of relying solely on rain-fed agriculture.

Mr Majomba further disclosed that more than 70 percent of Zambia’s farming community depends on rain-fed agriculture, making farmers particularly vulnerable to the effects of climate change.

Mr Manjomba stressed that providing farmers with timely and appropriate climate information will help them better prepare for changing weather patterns and improve their resilience resulting from climate change and the forthcoming El Nino catastrophe.

World.title: Chongwe Council welcomes newly nominated Councilors
World.content:
Chongwe Municipal Council has welcomed four newly nominated Councilors appointed under the proportional representation electoral system.

The four Councillors were nominated by the United Party for National Development (UPND) in accordance with the Electoral Process (Amendment) Act No. 12 of 2026, which provides for proportional representation in local government.

The newly nominated councilors are; Shamiso Makumbiro and Lexina Lungu, representing women, Agnes Mwakalombe representing the youth, and Beatrice Chama representing Persons with Disabilities.

Chongwe Municipal Council Assistant Public Relations Manager, Cecilia Musonda said the inclusion of the four Councilors would broaden representation and strengthen participatory governance at local government level.

Ms Musonda said the proportional representation system provides an opportunity for women, young people and persons with disabilities to participate more meaningfully in decision-making processes.

She said the Council looks forward to working with the newly nominated Councilors in advancing development programmes and improving service delivery to the people of Chongwe district.

Ms Musonda further said the Council remains committed to promoting inclusive governance by ensuring that different groups in society have an opportunity to contribute to the development of the district.

She said the addition of the four Councilors would complement the work of elected Councillors and strengthen the council’s efforts to respond to the needs and aspirations of the local community.

Ms Musonda congratulated the newly nominated Councilors and urged them to work closely with the council, fellow Councilors and residents in promoting sustainable development and effective service delivery.

World.title: Funeral scheme digital platform to be rolled out in October
World.content:
Government has reiterated its commitment to digitalize systems across all sectors to increase speed, improve accuracy and eliminate paperwork thereby helping to contribute to the fight against climate change.

Muchinga Province Deputy Permanent Secretary, Brian Sichande said moving to a digitalized system is part of the government’s broader reform agenda to modernize service delivery.

The Deputy Permanent Secretary said this when a delegation from the Public Service Management Division (PSMD) and Madison Life Insurance paid a courtesy call on him at his office in Chinsali yesterday.

Mr Sichande said the digital platforms will enable institutions to work faster and keep accurate data while reducing dependence on paper.

“Government is making strides to digitalize government systems and examples to the digitalization agenda include the Integrated Financial Management Information System (IFMIS) and the Electronic Health Record (EHR) system used in hospitals,” he cited

And PSMD Chief Human Capital Officer- Industrial Relations Misheck Ng’uni , said the funeral scheme digital platform is expected to be rolled out in the first week of October, this year with Chinsali selected as one of the first districts for sensitization.

Mr Ng’uni said that the digital platform for the funeral scheme will allow members to transact seamlessly access services using mobile phones, or computers.

He added that the digital system will allow stakeholders to update data on the portal, including membership details, registration of new family members and parents, without doing paperwork.

Mr Ng’uni stated that PSMD and Madison will however conduct sensitization meetings with stakeholders before it is rolled out.

“The sensitization will be two-fold. We will do the general membership and also going to specifics with the focal point persons that will be assisting members who may be facing challenges in handling the system,” he added

Mr Ng’uni further said once operational, stakeholders will be able to log in, update their details, register beneficiaries and track claims without traveling to offices.

He adds that the move is aimed at improving efficiency, transparency and convenience in the management of the funeral scheme.

World.title: Government trains 25 teachers in KGS Digital checklist verification
World.content:
The Ministry of Education in Lavushimanda District in Muchinga Province has trained 25 school guidance teachers in digital checklist verification for the Keeping Girls in School (KGS) Programme under the Girls’ Education and Women’s Empowerment and Livelihood (GEWEL) Project.

The guidance teachers have been provided with tablets installed with the KGS application, which they will use to screen and verify beneficiaries of the programme.

Speaking in an interview with the Zambia News and Information Services (ZANIS), Lavushimanda District Education Board Office Assistant Statistical Officer, Gregory Chitemfuma said the training is important as it will enable guidance teachers to effectively conduct verification of KGS beneficiaries in their Schools.

Mr Chitemfuma explained that the training is conducted three times in a year to equip guidance teachers with the necessary skills to ascertain whether the girls are still in school and follow up on those who have dropped out.

“The purpose of the training is to equip guidance teachers with the knowledge and skills on how to use the application which is used for KGS verification,” he said.

He added that digital checklist verification promotes transparency in the identification of KGS beneficiaries.

Mr Chitemfuma explained that previously, verification was conducted using paper forms, where someone could sign on behalf of the girls, but the digital system now requires the girls to be captured and sign for themselves through the digital platform.

He however, revealed that the district has 28 schools, but only 25 guidance teachers have been trained because the remaining schools currently do not have KGS beneficiaries.

Meanwhile, in his opening remarks, District Education Board Secretary Beatus Nshenda, who was represented by District Standards Officer for Special Education, Regina Makasa, emphasised the importance of conducting the checklist verification process consistently, accurately and fairly.

Ms Makasa encouraged the guidance teachers to follow the appropriate procedures and seek guidance rather than making assumptions whenever they encounter uncertainties.

“I would also like to emphasise the importance of accuracy, consistency, professionalism, and confidentiality throughout the verification process,” she said.

She further acknowledged the important role played by guidance teachers in supporting learners and ensuring that the information collected and verified is reliable and handled with the necessary care and confidentiality.

World.title: UPND Kabwe MPs pledge to work together
World.content:
United Party for National Development (UPND) Members of Parliament (MPs) in Kabwe District in Central Province have pledged to work together to spearhead impactful developmental projects in the area.

Speaking in separate interviews, Bwacha South MP, Sydney Mushanga said he will work closely with his Kabwe Central and Bwacha North counterparts Chrizoster Phiri and Percy Chato, respectively, to push for development in Kabwe district.

Mr Mushanga said Kabwe is a strategic town in need of tangible development.

“As UPND MPs, we have resolved to work together in developing Kabwe for the benefit of the people. We are aware of what the people want and we are equal to the task,” Mr Mushanga said.

Kabwe Central MP, Chrizoster Phiri said the increase in the number of constituencies has put Kabwe on a sound development trajectory through the expanded Constituency Development Fund (CDF).

She said she will work with other MPs in the district to identify projects that could transform Kabwe.

Ms Phiri said the CDF, which currently stands at K40 million, will be used as a vehicle to initiate more developmental projects in the three constituencies of the district.

“We have put behind politics to focus on development. We have already done a lot in the last five years through CDF in various sectors. We will build on that foundation to deliver development for the benefit of the people of Kabwe,” she said.

Meanwhile, Bwacha North MP, Percy Chato said time for politicking is over and that it is now time to focus on development.

Mr Chato said teamwork among elected leaders and those in opposition will be key to the development of Kabwe.

He said Bwacha North Constituency is yearning for development by virtue of being one of the newly-created constituencies.

Mr Chato has also pledged to work with Councilors in the constituency to identify developmental projects that need urgent attention.

World.title: Zambia Is Now A “Full-Blown Police State”, Says Kateka
World.content:
New Heritage Party (NHP) president Chishala Kateka has accused the United Party for National Development (UPND) government of turning Zambia into a “full-blown police state”. She said the security wings are being used to silence the opposition and anyone with divergent views on national issues.

Speaking in a radio interview, Ms Kateka said the crackdown had been planned long before Zambians went to the polls.

“The army was psyched way back before the elections and they were prepared to clamp down on the opposition,” she said.

The opposition leader said the UPND did not win the August 13 general election fairly. Instead, she said, it used the army to intimidate voters and instil fear. She added that Zambians were still waiting to be told why the Zambia Army was deployed to manage the vote in polling stations where the ruling party had lost.

“To be honest, I did not expect the UPND to win fairly and squarely, but in the manner in which they did things, which included manipulation,” she said.

Ms Kateka said the anger left behind by the polls has split the nation, and the country is more divided than it has ever been. That division, she said, cannot be left to fester and must be dealt with now.

She reserved some of her sharpest criticism for the closure of courts during the post-election period. She called it shameful that people seeking justice over the outcome were blocked when the Government shut courts across the country, and said the move was meant to stop election petitions.

The closures, she said, have damaged Zambia’s standing abroad and drawn condemnation from the international community.

“Can you imagine that an international organisation of lawyers issued a statement on the closure of courts? It paints a very bad picture because investors are watching,” she said.

Her words landed on a day that gave her argument fresh fuel. In Chienge District, Luapula Province, heavily armed soldiers and plain-clothes police officers picked up veteran politician Dr Katele Kalumba, an outspoken critic of the arrests and detentions of opposition figures. Police headquarters said it had no information about the matter.

Opposition leaders Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu also remain in detention after a security operation at Mr Mundubile’s residence, during which former Cabinet minister Mutotwe Kafwaya died.

The Government’s own picture of the country is very different. In New York, Foreign Affairs Minister Mulambo Haimbe accepted European Union praise of Zambia as a “beacon of democracy”. He urged citizens to accept that the election is over and move forward.

Ms Kateka’s call for the country’s divisions to be dealt with now also runs straight into State House’s position on dialogue. Clayson Hamasaka, State House Chief Communications Specialist, said President Hakainde Hichilema sees no need to start a reconciliation process. He added that those calling for talks must first submit a formal proposal.

That leaves the opposition’s grievances, from the army’s role at polling stations to the shut courts, without a forum. For now, State House’s position stands: no dialogue until a proposal lands on the President’s desk.

World.title: Resist Any Third Term Push, Miti Tells Zambians, Says Bill 7 Was Built “For Numbers”
World.content:
Human rights activist Laura Miti has urged Zambians to resist any attempt to remove the presidential two-term limit, warning that the constitutional changes brought in under Bill 7 were designed to hand the ruling United Party for National Development (UPND) the numbers it needs in Parliament.

The third term calls, she said, were coming from what she described as President Hakainde Hichilema’s “cronies”, following a pattern as old as the bid under former President Frederick Chiluba, when scattered voices came first and the campaign followed. “Zambians do not accept a third term,” she said. “But don’t be surprised that it is being called for.”

Asked whether the UPND, now holding a two-thirds majority with the help of nominated proportional representation seats and independent members, could rewrite the Constitution at will, Ms Miti turned the question on those expressing alarm. “Why are you worried now? You should have been worried when Bill 7 was being fast-tracked and you were singing and saying, no, it’s all right, it’s for the youth. Bill 7 was not for the people.”

The outcome, in her view, should have surprised no one. “You are driving straight into a brick wall, and when impact hits, you say you are surprised,” she said. “It was always going to be this way.”

The UPND, she said, knew many of its Members of Parliament would lose their seats, and shaped the reforms, including delimitation and proportional representation, to protect its position in the House. Proportional representation had nothing to do with women or young people. “It was for numbers. It was to give the ruling party numbers.”

Women remain few in Parliament despite the reform, she pointed out, and nominated members belong to their parties and can be removed at any time. “Do you think they will ever go against the Government? No. Those are a sitting vote for the Government.”

Ms Miti was careful to separate the President from the calls. Mr Hichilema had previously stated he was not interested in a third term, she said, and had said nothing since to suggest otherwise. “To be fair to President Hichilema, he hasn’t said anything about this. The day we hear it straight from his mouth, the conversation becomes very different.”

The country, she said, should not change its Constitution to suit one person. Zambia does need reform, but of a different kind, one that separates institutions and restrains the executive. “We need the constitutional amendment. What we don’t need is a third term.”

Her message to citizens was to set party loyalty aside. “Forget the name of who is in power. Forget the party of who is in power and look at your own interest,” she said. “Your own interest is that if the UPND tries to change the Constitution, they should face real resistance from the people.”

On the economy, she praised the Head of State’s first term, describing his work on redirecting the economy and social welfare as “brilliant”. Third term talk, she warned, could undo it. “If the UPND allows this kind of distraction around politics to start today, they can be sure that whatever they succeed to do on the economy will drown again in a whole lot of noise, a whole lot of anxiety, a whole lot of tension.”

Tribal politics came under equal fire. Between 2011 and 2021, Ms Miti said, she had spoken out, sometimes alone, against what was being done to the Tonga people, while many of those now complaining about tribalism stayed silent. Tensions first rose, she said, when the Patriotic Front (PF) under former President Edgar Lungu allowed Chishimba Kambwili and others to make hateful statements against the Tonga. Now the pendulum has swung, and the complaints come from the north and east.

“Our divisions are a political construct,” she said. “They have been created by politicians.”

Mr Hichilema, she added, should himself stop suggesting that people hate him because of who he is. “You are the President. You are the one enjoying the power. Don’t make the Tonga about you. Do not make a whole people an extension of you.”

Only elite families benefit when one of their own holds power, she said, through access to appointments and contracts, while a clique moves from one government to the next. “No one can tell me that the ordinary Tonga selling tomatoes at Soweto has benefited because President Hichilema is President. We, the ordinary citizens, don’t hate each other. Let’s not destroy our country for the benefit of a few people.”

On calls for dialogue, including a pastoral letter by Archbishop Lungu urging reconciliation, she said Zambia had been calling for dialogue for 20 years without change, because its problems are structural and systemic.

Ms Miti was frank about her view of the election result. She did not want Mr Mundubile in State House, she said, nor the PF back. “I think Brian Mundubile is a nice guy, but I don’t see a president in him.” She pointed to the brief period in which he declared himself President, when she said cadres went out to reclaim shops, as a sign of where the country would have been.

She was equally clear that he should be taken to court and freed, and allowed to continue his political career. “If one day he is able to convince Zambians to vote for him, if I’m alive, I will accept that he is the President.”

A caller, Mulenga from Lusaka, challenged her, saying Mr Mundubile was a different person from Mr Lungu and that she should be fair to everyone regardless of where they came from. Ms Miti welcomed the challenge and urged Zambians to become comfortable disagreeing with people they admire. “That is how we will get a good constitution. That is how we will get better institutions.”

Competence was her only test for the four Cabinet appointments made so far, and she was pleased with them. She described Finance Minister Situmbeko Musokotwane as one of the country’s best finance ministers ever and said the new Minister of Health brought wide experience and qualifications, though she questioned why a green economy portfolio had been filled ahead of education or home affairs.

She hoped for a small Cabinet but did not expect one. For the second term, her wish was simple: a team that works hard, does not steal and improves life in rural Zambia and the informal settlements. “I’m hoping that our democracy is protected,” she said. “And I pray that we change our Constitution to make it such that we are able to protect our democracy.”

President Hichilema has so far named four members of his Cabinet, with the rest of the appointments still to come.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - September 24, 2026
World.content:
press review

Monrovia — CAR Rebel Commander Convicted of Crimes Against Humanity

The International Criminal Court has found Central African Republic Seleka rebel commander Mahamat Said Abdel Kani guilty on four counts, including torture and persecution. The charges stem from the 2013 conflict, when predominantly Muslim Seleka rebels seized power and ousted President François Bozizé - an event that triggered opposition from mainly Christian anti-Balaka militias. Prosecutors accused Said of running a Bangui prison where suspected Bozizé supporters were beaten and tortured, with detainees testifying they were held in a windowless cell beneath his office floorboards. The country's Justice Minister, Arnaud Djoubaye Abazène, welcomed the ruling, saying that "no victim will be left behind, and justice will be delivered at every level.

DR Congo Ebola Outbreak Death Toll Exceeds 3,700 Deaths



The World Health Organization (WHO) has reported that over the last 21 days, Ebola infection cases dropped by approximately 26% in Ituri province and 15% in Haut-Uélé province. However, WHO said that North Kivu province recorded a 73% increase over the same period, indicating a distinct transmission profile across the seven affected provinces. Health experts said on Wednesday that response efforts have been scaled up significantly, showing "the first encouraging signs of progress" more than 130 days into the country's latest outbreak.

Malawi Imposes $1,000 Limit on Foreign Cash Possession

The Reserve Bank of Malawi (RBM) has introduced strict restrictions on the physical possession and movement of foreign currency. Under the new rule, anyone carrying more than $1,000 (roughly K1.75 million) or its foreign currency equivalent must secure prior approval from the central bank or face punitive action. The dramatic tightening comes as Malawi struggles with a severe foreign exchange shortage and a growing forex black market, with authorities attempting to curb unofficial cash flows.

Calls for De-Escalation as Tigray Militia and Ethiopian Army Clash

Tigray rebels in Ethiopia have confirmed they are in a state of "full-blown war" with the federal government, saying they've seized control of several towns and airports, as reports of heavy artillery attacks in neighbouring regions emerge.

The Tigray People's Liberation Front, which dominates the region, has seized control of three airports in the cities of Mekelle, Shire and Axum, taking prisoner the small number of federal police that guard them.

Police Investigate Murder of Ugandan Music Legend Moses Matovu

Veteran Ugandan musician Moses Matovu has died following an attack by unknown assailants in Kampala. Police confirmed the incident occurred on Thursday morning, September 24. Kampala Metropolitan Police spokesperson Rachael Kawala said that Matovu was attacked at Kibuli Market Zone B - a prominent commercial hub in Kampala - and was rushed to hospital, where he later succumbed to his injuries.

Close 

Matovu co-founded the iconic Afrigo Band in 1975 and remained a cornerstone of Uganda's live music industry for nearly five decades.

World.title: Sudan: Has the U.S. Adopted a Regime Change Policy in Sudan?
World.content:
Monrovia — There has been a flurry of diplomatic activity this week surrounding peace efforts in Sudan as world leaders gather in New York for the 81st session of the UN General Assembly. The conflict, which began in April 2023, has reached a stalemate, leaving the country virtually divided between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).

A committee of Sudanese doctors earlier warned that conditions in the country have reached "catastrophic" levels, particularly in conflict-affected areas including the capital, Khartoum. The group, the Preparatory Committee of the Sudanese Doctors' Syndicate, presented its report to the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva. It documented extensive damage to health facilities and environmental destruction that the group warned is fueling the spread of disease.

The committee's report comes after UN agencies warned they may be forced to cut back on humanitarian aid due to severe funding shortfalls. Sudan is currently home to the world's worst hunger and displacement crisis: according to the UN, nearly 8.6 million people remain internally displaced, and more than 19 million face crisis levels of food insecurity.

In response, the U.S. intensified its diplomatic efforts to bring an end to the violence. The American approach - spearheaded by U.S. President Donald Trump's Senior Advisor for Arab and African Affairs, Massad Boulos - focuses on applying diplomatic pressure on both the SAF and RSF to secure a ceasefire, establish humanitarian corridors, and enforce targeted sanctions against key perpetrators of violence.



As part of these efforts, the Trump administration proposed an immediate 90-day humanitarian truce in July to allow aid deliveries, strengthen civilian protection, and pave the way for negotiations on a permanent ceasefire, followed by a civilian-led political transition and elections. Although early reports suggested the warring factions had accepted the proposal, an op-ed by Sudanese Sovereignty Council Chief and Army Commander Abdel Fattah al-Burhan appears to contradict those claims.

Writing in Foreign Policy magazine under the title "How to Bring Peace to Sudan," Burhan argued that external efforts to secure a ceasefire over the years have failed to yield results, stressing that the latest U.S. proposal merely buys the RSF time. He argued that any genuine peace process must be an internally driven settlement leading to a permanent ceasefire, the consolidation of all armed groups under a single national army, and a national political dialogue culminating in a new constitution and elections. He added that the Rapid Support Forces do not hold legitimate state authority.

On the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, Boulos announced on social media that he had held "productive conversations" with the SAF-appointed Foreign Minister, Mohi El Din Salem, and Egyptian Foreign Minister Dr. Badr Abdelatty. Boulos said the discussions centered on the urgent need to "agree on a path to durable peace in Sudan," adding that the Sudanese people critically need a humanitarian truce that can "lead towards an inclusive civilian dialogue and a peaceful, unified Sudan."

His statement follows reports that the U.S. denied a visa to Army Chief Burhan, preventing him from attending the UN gathering. Observers view the move as an attempt to pressure him into accepting the proposed ceasefire. U.S. officials reportedly made Burhan's attendance contingent on his agreement to the 90-day truce proposed by Boulos. While neither the U.S. State Department nor the Sudanese government has officially commented on the reported visa denial, according to al-Jazeera, some Sudanese citizens took to social media to voice opposition to the U.S. stance, arguing that UN participation should not be conditioned on Khartoum's acceptance of the proposal.

Meanwhile, in a statement released Tuesday, September 22, the U.S. State Department reiterated President Trump's commitment to ending the conflict, stating that accepting the truce is an "essential step to achieving a durable peace" in Sudan. It emphasized that the administration stands ready to work with anyone who is a "serious partner" for peace.

Close 

"Neither the Sudanese Armed Forces, the Rapid Support Forces, nor their respective leaders represent legitimate, constitutional governance for Sudan - they rule through force of arms alone," the State Department added, saying the conduct of both leaders "renders them ineligible to govern the country."

Cameron Hudson, a senior fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), has said the State Department's statement essentially signals a policy of regime change in Sudan.

"There is no other way to read the statement," Hudson wrote in a post on X (formerly Twitter), arguing that the U.S. has painted itself into a corner. "First with its chemical weapons sanctions, then its arms embargo, then with its visa ban. Now, in order to justify the ban, it has doubled down on its regime of maximum pressure."

Hudson said the current U.S. approach leaves little room for negotiation: "Either Burhan bends his knee and signs whatever is put in front of him unconditionally, or the situation remains as is."

World.title: Uganda: Police Identify Suspect in Death of Afrigo Band Icon Moses Matovu
World.content:
Legendary Afrigo Band leader Moses Matovu has died after he was reportedly attacked while on his way to a mosque.

Kampala — Police have identified a male suspect in the suspected murder of veteran Afrigo Band musician Moses Matovu, who died on Thursday after sustaining serious injuries during a confrontation at Kibuli Depot in Kampala.

According to Kampala Metropolitan Police spokesperson Rachael Kawala, preliminary investigations indicate that Matovu went to the residence of his girlfriend at about 5:30 a.m. on September 24, 2026.

Police allege that Matovu and the woman were leaving the residence when they were confronted by a man who had previously been in a relationship with the same woman.

Kawala said the woman who was with Matovu has since been arrested and is assisting detectives with the investigation.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"Preliminary information indicates that the incident may have arisen from a physical altercation," Kawala said, while stressing that the exact circumstances surrounding the confrontation and Matovu's subsequent death had not yet been fully established.

Matovu sustained serious injuries and was rushed to Kibuli Hospital by a boda boda rider, where he later succumbed to his injuries.

Police said the male suspect has been positively identified but is believed to have fled the scene. Investigators are pursuing him to facilitate his arrest and establish what happened.

"The exact circumstances surrounding the confrontation and subsequent death are yet to be fully established," Kawala said.

Police are continuing to verify the different accounts surrounding the incident and have appealed to members of the public to remain calm and allow investigators to conduct their work without interference.

The death of Matovu, a veteran figure in Uganda's music industry and a leading member of Afrigo Band, has prompted condolences from colleagues, fans and members of the public.

Police said further updates will be provided as investigations progress.

World.title: South Africa: Local Elections Will Test Voters' Ability to Spot Fake News
World.content:
analysis

Public confidence in identifying disinformation is falling just as AI and hyper-local campaigning make election manipulation harder to detect.

South Africa's new code of conduct against election disinformation is a vital step ahead of what could be the country's most fiercely contested local polls on 4 November.

The Electoral Code of Conduct Countering Disinformation in the Local Government Elections (Disinformation Code) was gazetted by the Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC) on 4 September. These legal provisions are badly needed, considering that citizens are becoming less confident in their ability to identify fake news.



According to the IEC's latest Voter Participation Survey, the proportion of respondents who describe themselves as confident in recognising fake news declined from 62% in 2023 to 52% in 2025/26. Yet only 18% say they regularly verify election-related information before liking, sharing or reposting it.

As the polls approach, the survey shows that traditional media remains highly influential, with 71% of respondents relying on television and 38% on radio for voting information. At the same time, social media is gaining ground - 23% cite it as a source of election-related information, up from 8% in 2021.

While social media may not be a leading source of election information, South Africans spend a lot of time online. In 2025, an average of nine hours and 37 minutes online daily was recorded - the highest in the world. Roughly three and a half of those hours were on social media. But greater access to information has not translated into stronger verification practices.

The World Economic Forum's Global Risks Report 2026 ranks misinformation and disinformation among the top risks facing societies. Speaking at the Disinformation Dialogue 2026, IEC Chairperson Mosotho Moepya warned that the 2026 elections would likely see a shift from national misinformation and disinformation to 'ward-specific deceptions' driven by generative artificial intelligence (AI) and hyper-local campaigning.

Moepya's concerns align with Institute for Security Studies (ISS) research showing that disinformation and political messaging are becoming increasingly localised and targeted at specific communities and voter groups. Community WhatsApp groups and Facebook pages have become central arenas for political discussion at the ward and municipal levels. In these spaces, information travels quickly, and verification is often limited.

At the same time, political parties are investing more in digital campaigning. ISS research shows that online political advertising and influencer-driven campaigning are becoming increasingly important features of election strategies.

While these tools can enhance political engagement, they can also make it harder for voters to distinguish between authentic political discussion, sponsored content and coordinated influence campaigns. AI is further complicating the picture. South Africa has not yet experienced a major election crisis linked to deepfakes, but AI-generated content is becoming cheaper, more accessible and harder to detect.

As a result, information integrity will no longer be simply a media issue, but an integral part of citizenship, democracy and governance.

Technology is not inherently the problem. It can be used both to spread harmful falsehoods and to help voters access accurate information. South Africa's challenge is to ensure that the tools designed to strengthen democratic participation evolve as quickly as the technologies used to manipulate it.

Much of the public conversation around disinformation focuses on social media users. However, verification cannot be the sole responsibility of citizens. Professional and legacy media journalists remain one of democracy's most important lines of defence against false and misleading information. They investigate claims, provide context and test competing narratives before they reach the public.

Although newsrooms are increasingly pressured to produce more content with fewer resources, this does not necessarily mean that verification standards are being compromised. Newzroom Afrika told ISS Today that accuracy takes precedence over being first. It applies the three-step verification process and labels fabricated AI-generated content as fake. These standard practices are reflected in the Press Council of South Africa's guidance on the use of AI in journalism.

This year, the IEC has expanded its efforts to strengthen information integrity and public trust. Voter education campaigns and public roadshows have been accompanied by journalist training, digital outreach and new tools enabling voters to verify information through official channels.

The new Disinformation Code requires political parties and candidates to verify information before sharing it and to clearly label political advertising and AI-generated or synthetic content. They must also correct and retract false or misleading information within 36 hours. Anyone can report suspected election-related online disinformation through the IEC's Real411 platform.

Crucially, the Disinformation Code extends responsibility for information integrity beyond official party statements to the wider networks through which political content circulates.

Social media platforms also have a role to play. As political parties and candidates face greater expectations to take responsibility for the information they share, platforms should strengthen their responses to election-related disinformation. The IEC chairperson warns that breaches of the Disinformation Code carry the same legal consequences as violations of the core Electoral Code of Conduct.

Close 

While the Disinformation Code remains in force only until the election results are declared, the problem can persist long afterwards, as allegations of vote rigging after the 2024 elections demonstrated. South Africa will therefore need long-term information integrity solutions that extend beyond elections.

Safeguarding local democracy is a shared responsibility, but citizens are an important first line of defence. Small, deliberate actions - such as challenging a suspicious post in a community WhatsApp group or helping a family member verify a candidate's claim - can strengthen democratic resilience.

With six weeks left before voting starts, South Africans need access to information they trust. That requires a sustained commitment to verification from political parties, institutions, media organisations, platforms and citizens.

Adivhaho Ramaite, Research Officer, Executive Director's office, ISS Pretoria

World.title: Ethiopia: EU Calls for 'De-Escalation' As Tigray Rebels Clash With Ethiopian Forces
World.content:
The European Union has called for an "immediate de-escalation" after Tigray rebels in Ethiopia confirmed they were in a state of "full-blown war" with the federal government. The separatists have seized control of several towns and airports, amid reports of heavy artillery attacks in neighbouring regions.

Tensions have been rising for months between the federal government and the authorities in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region, who fought a devastating civil war in 2020-2022 that killed more than 600,000 people, according to African Union estimates.

The two sides accuse each other of triggering a return to open conflict with attacks this week, prompting alarm in the international community.

The EU on Wednesday called for an "immediate de-escalation" of the growing conflict and condemned strikes on humanitarian convoys.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"The European Union is deeply concerned by the rapidly deteriorating situation in northern Ethiopia and its impact on the population, including reports of military activity across multiple localities," said an EU spokesperson in a statement.

Renewed fighting in Tigray raises risk of a wider regional war

On Wednesday, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which dominates the region, seized control of three airports in the cities of Mekelle, Shire and Axum, taking prisoner the small number of federal police that guard them.

Ethiopian Airlines said it had suspended flights to all three.

"We are in the situation of full-blown war now," TPLF vice president Amanuel Assefa told French news agency AFP.

He confirmed fighting was ongoing in the neighbouring regions of Afar and Amhara, with Tigrayan forces joined by local armed groups.

New alliance in action

Humanitarian workers in Afar told AFP of fighting between TPLF and federal forces in Abala and the town of Erebti, around 100 kilometres further into the region.

"We are expecting it to expand. We just sent a truck with food to help the people displaced," one worked, who requested anonymity, said.

A foreign security source said the TPLF was in control of Abala, while a former TPLF senior official told AFP the rebels were in control of several towns in the region, which could not be independently confirmed.

The federal forces are "fast retreating", the former official said.

Conflict monitoring platform Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED) said Tigrayan forces had attacked positions in the Amhara region and were working alongside a local insurgent group known as the Fano, part of the new Alliance for Survival.

Seven of Ethiopia's armed groups announce anti-government alliance

"Today's episode will cause worry that the other agents in the alliance are about to act in their areas across the Ethiopian state," ACLED said in a briefing note, although it added that several of the groups have limited capabilities.

The federal government in the capital Addis Ababa, which is yet to comment on the clashes, has significant military advantages, having ramped up production of military drones since the last conflict.

Pushing into Afar and Amhara suggests the Tigrayans are planning a similar strategy to that seen in the civil war in 2020-2022 - seeking to cut off supply lines, and ultimately threaten Addis Ababa.

"Their stated aim is to take Addis, but its tactical manoeuvres to reach the city are not yet known," said regional expert Kjetil Tronvoll, of Oslo New University College.

Thousands displaced

Ethiopian authorities have also accused the TPLF of allying with neighbouring Eritrea, which it denies.

Close 

The TPLF ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018 before being sidelined with the rise of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, eventually triggering the civil war.

During the war of 2020-2022, the Fano group and Eritrea both fought with the government against the Tigrayans.

The Pretoria Peace Agreement ended the war and maintained an uneasy calm until late 2025, when clashes resumed. The federal government has since launched drone strikes in Tigray and massed troops at the regional border.

Rights groups have accused the TPLF of a campaign of forced recruitment this year, as it prepares for renewed conflict.

The region has not recovered from the last war, with around 1 million people still displaced and many aspects of the peace agreement unfulfilled.

(with AFP)

World.title: Burkina Faso: From Cotton to Uniforms, Burkina Faso Boosts its Textile Industry
World.content:
By introducing traditional fabrics into school, judicial and military uniforms, as well as some public-service attire, Burkina Faso is seeking to create a sustainable market for locally processed cotton. The policy could support spinning mills, women weavers and garment workshops, provided the sector can meet the required volumes, prices and deadlines.

In a small workshop equipped with two looms in the Taabtenga neighbourhood of Ouagadougou, Véronique Thiombiano Yonli and her colleagues are working hard to finish a length of cloth due the following day.

It is cencingu, also known as Tchintchingou in French, a fabric of Gourmantché origin deeply rooted in the traditions of eastern Burkina Faso.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The fabric gained national prominence when the government selected it for the parade uniform worn on 25 July 2026 at the graduation ceremony for the 25th class of active-duty officer cadets from the Georges Namoano Military Academy in Pô, about 140 kilometres from Ouagadougou.

Behind the cultural significance of the uniform lies a broader economic objective. By expanding the use of traditional fabrics, particularly Faso Dan Fani, across the public service and in schools, courts and the military, the state is stimulating demand for textiles produced in the country. The orders could support spinning mills, dyers, women weavers and garment workshops, while retaining more of the value generated by Burkina Faso’s cotton within the country.

The state creates a market for local fabrics

Since Captain Ibrahim Traoré came to power in 2022, the government has introduced a series of measures to promote Burkinabè fabrics. Following a national forum on Faso Dan Fani in May 2023, a decree adopted the next month encouraged the wearing and use of Faso Dan Fani, Koko Dunda and other traditional fabrics in the public service, at official ceremonies and in the decoration of public buildings.

The measure was subsequently extended to schools. During a pilot phase in the 2025–2026 school year, pupils in four municipalities wore Faso Dan Fani or Koko Dunda uniforms twice a week. The government said the trial was not compulsory but plans to roll out the policy more widely from the start of the 2026–2027 school year. The details have yet to be specified.

In October 2024, Faso Dan Fani also became the courtroom attire of magistrates and court clerks. Orders from the defence and security forces and other public institutions have added to this demand. Together, these decisions are gradually turning uniforms and official attire into markets for local textiles.

The challenge of producing parade uniforms

Abdoul Ben Isaac Compaoré, a garment engineer and founder of the Black brand, made the officer cadets’ parade uniforms. The order tested his workshop. “We had to make 252 suits in four weeks,” he says, describing it as “a suicide mission that we had to pull off — and we did.”

According to Compaoré, the made-to-measure suits were produced through an entirely Burkinabè supply chain. “The yarn comes from FILSAH. The fabrics were produced by women weavers I brought in from different places, the other accessories were also made locally, and I contributed the design,” he says.

For producers, the appeal of this market lies in both its volume and its regularity. Its impact, however, depends on how contracts are awarded and whether local-content requirements are enforced. If the yarn or fabric is imported, a significant share of the value still escapes the national economy.

Tailor Soumanou Kiéma believes the state should also organise trade fairs to raise awareness of Faso Dan Fani. “Public orders must be more regular,” he says.

He also calls for stronger training for women weavers to ensure the quality of the fabrics.

FILSAH seeks markets for its yarn

The local-uniform policy comes as Burkina Faso seeks to process more of its cotton domestically. Based in Bobo-Dioulasso, the Filature du Sahel, or FILSAH, is experiencing renewed activity after several difficult years.

The company, representing an investment of 18.5 billion CFA francs (US$32.7 million), turns cotton fibre into yarn supplied mainly to women weavers and producers of traditional cloth. At an open day on 30 April 2026, managing director Abdoulaye Nabolé announced an annual capacity of 10,000 tonnes of yarn and about 550 direct jobs, figures confirmed by the Ministry of Commerce.

According to Nabolé, the cotton-textile value chain “accounts for more than 10% of gross domestic product and supports more than 3.5 million people”.

But production capacity does not guarantee a market. FILSAH says fraudulent imports of yarn and cloth weakened its operations, contributing to unsold stock worth as much as three billion CFA francs (US$5.3 million). In 2026, enforcement agencies announced the seizure of fraudulent or illegally imported textile products valued at several hundred million CFA francs.

Public procurement could therefore support yarn manufactured by FILSAH. Its effect will nevertheless depend on the company’s ability to deliver the required quantities at competitive prices and within the prescribed deadlines.

Demand reaches the workshops

For some women weavers, the effects are already visible. Thiombiano Yonli says the promotion of traditional cloth has revived her business. “I have never seen my workshop this busy since I started this trade in 2020,” she says.

With only two looms, she sometimes manages “to weave as many as two lengths of cloth a day”. She received orders from schools at the start of the 2025–2026 school year and hopes the demand will continue.

Her prices vary according to the weight of the fabric, the yarn and the dye. “My cloth costs between 4,000 and 8,000 CFA francs, taking the economic situation into account so that I can keep my customers,” she explains. She says she no longer uses imported yarn: “With the state’s commitment to promoting traditional cloth, I now source 100% Burkinabè yarn from FILSAH.”

Her experience illustrates the intended mechanism: a school order provides work for the workshop and, further up the supply chain, creates demand for locally produced yarn.

In Loumbila, Alizèta Ouoba Nikiéma runs the Faso Impact training centre with her husband. She estimates that its turnover reached about 10 million CFA francs (US$17,700) over the past year, compared with approximately five million CFA francs two years earlier. She attributes the growth to the promotion of traditional fabrics, as well as to the rigour of their work.

“At Faso Impact, we weave all kinds of traditional cloth, including Faso Dan Fani, cencingu, Mandili and many others,” she explains. The work also requires mastery of dyeing because FILSAH’s yarn is sold white.

The National Federation of Women Weavers of Burkina Faso, FENATI/BF, has delivered 1,200 lengths of cloth worth 12 million CFA francs (US$21,200). In a report presented on 8 May 2026, it also cited its contribution to the production of Faso Dan Fani school uniforms.

Production capacity put to the test

Rising demand creates opportunities but also exposes the sector’s constraints. Thiombiano Yonli lacks the means to buy additional looms. At Faso Impact, cramped dormitories prevent the centre from accepting more trainees.

“My centre serves a social purpose. Most of the trainees have fled conflict zones or forced marriage,” says Nikiéma, who is calling for additional facilities.

The government is attempting to address some of these constraints by building the National Centre for the Support of Artisanal Cotton Processing, known as CNATAC. Built on a 10-hectare site, it is intended to bring together weaving, dyeing, cutting and sewing workshops, as well as training and exhibition spaces. The project could help artisans fulfil larger orders and meet common standards for quality and delivery times.

Close 

Progress remains uneven, however. In Fada N’Gourma and Ziniaré, Tanilemba Tankoano and Viviane Dayamba Bouda are still struggling to sell their cloth. Bouda sells only two pieces a week, earning an estimated profit of between 2,000 and 3,000 CFA francs (US$3.50–US$5.30). Her workshop, situated inside a large welding yard, has little visibility. She does not belong to an association and has no presence on social media.

Tankoano, meanwhile, did not consider weaving her main occupation until government policy encouraged her to invest more in it. The contrast with workshops receiving school orders shows that access to public contracts, equipment, finance, raw materials and commercial networks remains decisive.

From public procurement to industry

Alongside FILSAH and CNATAC, the government is developing TEXFORCES-BF, a textile complex intended to supply clothing to the defence and security forces as well as the wider population. It was inaugurated on 9 September.

These projects reflect the ambition to connect cotton production to spinning, weaving and, ultimately, the manufacture of finished garments. The challenge now is to turn uniform policies into sustainable, measurable orders that genuinely use Burkinabè cotton and yarn, while ensuring that small businesses and women weavers’ associations can access them.

For workshops such as Thiombiano Yonli’s, the initial effects are visible. But moving from a growing number of artisanal orders to a fully fledged textile industry will depend on Burkina Faso’s ability to organise the entire value chain, from cotton grown in its fields to uniforms worn in its schools and institutions.

World.title: Zimbabwe: Zimbabwe Turns to Cloud Seeding As Drought Threat Looms
World.content:
Zimbabwe is turning to cloud seeding as part of efforts to protect the 2026/27 agricultural season from the threat of below-normal rainfall linked to a forecast Super El Niño.

The government has identified three aircraft, alongside drones, for cloud-seeding operations as part of a wider six-pillar drought mitigation strategy aimed at protecting food production and livelihoods.

Agriculture, Mechanisation and Water Resources Development Minister Dr Anxious Masuka said the aircraft will operate from Harare, Bulawayo and Masvingo, with deployments dependent on suitable weather conditions.



"As you are aware, Government has already approved a drought mitigation plan with six pillars, and now this meeting came up with a contingency plan whereby this time we agreed to use our conventional aeroplanes and drones that will be availed to conduct cloud seeding when need be," Masuka said.

The intervention comes as Zimbabwe prepares for a potentially difficult summer cropping season, with forecasts pointing to below-normal rainfall and elevated temperatures.

For farmers who depend heavily on rain-fed agriculture, the prospect of prolonged dry spells presents a major risk to crop establishment, yields and livestock production.

Cloud seeding is a weather modification technique in which particles are introduced into suitable clouds to encourage the formation of rainfall. However, it cannot create rain where there are no suitable clouds or sufficient atmospheric moisture, meaning it will not replace irrigation, water harvesting or climate-smart farming practices.

The Government's cloud-seeding plan is therefore being positioned as one component of a broader drought response.

The six-pillar strategy includes strengthening strategic grain reserves, scaling up climate-smart agriculture, improving agricultural financing, protecting livestock, facilitating imports where necessary and strengthening early-warning systems.

The government has also placed greater emphasis on irrigation development as Zimbabwe prepares for a season expected to be drier than normal.

Permanent Secretary in the Agriculture Ministry Professor Obert Jiri said irrigation, climate-smart production and early planning would be critical in reducing the impact of the anticipated conditions.

"As we move into the next season, which is expected to be drier than normal, we must look ahead, set targets and budget accordingly. We are looking at irrigation development as we go into the El Niño season," Jiri said.

For smallholder farmers, experts have also urged greater emphasis on conserving soil moisture, harvesting water, protecting crop residues and considering drought-tolerant varieties.

Close 

The Meteorological Services Department has warned that farmers should not interpret the seasonal forecast as an indication that there will be no rainfall. Instead, rainfall could be erratic, poorly distributed and separated by prolonged dry spells, making planting decisions particularly important.

The Government's approach also reflects lessons from previous droughts, with authorities seeking to move towards acting on early warnings before climate shocks translate into major agricultural losses.

The Food and Agriculture Organisation has similarly called for anticipatory action ahead of the 2026/27 season, including stronger early-warning systems, water infrastructure, climate-smart agriculture and targeted support for vulnerable farming communities.

For Zimbabwe's farmers, cloud seeding could provide an additional tool when atmospheric conditions allow. But the success of the coming season will also depend on how effectively farmers and authorities combine rainfall interventions with irrigation, water conservation, appropriate crop choices, livestock preparedness and timely weather information.

With the planting window approaching, the message from Government is increasingly clear: preparations for a potentially difficult season need to begin before the rains -- not after they fail.

World.title: Lane Kiffin suggests Ole Miss broke rules with in-stadium music during LSU's loss to Rebels
World.content:
Lane Kiffin seems to believe that his LSU team was put in an unfair situation during the Tigers' loss at Ole Miss, and it had nothing to do with anything taking place inside the white lines, but instead, it involved someone pressing a button at Vaught-Hemingway Stadium.

During Wednesday's SEC coaches' teleconference call, Kiffin made a subtle yet pointed remark accusing Ole Miss' game operations of playing music for too long of a time when LSU's offense was on the field.

"Those games happen, and a lot of factors go into that," Kiffin said, referring to the atmosphere at Ole Miss on Saturday night. "We didn't protect really well around him [quarterback Sam Leavitt]; the crowd noise and music being played all the way through the snap when the center's hand is on the ball. Again and again."

SEC rules require stadium music to stop once the center touches the ball.

While Kiffin may have a case to be made that Ole Miss played music over its stadium speakers a bit too long, it's hard not to interpret his comments as an excuse.

LANE KIFFIN COULDN'T HELP HIMSELF, TAKES PETTY SHOT AT OLE MISS FANS AFTER LSU LOSS IN HIS RETURN TO OXFORD

Kiffin laid out the accusation when asked about Leavitt's struggles during the contest, and making a comment about music being played inside the stadium three days after the game ended seems unnecessary. By no means did he pin his team's loss on the fact that music was being played when his team possessed the football, but Kiffin bringing the topic up opens himself up to criticism.

Kiffin's return to Ole Miss in Week 3 made for one of the most emotionally charged atmospheres college football has ever seen after the head coach left Oxford for LSU just days before the Rebels played in their first-ever College Football Playoff game.

Ole Miss announced during the contest that it set a new all-time attendance record at Vaught-Hemingway Stadium with 70,033 fans in the stands.

The Rebels fed off the energy early and jumped out to a commanding 17-0 lead early in the second quarter before taking a 24-7 lead into halftime. Chambliss threw for 363 yards in the game, while Leavitt threw for 158 yards and picked up another 63 yards on the ground.

World.title: Gregg Popovich shocks NBA world with marriage to former assistant Mike Budenholzer's ex-wife

Love is in the air for Pop.

Former San Antonio Spurs head coach Gregg Popovich, 77, is officially a married man again, tying the knot with Mary Barth Budenholzer, according to marriage records filed in Bexar County, Texas, on Sept. 16, 2026.

Mary was previously married to former Phoenix Suns and Milwaukee Bucks head coach Mike Budenholzer for two decades, raising four kids together while he served as Popovich's top assistant during the Spurs dynasty.

Mike and Mary quietly divorced in 2016, and Popovich suffered his own tragedy two years later when his wife of 42 years, Erin, passed away following a long illness.

In November 2024, Popovich suffered a mild stroke at the arena right before a home game. Further medical complications ultimately forced him to step off the bench, handing the reins to Mitch Johnson as he shifted into a front-office advisory role as the Spurs' president of basketball operations.

World.title: NASCAR Hall of Famer diagnosed with frontotemporal degeneration, possible CTE from racing
World.content:
NASCAR Hall of Famer Darrell Waltrip has been diagnosed with frontotemporal degeneration (FTD), complicated by possible chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), according to a statement his family put out Wednesday.

Waltrip, now 79, won 84 races over a nearly 30-year NASCAR Cup Series career, including three championships. His family said the possible CTE stems from "injuries incurred during his racing career."

NASCAR HALL OF FAMER NED JARRETT, LEGENDARY DRIVER AND BROADCASTER, DIES AT 93

"While this disease will inevitably progress, thankfully it is currently limited to some minor noticeable symptoms," the statement, put out by Darrell and his wife, Stevie, said. "As a result, he will be stepping further away from the public limelight. Be assured, Darrell is happy and otherwise healthy — spending his time with his wife, Stevie, two daughters and his three young grandchildren. We are all grateful for your continued prayer, love and support!

"Boogity! Boogity! Boogity!"

Darrell Waltrip is a beloved racer and broadcaster

Stunning news out of the NASCAR world. You won't find a more universally loved racer in the series than Darrell Waltrip. He's a three-time champ, a Daytona 500 winner, and his 84 wins are fifth-most in NASCAR Cup Series history.

Of course, to a large portion of the fanbase, he's better known as the NASCAR on FOX analyst who coined the term "Boogity Boogity Boogity" at the start of every race.

Waltrip spent 19 years in the FOX booth before retiring in 2019. His first race was the infamous 2001 Daytona 500, where Dale Earnhardt died on the final lap, and Waltrip's brother, Michael, won his first race.

"I sure hope Dale's OK," Waltrip famously said from the booth while Michael was doing his victory lap.

NASCAR fans haven't seen nearly as much of Waltrip since he retired in 2019, but he has occasionally rejoined the broadcast booth for brief cameos. His most recent surprise visit came earlier this year, when he gave another "Boogity Boogity Boogity" from the booth at Darlington in March.

7 NEW DEMENTIA RISK FACTORS REVEALED — INCLUDING ONE MILLIONS STRUGGLE WITH

According to the American Brain Foundation, frontotemporal degeneration (also known as frontotemporal dementia), is a group of neurodegenerative disorders associated with changes in the brain’s frontal and temporal lobes. These areas of the brain control functions related to personality, behavior, and language.

The Mayo Clinic says this could impact the way one acts and could make someone impulsive or show less response to other people's feelings. Others lose the ability to use or understand language.

As for the possible CTE ...

Waltrip obviously got into hundreds of wrecks over his nearly 30-year racing career. That's just the nature of the beast. He also raced during a much different era in NASCAR.

KYLE SHANAHAN, RETURNING AFTER SERIOUS CAR CRASH, HAS NEW PERSPECTIVE ON TESLA AUTOPILOT AND CONCUSSIONS

The cars were not nearly as safe back then as they are now. Frankly, it's not even close. Drivers got seriously injured during Waltrip's racing career. Some died. Earnhardt's crash in 2001 changed things for good, but even his son, Dale Earnhardt Jr., famously dealt with concussions toward the end of his racing career.



Earlier this year, Hendrick Motorsports driver Alex Bowman missed several races because of vertigo. He missed five races in 2022 due to a concussion.
