World.title: Aeroméxico will offer Mexico’s first direct flights to Jamaica and the Bahamas
World.content:
Legacy airline Aeroméxico has announced new nonstop routes from Mexico City to Nassau, Bahamas, and Montego Bay, Jamaica, making it the first airline to offer direct service connecting Mexico and the two Caribbean destinations.

Before those two new routes — which begin operations in March — travelers departing from Mexico for the the Bahamas or Jamaica had to arrive through connections in the United States or Panama.

Chief Executive Officer Andrés Conesa linked the two new direct routes to Aeroméxico’s ongoing expansion. “We continue to strengthen the ‘Eagle Knight’s’ leadership position in the international market and bring our passengers closer to the world’s most iconic destinations,” he said in a in a statement on his official LinkedIn page.

(The Eagle Knight or Caballero Águila is Aeroméxico’s emblematic logo that appears on the tail of its aircraft.)

The Mexico City–Montego Bay flight will begin March 18, 2027, and operate three times a week: Thursdays, Saturdays, and Sundays. Departure from the Mexican capital is scheduled for 9:20 a.m., with arrival in Jamaica at 2 p.m. local time. The return flight will depart at 3:15 p.m. and land in Mexico City at 6:20 p.m.

The following day, March 19, Aeroméxico will launch the route to Nassau, which will also operate three days a week on Fridays, Saturdays, and Sundays. Flights will depart from Mexico City at 9:10 a.m. and arrive in the Bahamas at 3:00 p.m. The return flight will depart at 4:15 p.m. with a scheduled landing at 6:30 p.m.

According to the newspaper El Universal, both services are still subject to government approval. If approved, they will be operated onboard a 737 MAX 8 aircraft configured to seat 166 passengers.

The addition of Nassau and Montego Bay expands the airline’s presence in the Caribbean, where it already offers nonstop connections to Punta Cana and Santo Domingo in the Dominican Republic, as well as to Havana, Cuba.

Senior Vice President of Global Sales Giancarlo Mulinelli said that the addition of Jamaica and the Bahamas reflects the airline’s commitment to offering its customers more travel options to world-class destinations.

“These new routes will provide passengers with direct access to an extraordinary range of tourism, culinary, and cultural offerings, while strengthening our connectivity from Mexico City,” Mulinelli said in a press release cited by El Universal.

Looking forward to Holy Week 2027 (March 21 to 28), Aeroméxico will be offering more than 4,000 weekly seats to its Caribbean destinations across 27 weekly frequencies.

With reports from Aviación Al Día

World.title: A cheeky response to Trump and Sheinbaum’s first presidential trip to Asia: Wednesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🇺🇳 Sheinbaum fires back at Trump’s U.N. remarks: Responding to Trump’s U.N. General Assembly claim that Mexico is the “epicenter” of cartel violence and that it’s “unacceptable” for the U.S. to border a country “controlled by enemy cartels,” Sheinbaum said she could just as easily say it is “very difficult to live next to a country” with such high illegal drug use and gun production.

Responding to Trump’s U.N. General Assembly claim that Mexico is the “epicenter” of cartel violence and that it’s “unacceptable” for the U.S. to border a country “controlled by enemy cartels,” Sheinbaum said she could just as easily say it is “very difficult to live next to a country” with such high illegal drug use and gun production. 🇨🇳 Sheinbaum to attend APEC Summit in China: The president announced she’ll travel to Shenzhen, China, in November for the APEC Leaders’ Meeting — her first trip to Asia as president. Mexico will host the APEC summit in 2028.

The president announced she’ll travel to Shenzhen, China, in November for the APEC Leaders’ Meeting — her first trip to Asia as president. Mexico will host the APEC summit in 2028. 🚆 750-billion-peso investment in rail projects: Sheinbaum said Mexico is investing roughly 750 billion pesos (US $42.95 billion) in railroads this sexenio, with around 60,000 jobs tied to construction.

Why today’s mañanera matters

At her Wednesday morning press conference, President Claudia Sheinbaum offered a riposte to the Mexico-related remarks U.S. President Donald Trump made during a 37-minute speech to the U.N. General Assembly on Tuesday.

Her retort was significant as it demonstrated — once again — that Sheinbaum is prepared to forcefully counter Trump’s rhetoric on Mexico, while simultaneously seeking to maintain a positive and productive working relationship with the U.S. president and his administration.

Also of note at today’s mañanera was Sheinbaum’s disclosure that she will travel to China in November to attend the APEC Leaders’ Meeting. The trip will be Sheinbaum’s first to Asia as president. She has visited seven foreign countries since she was sworn in on Oct. 1, 2024: Panama, Brazil, Honduras, Canada, Guatemala, the United States and Spain.

Sheinbaum responds to Trump’s UN address

A reporter asked the president about Trump’s U.N. General Assembly address, highlighting that the U.S. president described Mexico as the “epicenter” of cartel violence and declared that it is “unacceptable” for the United States to share a 2,000-mile border with a country “controlled by enemy cartels.”

Sheinbaum’s first response was to note that Trump also said “something else.”

“Let’s see, what did he say?” she asked, prompting the reporter to acknowledge that the U.S. president also said that his administration has “a very good relationship with the Mexican government.”

“They take one part of the statement and not the other,” Sheinbaum said without specifying who she was referring to.

She then gave a pointed response to Trump’s declaration that it is “unacceptable” for the U.S. to share a border with a country “controlled by enemy cartels.”

“I could say it’s very difficult to live next to a country that has such a high level of illegal drug use,” Sheinbaum said.

“Or I could say it’s very difficult to live next to a country that produces so many guns,” she said.

“But I’m not going to say it,” Sheinbuam said, eliciting laughter from the press corps.

“I’m not going to say it because we have a good relationship with President Trump and the U.S. government,” she said.

“We’re working in a coordinated way [on security challenges] and we’re making progress,” Sheinbaum said.

La presidenta Sheinbaum no quiso pronunciarse sobre las declaraciones de Trump ante la ONU Afirma que es difícil vivir a lado de un país que es consumidor de drogas Nada menciona sobre la protección de su gobierno a narcopolíticos de Sinaloa pic.twitter.com/jTmGlGH0UU — Manuel Lopez San Martin (@MLopezSanMartin) September 23, 2026

Sheinbaum to attend APEC Summit in China

Asked why she decided not to travel to New York to participate in the 81st session of the U.N. General Assembly, Sheinbaum responded:

“There are moments and then there are moments when one decides to go or not go. I felt that this wasn’t the time to attend the [General] Assembly. I didn’t go last year either.”

Foreign Affairs Minister Roberto Velasco is representing Sheinbaum at the General Assembly. The president noted that he has not yet addressed the General Assembly.

She told reporters that she will attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 18 and 19. Sheinbaum noted that Mexico will host the APEC Leaders’ Meeting in 2028.

In China, “we’re going to receive the baton,” she said, although Vietnam will host the 2027 APEC event before Mexico gets its turn the year after.

Sheinbaum highlights 750-billion peso investment in rail projects

After an update on the various railroads currently under construction, Sheinbaum told reporters that the total investment in the projects is around 750 billion pesos (US $42.95 billion).

“That’s what we’re investing in trains in the sexenio,” she said, referring to her six-year period of government (2024-30).

Sheinbaum said that trains have “many virtues,” noting that they “connect regions” and “cities” and help to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by taking cars and buses off the roads.

She also highlighted that railroad projects create jobs. Sheinbuam told reporters that around 60,000 people are currently employed in jobs directly related to the construction of railroads. She also said that rail projects help drive economic growth.

“We’re very happy with the work being carried out,” Sheinbaum said, referring to the various railroad projects under construction, including lines linking Mexico City to Querétaro, Mexico City to Pachuca and Saltillo to Nuevo Laredo.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: Tolima Seismic Swarm: M4.5 Tremor Shakes Central Colombia
World.content:
Colombia · Disasters

Key Facts —The peak. A magnitude 4.5 tremor struck near Chaparral, in Colombia’s Tolima department, at 3:09 p.m. local time on Wednesday 23 September 2026, at shallow depth, and was felt in Pereira, Armenia and Bogotá. —The swarm. It was the strongest of at least ten tremors recorded around Chaparral on Wednesday alone, part of a sequence running since Sunday that included a magnitude 4.1 event among 32 movements logged in under 24 hours on Monday. —The source. All figures come from the Servicio Geológico Colombiano (SGC), the state geological service, which classifies the episode as an “enjambre sísmico” — a seismic swarm with no single mainshock. —The response. Schools in Chaparral and neighbouring Roncesvalles suspended classes on Monday as a precaution; no injuries or structural damage have been reported so far. —The context. Colombia is still counting the cost of the magnitude 7.4 Chocó earthquake of 10 August, which killed 321 people — a separate fault system, but one that has left the country sensitive to every new tremor.

Central Colombia has been shaking for days. A seismic swarm around Chaparral, in the coffee-growing department of Tolima, peaked on Wednesday afternoon with a magnitude 4.5 tremor felt as far away as Bogotá — and the state geologists say the sequence is not over.

Central Colombia’s Andean corridor, where the Tolima seismic swarm has been rumbling since Sunday. (Photo: The Rio Times archive)

What Happened in Tolima

The Servicio Geológico Colombiano recorded the day’s strongest shock at 3:09 p.m. local time on Wednesday: magnitude 4.5, shallow depth, with its epicentre near the municipality of Chaparral in southern Tolima. The nearest towns were Roncesvalles at 20 kilometres, San Antonio at 22 and Chaparral itself at 24.

The tremor was felt well beyond the epicentre. Residents reported shaking in Pereira and Armenia, the coffee-axis capitals to the northwest, and in Bogotá, more than 150 kilometres away — enough to send the word “temblor” trending across Colombia within the hour.

It did not come alone. SGC bulletins show at least ten events around Chaparral on Wednesday between late morning and mid-afternoon, most between magnitude 3.1 and 3.7, before and after the 4.5 peak. The latest bulletin at the time of writing logged a magnitude 4.1 event at 9:34 p.m. local time.

A Swarm, Not a Single Quake

The sequence began on Sunday 20 September, when the SGC registered a magnitude 4.1 tremor near Chaparral in the early hours, followed by smaller shocks through the morning. Monday brought the busiest day so far: 32 movements in the region in under 24 hours, including another magnitude 4.1.

The SGC’s own analysis describes the episode as an enjambre sísmico — a seismic swarm. In a swarm there is not necessarily one mainshock followed by aftershocks; instead, frequency rises and falls over days or weeks, and the largest event can arrive well into the sequence. That is why Wednesday’s 4.5, four days in, does not close the episode.

Local authorities moved early. Classes were suspended at schools in Chaparral and Roncesvalles on Monday as a safety precaution, and the SGC has asked residents to log what they feel through its Sismo Sentido platform, which maps reported intensity across the country.

Bogotá, more than 150 kilometres from the epicentre, felt Wednesday’s strongest tremor. (Photo: The Rio Times archive)

Why Tolima Shakes

Colombia sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire, where the Nazca Plate dives beneath South America. Tolima lies in the Central Cordillera, home to the Nevado del Tolima volcano, and the department is no stranger to either tectonic or volcanic tremors.

Wednesday’s events were shallow — the SGC lists them as superficial — which is why moderate magnitudes were felt so widely. Shallow shocks dissipate less energy with depth and tend to rattle a broader area than deeper events of similar size.

The swarm is unrelated to the aftermath of the magnitude 7.4 Chocó earthquake of 10 August on the Pacific coast, which killed 321 people and has generated more than 1,300 aftershocks. But that disaster, barely six weeks old, is the backdrop against which every new Colombian tremor is now read — and one reason Wednesday’s tremor dominated search traffic within minutes.

What It Means for Residents and Travellers

For now, the practical impact is precautionary rather than destructive. No injuries or structural damage have been reported from the Tolima sequence, and the SGC has issued no evacuation order beyond the school closures in the two municipalities nearest the epicentre.

Residents in the coffee axis and Bogotá should expect further perceptible tremors while the swarm continues. The standard guidance applies: drop, cover and hold on; stay away from façades and steep slopes on the region’s mountain roads; and follow SGC bulletins rather than social-media rumours for magnitude and location.

Travellers heading to or through Tolima — a region popular for its coffee fincas and the Combeima canyon — should check with local operators and allow for short-notice changes, particularly if the swarm intensifies.

What We Could Not Confirm

Whether any injuries or damage have occurred in the Tolima sequence — none were reported in the bulletins and coverage we reviewed. Whether classes in Chaparral and Roncesvalles remain suspended on Thursday. How long the swarm will run or whether a larger event will follow; the SGC has made no such forecast. And whether the swarm carries any volcanic component linked to the Nevado del Tolima — SGC bulletins so far list only location, magnitude and depth.

Frequently Asked Questions

How strong was the Tolima earthquake on 23 September 2026?

The strongest event was magnitude 4.5 at 3:09 p.m. local time, at shallow depth near Chaparral, Tolima, according to the Servicio Geológico Colombiano. It was felt in Pereira, Armenia and Bogotá, and a magnitude 4.1 followed at 9:34 p.m.

What is a seismic swarm?

A seismic swarm — enjambre sísmico in Spanish — is a sequence of tremors in one area without a clear single mainshock. Frequency rises and falls over days or weeks, and the largest event can arrive well into the sequence, as Wednesday’s 4.5 did four days in.

Is the Tolima swarm linked to August’s Chocó earthquake?

No. The magnitude 7.4 Chocó earthquake of 10 August struck a different region on the Pacific coast and has its own aftershock sequence. The Tolima events are in the Central Cordillera, hundreds of kilometres away, on separate fault structures.

Are there casualties or damage in Tolima?

None have been reported so far. Schools in Chaparral and Roncesvalles suspended classes on Monday as a precaution, and the SGC continues to monitor the swarm around the clock.

World.title: Argentina Explained 2026: Milei’s Experiment, the Economy and What to Watch
World.content:
GUIDES · ARGENTINA

Key Facts — Capital Buenos Aires, an autonomous federal district with its own government and its own directly elected head of government, separate from the surrounding province.

— Population 46.2 million, from the 2022 census with its undercount adjustment. International estimates run a few hundred thousand lower.

— Currency The peso, and there is more than one price for it. On 23 September 2026 the wholesale reference rate was 1,516 to the US dollar and the parallel rate about 1,555.

— Language Spanish. Argentine Spanish uses vos rather than tú , and the accent is closer to Italian than to any other Spanish in the region.

— Economy Grain, beef, shale oil and gas from Vaca Muerta, lithium and a large software and services sector. Argentina has defaulted on sovereign debt nine times.

— Government A federal presidential republic. Four-year terms with one consecutive re-election allowed, 257 deputies and 72 senators, and no prime minister.

Argentina explained without the noise: what the stabilisation programme actually did, what it has not done, and the dates that will decide whether it holds.

Argentina explained in 2026 means explaining one experiment. A libertarian economist took office promising to end chronic inflation by cutting the state, and three years in the monthly numbers have fallen a long way while the twelve-month numbers have stopped falling. Both of those things are true at once.

What kind of country is this?

Argentina runs nearly 3,700 kilometres from the subtropical north to Tierra del Fuego. The core of it is the pampas, a flat, deep-soiled plain around Buenos Aires that is among the most productive farmland anywhere. West of that is the Andes and the lithium triangle. South is Patagonia, with Vaca Muerta underneath it.

Almost all of the population lives in cities, and roughly a third of it in greater Buenos Aires alone. That concentration matters politically. A president who loses the province of Buenos Aires has lost most of the argument. It is why national politics so often looks like a fight between one metropolitan area and everywhere else.

The country was among the ten richest in the world per head in the early twentieth century. It is not now. Between then and now sit military coups, Peronism, the dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, the return of democracy, and nine sovereign defaults. That long descent is the backdrop against which Argentines assess any new economic plan, and it explains a scepticism that outsiders often read as pessimism. Any honest Argentina explained guide starts there rather than with the current headline.

The Obelisco on Avenida 9 de Julio, the centre of a metropolitan area holding roughly a third of the population (Photo: Dpalma01, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Who runs Argentina and how

Javier Milei, an economist who describes himself as an anarcho-capitalist, has been president since 10 December 2023, elected at the head of La Libertad Avanza. He inherited monthly inflation of 25.5 percent and an annual rate of 211.4 percent in his first month in office.

Congress has 257 deputies, half renewed every two years, and 72 senators, a third renewed every two years. The midterm elections of 26 October 2025 were the hinge of the term. Milei’s party took 40.66 percent and 64 of the 127 contested lower-house seats against 33.70 percent for the Peronist bloc, on the lowest turnout of any national election since 1983.

What that changed is worth stating precisely, because it is widely overstated. From 10 December 2025 La Libertad Avanza became the largest bloc in both chambers. It still has no majority. In the Chamber it holds 95 seats against 93 for the Peronists, with the rest scattered across Provincias Unidas, the PRO, the radicals and a long tail of provincial parties. Every law is still a negotiation with governors.

That is the standing feature of Argentine government rather than a quirk of this one. Provinces control their own revenue shares and their own legislators, so a president bargains with governors the way a Brazilian president bargains with party blocs. Anyone assessing a reform announcement should ask first whether the governors are in it.

How the economy works

Argentina sells grain, soy products, beef, and increasingly oil and gas. Vaca Muerta, the shale formation in Neuquén, has turned a net energy importer back into an exporter. Lithium from the northwest and a substantial software and business-services export sector sit alongside that. The agricultural export tax, called retenciones, is a permanent political argument because it funds the state and squeezes the sector that earns the dollars.

The stabilisation programme has two legs. The first is a hard fiscal anchor. Through August 2026 the Treasury had accumulated a primary surplus of 1.1 percent of output and an overall surplus of 0.2 percent. The International Monetary Fund target for the year is 1.4 percent primary. The second leg is a managed exchange rate inside a band whose limits reset monthly by past inflation.

On inflation the arc is real and the caveat is important. Monthly inflation ran at 25.5 percent in December 2023, 2.7 percent in December 2024, 2.8 percent in December 2025 and 1.7 percent in August 2026, a fourteen-month low. But the twelve-month rate rose over 2026, from 31.5 percent at the end of 2025 to 33.5 percent in August. Disinflation has stalled on an annual basis even as the monthly print improved.

There is no policy interest rate to quote. The central bank abolished its formal policy rate in July 2025 and moved to steering monetary aggregates through open-market operations, repos and reserve requirements. Anyone citing an Argentine policy rate after mid-2025 is quoting a series that stopped being updated.

Markets have turned less friendly through September 2026. Country risk rose for eight consecutive sessions to around 556 to 566 basis points on 23 September, a five-month high and more than 150 points above July’s low. Reserves fell US$481 million in a single day to US$48.9 billion. The programme is not in crisis, and it is not comfortable either.

Puerto Madero in Buenos Aires, where the banks and the country-risk screens are (Photo: Vlasta x, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

What is happening right now

As of 24 September 2026 the poverty figure for the first half of the year is the number everyone is waiting for. The last official reading was 28.2 percent for the second half of 2025, the lowest since 2018. Private estimates for the first half of 2026 cluster between 30 and 32 percent, which would mean between 1.5 and 1.7 million more people below the line since December. The official number had not been published when this guide was written.

The second story is American money. On 23 September 2026 the two governments launched the Andes-Atlantic Corridor, the first Western Hemisphere corridor under the Partnership for Global Infrastructure and Investment. The United States export credit agency is to provide financing of up to US$7 billion by 2027. A separate non-binding term sheet of up to US$6 billion is attached to the US$51 billion Argentina liquefied natural gas project in Vaca Muerta.

The third is the International Monetary Fund. A technical mission for the third review under the Extended Fund Facility arrived on 21 September 2026. On the precedent of the second review, a staff-level agreement would be followed by board approval about five weeks later. No board date has been announced.

Underneath all three sits the exchange-rate question. The peso is trading well below its band ceiling, which looks comfortable. But corporate hedging against the dollar roughly doubled to about US$12 billion between March and August 2026, and the central bank has slowed its own dollar purchases. That combination is what analysts are watching, not the spot rate.

What to watch

The statistics institute publishes on a fixed calendar and those dates are the spine of the year. Consumer prices for September land on 13 October 2026, October’s on 12 November and November’s on 15 December. Monthly activity data follow on 21 October, 24 November and 21 December. Third-quarter output arrives on 16 December.

The exchange-rate band resets every month, with the ceiling set by inflation two months earlier. The October 2026 ceiling is already fixed at 1,951.50 pesos to the dollar, up from 1,919.63 in September. November’s ceiling will be set by the September inflation print published on 13 October. That mechanism is public, so the band’s path is knowable even when the peso’s is not.

Then there is the third Fund review, which has no published board date, and beyond that the general election of October 2027. Between now and then the practical test is whether the fiscal surplus survives a year in which real wages have fallen and poverty has risen. That is the tension the whole programme rests on.

What this means for foreigners

The rules changed sharply in 2025 and a lot of published guidance is now wrong. A decree of 29 May 2025 requires non-permanent residents to hold health insurance or pay for public health services. It ends free public university for anyone who is not a citizen or permanent resident. It requires permanent-residency applicants to show sufficient means and a clean record, and it moves citizenship decisions from the courts to the migration authority. Emergency care remains free regardless of status. This is the Argentina explained change that most outdated guides miss.

The common route for people with passive income is the rentista temporary residency. It requires proof of income from assets rather than from work, at five times the statutory minimum wage, and the minimum wage is indexed, so the threshold moves. You will also need an Argentine police certificate and foreign police certificates from anywhere you lived a year or more in the last three. Documentation that the money entered through authorised financial institutions is required too.

Tax residency works on a longer clock than most countries. A foreigner living in Argentina for reasons other than work becomes a tax resident after more than twelve months, with residency taking effect from the thirteenth. That is more forgiving than the 183-day tests common elsewhere in the region, and it is one reason Argentina appears on remote-worker shortlists despite everything else.

On daily costs, the honest answer is that they depend on which exchange rate you live on. The gap between the official and parallel rates has narrowed to a few percent. That is historically unusual, and it removes the arbitrage that once made Buenos Aires extraordinarily cheap for dollar earners. Say it plainly: the country is no longer the bargain it was in 2023, because the peso is closer to being one currency again.

The Perito Moreno glacier in Santa Cruz province, at the far south of a country that runs nearly 3,700 kilometres (Photo: Luca Galuzzi (Lucag), CC BY-SA 2.5 via Wikimedia Commons)

Sources: Inflation, poverty and the release calendar from INDEC, exchange rates, reserves and monetary data from the central bank, fiscal results from the economy ministry, residency rules from the national migration directorate and the official gazette, and the corridor agreement from the United States State Department.

What Is Not Known

The official poverty rate for the first half of 2026. It was due for publication on the day this guide was written and had not appeared. Private estimates cluster at 30 to 32 percent against 28.2 percent officially for the second half of 2025. Alternative methods that update the consumption basket and account for rent would put it far higher, and that methodological dispute is itself unresolved.

Whether inflation is still falling. The monthly print hit a fourteen-month low of 1.7 percent in August 2026, but the twelve-month rate rose from 31.5 percent at the end of 2025 to 33.5 percent. The 21.3 percent accumulated in eight months annualises to roughly 33 percent, which makes the Fund’s projection of around 25 percent for the year look out of reach.

The growth number for 2026. Three credible forecasters give three answers: the Fund projected 3.5 percent in May 2026, the OECD cut to 2.6 percent in September, and market consensus had fallen to about 2.1 percent by mid-September. Second-quarter output fell 0.6 percent on the quarter. There is no settled figure.

Whether the exchange-rate band holds to the October 2027 election. The peso sits well below the ceiling, which reads as comfort. Against that, corporate dollar hedges roughly doubled to about US$12 billion between March and August 2026, the central bank has slowed its purchases, and country risk has risen more than 150 basis points since July. This is the central open question of the programme.

Whether the remaining capital controls on companies are lifted. The central bank’s president said in May 2026 that it is not among their priorities, and no timetable has been published. That directly affects whether a foreign company can repatriate profits earned before 2025.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is the president of Argentina and what is he trying to do?

Javier Milei, an economist who calls himself an anarcho-capitalist, in office since 10 December 2023. His programme rests on a hard fiscal surplus and a managed exchange-rate band, aimed at ending the chronic inflation he inherited at 211.4 percent a year.

Has inflation in Argentina actually come down?

On a monthly basis, a long way: from 25.5 percent in December 2023 to 1.7 percent in August 2026. On a twelve-month basis it has stalled and even risen, from 31.5 percent at the end of 2025 to 33.5 percent in August 2026. Both statements are true and they describe different things.

What is the exchange rate in Argentina?

There is more than one. On 23 September 2026 the wholesale reference rate was about 1,516 pesos to the US dollar and the parallel rate about 1,555. The gap has narrowed to a few percent, which is historically unusual.

Can foreigners still use free healthcare and universities in Argentina?

Not as before. A decree published on 29 May 2025 requires non-permanent residents to hold health insurance or pay for public health services, and ends free tuition at state universities for anyone who is not a citizen or permanent resident. Emergency care remains free regardless of status.

When does a foreigner become an Argentine tax resident?

After more than twelve months of living in the country for reasons other than work, with residency taking effect from the thirteenth month. That is a longer runway than the 183-day tests used in much of the region.

What does Argentina export?

Grain, soy products and beef above all, and increasingly oil and gas from the Vaca Muerta shale formation in Neuquén. Lithium from the northwest and a sizeable software and business-services sector sit alongside them.

World.title: Recife Wreck Diving Complaint Goes to Brazilian Federal Prosecutors
World.content:
Pernambuco · Environment

Key Facts — What happened Divers and dive operators reported murky water and litter over Recife’s sunken ships, and a lawyer took the reports to federal prosecutors.

— Where this is Pernambuco is a state on Brazil’s north-eastern coast. Recife, its capital, faces the Atlantic.

— Why it matters Brazil’s tourism board calls Recife the country’s capital of shipwrecks, with more than 26 sunken vessels along the state coast.

— The catch No visibility reading has been reported, and the port says no confirmed technical evidence links the dredging to the pollution.

— What it costs The dredging is budgeted at R$95 million (about US$18.5 million), converted at a rate of 5.14 to the US dollar.

— Who is looking at it A federal prosecutor already opened a procedure on the same dredging in July 2026, after a complaint by Recife fishermen.

Divers off Recife, which Brazil’s tourism board calls the country’s shipwreck capital, say the water above the sunken ships has turned cloudy. The Porto do Recife, which is deepening its shipping channel under a state licence, says no confirmed evidence ties the work to the litter.

File photograph of Carneiros beach at Tamandaré, on the Pernambuco coast. The sunken ships divers visit lie in deeper water off the state capital. (Photo: Rio Times media library)

Recife wreck diving is the subject of a complaint now sitting with Brazil’s federal prosecutors. Divers say the water over the city’s sunken ships has turned cloudy and full of litter.

The complaint asks whether a licensed dredging project at the Porto do Recife is behind it. The port says no confirmed technical evidence supports that link.

This matters to anyone who was thinking of going. The wrecks are one of the reasons foreigners fly to Pernambuco at all.

What the divers reported

Dive operators told Leonardo Accioly, a lawyer and a diver, that litter and sediment had spoiled dives off the city. He filed a report on Monday 21 September 2026.

It went to the Ministério Público Federal, Brazil’s federal prosecution service. That body can open civil environmental inquiries and ask agencies for information.

Accioly described “the complete unviability of diving at most of the wrecks in the park”. The water, he said, “is cloudy and with a lot of rubbish”.

Those words were quoted by the Diario de Pernambuco, the Recife newspaper that reported the filing on Wednesday 23 September 2026. Accioly also spoke of harm to fragile marine life.

He is not presenting the dredging as a proven cause. He told the paper there is no proof that the litter comes from it.

The point of the filing, he said, is to have that possibility investigated.

The filing asks prosecutors to look at dredger tracking data, dumping records and sediment dispersion studies. It also asks for an expert survey of the wreck park itself.

Why Recife wreck diving draws foreigners

Embratur, Brazil’s national tourism board, counts more than 26 submerged vessels along the Pernambuco coast. It calls Recife “the Brazilian capital of shipwrecks”.

Embratur names the Servemar, Virgo, Taurus, Pirapama and Servemar X as the most visited. It puts the dive sites at depths of 25 to 50 metres.

Many of the ships were put on the bottom deliberately, to grow artificial reefs. They lie off the Recife coastline and are reached by boat.

The Diario de Pernambuco names three wrecks in the affected area: the tugs Mercurius, Saveiros and Taurus. The Taurus also sits on the tourism board’s most-visited list.

A trailing suction hopper dredger of the kind used for port maintenance work. File photograph of the Pallieter, of Belgium’s Jan De Nul, at Zeebrugge; this is not the vessel working at the Porto do Recife. (Photo: Marc Ryckaert, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

The dredging, and what its permits require

The work began in June 2026 at the Porto do Recife, the port beside the old city centre. It deepens the access channel, the turning basin and the berths.

It is budgeted at R$95 million (about US$18.5 million) in federal money. Another R$15 million (about US$2.9 million) is going on 97 new fenders along the quays.

Those conversions use a rate of 5.14 to the US dollar. That is the Central Bank of Brazil reference rate for 23 September 2026.

The contractor is DTA Engenharia and the vessel is the Dutch-flagged dredger Amazone. Dredged material goes to an ocean dumping ground about six nautical miles offshore.

Six nautical miles is a little over 11 kilometres. The complaint says the southern edge of that ground lies about 1.5 kilometres from the wreck park.

The port names two authorisations for the first phase. One is a technical note from CPRH, the Pernambuco state environment agency that licensed the project.

The other is an order from the Capitania dos Portos de Pernambuco, the Brazilian Navy’s harbourmaster for the state. The Capitania says it cleared maintenance dredging of the channel, with completion expected in December 2026.

CPRH told Marco Zero Conteúdo in July 2026 that it had imposed continuous monitoring by small boats. Anything that surfaces must be collected at once.

What the port says

The Porto do Recife told the Diario de Pernambuco that the dredging holds CPRH authorisation. Its procedures, it said, include monitoring of water quality and sediments.

There is “no confirmed technical evidence that the dredging is related to the pollution”, the port said. It used the same wording about waste settling on the wrecks.

The port also said it will widen its monitoring around the main wrecks. The new readings are to cover litter, turbidity and water transparency.

It said it had met divers and operators recently to hear their accounts. It says it has pulled more than 10 tonnes of solid waste out of the estuary since the work began.

Wagner Maciel, the port’s chief executive, has argued for the project on tourism grounds. He says deeper water will let cruise ships berth at the passenger terminal rather than between two warehouses.

The argument has a history

The divers’ report is not the first complaint aimed at this project. Lobster fishermen made a similar one in July 2026 about plastic in their traps.

The federal prosecutor Antonio Nilo Rayol Lobo Segundo signed the opening of a procedure on 29 July 2026. He asked CPRH and the port for information on the works and their approvals.

That procedure came from the Colônia de Pescadores Z-1 do Pina, a Recife fishing guild. Prosecutors took it because the dumping ground sits inside Brazil’s territorial sea.

CPRH acknowledged then that suction can stir up material buried in the riverbed. Sediment may rise into the water column and reach the surface, the agency said.

The same agency ruled the dredging out as the cause of a February 2022 wave of beach litter. Heavy rain and strong winds explained that episode, it said.

What would settle it

The Diario de Pernambuco report carries no visibility measurement. The turbidity and transparency readings the port has promised would be the first numbers to test the divers’ account.

Prosecutors can also seek the expert survey the filing asks for. They have already asked CPRH and the port for information about the works.

No authority has found wrongdoing and nobody has been charged. The port says the works meet every technical and legal requirement that applies.

The first phase covers about 76% of the planned volume, according to the port. The designs for the harder second phase have still to be approved.

For a visitor who has booked Recife wreck diving, the question is simply when the water clears. The port has forecast finishing in November 2026, and the Capitania expects the work to end in December 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Recife wreck diving still going ahead?

Dive operators told the lawyer who filed the complaint that litter and sediment had spoiled dives, and he described most of the park as unviable. The Porto do Recife says it has met divers and operators and will extend its monitoring to the main wrecks, covering litter, turbidity and water transparency. Anyone with a trip booked should ask their operator about conditions on the day.

What is the dredging for?

The Porto do Recife is deepening its access channel, turning basin and berths so that larger vessels can come in. The work is budgeted at R$95 million (about US$18.5 million) in federal money and is being carried out by DTA Engenharia with the Dutch-flagged dredger Amazone. The port’s chief executive, Wagner Maciel, has argued that deeper water will also let cruise ships berth at the passenger terminal instead of alongside warehouses.

Who is investigating, and has anyone been blamed?

Brazil’s federal prosecution service, the Ministério Público Federal, opened a procedure on 29 July 2026 after a complaint from a Recife fishing guild, and received the divers’ report on 21 September 2026. No authority has found wrongdoing and nobody has been charged. The port says no confirmed technical evidence links the dredging to the pollution, and the state environment agency ruled the dredging out as the cause of a comparable episode in February 2022.

Who licensed the work?

CPRH, the Pernambuco state environment agency, issued the environmental authorisation and set the conditions, including continuous monitoring by small boats and immediate collection of anything that surfaces. The Capitania dos Portos de Pernambuco, the Brazilian Navy’s harbourmaster for the state, separately authorised the maintenance dredging of the access channel and has said it expects the work to end in December 2026. The disposal ground lies in the territorial sea, which is federal, and that is why federal prosecutors have a role.

World.title: Porto Digital Built a Tech Hub on a Tax Break Brazil Is Phasing Out
World.content:
Brazil · Technology

Key Facts — What happened Porto Digital ended 2025 with 541 companies and 24,079 employees in Recife’s old port district, its own figures show.

— Where this is The Bairro do Recife, an island district in Recife, capital of Pernambuco state in Brazil’s Northeast.

— How the money works Technology firms inside the perimeter pay a 2 percent municipal services tax, set by city law and the lowest Brazil allows.

— What the companies bill They billed R$7.4 billion in 2025 (about US$1.4 billion), 19 percent more than in 2024.

— The catch Brazil’s tax reform strips municipalities of that power and cuts services-tax rates in stages from 2029, abolishing the tax in 2033.

— What comes next The state and the park are spending R$51 million (about US$9.9 million) to 2028 on units outside Recife.

Porto Digital turned a derelict port district in Brazil’s Northeast into one of the country’s largest technology clusters. The city tax rule that built it starts winding down in 2029 and disappears in 2033.

Avenida Rio Branco at night in the Bairro do Recife, the port district that houses Porto Digital. File photograph. (Photo: Marcos Elias de Oliveira Júnior, CC0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Porto Digital, the technology park inside Recife’s old port district, ended 2025 with 541 companies and 24,079 employees. Those companies billed R$7.4 billion (about US$1.4 billion), 19 percent more than in 2024.

Recife is the capital of Pernambuco, a state in Brazil’s Northeast. The park occupies a small island of warehouses and period buildings that had fallen derelict.

For anyone weighing where to put a technology operation in Brazil, the mechanism matters more than the totals. Porto Digital rests on a city tax rate that Brazil’s tax reform will take away.

A 2 percent tax rate, written into city law

The park began in 2000 as a state policy rather than a private venture. Its address is Cais do Apolo, 222, on the island known as the Bairro do Recife.

Recife’s council cut the municipal services tax, known by its Portuguese initials ISS, to 2 percent. That applied to information technology firms in the old port, under a city law of 2004.

Later laws widened both the map and the list of eligible trades. A 2011 law brought in the neighbouring Santo Amaro district and creative-economy work.

Laws of 2013 and 2015 widened the perimeter again. It now covers the historic port site, a block of Santo Amaro and two downtown avenues.

The building rule is a separate law

Relief tied to restoration came later, and it is a different instrument. Recife’s Recentro law, number 18,869 of 9 December 2021, rewards owners who rebuild central properties.

Exemption from IPTU, the property tax, runs at 100 percent for ten years for recovery and renovation work. Ordinary repairs earn 60 percent for three years.

The same law cuts the services tax to 2 percent for listed activities for ten years. It also refunds the transfer tax on first sales and waives urban and environmental licensing fees.

City hall publishes those terms on the programme’s own site. The covered area is Boa Vista, Santo Antônio, São José and the Bairro do Recife.

What Porto Seguro does. Porto Seguro S.A., together with its subsidiaries, provides a range of insurance products and services in Brazil and Uruguay. It offers auto, residential, travel, cell phone, life, motorcycle, notebook and tablet, photo and video, smart and games, bike, real estate, green card, bail, and moving insurance products, as well as reinsurance, combined…

Who runs the park, and on whose money

The park is run by the Núcleo de Gestão do Porto Digital, a private non-profit set up in December 2000. Pernambuco and Recife both qualify it as a social organisation.

That status in Brazilian law lets a government contract a non-profit to deliver a public service. The body says it works with industry, government, universities and civil-society groups.

In December 2024 the state signed a four-year management contract worth R$44.5 million (about US$8.7 million). The money flows through the state science, technology and innovation secretariat.

The Bairro do Recife island from the air, water on both sides and the breakwater beyond. File photograph. (Photo: Rio Times media library)

The tax lever has an expiry date

Brazil’s 2023 constitutional amendment and its 2025 implementing law replace the services tax with national levies. Cities lose the power to grant their own consumption-tax breaks.

The amendment sets the timetable itself. Services-tax rates fall to nine tenths of their legislated level in 2029, then to six tenths by 2032.

Local tax breaks shrink in the same proportion, and the tax disappears in 2033. Until 2029 Recife’s 2 percent rate applies in full.

Two percent is already the lowest rate Brazil’s constitution lets a city charge. Lawyers writing in the legal journal Conjur on 21 September 2026 expect effective rates to fall below it.

An analysis published by the digital imprint of Pernambuco’s bar association reaches the same conclusion for the park. Unlike the state tax, it notes, the services tax carries no compensation scheme.

The new code does keep one thing for old districts. Its article 158 cuts the new levies by 60 percent on rehabilitation work in historic zones.

Municipalities must define those zones by their own law. Projects then go to a commission of two federal ministries and the new tax committee.

What holds the district up, and what could tip it

Research sits inside the perimeter, not beside it. CESAR, an innovation institute founded in Recife in 1996, four years before the park, is among its largest employers.

Restoration is real and countable. Porto Digital has itself requalified 19 historic buildings, about 40,000 square metres, Folha PE reported in April 2026.

More than 200 further buildings inside the perimeter were restored by their private owners, the same report said. Housing has started to follow the offices.

Moura Dubeux, a Recife developer, delivered 251 flats on 28 January 2026. They sit in two towers retrofitted from the century-old Moinho Recife grain silos.

The wider centre is in worse shape. Recife’s civil defence rated 136 buildings there at high or very high risk in 2025, Diário de Pernambuco reported.

Pay is the other pressure. Movimento Econômico reported in May 2026 that senior Brazilian developers earn R$12,000 to R$18,000 a month (about US$2,300 to US$3,500).

Foreign employers pay far more for the same people without asking them to move. The hiring platform Deel recorded a 53 percent rise in foreign hiring of Brazilian technology workers in 2024.

Public support also carries dates. The state management contract runs four years from December 2024, and the inland programme is funded through 2028.

The next bet is inland

In June 2026 the state and the park announced R$51 million (about US$9.9 million) through 2028 for sites outside Recife. Of that, R$12.9 million (about US$2.5 million) goes to Petrolina.

Petrolina sits on the São Francisco river in Pernambuco’s irrigated fruit belt. Its unit will take about 2,500 square metres on the campus of the federal university there.

Smaller outposts are planned for Garanhuns and Araripina. An inland site opened in Caruaru in August 2025, inside the old Caroá factory.

Conversion figures here use a rate of 5.14 to the US dollar. That is the Brazilian Central Bank PTAX reference for 23 September 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

What exactly is Porto Digital?

It is a technology park in the Bairro do Recife, the old port district of Recife, capital of Pernambuco state in north-eastern Brazil. It started in 2000 as a state public policy, not as a private development. It is an open urban park rather than a gated campus, so its companies occupy ordinary buildings across the district. Its own figures for 2025 give 541 companies, 24,079 employees and combined billings of R$7.4 billion (about US$1.4 billion).

What tax break do companies get there?

Recife’s council cut the municipal services tax, ISS, to 2 percent for information technology firms in the old port under a city law of 2004. Later laws of 2011, 2013 and 2015 widened the area and added creative-economy activities. A separate city law, Recentro, number 18,869 of 9 December 2021, deals with buildings. It exempts owners from the property tax for up to ten years when they recover or renovate central properties, and waives licensing fees.

Is the tax break really ending?

Brazil’s 2023 constitutional amendment and its 2025 implementing law replace the municipal services tax with national levies, and municipalities lose the power to grant their own consumption-tax breaks. Under the amendment itself, services-tax rates fall in stages from 2029 and the tax is abolished in 2033. A study published by the digital imprint of Pernambuco’s bar association notes that, unlike the state tax it replaces, the services tax carries no compensation scheme for lost benefits.

Which companies are based in the park?

Exame reported in March 2026 that the largest by revenue included Accenture, Avanade, CESAR, Deloitte, Extreme Group, Incognia, Neurotech, Globo, Safetec and Tempest. The largest employers it listed were Accenture, Avanade, CESAR, Datamétrica, Deloitte, FITec, Neurotech, Provider, Serttel and Speedmais. Movimento Econômico reported in August 2026 that Banco Inter was setting up its technology base in the district.

World.title: Mato Grosso Cotton Margins Narrow as Full Costs Outrun the Price
World.content:
Brazil · Agriculture

Key Facts — What happened Cotton in Mato Grosso is selling above its cash cost of production but below its full cost, IMEA says.

— The catch Covering every cost, including depreciation and a return on capital, needs R$147.47 an arroba of lint (about US$28.68).

— Where this is Mato Grosso is a vast state in central Brazil, and the country’s biggest producer of cotton, soy and maize.

— Its share of the crop Mato Grosso grows close to 70 percent of Brazil’s cotton, and Bahia about 21 percent, the US Agriculture Department says.

— Why it matters abroad Brazil is the world’s largest cotton exporter, shipping a record 3.37 million tonnes in the year to July 2026.

— What the currency is worth Brazil’s real traded at a rate of 5.1414 to the US dollar on 23 September 2026, on Banco Central PTAX data.

Growers in Brazil’s biggest farm state are covering what they spend in cash, but not what a hectare truly costs. The institute that tracks the numbers calls the margin tight.

Self-propelled pickers harvesting cotton on a large Brazilian farm, seen from the air. File photograph. (Photo: Rio Times media library)

Mato Grosso cotton is selling for enough to cover what growers spend in cash, and little more. The state’s farm-economics institute published that arithmetic this week.

That matters well beyond Brazil. Mato Grosso cotton margins help decide how much fibre the world will have to spin next year.

Brazil is the largest cotton exporter on earth, and this one state is its engine. The state grows close to 70 percent of national output, the United States Department of Agriculture says.

The numbers behind the squeeze

The Instituto Mato-Grossense de Economia Agropecuária, known as IMEA, tracks farm costs across the state. Its August reading for the 2026/27 season puts the full cost of a hectare at R$18,709.02 (about US$3,639).

That figure includes depreciation and a return on the capital tied up in land and machinery. The effective operating cost, the cash a grower pays out, is R$15,250.61 (about US$2,966).

Forward sales of the 2026/27 crop have averaged R$129.67 an arroba of lint (about US$25.20). An arroba is a Brazilian weight unit of 15 kilograms, or 33.07 pounds.

Covering the operating cost needed R$120.06 an arroba (about US$23.35). Covering every cost needed R$147.47 (about US$28.68).

Conversions use the Banco Central do Brasil closing quote of 23 September 2026, a rate of 5.1414 to the US dollar. At that rate the lint price is near 76 US cents a pound.

Full cost, on the same conversion, sits near 87 cents. Sales are running about 12 percent below that full-cost line.

Cotton costs are not the problem

The squeeze is real, but its cause is not a cost explosion. IMEA’s July comparison put this season’s spending on inputs 1.44 percent below last season’s.

Full cost rose only 1.04 percent on the same comparison. Soybeans, the state’s other great crop, saw input spending rise 3.35 percent.

What did jump was rent. Payments to landlords rose 4.72 percent in August alone, IMEA said.

Fertiliser is the other pressure point. In July a tonne of ammonium sulphate cost 19.43 arrobas of lint, 18.73 percent above the three-year average.

In February 2026 that ratio sat just below the average. Growers now hand over more fibre for the same sack of nutrients.

Open cotton bolls on the plant, ready for picking. File photograph from the library record titled Lavoura de algodao. (Photo: Rio Times media library)

Why the crop grows in soy’s shadow

Most cotton here is a second crop, IMEA data show. Farmers take off their soybeans first, then plant cotton into the same field in the same season.

That makes timing everything. A late soy harvest pushes cotton sowing past its best window and costs yield.

It also ties the two crops together financially. The same fertiliser, diesel and chemicals feed both, and one rent cheque covers both.

Soy sowing for the coming season has only just begun in the state. IMEA put it at 1.15 percent of the area on Friday 18 September 2026.

In the state’s south-east the earliest sowers were irrigated farms and cotton growers, the institute said. Cotton itself goes in after the soy harvest, gathering pace in January.

Growers already cut back once

The pressure showed up in the ground last season. The Mato Grosso cotton area fell 11.18 percent, to 1.37 million hectares.

IMEA blamed high costs and unattractive prices at the moment growers were deciding. It measured the area by satellite mapping of planted fields.

The weather then rescued the harvest. Yields reached a state record of 323.37 arrobas of seed cotton per hectare.

Even so, state output fell 8.86 percent, to 6.67 million tonnes of seed cotton. Nationally, the federal crop agency Conab logged a record 4.14 million tonnes of lint.

Where next season is heading

Every published projection for 2026/27 points up rather than down. Conab expects Brazil’s cotton area to reach 2.09 million hectares.

That would be 3.68 percent more than this season, Conab says. Mato Grosso would add more hectares than any other state, a rise of 3.38 percent.

Conab also expects national yields to fall 3.23 percent. It cites uncertainty over El Niño, the Pacific warming pattern that shifts Brazilian rainfall.

Agroconsult, a consultancy that advises the farm sector, is more bullish. It told the Brazilian Cotton Congress in Belo Horizonte on Wednesday 23 September 2026 that area could reach 2.22 million hectares.

André Pessoa, a director of Agroconsult, put that rise at about 7 percent. He pointed to prices above 80 US cents a pound and much heavier trading.

What the world buys from here

Brazil shipped a record 3.37 million tonnes of lint in the year to July 2026. That was 19 percent more than the year before, according to Abrapa.

Abrapa is the Brazilian Association of Cotton Producers, the growers’ own national body. Its figures put United States exports at about 2.66 million tonnes and Australia at 1.24 million.

The Brazilian sales earned US$5.3 billion. China was the largest single buyer.

The New York cotton benchmark stood near 83 US cents a pound on Thursday 24 September 2026, on Trading Economics data. That is roughly 30 percent above a year earlier, and about 6 percent below a month ago.

So the fibre is dearer than it was, and the hectare still barely pays. That tension will decide how much cotton the world gets in 2027.

More: Brazil coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why should a shopper abroad care about one Brazilian state?

Brazil is the world’s largest exporter of cotton lint, and Mato Grosso cotton makes up close to 70 percent of the Brazilian crop, according to the United States Department of Agriculture. Bahia is next, at roughly 21 percent. What growers in Mato Grosso decide to plant therefore moves a large slice of the raw material that mills in China, Bangladesh, Vietnam and Turkey spin into cloth. Thin margins now can mean less fibre, and dearer fibre, a year later.

What do IMEA’s cost measures actually mean?

IMEA publishes three layers. The effective operating cost is the cash a grower actually pays out in a season, including seed, fertiliser, chemicals, fuel, labour and land rent. The total operating cost adds depreciation on machinery and buildings. The total cost adds a return on the capital tied up in the business. A crop that covers the first two but not the third is paying its bills while slowly eating its own balance sheet.

Is Brazil really ahead of the United States in cotton exports?

Yes, and not narrowly. Abrapa, using Brazilian customs data and United States Department of Agriculture figures, puts Brazilian shipments at 3.37 million tonnes in the commercial year to July 2026, against about 2.66 million tonnes for the United States and 1.24 million for Australia. USDA’s own annual report on Brazil, published on 6 April 2026, says Brazil is set to keep that lead.

Will there be more Brazilian cotton next year or less?

Both published forecasts point to more area. Conab, the federal crop agency, projects 2.09 million hectares for 2026/27, up 3.68 percent, with Mato Grosso adding the most hectares of any state. Agroconsult, a private consultancy, told the 15th Brazilian Cotton Congress in Belo Horizonte on 23 September 2026 that the figure could reach 2.22 million hectares, a rise of about 7 percent. Both are projections, and Conab expects average yields to fall because of El Niño.

Sources: Revista Cultivar on IMEA’s August cost and break-even figures, Mais Soja reproducing IMEA’s weekly cotton bulletin, Notícias Agrícolas on IMEA’s year-on-year cost comparison, Agrolink on fertiliser spending and the exchange ratio, Agrolink on the 11.18 percent cut in planted area, Conab’s 12th crop survey of 15 September 2026, Conab’s outlook for the 2026/27 season, Abrapa on record cotton exports, Portugal Têxtil on the world export ranking, CNN Brasil on the export record and its destinations, USDA Cotton and Products Annual for Brazil, Boca Notícias on Agroconsult’s congress projection, CenárioMT on IMEA’s soy sowing report, Trading Economics on the New York cotton benchmark, Banco Central do Brasil for the exchange rate

World.title: Mato Grosso Farm Output Hit US$32 Billion in 2025, IBGE Crop Data Show
World.content:
Brazil · Agriculture

Key Facts — What happened Mato Grosso’s 2025 crops were worth 165.6 billion reais (about US$32.2 billion), the most of any Brazilian state.

— The state in question Mato Grosso is Brazil’s third-largest state by area, in the centre-west, with no coastline and no nearby port.

— Why it matters The state grew 30.4% of Brazil’s soybeans and 38.5% of its maize in 2025, on IBGE volume figures.

— The catch A study by Senar-MT and IMEA puts total soybean cost up 16.69% a hectare for the 2026/27 season.

— The cost of distance Trucking soybeans from Sorriso to the port of Santos cost 500 reais a tonne (about US$97) in July 2026.

— What the currency is worth Brazil’s real traded at a rate of 5.1414 to the US dollar on 23 September 2026, on Banco Central PTAX data.

Mato Grosso farm output set a record in 2025, with crops alone worth about US$32.2 billion on figures from Brazil’s statistics agency. Its growers say costs are rising faster than the crop pays.

Combine harvesters working a soybean field in Brazil. File photograph. (Photo: Rio Times media library)

Mato Grosso farm output was worth 165.6 billion reais in 2025, or about US$32.2 billion. It was the largest crop total of any Brazilian state.

The figure comes from IBGE, Brazil’s national statistics agency, which published it on 17 September 2026. It counts crops only, at the prices growers actually received.

That matters well beyond Brazil. This one state grew about as many soybeans in 2025 as the whole of Argentina.

Mato Grosso is Brazil’s third-largest state by area, bigger than France. It has no coastline, and its crops reach a port only after 1,000 to 2,000 km by road.

What the number actually measures

The survey behind it is called Produção Agrícola Municipal, or municipal crop production. It tracks 70 crops in every Brazilian municipality, year by year.

The values are at current prices, so inflation is not stripped out. Livestock is excluded, which leaves the state’s large cattle herd outside the total.

Nor is this the size of the state’s economy. IBGE put Mato Grosso’s gross domestic product at 273.0 billion reais (about US$53.1 billion) in 2023, the latest year published.

It is not export earnings either. Conversions here use a rate of 5.1414 to the US dollar.

That is the closing PTAX rate published by Banco Central do Brasil, the central bank, for 23 September 2026.

Three crops, one state

Soybeans, maize and cotton together made up 95.9% of the state’s crop value. Soybeans alone were worth 90.3 billion reais (about US$17.6 billion).

Maize brought 38.7 billion reais (about US$7.5 billion) and cotton 29.9 billion reais (about US$5.8 billion). Mato Grosso supplied 17.9% of Brazil’s crop value.

By volume the concentration is starker. In 2025 the state grew 30.4% of Brazil’s soybeans, 38.5% of its maize and 72.3% of its cotton.

One municipality, Sapezal, earned more from crops than any other in Brazil, at 8.6 billion reais (about US$1.7 billion). Five of the national top ten sit in Mato Grosso.

A satellite view of farmland at Alto Taquari in Mato Grosso. File image. (Photo: “Alto Taquari” by Coordenação-Geral de Observação da Terra/INPE, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.)

A 37% jump, and what drove it

The 2025 value was 37.1% above 2024. Volume explains part of that, as the state’s soybean harvest rose 30.7% and its maize crop 14.5%.

Prices explain much of the rest. IBGE said the 2024 crop had been hurt by El Niño, and that maize, cotton and soybean prices firmed during 2025.

The agency also pointed to the tariff dispute between the United States and China. Chinese buyers turned to Brazilian soybeans, which held domestic prices steady late in the year.

How that looks from outside Brazil

Mato Grosso harvested 50.2 million tonnes of soybeans in calendar 2025, on IBGE’s count. That is close to the entire crop of Argentina, the world’s third-largest producer.

The United States Department of Agriculture put Argentina at 51.1 million tonnes for 2024/25 and 49.5 million for 2025/26. Those estimates are from its September 2026 world production report.

Maize tells the same story. The state’s 54.3 million tonnes in 2025 exceeded the combined 2025/26 crops of Ukraine and South Africa.

The same American agency puts those two at 30.9 million and 18.1 million tonnes.

Why growers are not celebrating

Record value has not meant record profit. A cost study was presented to farmers in Brasnorte, in the north-west of the state, on 9 September 2026.

It is run by Senar-MT, the Mato Grosso arm of Brazil’s rural training service, and IMEA, the state’s farm economics institute. It projects total soybean cost at 8,171.41 reais a hectare (about US$1,589), up 16.69%.

The same study projects earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation down 35.05% a hectare. Yields are expected to slip 5.43%, to 62.44 sacks a hectare.

Maize looks worse on the same numbers. For the high-technology second-crop system that profit measure falls 88.16%, to 122.26 reais a hectare (about US$24).

Milena Habeck, an IMEA production-cost analyst, said gross revenue does not cover total cost. That measure includes the opportunity cost of a grower’s own capital, she added.

Aprosoja-MT, the state’s soybean and maize growers’ association, presses the same case. Its press office issued these remarks by its administrative director, Diego Bertuol, on 17 September 2026.

“We are coming off four years of pressured margins, high interest rates, inputs at historic prices and commodities without matching gains.”

The road and the railway

Distance is the permanent tax on all of this. Trucking soybeans 1,961 km from Sorriso to the port of Santos cost 500 reais a tonne (about US$97) in July 2026.

Those rates come from Conab, Brazil’s national food supply agency, in its August 2026 logistics bulletin. The shorter northern run to the river port of Miritituba cost 290 reais a tonne (about US$56).

The same agency’s July 2026 bulletin put Mato Grosso at 74% of Brazil’s maize exports in the period it covers.

Most of that load leaves on the BR-163, the federal highway running north from Mato Grosso into Pará. Its concessionaire, Nova Rota do Oeste, is widening the state stretch.

It had 230 km open as dual carriageway by late June 2026, with 96 km left. It aims to finish those by December 2026.

That northern route is why the Ferrogrão railway matters. The planned 933 km line would run from Sinop in Mato Grosso to Miritituba in Pará.

Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court cleared a legal obstacle on Thursday 21 May 2026. It upheld the 2017 law that cut protected land from the Jamanxim National Park in Pará.

The case, ADI 6553, was brought by the left-wing Socialism and Liberty Party, known as PSOL. The majority followed Justice Alexandre de Moraes and held that the line still needs every licence the law requires.

The court’s president, Justice Edson Fachin, was the only member to uphold the challenge.

ANTT, the land transport regulator, approved updated studies and a new concession model on 11 September 2026. The papers went to the federal audit court, the TCU, for review.

CenárioMT, a Mato Grosso news site, put the investment in the line at 33.3 billion reais (about US$6.5 billion). It reported that the auction is projected for 2027.

Until then, the trucks do the work.

What it means outside Brazil

The 2025 record shows how much of the world’s animal feed now leans on one Brazilian state. The cost figures show how thin the margin behind it has become.

More: Brazil coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where is Mato Grosso and what is it known for?

Mato Grosso is a state in Brazil’s centre-west, bordering Bolivia, and the country’s third-largest by area. Its capital is Cuiabá. It has no coastline, so its crops move to port by road, rail and river. Soybeans, maize and cotton dominate, and towns such as Sorriso and Sapezal are among the highest-earning farm municipalities in Brazil. Cattle ranching is also large, although IBGE’s crop survey does not count it.

Does the Mato Grosso farm output figure include cattle?

No. The 165.6 billion reais total, about US$32.2 billion, covers crops only. IBGE’s Produção Agrícola Municipal survey measures 70 crops at the prices growers received, in calendar 2025 and at current prices. It is not the state’s gross domestic product, which IBGE put at 273.0 billion reais, about US$53.1 billion, in 2023. It is not export revenue either.

How does one Brazilian state compare with whole countries?

Mato Grosso harvested 50.2 million tonnes of soybeans in 2025, on IBGE figures. In September 2026 the United States Department of Agriculture put Argentina’s whole crop at 51.1 million tonnes for 2024/25 and 49.5 million for 2025/26. The state’s 54.3 million tonnes of maize exceeded the same agency’s 2025/26 estimates for Ukraine and South Africa combined, at 30.9 million and 18.1 million tonnes.

If output is a record, why are farmers complaining?

Because costs rose faster than prices. A study by Senar-MT and IMEA, presented on 9 September 2026, projects total soybean cost at 8,171.41 reais a hectare, about US$1,589, for the 2026/27 season, a rise of 16.69%. It projects earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation down 35.05% a hectare. Freight is part of the squeeze: Conab recorded 500 reais a tonne, about US$97, from Sorriso to Santos in July 2026.

Sources: IBGE, Produção Agrícola Municipal 2025 (informativo), IBGE on the record national crop value, IBGE SIDRA table 5457 for the state and national values, United States Department of Agriculture, World Agricultural Production, September 2026, Conab logistics bulletins on freight rates and export shares, CenárioMT on the Senar-MT and IMEA cost study, Olhar Direto on costs, yields and margins, Supremo Tribunal Federal on its ruling in ADI 6553, CenárioMT on the ANTT model for the Ferrogrão line, Agência Estado on ANTT sending the Ferrogrão studies to the TCU, Nova Rota do Oeste on the BR-163 widening timetable

World.title: São Paulo Nightlife Tonight — September 24, 2026
World.content:
São Paulo · Nightlife

If You Only Go to One Place Walerie Gondim Sings Gal Costa at Blue Note She played Gal Costa on stage in “Gal – O Musical”, and the club calls this her first show. Her set starts at 10.30 p.m., after a Ray Charles and BB King celebration at 8 p.m.

Tonight at a Glance — Walerie Gondim · Blue Note “Estado de Graça”, the late set, at 10.30 p.m.

— Adriano Grineberg · Blue Note A Ray Charles and BB King celebration, at 8 p.m.

— Neither flagged Neither of tonight’s sets carried a last-tickets label on the club’s programme today.

— Late-set price Press listings give R$140 full and R$70 half, about US$27.40 and US$13.70. The club publishes none.

— Free at the weekend The club marks entry to its Saturday and Sunday daytime music sessions as free.

— Book the weekend now Friday and Saturday both carry the club’s last-tickets label.

— Under-18s The club admits minors only with a parent or legal guardian.

Tonight, Thursday 24 September 2026, the jazz room on Avenida Paulista runs two sets and neither is flagged as running low. All times below are São Paulo time, four hours behind London.

Avenida Paulista at night, the avenue above the Blue Note’s room in the Conjunto Nacional (Photo: Sailko, CC BY 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

What’s On Tonight

Blue Note São Paulo lists two separate shows tonight. Adriano Grineberg opens at 8 p.m. with a Ray Charles and BB King celebration.

The late set at 10.30 p.m. is Walerie Gondim with “Estado de Graça”. The club’s own page for the show calls it her first, built on the songs of Gal Costa.

Gondim played Gal Costa on stage this year in “Gal – O Musical”. She performs with a quartet, and the club says the show carries its own arrangements rather than copies of the records.

That page names “Baby”, “Tigresa” and “Flor de Maracujá” among the songs. It says the set also reaches for hidden corners of the catalogue.

Neither set carried a last-tickets label on the club’s programme on 24 September. Friday and Saturday both did.

The club publishes no price, on its programme index or on either show page. The figure appears only at the Eventim checkout that the buy button opens.

One ticket covers one session, and the club clears the room within 15 minutes of the first set. Anyone staying for the second must buy again, subject to space, and rejoin the queue.

Two Ways into the Same Room, for Nothing

The club marks its daytime music sessions “entrada gratuita” on its own homepage, apart from the ticketed evening programme. Saturday brings Feijoada Raiz, from midday to 4 p.m.

Sunday brings Brunch Music, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Both carry live music, a samba circle on Saturday and jazz on Sunday, and the club marks entry to both as free.

Food and drink are charged separately in each case. The feijoada and brunch buffets are free for children up to five and half price from six to eleven.

The music is the part that costs nothing.

That matters for a first visit. You can see the room, the stage and the sightlines before you commit to a ticket.

A weekday lunch session, Tuesday to Friday from midday to 3 p.m., carries the same free-entry mark.

It is also the answer if the weekend evenings sell through. Friday and Saturday both carry the club’s last-tickets label.

The club takes bookings for the daytime sessions, for up to 25 people, on (11) 7577-0900.

The Rest of the Weekend

Friday brings Amy Reggaehouse in two sets, at 8 p.m. and 10.30 p.m. The club says the tribute was founded in Salvador and is led by the singer Clariana.

It was named best Amy Winehouse tribute in the world in 2020, the club says.

Saturday brings Demônios da Garoa with “Clássicos & Bossas”, also at 8 p.m. and 10.30 p.m. Both nights already carry last-tickets labels.

Sunday is a single early show at 7 p.m., Frã Finamore’s Tim Maia birthday tribute. No show is listed for Monday, and the programme resumes on Tuesday.

Two Things to Check First

Only the late set has a price in circulation, and it comes from press listings rather than from the club. The 8 p.m. set has no published price at the club or in those listings.

Canto da Ema, the forró house in Pinheiros, has published no act for tonight. Forró is a couples dance from the northeast, and the only dated entry on the house’s own agenda page is 31 December.

Nothing on the house’s site says whether it opens tonight or who plays. Ring (11) 2503-2915 before crossing the city.

Where to Go

Blue Note São Paulo — Paulista The São Paulo branch of the New York jazz club, open since February 2019. It fills a hall of about 800 square metres on the second floor of the Conjunto Nacional. Tonight Adriano Grineberg at 8 p.m., then Walerie Gondim at 10.30 p.m.

Status No last-tickets label on either set, checked on 24 September.

Box office Ground floor 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., Monday to Saturday. Second floor on show days only: 7 p.m. to 11 p.m. Wednesday to Saturday, 7 p.m. to 8.30 p.m. Tuesday, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Sunday.

Free sessions Feijoada Raiz, Saturday midday to 4 p.m. Brunch Music, Sunday 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.

Seating Tables go by arrival order. Minors only with a parent or legal guardian.

Address Avenida Paulista 2073, second floor. Consolação station, on line 2-Green, is 200 metres away.

Money and How Paying Works

The club sells through its own site and through Eventim, and it says it takes no responsibility for tickets bought anywhere else. Neither of tonight’s prices is published on its pages, so read the figure at the checkout before you pay.

Mídia NINJA’s listing for the late set gives R$140 full and R$70 half, or about US$27.40 and US$13.70. That figure is the press’s rather than the club’s, which publishes no price for either set tonight.

Canto da Ema publishes a standard door price of R$55 full and R$27 half. That is about US$10.76 and US$5.28 at about 5.11 reais to the dollar.

The house says both price and hours change with the event, and it lists no event for tonight.

Food and drink are billed separately from any ticket. Restaurants usually add a service charge of about 10 per cent, called serviço.

It is customary rather than compulsory, and staff remove it if you ask.

What This Means for Your Evening

Tonight is a real choice between two evenings in one room. The 8 p.m. set suits dinner, and the late one runs past midnight.

Tables go by arrival order rather than by booking. The second-floor box office opens at 7 p.m. tonight, and arriving near that is the way to sit close to the stage.

If the weekend interests you more, book it today. Both Friday and Saturday evenings carry the club’s last-tickets label.

Getting Home Safe

The 8 p.m. set finishes inside normal metro hours. The 10.30 p.m. set will not, so plan a car if you take the late one.

Consolação is on line 2-Green, and weeknight service ends around midnight. Check the last train for your own line on the Metrô or ViaQuatro sites before you go.

Avenida Paulista stays busy and well lit into the night. Wait for a ride-hailing car on the avenue rather than on a side street.

The club’s parking is inside the Conjunto Nacional, entered from Rua Padre João Manuel 60. It is not affiliated with the venue.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is on at Blue Note tonight?

Two separate sets. Adriano Grineberg plays a Ray Charles and BB King celebration at 8 p.m., and Walerie Gondim sings Gal Costa at 10.30 p.m.

Can I still get a ticket?

Neither set carried the club’s last-tickets label on 24 September. That is a status rather than a guarantee, so buy online before you travel.

Is there a way in without a ticket?

Yes, in the daytime. The club marks entry free at Feijoada Raiz on Saturday from midday and at Brunch Music on Sunday from 10 a.m.

Can I bring someone under 18?

Only with a parent or legal guardian. The club states that rule on its own information page.

World.title: Rio de Janeiro Nightlife Tonight — September 24, 2026
World.content:
Rio de Janeiro · Nightlife

If You Only Go to One Place Samba da Constituição at Carioca da Gema Thursday is the last night of the week at the lower midweek price in Lapa. Doors open at 7.30 p.m., the main show starts at 8.30 p.m., and entry is R$30 (about US$6).

Tonight at a Glance — Samba da Constituição · Carioca da Gema Doors 7.30 p.m., show 8.30 p.m., entry R$30 (about US$6).

— No description published The house names tonight’s act but says nothing more about it.

— Last cheap night The price rises to R$35 (about US$7) from tomorrow.

— Tables The house holds reserved tables until 9 p.m., then releases them.

— Age The ticket page sets 18 as the minimum, with under-18s admitted only alongside a parent or legal guardian.

— Tomorrow Família Moadir, main show 10 p.m. The house site and the ticket page disagree on doors, 7.30 p.m. against 8.30 p.m.

— Arts week ends Sunday The Semana de Arte do Rio closes on 27 September.

Tonight, Thursday 24 September 2026, Lapa runs its last night at the midweek price before the weekend rate begins. All times below are Rio de Janeiro time, four hours behind London while British Summer Time lasts.

The Lapa Arches at night, the landmark at the centre of Rio de Janeiro’s live-music district (Photo: Carlos Lucio, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)
