World.title: Venice-winning Gaza documentary 'NAZA' set for European release
World.content:
The award-winning documentary NAZA is set to be released in cinemas across 56 countries, including European territories.

 

The film premiered at the Venice Film Festival earlier this month, where it was met with a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record – and was awarded the Special Jury Prize.

NAZA shows “in detail the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza,” according to its official synopsis. It builds on reporting between 2023 and 2025 published by the Israeli-Palestinian +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call, and The Guardian.

A theatrical release in partnership with French sales company MK2 Films is planned at the end of September and during October in territories including the UK, France, Spain, Portugal, Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands, Austria, Poland, Greece, Denmark, Norway, as well as Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Hong Kong, Thailand, Brazil and Central America.

After its run in cinemas, the film will stream on the Guardian’s website, for free.

The film has also “been offered to a number of distributors and cinemas in Israel,” a statement said, and The Guardian stated that they will be exploring other ways to enable the film to be seen in the occupied Palestinian territories.

“NAZA is grounded in rigorous journalism published over the past three years,” said Harry Davies, a Guardian investigations correspondent and one of NAZA’s producers. “But it is also a powerful piece of cinema that will soon be available on screens, large and small, around the world.”

Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham, winners of the special jury prize for the film 'NAZA' AP Photo

NAZA was shot in secrecy at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv during the ongoing Gaza war, and features interviews with 24 Israeli military intelligence officers, soldiers and whistleblowers. They describe how Palestinians are targeted and how strikes are carried out despite Israel being aware that civilians are present in targeted areas – hence the title of the film, a military acronym used by Israeli Military Forces to refer to the number of civilians expected to be killed in an airstrike in Gaza. It stands for "Nezek Agavi": collateral damage.

The participants' faces and voices were digitally altered to protect their identities.

Since its premiere in Venice, NAZA and its filmmakers, Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, have been under the spotlight as the film has sparked a political storm in Israel.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu attacked the makers of the documentary, accusing them of contributing to “global antisemitic incitement”.

“It’s shocking. We are fighting global antisemitic incitement and when it comes from within us it is intolerable,” Netanyahu said in a video posted on Telegram. “And now two Israeli directors portraying the IDF (Israel Defense Forces) as war criminals receive applause at the Venice festival.”

Netanyahu’s attack on the film has been interpretated as a reflection of his concern for its potential impact on the upcoming Israeli elections, which are set for 27 October. His comments also followed those of Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar, who directly equated criticism of Israel's actions to antisemitism and announced that he would “act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship” of the Israeli directing duo Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor.

Zohar called NAZA “vile” and the Venice Film Festival honour “shocking,” adding: “The self-loathing that burns in the creators, who are willing to harm their homeland just to get applause from antisemites around the world, is inconceivable and constitutes a betrayal of the state.”

National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir also described Abraham and Szor as a “disgrace and an embarrassment” and told them to leave the country. “I am certain that your friends, that is to say our enemies Hamas in Gaza, will welcome you with open arms," he wrote on X.

Graffiti showing directors Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham with the Hebrew writings "traitors" in Ashdod, Israel - Tuesday 15 September 2026 AP Photo

Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor's previous film, No Other Land, was released in 2024 and followed Israeli settler violence against Palestinian communities in the West Bank. It won the Oscar for Best Documentary.

Last week, 43 local human rights organisations issued a joint statement urging Israeli authorities to stop what they described as incitement and threats against the filmmakers, and not to prosecute either them or their sources.

More than 1,500 Israeli filmmakers have also signed a petition defending “freedom of expression and creation” and expressing solidarity with Szor and Abraham.

“In recent days, we have witnessed an unprecedented campaign of vilification and incitement against the film’s creators,” it says, warning that the rhetoric was moving increasingly close to “effectively sanctioning violence” and posed a physical threat to their lives.

Tricia Tuttle, director of the Berlin Film Festival, said: “Artists must be free to critically examine the world. Films can provoke discussion, disagreement and criticism, but in a democratic society, the response to art must be dialogue and scrutiny, not intimidation or punishment by the state. Our team at the Berlinale stands with Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and all artists who exercise these rights.”

NAZA will screen at the New York Film Festival on 26 September. A theatrical rollout will commence in the US afterwards and in Europe as soon as 9 October.

World.title: At least eight killed in wave of Russian strikes across Ukraine as attacks intensify
World.content:
A barrage of Russian drone and missile strikes pummelled Ukraine on Thursday, killing six agricultural workers in the east alongside two in the capital Kyiv in the latest in an intensifying exchange of attacks.

 

The strikes, which triggered air raid sirens and sent locals rushing underground for shelter, came after both Kyiv and Moscow were at the United Nations and vowed no let-up in their long-range attacks, dimming any immediate prospects for peace in Europe's worst conflict since World War II.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who was in New York seeking more Western support for stronger sanctions against the Kremlin, accused Russia of deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure.

The increase in attacks, particularly on Kyiv, has prompted residents to consider contingency plans for the winter, if Russian strikes once again knock out the energy system vital for heating in bitter sub-zero temperatures.

Burnt-out cars and the smouldering remains of buildings were seen in Kyiv, emergency service images showed, after the early morning attacks that the authorities said included powerful ballistic missiles.

A woman walks in front of a house destroyed in a Russian strike on a residential neighbourhood in Kyiv, 24 September, 2026 AP Photo

At least two people were killed across the city, Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said.

In the Kharkiv region, the regional prosecutor's office published images showing the inside of a destroyed warehouse, with what appeared to be piles of apples strewn on the floor and a gaping hole in the roof.

The storage facility in the Chuguiv district, southeast of Kharkiv, was hit as employees were sorting vegetables, it added.

Drone-missile hybrid

"Preliminary data indicate that the enemy used a small-sized cruise missile known as 'Banderol'," a statement read.

A Banderol is a low-cost hybrid weapon combining characteristics of a cruise missile and an attack drone. The Russian military has used them on a large scale, notably to overwhelm Ukrainian air defences.

Eight settlements in the region had been attacked in the last 24 hours, its governor Oleg Synegubov said.

In and around Ukraine's Black Sea port of Odesa, officials said Russian strikes caused a fire at a shopping mall and also hit houses and businesses.

The latest attacks came a day after a series of Russian strikes killed at least seven people in Ukraine and sparked fires in Kyiv.

The capital, which is home to some 3 million people, has been the target of particularly intense drone attacks in recent days, hitting petrol stations and the rail network.

The Nova Post postal and courier company said one of its branches was destroyed and its sorting depot was damaged in Thursday's strikes.

AFP analysis of data from the ACLED armed conflict monitor showed that there were more Russian strikes on the Kyiv region in the first 18 days of September than in any full month since the start of the war apart from March 2022.

Zelenskyy met NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in New York to brief him on the latest security situation and made a renewed push for US-made interceptors against ballistic missiles and tougher sanctions on Russia.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has urged both sides not to target the other's energy sector.

But Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said on Wednesday there would be no "pause" in the war, while Zelenskyy said Moscow would leave Kyiv "no choice" but to do likewise if the Kremlin again weaponised the region's brutal winter with attacks on energy facilities.

World.title: EU says US diesel export plan is 'bad idea' that risks hurting both sides
World.content:
The European Union has hit out at a possible US diesel export ban being considered by President Donald Trump, calling it a "bad idea" that could damage both economies.

 

Trump signalled support for a ban this week as surging fuel prices — driven by the war in the Middle East — threaten to cost his Republican party control of Congress in November's midterm elections. But European Commission spokesman Olof Gill said Brussels viewed the plans "with concern".

"We believe this is a bad idea," Gill told a press conference. "We believe it potentially can have a negative impact on both sides. We're making that point to our US counterparts at the highest level."

Europe has also grappled with high fuel prices since the US-Iran war began in late February, but it is far more reliant on imports than the US. The average diesel price across the EU's 27 member states hit a record €2.23 per litre, according to an AFP analysis of commission data published on Thursday. The US supplied around 50% of the bloc's diesel imports in August.

"We expect close partners to consult each other before taking measures that affect shared markets," Gill added.

Industry pushes back

The comments came after US Energy Secretary Chris Wright sought to clarify the administration's plans on Wednesday, saying the US would not impose an outright ban but would instead introduce restrictions on diesel exports. Speaking to WSJ's Journal House on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, Wright said the US needed to keep global markets supplied while changing the trajectory of domestic prices, and that any measures would be voluntary.

"We're trying to avoid a blunt hammer of a government policy, understanding the complexity of refining," he said.

Trump first floated the idea of restricting diesel exports on Tuesday, prompting alarm across the oil and gas industry, which has warned that curbing exports could trigger unintended consequences and push up domestic prices for both diesel and petrol.

Wright's comments were light on detail, and some industry lobbyists have noted that any coordination among refiners over restrictions could raise antitrust concerns.

Industry trade groups have voiced strong opposition, marking one of their most forceful pushbacks against the administration since Trump returned to office. The American Exploration & Production Council said "policymakers should reject this short-sighted approach and instead focus on solutions that will actually lower prices at the pump."

World.title: Germany news: Berlin officially withdraws Olympics bid
World.content:
Skip next section German business confidence up in September — Ifo

The monthly business climate index put out by the Ifo economic research institute has risen 1.1 points to 89.9 points, the highest level in more than three years.

The index, Germany's most important economic barometer, has been rising constantly over the past five months, indicating that the country is slowly returning to economic health after years of struggle.

The business optimism comes despite an energy price ​shock that has pushed fuel costs to record highs.

"The German economy continues its recovery," said Ifo president Clemens Fuest.

The ​gauge of business expectations accompanying the index rose to 90.4 ​from 89.1 in August, while companies also gave a rosier assessment of their current situation than the month before, improving to 89.5 to 88.5 points.

Ifo said, however, that the automotive sector was still in "difficult terrain."

The index is based on a monthly survey of 9,000 companies.

The news from Ifo comes as ​the country's five leading economic institutes presented a joint fall forecast raising 2026 GDP growth expectations to 1.3% from ⁠0.6%.

World.title: Czech PM Andrej Babis reiterates importance of NATO for his country but rejects calls to increase defense spending
World.content:
The US and NATO want Czechia to spend more on defense. Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis says Prague cannot afford faster increases, despite growing warnings about the threat from Russia.

The Czech Republic "must remain committed to increasing defense spending," Matthew Whitaker, the US envoy to NATO, demanded in Prague last week. "We ⁠expect our allies to step up," he said.

The call is nothing new. As warnings about the threat emanating from Russia increase, and Washington demands European allies take greater responsibility for security, NATO has raised its target for defense spending from 2% to 3.5% of GDP, and pressure on those lagging is rising.

Czechia, alongside Slovenia and Albania, has yet to meet the old target. But Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis, whose government cut the defense budget for 2026 to around 1.7% of GDP when it took office late last year, pushed back against the latest barb from Washington.

While reiterating that NATO membership is crucial for Czechia, the premier bluntly stated that the government cannot afford to accelerate spending. He has pledged to hit the 2% target in 2027 but plans no further increases.

US Ambassador to NATO Matthew G. Whitaker (pictured here in Iowa earlier this month) has made the US position clear to Prague: Czechia 'must remain committed to increasing defense spending' Image: Tim Evans/REUTERS

That leaves the populist billionaire hoping that a personal rapport with US President Donald Trump will protect the country amid the burgeoning row.

Warnings of a growing threat

Whether Trump will protect Czechia from the threat of Russian hybrid warfare targeting Central European NATO allies is another question.

A growing wave of stray drones and Russian intelligence operations — suspected bombings, sabotage and cyber warfare — have spread alarm in the neighborhood.

Germany and Poland — key Czech partners — have reported high-profile incidents and linked them to attempts to intimidate Ukrainian allies.

Czechia should understand the threat better than most, having been among the first to experience such an attack.

Czechia's Security Information Service (BIS) reported in 2021 that the bombing of a depot storing weapons linked to Ukraine seven years previously had been carried out by Russia's domestic intelligence agency, the Federal Security Service (FSB).

Babis, then in his first stint as PM, responded by expelling around 100 Russian diplomats and embassy staff, freezing relations with Moscow.

The BIS remains in step with other intelligence agencies across the region in warning that the threat from Russia is growing.

However, like its predecessors, the Babis government has failed to keep pace in terms of the national defense budget, even as neighbors have leapt into action.

Prague spent just 1.86% of GDP on defense last year; Poland and the Baltic States have already met the new NATO target and will hit 5% next year.

Prague's priorities

Babis has made it clear this approach will not change. However, his claim that Czechia can't afford to boost defense spending is at odds with the 2027 budget his government approved on September 22.

The fiscal plan will expand expenditure generously and targets Czechia's second-highest deficit ever at 386 billion Czech crowns (€15.8 billion or $18 billion).

While finally catching up to the old NATO target will account for some of that spending, most of the increased outlay will reflect the coalition government's domestic political priorities.

The plan clearly reflects the election campaign promises of Babis's ANO party and its junior partners, the far-right Freedom and Direct Democracy party (SPD) and radical-right Motorists for Themselves party. They all say defense can't be allowed to disrupt the urgent need to spend on pensions, education, healthcare and infrastructure.

"The claim that the country cannot spend more on defense is primarily rooted in domestic politics," Ales Michal, a political scientist at Prague's Charles University, told DW. "The major priority is investment in the social system."

That will be welcomed by supporters of the governing parties, who skew older and less well off, and resent the support being given to 300,000 or so Ukrainian refugees.

"None of the governing parties promised voters higher defense spending," in campaigning for last year's election, Michal notes.

Critics, however, say that's because the government is downplaying the threat from Russia. The government's spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.

'We don't want World War III'

The reticence to raise defense spending also reflects political narratives around the war in Ukraine.

Two days after Whitaker's rebuke, Babis appeared in a video dressed in a T-shirt emblazoned with the words "No War" in blue and yellow letters. While he noted the threat from Russia, he called for greater efforts to find peace.

"We don't want World War III, do we?" he pronounced, repeating his claim that Europe should work harder to end the conflict.

It was a performance echoing the stance of Europe's radical right-wing, and the sort that has seen the Czech PM labelled "pro-Russian" in some international media.

The truth is more mundane. Babis is a pragmatist. The ANO electorate is populist and anti-Ukrainian, but also strongly pro-Western. Surveys show that the plan to keep defense spending at 2% of GDP precisely matches its views.

Yet Babis's divisive personality leaves the party dependent on extremist partners for enough support to govern, and so he must also try to speak the anti-system, pro-Russian language of the SPD, which, despite controlling the defense ministry, was pushing to cut spending further in the 2027 budget.

"A critical stance towards Ukraine also shapes the government's position on spending," said Michal. The pro-peace stance downplaying Russia's aggression moves ANO "closer to the European radical right," he notes, but Babis is "guided by opinion polls," and must try to find a "balance between two polarizing positions."

Strategic understanding

The opposition sees this dichotomy as the government's Achilles' heel.

Martin Kupka, leader of the center-right Civic Democrats (ODS), welcomed Babis's reiterated NATO commitment before asking the PM: "When will you get rid of the Kremlin fifth column, which you took into the government and even entrusted with the Ministry of Defense?"

However, although the ODS-led government that held office between 2021 and 2025 offered fervent support to Ukraine, like all its predecessors, it also failed to meet the NATO spending target.

"Our partners may be unhappy about the approach to spending, but it's the reality of the political situation in our country," Andor Sandor, a defense analyst and former commander of Czechia's Military Intelligence Service, told DW.

However, he added that while weak defense spending growth "is not optimal," the biggest issue is a lack of strategic understanding regarding the military's size and role.

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

World.title: 'Pope fever' takes hold as Pope Leo visits France
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV is expected to draw large crowds during his visit to France. As part of his trip to Europe, he's also set to address the continent's future and some of the challenges ahead.

France is gripped by "Pope fever." Since the 1905 French law on separating church and state, the country has embraced secular traditions. But over the next few days, the streets will tell a different story.

From Friday, Pope Leo XIVwill spend four days in France, visiting the capital Paris, Lourdes and Metz. All his public events have been sold out for weeks. Organizers expect around one million people to fill the streets of Paris on Saturday for a massive open-air mass at the Place de la Concorde.

"The pope is popular among both believers and nonbelievers," political scientist Olivier Roy told DW. He added that Leo XIV's conflict with US President Donald Trump in particular had lent him "a moral standing that extends far beyond the Catholic Church."

Paris gears up for influx

And massive crowds are expected. Some 600,000 people who were able to get tickets will fill the entire Champs-Elysees, going right up to the Arc de Triomphe. Many more are expected to show up without tickets. Authorities have announced that a number of metro stations will be closed. Across the city, churches have been draped with large portraits of the pope and Vatican flags. Security forces are gearing up for a major challenge.

With France's presidential elections just over six months away, the visit comes at a delicate time. The left, Roy said, "appreciates Leo's personality but is skeptical about the state's involvement in organizing the reception."

Those on the far right, he continued, welcomed the visibility of Catholicism but had objected, for example, to an interfaith meeting planned in the eastern city of Metz, which they say places Islam on an equal footing with Christianity.

Because of the separation of church and state, the president will not be able to attend the large public masses.

Pope Benedict XVI celebrated an open-air mass at the Invalides in Paris Image: Osservatore Romano/ansa/epa/dpa/picture alliance

Leo's visit is likely to boost the pope's profile in the country, which last saw a papal state visit in 2008, when Benedict XVI (2005-2013) traveled to Paris and Lourdes, the world-famous pilgrimage site in the southwest of the country. He drew smaller crowds than those expected for Pope Leo.

Pope Francis (2013-2025) visited Strasbourg in 2014 and Ajaccio in Corsica in 2024 on one-day trips, and in 2023 he spent a night in the Mediterranean port city of Marseille. But each time, he came for a specific occasion rather than visiting the country as a whole. In his speeches to the European Parliament and Council of Europe in Strasbourg, he criticized the migration policies of what he described as an "aged and weary" Europe.

Roy described the contrasting perspectives of recent popes. John Paul II (1978-2005), he said, viewed Christianity as "primarily European," while Francis saw it as "more shaped by the Global South."

This, Roy argued, explained Francis' "certain disregard for Europe." Leo was likely to assume the middle ground, while extending his predecessor's message, Roy said: "He affirms the universality of the Catholic Church, while also recognizing Europe's weight within that universality."

Europe's key role for the pope

For Augsburg-based church historian and papal expert Jörg Ernesti, Europe has remained "the most important political point of reference for popes since the late 19th century," despite the growing internationalism of Catholicism Ernesti pointed to the demographic shift: In 1900, more than two-thirds of all Catholics lived in Europe, he said; today, the figure is only around 20%. This internationalization had also shaped the College of Cardinals, albeit with a time lag. "While Europeans have historically always made up the majority, they now account for just 39%."

During his four-day visit, Leo is scheduled to deliver 15 speeches and homilies. Most of those in Paris will be aimed at wider French society and its political leaders, while the large masses and events in Lourdes will focus primarily on France's Catholics.

In April 2026, Pope Leo received French President Emmanuel Macron and his wife, Brigitte Macron, at the Vatican Image: Vatican Media/Catholic Press Photo/ipa-agency/picture alliance

The most keenly awaited speech is one scheduled for the final day in Metz, which French President Emmanuel Macron will introduce. It is titled "To the roots of Europe for peace and unity."

The choice of Metz itself is symbolic. Once a center of the Carolingian Empire, the city has changed language and allegiance several times over the centuries, at times being German, at others French.

Leo will be able to invoke the name behind the Robert Schuman Convention Center. Born in Luxembourg, Robert Schuman (1886-1963) was a French statesman who had inherited his father's German citizenship at birth. In the aftermath of World War II, he was an early advocate of Franco-German reconciliation. He pushed for a new, united Europe and in 1958 became the first president of the newly established European Parliament. After his death, he was buried in a small church in Scy-Chazelles, near Metz.

Robert Schuman's tombstone in a church in his hometown Scy-Chazelles Image: Jean-Christophe Verhaegen/AFP

For Pope Leo, Roy said, "Europe is a real entity that must be sustained and developed beyond nationalism." That, he said, "has always been the message of the Catholic Church since World War II. It is Schuman's message."

Roy will be watching closely to see whether, and how openly, Pope Leo criticizes populism and nationalism in his call to strengthen the EU and whether he will speak about a form of nationalist Catholicism found in France. He said that defenders of the traditional Latin Mass were not infrequently "identitarian nationalists or even close to far right circles."

Leo to meet abuse survivors

It is hard to imagine a papal trip without mention of the long-running issue of abuse. When Pope Benedict visited France in 2008, he did not take the chance to meet any survivors of sexual abuse in the French Catholic Church. His successors did, though the institution has been slow to confront its past amid a spate of new scandals.

This grotto is at the heart of religious life in Lourdes. According to legend, the Virgin Mary appeared several times to a young woman in 1858 Image: Lionel Bonaventure/AFP/Getty Images

This time round, a meeting with survivors is on the pope's agenda in Lourdes. But something else has changed. During the pontificates of Benedict and Francis, those who met with them were usually not named. At times, it appeared that access to the Vatican came in exchange for silence. In France, the seven survivors who will meet Leo have spoken out together ahead of the meeting, with five of them also making their names public.

"Dialogue does not mean approval," they said. "Being received does not mean giving up our demands." The issue is likely to remain a thorny challenge for the Catholic Church — in France and elsewhere for a long time to come.

This article was translated from German.

World.title: UNGA: Netanyahu, Abbas to speak as Middle East dominates day
World.content:
Before the more predictable broadside against the UK, Milei trained his sights on the UN itself Image: Heather Khalifa/AP Photo/picture alliance

Argentina's President Javier Milei issued a fiery rebuke not just against the UK, amid renewed tensions with the UK over the Falkland Islands, but also against another pet peeve of his — the UN itself.

He said he wanted to highlight the shortcomings he perceived in the UN "in a constructive spirit," decades after it undertook to "uphold international law, defend the sovereignty of nations and provide a forum through which conflicts could be resolved through cooperation, rather than immediately through the force of arms."

That, he said, was the original contract member states signed, but this "sacred covenant" had in practice been broken.

"That's to say it's become a useless organization whose only purpose is to sustain a cast of fatally arrogant parasites masquerading as well-intentioned bureaucrats," Milei said.

He said they had failed in their task of ensuring collective global security and human rights: "Instead, they allowed chaos, violence and international terrorism to flourish."

Milei accused these "alleged defenders of human rights" of sheltering "bloodthirsty dictators and regimes that stone women in the streets" and of "systematically" voting against Israel "while remaining silent in the face of Islamic terrorism and the genocide of Christians in Africa."

From this point, he turned his gaze directly to the isolated Falkand Islands of some 2,000 residents, some 550 kilometers (350 miles) off Argentina's coastline. He referred to them using their Spanish name, the Malvinas.

"And, as if that were not enough, an organization established to defend the territorial sovereignty of its members decided to look the other way with regard to the situation of the Malvinas Islands, South Georgia Islands and South Sandwich Islands and the surrounding maritime areas," he said of the disputed British territory that Argentina's defunct military dictatorship invaded in the 1980s, just a matter of months before it collapsed.

"For us, the Malvinas are a national cause," he said, before repeating for emphasis. "They are also a test of the gulf that can exist between the words of international institutions and the reality upon which they purport to act."

He complained, for instance, about UK oil extraction operations in waters that Argentina claims, saying this violated a past UN resolution designed to prevent further tensions in the dispute. Milei said that "for far too long" Argentina had opted for a "rhetorical" and "peaceful" defense in this dispute, and said his country again called on the UK "to resume negotiations with a view to finding a peaceful solution to the sovereignty dispute, as required by international law."

World.title: As the EU advances free trade with Southeast Asia, why is there no ASEAN-wide deal?
World.content:
After years of arduous negotiations, the EU is closing on a string of bilateral trade deals with countries in Southeast Asia. And yet, a bloc-to-bloc agreement between the EU and ASEAN remains a distant prospect.

The EU and several Southeast Asian nations are nearing the finish line on bilateral trade deals, and if the current deadlines hold, the European bloc will have agreements in place with six out of 11 ASEAN states by the middle of next year.

Free trade agreements with Singapore and Vietnam are already in force. Negotiations with Indonesia have concluded, and Jakarta aims to sign the agreement in October, with implementation targeted for early 2027.

Trade Reset: How Europe is replacing China and the US To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Talks with Thailand, relaunched in 2023, have reached nine negotiating rounds, while Malaysia resumed negotiations in early 2025 after a 13-year pause. Both are expected to be finalized by the end of the year or early 2027.

Earlier this week, the EU and the Philippines announced that they had reached "substantial agreement" on their free trade agreement, putting it on course for formal conclusion in the coming months.

Trade up by more than half in single decade

Speaking to DW, Chris Humphrey, executive director of the EU-ASEAN Business Council, described EU engagement with ASEAN on trade and investment issues as "at an all-time high."

EU-Southeast Asia goods trade reached €274.9 billion ($313.7 billion) last year, up around 6% from the previous year and more than 50% from the €177.9 billion recorded in 2016, according to EU data.

The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) is now the EU's third-largest goods trading partner outside Europe, behind only the United States and China.

The Philippines is chair of ASEAN — these are its goals To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

This week, Manila hosted both the ASEAN–EU Business Summit and the 22nd meeting of ASEAN economic ministers and the EU's trade commissioner. The two blocs pledged greater cooperation to protect themselves from rising geopolitical tensions, including unilateral trade actions and regional conflicts, that "collectively threaten the rules-based international order."

Why is Southeast Asia so important for Europe?

Brussels is expanding its network of trade agreements globally as it looks to expand to new markets and form more resilient supply chains. Southeast Asia, in turn, sits at the center of supply chains for semiconductors, electronics, electric vehicles and batteries, with investment pouring into data centers, renewable energy and digital services.

EU-Mercosur free trade deal: Who gains the most? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

An article published this month by the International Monetary Fund said ASEAN's 11 economies already form a $4.5 trillion bloc, growing at more than 4.5% a year.

Such economic expansion, combined with multinational firms' efforts to diversify production beyond China, has made access to Southeast Asian markets more attractive for European companies.

Alfred Gerstl, an expert on Indo-Pacific international relations at the University of Vienna, told DW that geopolitical and geo-economic changes are also accelerating cooperation between the two regions.

US President Donald Trump's "protectionist and erratic trade policies" have acted as a crucial catalyst, he said, while the EU's strategy of "de-risking from China" and diversifying supply chains boosted Southeast Asia's strategic importance.

A stronger partnership with European nations also plays in favor of Southeast Asia governments, who have long tried to maintain broad economic relationships with competing powers rather than becoming excessively dependent on China, the United States or any other single partner.

EU companies push for an ASEAN-wide deal

The EU-ASEAN Business Council, said Humphrey, is calling for a region-to-region economic framework with a clear pathway to an eventual region-to-region free trade deal, "something European business has consistently called for."

"This would adopt a modular approach, perhaps starting with a region-to-region Digital Trade Agreement and an Investment Protection Agreement," Humphrey told DW.

The idea is not exactly new — the EU and ASEAN launched negotiations for a region-to-region agreement in 2007, but the talks bogged down over enormous differences between ASEAN economies and disagreements over the agreement's scope.

The talks were put on ice by mutual agreement in 2009, after which Brussels switched to negotiating bilateral deals with individual ASEAN members.

The main difficulty preservers to this day, as ASEAN includes Singapore, one of the world's wealthiest economies, alongside developing and least-developed members, making it difficult to agree on common commitments acceptable to Brussels.

"In addition, meeting the EU's high social, labor and environmental standards is difficult for the less-developed ASEAN members," said Gerstl.

Is the Commission ready to up the stakes?

Yet, even without an immediate prospect of a full region-to-region agreement, completing the current bilateral deals would give the EU preferential trade arrangements with most of ASEAN's largest economies and demonstrate that Southeast Asia has moved higher up Brussels' trade agenda.

For Humphrey, however, that should be the starting point rather than the endpoint. The concern, he said, is the European Commission might not be willing to move towards region-to-region agreements.

"With 2027 marking the 50th Anniversary of EU-ASEAN relations, we remain hopeful that the Commission will take this milestone seriously and ramp up work on a region-to-region economic architecture," he told DW.

"Failing to do so will only make ASEAN think that the EU does not take the region seriously."

World.title: Tensions between India and Bangladesh are in focus after Dhaka skipped the BRICS summit in Delhi
World.content:
Bangladesh's absence from the BRICS summit in New Delhi has raised fresh questions about strained ties. Ousted PM Sheikh Hasina's exile in India remains a major obstacle to normalizing relations.

When India hosted a BRICS leaders' summit in New Delhi earlier this month, a notable absentee was Bangladesh's Prime Minister Tarique Rahman.

The Indian government says Rahman received two invitations: one to attend a BRICS outreach session as the chair of a regional group of nations around the Bay of Bengal, known as BIMSTEC, and another for a bilateral visit to India.

Invitation or snub?

But in Dhaka, these invitations were viewed as a snub, as Rahman was not formally invited to the summit proper in his capacity as prime minister, but only as the chair of BIMSTEC.

This represents a departure from Bangladesh's previous prime minister, Sheikh Hasina, who was invited as premier to previous BRICS summit events, even though Bangladesh is not a member.

The case is the latest example of the frosty ties between the two South Asian neighbors that have developed since Hasina's ouster in 2024 following huge protests and a deadly crackdown.

Hasina fled to India, and last year was sentenced to death after being convicted in absentia of crimes against humanity over the response to the protests.

Bangladesh has called on India to extradite Hasina so that she can face justice.

Hasina has rejected the verdict, calling it politically motivated.

After her ouster in 2024, bilateral relations entered their worst period in years — visa services were curtailed as disputes mounted over her presence in India as well as the management of the border and alleged forced returns without due process of undocumented, mostly Muslim, Bengali-speaking migrants — known as "push-ins."

India forces Bengali-speaking Muslims into Bangladesh To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Since Rahman's Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) won February's election, that drift has partly reversed. India resumed tourist visas in June and appointed Dinesh Trivedi as its new high commissioner.

But while a bilateral summit is being discussed for November, Hasina's exile in India remains a major obstacle to normalizing relations.

Former Indian diplomat Ajay Bisaria told DW that Bangladesh had "missed a trick" by staying away.

"It was a chance to engage not just with India but with other global leaders," he said. "But the lost ground is easily recovered."

Has the India-Bangladesh relationship fundamentally changed?

Both sides, he added, would need to manage the "irritant" of Hasina's presence in India. A positive bilateral summit later this year could reset ties, he added.

Humayun Kabir, a former Bangladeshi diplomat, said the relationship is not what it was before Hasina fled to India.

"Ties were one-sided before the uprising, and Dhaka is now looking for something different," Kabir told DW. "There has to be dignity and equality."

Dhaka is willing to engage, but New Delhi must create a congenial atmosphere for a Rahman visit, Kabir said, including by keeping Hasina from making "provocative" remarks and acknowledging the court verdict against her.

Zafar Sobhan, a Bangladeshi political analyst, told DW that Bangladesh will now engage only on equal terms.

"It was hoped that with the exit of the (Mohammad) Yunus-led interim government, New Delhi could mend ties with the elected BNP government," he said. "However, both sides are held hostage by hardliners, giving them limited room for maneuver."

Sobhan said the best way for India to rebuild trust with authorities in Bangladesh is "not to allow Hasina to destabilize Bangladesh with provocative statements."

"Failure to rein her in is seen as an act of unfriendliness," Sobhan explained.

Others read Rahman not taking part in the BRICS summit more sharply.

Shanthie Mariet D'Souza, founder of the Mantraya Institute for Strategic Studies, called it "clearly a snub," even though Dhaka cited procedural problems with the invitation.

She said the episode must be viewed alongside the unresolved Hasina question, stalled talks on the Ganga Water Sharing Treaty — which is set to expire in December — and Bangladesh's deepening ties with China and Pakistan.

"The BNP is clearly on its way to diversifying its relations amid China's growing overtures and India's hard postures," D'Souza told DW, describing it not as a pivot away from India but a "recalibration toward hedging and greater autonomy."

Sreeradha Datta, a Bangladesh expert at the Jindal School of International Affairs in India, offers a more cautious take.

"India will always remain an important neighbour for Bangladesh," Datta told DW, "but India holds few advantages over Dhaka, and both sides understand that."

"It's too early to suggest the two neighbours have moved apart," she said. "Delhi and Dhaka seem measured in their overtures to each other."

The China factor

That caution matters because the China relationship is not new. Beijing has spent a decade building its economic and strategic presence in Bangladesh, spanning infrastructure, energy, trade and defence, since Dhaka joined the Belt and Road Initiative in 2016.

China is now Bangladesh's largest trading partner and a major defence supplier.

Beijing also pledged support for Bangladesh's long-delayed Teesta initiative, a major river-management and infrastructure project to control floods and improve water supply on the Teesta River, which flows between India and Bangladesh.

Despite years of talks, Bangladesh and India failed to sign a Teesta water-sharing treaty.

On his June visit to Beijing, his first overseas trip in office, Rahman leaned into that relationship, securing agreements on trade, investment, infrastructure and defence.

"It is normal for a mid-sized state like Bangladesh to seek relationships with Beijing and other nations," D'Souza said, warning that heavy-handed pressure from India could push Dhaka further that way.

D'Souza advises New Delhi to separate the bilateral agenda from the Hasina question, offer Rahman a concrete package on water, trade and connectivity, and hold firm red lines on any Chinese military presence near the Siliguri corridor and the Bay of Bengal.

Shahab Enam Khan, a Bangladeshi scholar of international relations, pushed back on the idea that improving ties is only in Dhaka's interests.

"If anyone should worry about this relationship, it is New Delhi," Khan told DW, citing India's trade surplus and its dependence on Bangladeshi goodwill for its own security.

India, he said, treated the 2024 uprising "as the loss of a client rather than a neighbour's political transition," pointing to suspended visas, closed land ports and shelter for Hasina.

"Bangladeshis took it as a message that Delhi's goodwill depended on who held power in Dhaka," Khan said.

Rebuilding trust, he said, means ending Hasina's party activity in Delhi, resolving bilateral disputes, and lifting post-2024 trade restrictions.

What India still holds

Geography still complicates any clean break. Bangladesh and India share a 4,096-kilometer (2,400-mile) border, the longest either country has. Bangladesh still depends on India for trade routes, transit, electricity, fuel, medical travel and regional connectivity. The two countries also share 54 rivers.

But those dependencies are also friction points. The 1996 Ganga Water Sharing Treaty expires in December, the Teesta dispute remains unresolved, and alleged Indian push-ins of undocumented migrants across the border remain a sore point.

Bisaria sees some balancing of its ties between India and China as "natural." "India can live with that, as it does with its other neighbours," he said.

The real question, then, may not be whether India is losing Bangladesh outright, but whether it is losing its old ability to shape the relationship on its own terms with an increasingly assertive Dhaka.

World.title: India news: Cockroach party demands Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation
World.content:
09/24/2026 September 24, 2026 CJP targets Gyanesh Kumar over SIR, alleges voter deletions benefit BJP

Cockroach Janata Party founder Abhijeet Dipke has accused India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar of undermining the country's democracy and alleged that the Election Commission's voter-roll revision is being used to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

Speaking at a press conference on Thursday, Dipke called Kumar "the biggest threat to India's democracy" and demanded his resignation.

CJP said it would launch protests across the country ‌if ⁠India's ⁠chief election officer does not resign in 48 ​hours.

The CJP's demands are:

Initiate criminal proceedings against Kumar

All upcoming elections put on hold, freeze Special Intensive Revision (SIR)

Repeal the 2023 law on the appointment of the Election Commissioners of India

Kumar overruled fellow election commissioners' concerns

Dipke's accusations came after the Indian Express published an investigation that fellow Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised at least 14 formal objections over 10 months to decisions concerning voter registrations, deletions and restorations, as well as control of electoral-roll data, the report said.

In one of the objections, Sandhu complained that the Election Commission acted against the written advice of two commissioners and claimed its action was "unauthorized and illegal."

Sandhu and Joshi, along with Kumar, are responsible for overseeing the Special Intensive Revision (SIR). The process is meant to remove redundancies in India's electoral rolls, but the process is accused of having gone far beyond that remit and removed millions of legal voters.

According to the Election Commission, the revision was needed to remove the names of deceased individuals, those who have permanently moved and duplicate entries — as well as avoiding the "inclusion of the names of foreign illegal immigrants."

In one of the objections, Sandhu complained that the Election Commission acted against the written advice of two commissioners and claimed its action was 'unauthorized and illegal' [FILE: March 15, 2026] Image: Ishant Chauhan/Hindustan Times/Sipa USA/picture alliance

'Kumar's actions benefit BJP'

Dipke alleged that more than 130 million names have been struck off draft electoral rolls across 30 states and union territories during the SIR process.

Dipke alleged the removals from voter registries were intended to widen the BJP's electoral advantage as voter deletions had disproportionately affected opposition strongholds.

Dipke pointed out that during the 2024 election the difference in total votes between the ruling party and the opposition coalition was 2%.

"Deleting 130 million votes means deleting approximately 13 to 14 percent of the votes," Dipke said. "So, is Gyanesh Kumar intentionally deleting them so that the two-percent gap, where it appears that the BJP could lose, becomes larger, so that they never have to leave power?"

Congress leader Rahul Gandhi also alleged earlier that the SIR process benefits the BJP. The ruling party has dismissed such claims, arguing that those removed largely involve dead voters and illegal immigrants, thereby protecting India's democracy.

World.title: Poland says Starlink station fire 'act of sabotage'
World.content:
Polish Deputy Prime Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said Warsaw believed the attack aimed to disrupt internet access for the Ukrainian military, calling it "an element of the next phase of hybrid warfare."

Warsaw considers a fire that broke out at a Starlink station in central Poland to be an act of sabotage, Deputy Prime Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said on Thursday.

"This act of sabotage was deliberately designed to disable the station ... disrupting internet access for various institutions, including the Ukrainian army," Gawkowski, who also serves as digital minister, told public broadcaster TVP.

He said the fire at the station belonging to Polish state-owned telecom company Exatel broke out late on Wednesday.

"There is much to suggest that we are dealing with an element of the next phase of hybrid warfare," he said.

The deputy premier said that the station was used to transmit internet traffic through Poland, including to neighboring Ukraine.

He also said there were "many indications" suggesting the incident "fits into this new Russian doctrine of attack."

Gawkowski warned that the incident could reflect a 'new Russian doctrine of attack' Image: Klaudia Radecka/NurPhoto/picture alliance

Poland accuses Russia of 'hybrid' warfare

Poland and other EU and NATO member states have accused Russia of engaging in hybrid warfare, including acts of sabotage, against Ukraine's allies, since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

Lying on the EU and NATO's eastern flank, Poland borders Ukraine, the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad and Moscow ally Belarus. It is one of Kyiv's strongest supporters in Europe.

Warsaw also joined the new "Carpathian Eight" regional summit launched by Ukraine last Friday.

Earlier in September, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that Russia plans to carry out "hybrid" drone and missile strikes against Ukraine's allies.

Late last year, Poland accused Russia of carrying out "state terrorism" over an act of sabotage on the Polish rail network.
