A fire last night at a ground station in Poland used by Starlink, Elon Musk’s satellite internet company, was caused deliberately, says digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski. The facility is used to provide internet services across the region, including in Ukraine, which relies heavily on Starlink connections. Although the fire is still being investigated, “the modus operandi in this case is clearly Russian”, says Gawkowski. 🔴 Gawkowski o pożarze stacji Starlink. "Element wojny hybrydowej" Wicepremier Krzysztof Gawkowski ocenił pożar stacji Starlink na Mazowszu jako celową próbę zakłócenia łączności. – Wiele wskazuje na to, że pożar stacji Starlinków na Mazowszu to kolejny element wojny hybrydowej… — Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) September 24, 2026 Firefighters were called out at around 9 p.m. on Wednesday to the facility, which is located in the village of Wola Krobowska, just south of the capital Warsaw. Due to suspicions that the fire had been caused deliberately, police and officers from the Internal Security Agency (ABW) were also later dispatched to the scene. “We’re dealing with an arson attack that was intended to impact critical telecommunications infrastructure that influences internet operation,” Gakowski, who also serves as deputy prime minister, told broadcaster TVN on Thursday morning. In a separate interview with TVP, the minister said that the facility is owned by Polish state telecommunications operator Exatel and “provides internet transmission through Poland, and also to Ukraine”. He noted that other internet providers use Exatel’s facility, including Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which is the owner of Starlink. Starlink terminals have been vital in Ukraine during Russia’s war against the country. Gawkowski told TVN that “the modus operandi in this case is clearly Russian” and “is another element of the hybrid warfare we are facing”. Poland has been one of the primary targets for Russian sabotage operations in Europe, including a series of arson attacks. “The Russians want to paralyse critical infrastructure, cut off water, gas and electricity, paralyse the internet,” said the minister. “All these processes have one goal: to incite panic and stir up emotions.” However, in his remarks to TVP, Gakowski acknowledged that, for now, “it is impossible to say” for sure whether Russia was behind the attack. Poland is the "primary focus" of Russia's sabotage campaign in Europe, finds a new report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism. Among 151 incidents identified since 2022, 31 of them took place in Poland – more than in any other country https://t.co/QXfSI00FD6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 3, 2026 The spokesman for Poland’s security services, Jacek Dobrzyński, likewise told TVN that “at this stage it is still too early to talk about the causes or motives of this fire”. However, he confirmed that “everything points to arson”. Justice minister Waldemar Żurek also told broadcaster RMF that “this could be an act of sabotage, and we are taking that into account, so nothing can be ruled out here, especially since these are sensitive elements that ensure satellite communications”. Polish news service Defence24 notes that ground stations are used by Starlink to connect its satellite constellation with terrestrial communications infrastructure. The facility in Poland, alongside one in Lithuania, serves the entire Central and Eastern Europe region, including Ukraine. Tu nieco więcej o roli stacji naziemnych w systemie Starlink. https://t.co/EYys481dSi — Mariusz Marszałkowski (@MJMarszalkowski) September 24, 2026 Earlier this month, a fire broke out at a drone plant in Poland belonging to WB Electronics, which supplies the armed forces of Ukraine and Poland, among others. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that there was “no doubt” the fire was caused deliberately, and that Russia was likely behind it. The Polish government has in recent months warned that Russia is planning to escalate its hybrid actions against Poland and other countries in the region, including through acts of sabotage, disinformation, and potential airspace and border violations. In July, a Russian missile entered Polish airspace before landing in a field in eastern Poland. On Wednesday this week, the same day as the fire in Wola Krobowska broke out, a Russian helicopter briefly entered Polish airspace. World.title: Poland and Belarus seek thaw in relations as foreign ministers meet for first time in a decade
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The foreign ministers of Poland and Belarus have met for the first time in a decade, as both sides indicated that they are open to thawing their long-frosty relations. The two countries have regularly clashed in recent years, in particular over Minsk’s alliance with Moscow, the migration crisis Belarus has engineered on the Polish border, and the persecution of Belarus’s ethnic Polish minority. Warsaw, meanwhile, has supported the Belarusian democratic opposition. However, on Tuesday this week, Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski confirmed to reporters that he had met with his Belarusian counterpart, Maxim Ryzhenkov, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. Sikorski said that the initiative had come from the Belarusian side. “When a neighbour wants to unfreeze and improve relations, Poland is the first to reach an agreement,” said Sikorski, quoted by broadcaster RMF. “This is a first, introductory meeting, but meetings with other ministries and at other levels are also taking place,” he added, noting that Poland will also “soon be opening a new embassy building in Minsk”. When asked what topics had been discussed, Sikorski said that they had included the border situation and regional security. Asked if he had requested that Belarus not allow Russia to fly drones and missiles through its territory, he said that this was discussed “among other things”. The last known time that the Polish and Belarusian foreign ministers met was in October 2016, when Belarus’s Vladimir Makei visited Witold Waszczykowski in Warsaw. Sikorski said that this week’s meeting with Ryzhenkov had been possible because the situation on their shared border – where Belarus has since 2021 encouraged and assisted tens of thousands of migrants, mainly from Asia and Africa, to cross into Poland – is now “more normalised”. Poland has installed physical and electronic barriers along the border, sent thousands of armed officers to guard it, and has banned asylum claims by migrants who cross irregularly. Following those measures, the number of attempted crossings has fallen dramatically this year. Sikorski also noted that relations have been improved by Belarus’s recent decisions to release political prisoners, including Polish ones. Most prominent among them is Andrzej Poczobut, a leader of the Polish community in Belarus, who had been imprisoned on trumped-up charges for five years. The number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants from Belarus to Poland fell from 15,500 in the first half of 2025 to 235 this year – a drop of over 98% Poland also now claims a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally https://t.co/RFZkd7CeIk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 20, 2026 Minsk’s recent actions have provided “more freedom and greater reasons to try to stabilise relations”, said Sikorski. “A snowdrop can bloom if the weather is favorable.” Belarus’s foreign ministry continued that metaphor in a post on social media on Wednesday, sharing a photo of Sikorski meeting with Ryzhenkov and writing that “snowdrop diplomacy is a nice restart”. “But we’re in it for the harvest,” added the ministry. “Let’s plant an orchard – it needs nurturing every year, not once a decade. Minsk is ready to host.” Last year, Belarus called for “dialogue” with Poland in order to “reduce the risk of armed clashes” amid a military build-up around the border. However, it also issued a formal protest to Poland over a demonstration in Warsaw organised by exiled opponents of Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko. .@sikorskiradek, snowdrop diplomacy is a nice restart. But we’re in it for the harvest. Let’s plant an orchard 🍎 – it needs nurturing every year, not once a decade. Minsk is ready to host 🇧🇾🇵🇱 pic.twitter.com/WSN5n4uOtE — Belarus MFA 🇧🇾 (@BelarusMFA) September 23, 2026 News of Tuesday’s meeting was criticised by Stanisław Żaryn, who served as spokesman for the Polish security services under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government and later as an advisor to President Andrzej Duda. In a social media post, he said that Sikorski and media outlets are “forcibly pushing us into another reset with Belarus (and perhaps even with Russia)”. However, “Belarus chose its strategic path long ago and won’t turn away from Russia”, he added. He asked if Poles are meant to forget about the death of Mateusz Sitek, a Polish soldier killed by a migrant from a group trying to force its way over the border from Belarus. His suspected killer, a Moroccan national, is believed by Polish prosecutors to still be in Belarus, which has refused to extradite him. Should “we just move on as if nothing happened regarding Belarus’s involvement in the war against Ukraine and the intelligence war against Poland?” continued Żaryn. ⚠️Radosław Sikorski spotkał się z Szefem MSZ Białorusi. Media już piszą o „przełomie”, a Sikorski zapewnia, że „Polska jest pierwsza do zgody”. Na siłę wtłaczają nas w kolejny reset z Białorusią (a być może i Rosją). Na czym mają polegać przełomy i „zgoda” w stosunkach z… pic.twitter.com/DZ41wSgjL0 — Stanisław Żaryn (@StZaryn) September 23, 2026 Francišak Viačorka, a leading figure in the exiled Belarusian democratic opposition, also expressed scepticism in an interview with Polish newspaper Fakt. “We believe that the authorities in Minsk cannot be trusted,” he said. “Of course, when the authorities communicate with Western partners, they promise that everything will be fine, that they want dialogue, but then their words fail to match their actions.” “I understand that Minister Sikorski is doing everything to protect Polish interests and the sovereignty and security of his country, but I think that in Minsk they see it differently.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Russian military helicopter violates Polish airspace
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. This is a breaking news story and may be updated as further details emerge. A Russian military helicopter briefly entered Polish airspace on Wednesday morning, the operational command of Poland’s armed forces has announced. The incident is the latest in a series of airspace violations by Russia, which have also involved drones and, most recently, a missile. It follows recent warnings by the Polish government that Moscow has been planning further “provocations” intended to test NATO’s defences and unity. ❗️ Informujemy, że 23 września br. o godz. 11.08, na północ od miejscowości Braniewo, doszło do krótkotrwałego naruszenia przestrzeni powietrznej Rzeczypospolitej Polskiej przez śmigłowiec Mi-8 Sił Zbrojnych Federacji Rosyjskiej. Śmigłowiec wykonywał lot z Obwodu Królewieckiego.… pic.twitter.com/afULQdSeTc — Dowództwo Operacyjne RSZ (@DowOperSZ) September 23, 2026 On Wednesday afternoon, Polish operational command announced that, shortly after 11:00 a.m. that day, an Mi-8 helicopter belonging to the Russian armed forces had briefly entered Polish airspace near the town of Braniewo, after crossing from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. The helicopter did not travel further than 300 metres into Polish airspace and remained there for 42 seconds. In response, the Polish military scrambled fighter jets and placed ground forces on standby. “The nature of the incident indicates that Russia is once again testing the readiness of our air defences,” wrote operational command. At the time of writing, Russia has not commented on the incident. Today’s violation appears to be the first publicly reported instance of a Russian military helicopter crossing Poland’s land border. Last year, in two separate incidents, a Russian Su-24 bomber and a naval helicopter flew over Poland’s territorial waters in the Baltic Sea. In 2023, two helicopters belonging to the armed forces of Belarus, a close ally of Russia, briefly entered Polish airspace before crossing back over the border. On one night in September last year, around 20 Russian drones entered Poland over its eastern borders amid Russian attacks on Ukraine. Polish and allied forces shot down some of them, while others hit the ground without causing casulaties. In July this year, a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile carrying a significant explosive payload entered Polish airspace before landing in a field in eastern Poland. The object that crashed in the Lublin region on Thursday was a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile carrying a "significant amount" of explosive material. The missile was "potentially very dangerous,” Poland's defence ministry confirmedhttps://t.co/NoqZwIcaWp — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 31, 2026 In recent months, Poland and other NATO countries have been warning of Russian plans to carry out further “provocations” intended to test the alliance’s defences and unity, saying that they could include border and airspace violations. In recent weeks, Poland has regularly intercepted Russian aircraft that have flown close to Polish territorial waters in the Baltic Sea. This month, Russian drones have repeatedly hit targets in Ukraine close to the Polish border, including a passenger train travelling from Kyiv to Warsaw. Just last week, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that, according to intelligence sources, Russia is planning drone and missile strikes on eastern NATO countries, which it would present as accidental. World.title: Senior Polish presidential official detained amid probe into misspending of funds
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Agents from Poland’s Central Anti-Corruption Bureau (CBA) have detained a senior official from opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki’s chancellery as part of a probe into alleged misspending of funds under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government. An employee of a major right-wing broadcaster, Republika, was also taken into custody as part of the same investigation, which relates to the activities of the Polish National Foundation (PFN), a body created under the PiS government to promote Poland abroad but which was also used to further the party’s political interests. Dzisiaj rano w Warszawie na polecenie Prokuratury Regionalnej w Rzeszowie agenci @CBAgovPL zatrzymali Piotra M. i Annę P. ▶️ Zatrzymane osoby przewożone są do @Prok_Regio_RZE, która prowadzi śledztwo dotyczące nieprawidłowości w Polskiej Fundacji Narodowej. ▶️ Na tym etapie… — Jacek Dobrzyński (@JacekDobrzynski) September 23, 2026 On Tuesday morning, Jacek Dobrzyński, the spokesman for the security services, announced that two individuals, named only as Piotr M. and Anna P. under Polish privacy law, had been detained by the CBA at the request of prosecutors investigating irregularities in the PFN. Both suspects previously worked in the chancellery of Prime Minister Beata Szydło, who was head of the PiS government from 2015 to 2017. Piotr M. was head of the Government Information Centre (CIR) and Anna P. led the media services department. Anna P. now works for Nawrocki, who was elected as president last year with the support of PiS. She is director of the Presidential Events Office, which organises the president’s schedule. Piotr M. currently works as a commentator for Republika, a station generally supportive of Nawrocki and PiS. Agenci CBA zatrzymali w Warszawie Piotra M. i Annę P. Sprawa dotyczy nieprawidłowości w Polskiej Fundacji Narodowej! pic.twitter.com/e3jw3ekdOA — Iwona Hartwich (@iwonahartwich) September 23, 2026 In 2017, while still working in Szydło’s chancellery, Piotr M. and Anna P. founded a PR company called Solvere. Later that same year, the company was hired to run a prominent and controversial campaign for the PFN called “Fair Courts”, receiving a reported 1.2 million zloty (€275,000) for the project. The PFN had been set up the previous year under Szydło’s government with funding from 17 state-owned companies. Its publicly declared and statutory mission was to promote Poland abroad. However, the “Fair Courts” campaign, which cost around 8.4 million zloty, was run in Poland itself, with material in Polish, and aimed to show the alleged failings of the justice system in Poland in order to justify why controversial reforms being implemented by PiS were necessary. Echoing PiS rhetoric, the campaign suggested that judges saw themselves as a “special caste” and highlighted cases of alleged wrongdoing by individual judges, including one who had been caught stealing a sausage. (The judge in question had not ruled on a case since that incident in 2006 and had died in 2015.) In 2018, a Warsaw court ruled that the “Fair Courts” campaign was inconsistent with the PFN’s statutory goals, saying that not only did the adverts fail to enhance Poland’s image abroad, “on the contrary, they significantly weakened it, creating a negative image of the judiciary based on individual cases”. In February 2025, just over a year after PiS lost power, a newly appointed PFN board accused its predecessors of criminal negligence that caused damages of over 30 million zloty to the foundation’s finances. They notified prosecutors of potential crimes. In July this year, two men who had served as PFN board members at the time of the campaign were detained as part of an investigation into the misspending of the foundation’s funds. At that time, the CBA also announced that it had searched the homes of Anna P. and Piotr M. A senior official under the former PiS government has been charged over alleged misspending of funds. The case relates to a campaign in 2017 that used money meant for promoting Poland abroad to instead advertise PiS's judicial reforms domestically https://t.co/tH64Bekhec — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 15, 2026 Today’s detentions of Anna P. and Piotr M. were welcomed by Prime Minister Donald Tusk. He told Polsat News that the “Fair Courts” campaign was a “double scandal” because it was “not only an abuse of public funds, but also for the very clearly malicious purpose” of “attacking the independent judiciary”. Meanwhile, Waldemar Żurek, the justice minister and prosecutor general, told the media that the authorities intended to find out “who stood behind” the actions of Anna P. and Piotr M., because “it’s hard to believe this was their initiative”. However, Jarosław Olechowski, a senior executive at Republika, condemned the detentions, calling them an act of “political revenge by the Donald Tusk regime for an information campaign exposing pathologies in Polish courts”. At the time of writing, the presidential chancellery had not commented on the detention of Anna P., the head of its events office. Earlier this year, Nawrocki’s deputy chief of staff was charged with ordering the falsification of documents, an accusation he denies. ❗️❗️❗️❗️❗️ Funkcjonariusze @CBAgovPL zatrzymali @Matczuk_ publicystę @RepublikaTV Przewożą go do prokuratury w Rzeszowie. Powodem zatrzymania jest zemsta polityczna reżimu @donaldtusk za kampanię informacyjną pokazującą patologie w polskich sądach — Jarek Olechowski (@OlechowskiJarek) September 23, 2026 The “Fair Courts” campaign was just one of a number of controversial initiatives launched by the PFN under the PiS government. The foundation was regularly accused of spending money to support PiS’s political goals or on seemingly wasteful projects. One of its most famous initiatives involved the purchase of a yacht for almost €1 million, which was renamed “I Love Poland” and sent on an around-the-world cruise to mark the centenary of Poland’s independence in 2018 (though it suffered damage and spent weeks stuck in a port, accruing further costs). In 2021, the Supreme Audit Office (NIK) accused the PFN of violating the law by refusing to provide documents required for an audit. World.title: New US “Fort Trump” military base in Poland “confirmed”, says President Nawrocki
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish President Karol Nawrocki says that a planned new permanent US military base in Poland is “confirmed” because his American counterpart, Donald Trump, is “famous for keeping his word”. He also suggested that the new facility will be called “Fort Trump”. Trump himself declared last week that “major progress” was being made towards establishing the base, saying it was thanks to the “bold leadership of my friend, Karol Nawrocki”, who is a conservative ally of the US president. Meanwhile, earlier this week, a Polish deputy defence minister, Stanisław Wziątek, also expressed confidence that the new base would soon be confirmed and said that it could see the number of US troops stationed in Poland rise to around 15,000. President Karol Nawrocki said he hopes the US will finalize plans to establish a permanent military base in Poland and, if it does, the compound will be christened ‘Fort Trump' https://t.co/SB4DOy5Qp1 pic.twitter.com/aPmvl4JoFO — Bloomberg TV (@BloombergTV) September 22, 2026 The US military presence in Poland has become a big issue this year following Washington’s unexpected last-minute decision in May to cancel the rotational deployment of almost 4,000 troops. Shortly afterwards, Trump declared that he would deploy 5,000 additional troops to Poland. In June, Poland formally submitted a request for the US to establish a new permanent US military base on its territory. In a post on his social media platform, Truth Social, last week, Trump announced “major progress” in those plans and said that “if this happens, the location [of the base] will be announced very soon”. He called it a “historic step for our Great US/Polish Alliance”. On Tuesday this week, speaking to Bloomberg during a visit to the US for the United Nations General Assembly, Nawrocki confirmed that plans for the base were at an advanced stage. “The infrastructure is being chosen right now. Consultants from the US have already visited Poland,” he said. “I think that it’s hard for me to give specific dates, but I think that this matter is for sure confirmed because President Trump is famous for keeping his word.” Nawrocki also expressed confidence that “President Trump will personally be able to participate in the inauguration of Fort Trump”. That name, Fort Trump, was first suggested in 2018 by Nawrocki’s predecessor, Andrzej Duda, when, during Trump’s first term, he sought a permanent US base in Poland. Poland’s government, which regularly clashes with the opposition-aligned Nawrocki and has also at times had tense relations with the Trump administration, has not commented on the idea of naming the new base after the US president. However, the government is keen for the project to move ahead, and has been doing much of the legwork on making it happen. Although Poland’s president is commander-in-chief of the armed forces, his position is largely ceremonial, and it is the government that is responsible for implementing policy. On Monday this week, deputy defence minister Stanisław Wziątek told broadcaster RMF that he was “convinced there is full agreement” on establishing the base, with the remaining question being the precise location. Wziątek said that the announcement could be made before November’s midterm elections in the US, as Trump will be keen to encourage Polish Americans to vote Republican. 💬Kiedy poznamy ostateczną decyzję w sprawie stałej bazy amerykańskiej w Polsce? 💬Jestem przekonany, że pan prezydent @realDonaldTrump będzie chciał zrobić wszystko, aby tak decyzja zachęcająca Polaków do głosowania na Republikanów mogła zapaść przed wyborami – Stanisław… pic.twitter.com/uPWkmdGQod — RozmowaRMF (@Rozmowa_RMF) September 21, 2026 The deputy defence minister said that the base would be likely to host between 3,000 and 5,000 US troops, with 4,500 the “most realistic estimate, because that is the size of a brigade”. In total, said Wziątek, Poland hoped to have “around 15,000” US soldiers in Poland, including the roughly 10,000 that have up until now been present on a rotational basis. The minister admitted that the current rotational presence was lower, around 6,500-7,000, following the cancellation of May’s planned deployment. But he said that the figure should “soon” return to the previous higher level. When asked about the cost to Poland of establishing the new permanent US base, Wziątek said it would “definitely be more than 15 billion zloty (€3.4 billion) but will depend on the level of involvement of the United States”. 💬Ilu w tej chwili w Polsce jest żołnierzy amerykańskich? Ilu będzie docelowo rotacyjnych żołnierzy i w stałej bazie? Odpowiada Stanisław Wziątek @MON_GOV_PL w #RozmowaRMF o 7:00 w @Radio_RMF24@RMF24pl @Radio_RMF24 pic.twitter.com/1Zl66upkp8 — RozmowaRMF (@Rozmowa_RMF) September 21, 2026 The US has long been Poland’s most important security partner. On Tuesday, the National Prosecutor’s Office announced that the main suspect, who can be named only as Paweł G. under Polish privacy law, had been detained last week by the Internal Security Agency (ABW) and charged by prosecutors with three alleged crimes. World.title: Poland has begun paying benefits to same-sex couples who married abroad
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has begun paying state benefits to same-sex couples who married abroad and have had their wedding certificates transcribed into the Polish registry, the minister for family, labour and social policy, Agnieszka Dziemianowicz-Bąk, has confirmed. Poland was recently ordered to start recognising such marriages by the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU). Dziemianowicz-Bąk says there are indications that Polish same-sex couples are now travelling abroad to marry so as to gain rights in Poland, where domestic law still does not allow them to form recognised unions. Wiedzieliście, że ZUS wypłaca już pierwsze zasiłki "małżeństwom jednopłciowym" po transkrypcji aktów wydanych za granicą❓❓❓ To już wiecie 👇 pic.twitter.com/W99ymV3T31 — ɐllǝnuɐɯı (@szef_dywizji) September 18, 2026 In November 2025, the CJEU ruled that Poland must recognise same-sex marriages conducted in other EU member states, finding that failing to do so infringes the freedom to move and reside within the EU as well as the right to respect for private and family life. In light of that ruling, in March this year, Poland’s own Supreme Administrative Court (NSA) ordered Warsaw’s registry office to recognise a marriage conducted by two Polish men in Germany by transcribing it into the Polish civil registry. In May, the Polish government issued a regulation allowing such transcriptions of foreign same-sex marriages to take place nationwide. It went into force in August. However, even before then, some cities had begun transcribing marriage certificates, beginning with Warsaw and Wrocław in May. At the end of August, digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski reported that 84 same-sex couples had already transcribed their foreign marriages under the government’s new regulation. All Polish registry offices can now recognise foreign same-sex marriages, after a new regulation went into force. The government’s plenipotentiary for equality warned local authorities they will be breaking the law if they do not comply with the new rules https://t.co/EWGkuvm7EE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 24, 2026 While foreign same-sex marriages can now be entered into Poland’s civil registry, questions have remained as to what that will mean in practice for such couples, especially as domestic law does not recognise same-sex relationships. However, speaking to news service Wirtualna Polska on Friday, Dziemianowicz-Bąk confirmed that “the Social Insurance Institution (ZUS) is already paying the first care allowances to same-sex couples”. Such allowances are paid to someone who is required to provide care for a spouse. The level of the allowance is set at 80% of the recipient’s average salary from the last 12 months, and it is available for up to 14 days per calendar year. Poland has begun recognising foreign same-sex marriages. But the legal consequences for such couples remain unclear, especially as Polish law does not allow any form of same-sex union We asked five experts for their view on what this will mean in practice https://t.co/h2KHmW8sMI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 Dziemianowicz-Bąk welcomed the fact that “ZUS, one of the most important institutions, knows and understands that love is love, marriage is marriage, and these rights will be respected”. She is from The Left (Lewica), a junior partner in Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition and the most enthusiastic supporter of LGBT+ rights. The minister confirmed that her colleague from The Left, Katarzyna Kotula, the government’s plenipotentiary for equality, is “in dialogue with the finance ministry and National Revenue Administration (KAS)” to ensure that same-sex couples who married abroad receive the tax benefits available to other married couples. Dziemianowicz-Bąk also argued that the right-wing opposition and conservative President Karol Nawrocki are unintentionally encouraging Polish same-sex couples to marry by preventing the government from introducing a domestic law on recognising same-sex relationships. In July, Nawrocki vetoed a government bill that would have allowed unmarried partners, including same-sex couples, to obtain certain rights available to married couples, including relating to taxation, property, and access to medical information. However, it would not have allowed same-sex couples to marry or even form civil partnerships. Instead, they would have signed a contract before a notary, formalising their relationship. Yet this step was still too far for Nawrocki, who said that it threatened the institution of marriage, which is enshrined in the constitution. Opposition-aligned President @NawrockiKn has vetoed government bills granting certain rights to unmarried partners, including same-sex couples, for the first time in Poland. He argued that the proposal would have threatened the institution of marriage https://t.co/UXdrNfGfup — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 Last week, the ruling coalition attempted to overrule the president’s veto in parliament, which requires the support of a three-fifths majority. However, the vote fell short of that figure after the right-wing opposition voted to uphold the veto. Dziemianowicz-Bąk said that the government’s opponents were “essentially encouraging marriage equality” because they left same-sex couples with only one option to have their relationships recognised: getting married abroad and then having the certificate transcribed into the Polish registry. She told Wirtualna Polska that “we’ve heard indications” that this is precisely what such couples are now doing. State research agency @CBOS_Info has found its highest-ever level of support in Poland for the introduction of same-sex civil partnerships. Over 62% are now in favour, up from 52% last year and just 25% in 2011, when the question was first asked https://t.co/Y9ydpbwsoU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 14, 2025 However, opposition figures have argued that recognition of same-sex marriages violates Poland’s constitution, article 18 of which says: “Marriage, being a union of a man and a woman, as well as the family, motherhood and parenthood, shall be placed under the protection and care of the Republic of Poland.” In July, the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), which has a majority of judges appointed by the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, ruled that the government’s regulation allowing the transcription of foreign same-sex marriages is unconstitutional. But the government regards the TK as illegitimate since it contains judges unlawfully appointed under PiS. It therefore ignores the tribunal’s rulings. Poland's Constitutional Tribunal has ruled that a new regulation allowing foreign same-sex marriage certificates to be registered in Poland is unconstitutional. The government says it will not implement the rulinghttps://t.co/xDAzLjcJQ4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 28, 2026 In response to Dziemianowicz-Bąk’s announcement that ZUS has begun paying benefits to same-sex couples, Krzysztof Bosak, one of the leaders of the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) group, said that it showed how “the left is ready to trample every law, including the constitution, just to get their way”. “What drives them and what they believe in is ideology, and what guides them is the instinct for domination,” added Bosak, who is also a deputy speaker of the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament. World.title: New Sports Complex Opens in Prague’s Riegrovy Sady
World.content:
A new sports complex has opened in Riegrovy Sady, giving residents of Prague 2 access to a refurbished court, parkour equipment, a climbing wall and an outdoor fitness area.

The facility, next to the TJ Sokol Královské Vinohrady building, was officially opened Tuesday afternoon. The renovation and installation of new equipment cost CZK 8.7 million, excluding VAT.



The site is intended for people of different ages and can be used for several sports. The refurbished court is suitable for football and basketball, while the new equipment includes a parkour area, climbing wall and a small fitness zone.

The project forms part of the district’s longer-term plans for Riegrovy Sady. Officials said the upper section of the park has lacked sufficient space for outdoor sports and exercise.

The sports area occupies land that until last year was used by two unauthorized structures, the Ice Magic ice sculpture exhibition and the Containall sports and cultural center.

The district is also considering a much larger project for the site. A multifunctional hall for sports and cultural events could eventually replace the current outdoor facility.

Petr Janů, deputy chairman of TJ Sokol Královské Vinohrady, previously said the goal was to create a building designed to remain in place for decades or longer.

The project is still at an early stage. Prague 2 plans to discuss the design with local residents, heritage authorities and Prague’s Institute of Planning and Development. An architectural competition is also expected to be held.

World.title: Prague Taxi Drivers Could Be Tested on Czech and Local Geography
World.content:
Prague taxi drivers could soon be required to demonstrate their knowledge of Czech and the city’s geography.

The Chamber of Deputies approved the change on Wednesday as part of an amendment to the Road Traffic Act. The legislation does not automatically introduce testing in Prague or other Czech cities. Instead, it would give municipalities the authority to impose such requirements.



Under the amendment, municipalities could test taxi drivers on their legal rights and obligations, their Czech language skills to the extent necessary for the job, and their knowledge of locations within the municipality that are relevant to taxi services.

The bill now goes to the Senate.

What the new rules could mean for taxi drivers

The issue has been debated in Prague for some time, particularly as the taxi industry has changed with the rapid growth of app-based services.

Pirate Party leader Zdeněk Hřib introduced a more detailed proposal in May. That version included specific provisions defining what drivers could be required to know and what would fall outside the scope of the tests.

For example, the proposal said drivers should not be expected to demonstrate encyclopedic knowledge of Prague’s landmarks. Transport Minister Ivan Bednárik of the SPD, however, argued that the Pirate Party’s proposal had legal shortcomings.

A shorter amendment submitted by ANO MP Patrik Nacher ultimately became the version approved by the Chamber of Deputies.

Supporters of the change say taxi driving has increasingly become a profession with few formal qualification requirements beyond holding a driving licence.

The explanatory report accompanying the legislation argues that the sector has attracted foreign workers who may have limited knowledge of Czech, local traffic rules and the city in which they operate.

Critics, meanwhile, have raised concerns about the potential impact on fares. They argue that additional requirements could increase the cost of entering the profession and eventually lead to higher prices for passengers.

No English requirement in the legislation

The approved amendment refers specifically to knowledge of the Czech language. It does not introduce an English-language requirement, even though some taxi drivers in Prague also have limited English skills.

The legislation would apply to taxi drivers regardless of whether they operate independently or through digital platforms such as Uber and Bolt.

Foreign nationals make up roughly half of Prague’s registered taxi drivers, reflecting the sector’s long-standing reliance on foreign workers and recently arrived migrants.

World.title: More Than 250 People Fall Ill in Salmonella Outbreak at Prague School
World.content:
More than 240 children and 10 adults have developed gastrointestinal symptoms in connection with a suspected Salmonella outbreak at a school in Prague’s Újezd nad Lesy district.

Masaryk Elementary School, which has around 1,100 pupils, is being temporarily closed while health authorities investigate the source of the infection. The school’s kitchen and cafeteria will also undergo thorough disinfection.



Salmonella has so far been confirmed by laboratory tests in four children, according to Petra Batok, a spokesperson for the Prague Public Health Authority. Officials are continuing to investigate how the infection entered the school.

The first cases were reported earlier this week. The largest number of illnesses has been recorded among upper-level pupils and children attending Montessori classes. Classes for those groups were cancelled on Wednesday, while all pupils have been given Thursday and Friday off.

Food samples taken from the school cafeteria have been sent for laboratory testing, with results expected on Friday.

The final number of people affected is not yet known. Health officials are collecting additional information through questionnaires completed by parents and adults who visited the cafeteria.

The Prague public health authorities have described the incident as an epidemic.

Prague emergency services have received 55 calls from people reporting gastrointestinal symptoms in connection with the outbreak.

Twenty patients were transported to hospitals for treatment, while another 24 were examined and treated without being admitted. The remaining people received medical advice by telephone.

Salmonellosis is usually contracted by consuming contaminated food. Common sources include eggs, insufficiently cooked meat, unpasteurized milk and foods containing raw or unpasteurized eggs. Symptoms generally appear between 13 and 36 hours after infection.

World.title: Prague Metro and Tram Disruptions Planned for September 28 Weekend
World.content:
Prague commuters should expect changes to metro and tram services from Saturday, September 26, through Monday, September 28, as maintenance work affects Metro Line C and tram routes in Libeň.

Metro Line C will be suspended between Pražského povstání and Chodov for the entire long weekend. Trains will continue running between Letňany and Pražského povstání, while the southern section between Chodov and Háje will operate as a shuttle service.



Four stations will be affected by the closure: Pankrác, Budějovická, Kačerov and Roztyly. Passengers can use replacement bus XC, which will run between Pražského povstání and Chodov via all four stations.

Hundreds of railway sleepers to be replaced

The closure will allow Prague Public Transit Company (DPP) workers to replace several hundred wooden sleepers with concrete ones.

Once the work is completed, around 17,000 of the approximately 20,000 original sleepers between Florenc and Kačerov will have been replaced.

DPP said the work is scheduled during long weekends because the materials used to secure the new sleepers need more time to harden than a standard weekend allows.

Tram services suspended in Libeň

Tram services will also be disrupted between Palmovka and Ke Stírce from early Saturday morning until 6 p.m. Monday.

Several lines will operate on modified routes. Tram 3 will run via Těšnov, Vltavská, Strossmayerovo náměstí, Výstaviště, Nádraží Holešovice, Hercovka, Ke Stírce, Kobylisy and Ládví before terminating at Sídliště Ďáblice.

Line 10 will run from Palmovka via Balabenka and Arena Libeň jih to Nádraží Libeň, while lines 24 and 95 will terminate at Palmovka.

Replacement bus X3 will operate during the day between Palmovka, Bulovka, Ke Stírce and Kobylisy. Night service will be provided by bus X95, which will continue to Vozovna Kobylisy.

Passengers using Prague public transport over the long weekend should allow extra travel time and check the latest DPP information before travelling.

World.title: Czech Man Jailed 13 Days After Protest on Moscow’s Red Square
World.content:
A judge at Moscow’s Tverskoy District Court sentenced a Czech man to 13 days in jail on Tuesday for staging a protest on Red Square.

Identified as Michal Plamenek, the man was arrested for holding up a sign in English next to Lenin’s Mausoleum on Sunday afternoon, the court’s press service said in a statement.



No details were provided as to what was written on Plamenek’s sign, but the court press service said a judge ruled that the inscription was “aimed at discrediting the Russian Armed Forces.”

Police officers arrested Plamenek because Red Square directly adjoins the Kremlin, where protests are banned. He allegedly refused to listen to a request by officers to accompany them to a police station and resisted arrest.

A judge found Plamenek guilty on three separate administrative counts of discrediting the Russian military, violating protest rules and disobeying a police officer.

He was also fined a total of 60,000 roubles, around CZK 15,000.

The Czech Foreign Ministry said its embassy in Moscow has been providing the detained man with consular assistance from the outset. It declined to comment further because of the sensitivity of the case.

World.title: Gipsy Kings by André Reyes to Perform in Prague This November
World.content:
The legendary Gipsy Kings by André Reyes will perform in Prague this November, bringing their distinctive mix of flamenco guitar, rumba and Latin rhythms to Lucerna Great Hall on November 29, 2026.

Led by founding member André Reyes, the group will perform some of the songs that made the Gipsy Kings famous around the world, including “Bamboleo,” “Djobi Djoba” and “Volare,” alongside newer material.



The concert is being presented by Gotobeat and will begin at 7 p.m. Tickets are online here.

From southern France to the world

The Gipsy Kings’ story began with the Reyes family and their musical roots in the south of France. André Reyes was one of the founding members of the group, which went on to combine traditional flamenco with rumba, Latin rhythms and pop influences.

Their energetic guitar playing and Spanish-language songs helped turn rumba flamenca into an international sound. Tracks such as “Bamboleo” and “Djobi Djoba” became global hits, while their version of “Volare” introduced the group to an even wider audience.

Music associated with the Gipsy Kings has sold more than 60 million records worldwide, making the group one of the most successful international acts to emerge from the flamenco-rumba tradition.

Their music has also appeared in popular culture, including their version of “Hotel California,” which featured in The Big Lebowski.

A new generation of the Reyes family

André Reyes continues the tradition today with Gipsy Kings by André Reyes, performing alongside younger members of the Reyes family.

The current show combines the group’s best-known classics with newer music, including material connected to Nací Gitano, the band’s latest project. The group is also touring internationally in 2026 as part of its Viva el Arte Tour.

For audiences, the concert offers a mix of familiar songs and new material, with the performance centred on the fast-paced guitar playing, percussion and vocals that have defined the Gipsy Kings sound for decades.

Date: Sunday, November 29, 2026

Time: 7 p.m.

Venue: Lucerna Great Hall, Štěpánská 61, Prague 1

Promoter: Gotobeat

World.title: Heating Season Starts Across Czechia as Temperatures Fall
World.content:
District heating plants across the Czech Republic are beginning to supply heat as temperatures drop, with conditions for the start of the heating season now being met in much of the country.

Some plants have already begun providing additional heat during the colder morning and evening hours. The first systems to respond were mainly in mountainous parts of northern and western Czechia and in the Vysočina region.



Other heating plants are expected to gradually start operating in the coming days, depending on local temperatures and weather forecasts.

Since 2010, district heating systems have generally started supplying heat after September 20, although the exact timing varies considerably from year to year.

If temperatures rise again in late September or early October, heating can be suspended. Under the standard rules, heating is normally interrupted when the average outdoor temperature exceeds 13°C for two consecutive days and the forecast indicates that temperatures will continue to rise.

Last winter was colder than average

The previous heating season placed greater demands on heating systems than the years immediately before it.

According to figures from the Czech District Heating Association, the season was 4.9 percent colder than the previous year. It was also 3.2 percent colder than the average of the preceding 15 years.

The colder conditions translated into higher demand for heat, particularly during periods of sustained low temperatures.

Heating costs could increase next year

Households are not currently expected to face a direct increase resulting from a recent change in the interpretation of a fuel tax exemption, but some other users of district heating could see higher costs.

The issue concerns combined heat and power (CHP) generation. This year, the state changed how an existing fuel tax exemption is interpreted, limiting its application to the amount of heat supplied to households.

Heating companies say the change could increase annual heating bills for institutions such as hospitals and schools by tens or even hundreds of thousands of Czech crowns.

World.title: Crowdfunding Campaign Launches for Book Tracing the History of Prague’s Roxy Club
World.content:
A new book documenting the history of Prague’s Roxy club and the alternative cultural scene that grew around it is seeking public support ahead of its planned publication this autumn.

Titled Kopneš do plechovky a dva dny se tančí (“Kick a Can and Dance for Two Days”), the book looks at Roxy’s development from its beginnings in the early 1990s to its current role in Prague’s music scene.



A crowdfunding campaign to finance the publication has been launched on Donio.cz.

Rather than focusing solely on the history of one nightclub, the project examines the people, artists and cultural movements connected with the venue.

More than 40 musicians, promoters, artists and other figures associated with Roxy contribute their memories and perspectives.

Roxy opened in 1992 and quickly became an important venue for alternative music in Prague. Over the years, its programme has covered genres including hardcore, house, trip-hop, hip-hop and drum’n’bass.

The book is the result of almost five years of research by cultural journalist Ondřej Horák. He examined thousands of archival documents, located previously unpublished photographs and interviewed nearly 50 people connected with Roxy and its history.

The campaign will also feature newly created artwork. Graphic designer and typographer Jozef Ondrík has produced a series of three screen-printed posters based on visual elements from Roxy’s history.

The design draws on three pages from the original handover document for the non-residential premises at Dlouhá 33, which were transferred to the Linhart Foundation.

Large-format photographs and works by artists connected with Roxy and the NoD Gallery are also expected to be among the campaign rewards.

World.title: Why children often get sick after starting nursery?
World.content:
For many families, the first months of nursery can feel like a cycle of runny noses, coughs, and missed days. Children who were rarely ill before may suddenly seem to be sick all the time, leaving parents wondering whether something is wrong.

Written by: Dorottya Fekete

Medical reviewer: Dr. Veronika Boros, Pediatrician, FirstMed Budapest

In most cases, this pattern doesn’t signal a serious health problem. Starting nursery or preschool means spending more time around other children and encountering viruses that the child may not have met before. The frequent minor infections that follow each other are a common part of early childhood.

For families arriving from abroad and beginning life in Budapest, there can also be an added challenge: knowing what is considered normal, when to keep a child home, and when medical advice is warranted. Dr. Veronika Boros, a pediatrician at FirstMed, explains what parents should know.

Children often get sick after starting nursery. (Source: Getty Images)

The first nursery year can mean a lot of illnesses

Toddlers have many opportunities to exchange viruses when they spend time together in a group. They play closely, share toys, and are still developing everyday hygiene habits such as covering coughs and washing their hands properly.

As a result, the beginning of nursery or kindergarten often brings more respiratory infections than parents were used to seeing before. One cold may seem to end just as another begins during the autumn and winter months.

Starting nursery means children suddenly spend much more time around other children and meet viruses they have never encountered before. (Source: Getty Images Signature)

This does not necessarily mean that a child’s immune system is weak. Exposure to common infections is part of normal childhood development, and the frequency of illness often becomes less disruptive as children get older and encounter fewer unfamiliar viruses.

It can nevertheless be difficult for parents to judge where normal childhood illness ends and a problem begins. The overall picture matters, including how the child behaves between illnesses, whether they recover as expected, and whether symptoms are becoming more severe or persistent.

A child’s wellbeing is part of the adjustment

Starting nursery is more than an increase in exposure to germs. It is also a major change in a young child’s everyday life.

New company, different routines, and many new experiences to process. Some children settle quickly, while others need considerably more time to feel comfortable. The adjustment itself can be tiring and stressful, mostly during the first weeks.

For parents, familiar routines can help make the transition easier. Consistent sleep and mealtimes, reassurance, and enough rest can support a child as they adapt to their new environment.

If a child remains very distressed about nursery or seems to be struggling with the transition for a prolonged period, parents can raise this with their pediatrician. A pediatrician can help consider the child’s overall wellbeing and advise whether any additional support may be appropriate.

If you missed it – Men’s health screening in Budapest: A guide for expats

What can parents do between one cold and the next?

There is no way to prevent every infection a child encounters at nursery, but everyday habits can reduce the spread of illness and support general health.

Applying everyday hygiene practices, adequate sleep, and a varied, balanced diet can reduce the spread of infections and support recovery. Routine childhood vaccinations protect against a range of serious infections.

Handwashing: This is one of the simplest preventive measures. Encourage children to wash their hands regularly, primarily before eating and after using the bathroom or arriving home from nursery. Parents can reinforce the habit by making handwashing part of the family’s routine.

Adequate sleep and a varied, balanced diet: These are also important aspects of caring for a growing child. When a child is unwell, rest and fluids become vital.

Vaccination is another significant part of prevention. Routine childhood vaccinations protect against a range of serious infections, while seasonal influenza vaccination can help reduce the risk of flu. Families should discuss their child’s vaccination needs with a healthcare professional. FirstMed provides information about influenza vaccination and other preventive care for children.

It is also worth following the nursery’s illness rules. Keeping a sick child at home gives them time to recover and reduces the chance of passing an infection to classmates and staff.

One common misconception is that antibiotics are needed whenever a child has a cold. Most ordinary colds are caused by viruses, and antibiotics do not treat viral infections. A pediatrician can help determine when medication may be appropriate and when supportive care is better.

When is it time to call the pediatrician?

Frequent minor illnesses in little children after starting nursery do not automatically require a medical appointment. However, some symptoms deserve professional attention, especially when a child appears significantly unwell or is not recovering as expected.

Parents should seek medical advice if a child has a high or persistent fever, difficulty breathing, signs of dehydration, or symptoms that are not improving. An unusually sleepy child who is difficult to wake, significantly less active than usual, or generally appears much more unwell than expected should also be assessed.

The same applies when parents are simply concerned that something is different from their child’s usual pattern. Parents do not need to work out the diagnosis themselves before contacting a pediatrician.

For international families in Budapest, FirstMed provides English-speaking pediatric care at its clinic in Hattyú utca, near Széll Kálmán tér. Pediatrician Dr. Veronika Boros is among the doctors caring for children and families at the clinic. Parents can seek advice even when they are unsure exactly what is causing their child’s symptoms.

Questions parents often ask about nursery illnesses

Is it really normal for a child to be ill so often after nursery starts?

It can be. The first months of group childcare often involve frequent minor infections because children encounter viruses they haven’t been exposed to before. This pattern does not automatically indicate an underlying health problem. What matters is how severe the illnesses are, how well the child recovers, and whether they remain well between episodes.

How many colds should a young child have?

There is no single number that applies to every child. Young children in group childcare can have repeated respiratory infections, particularly during the first nursery year. The frequency may look quite high when one infection follows closely after another. If illnesses are unusually severe, prolonged, or accompanied by other concerning symptoms, a pediatrician can assess the individual child.

Should my child stay home from nursery when they are ill?

A child who is unwell generally needs time to rest and recover at home, and staying home also helps reduce transmission to other children and staff. The appropriate return-to-nursery point depends on the illness, the child’s condition, and the nursery’s rules. If you’re unsure, ask your pediatrician for guidance.

How do I know when a cold needs medical attention?

A typical mild cold can often be managed with rest, fluids, and observation. Seek medical advice if symptoms are severe or persistent, the child has difficulty breathing, has a significant fever, shows signs of dehydration, or isn’t improving. You may also consult a pediatrician if your child seems unusually unwell or if your instincts tell you something is not right.

The bigger picture

The first nursery year can be exhausting for parents who feel they are constantly dealing with another cold. In many cases, however, frequent minor illnesses are part of a child’s adjustment to group childcare, not evidence that something is seriously wrong.

Keeping expectations realistic can help. Children will get sick, mainly when they first enter a group setting, and parents cannot prevent every infection. Good daily habits, appropriate vaccinations, enough rest, and knowing when to seek medical advice can make the period easier to navigate.

If you would like to explore the topic in more detail, FirstMed’s full guide covers childhood illness after starting nursery and provides further information for parents in Budapest.

World.title: Investment in Hungary: the next question is not where capital comes from, but how long it stays
World.content:
Hungary has spent years building a position within Europe’s manufacturing and investment landscape. New factories, logistics projects and international companies have expanded the country’s industrial base and strengthened its links with wider European supply chains. But attracting capital is only the first part of the equation. The more difficult question is whether that capital has enough reasons to remain, expand and support the next stage of economic activity.

Written by Abdulla Saeed Alhebsi (A.S. Alhebsi)

For investors making decisions over several years rather than several quarters, the quality of an investment destination is measured by more than the initial cost of entering a market. They look at infrastructure, logistics, access to skilled workers, the reliability of institutions, the ability to expand operations and the predictability of the environment in which a project will operate.

This distinction matters because long-term capital behaves differently from short-term capital. A short-term investor can react quickly to changing conditions. A company building a factory, logistics network or research operation cannot move its assets with the same speed. Once capital is committed to physical infrastructure, the quality and continuity of the surrounding environment become part of the investment itself.

Hungary already provides useful examples of this dynamic.

Consider Debrecen. BMW’s investment there is not simply a factory project. The company developed a major manufacturing site dedicated to electric vehicles, while related activities have expanded around the investment. This illustrates how an initial manufacturing commitment can generate additional economic activity when the surrounding ecosystem is capable of supporting it.

A similar lesson can be seen in southern Hungary. METRANS is developing an intermodal rail and road terminal in Szeged, strengthening connections between manufacturers in the region and wider European transport networks. The importance of such infrastructure is not simply the value of the terminal itself. It is the additional connectivity it can provide to companies making longer-term decisions about production and distribution.

These examples point to a broader principle: investors do not assess an industrial project in isolation. They assess the system around it.

That system includes roads and railways, energy and telecommunications, customs procedures, suppliers, education and workforce development, financial services and the capacity to respond when conditions change. A company may enter because of an attractive initial opportunity, but its decision to expand depends increasingly on whether the wider system continues to work.

If you missed it: CATL launches trial operations at Debrecen battery factory

This is where institutional clarity becomes important

Global investors managing long-term capital increasingly operate in an environment where infrastructure needs are growing while traditional sources of financing face constraints. BlackRock has highlighted the growing role of private capital in financing infrastructure and other long-duration assets. Its discussion of infrastructure and private markets reflects a broader shift in the investment landscape.

The World Bank Group has made a related point from a development perspective. Its Private Sector Investment Lab identifies regulatory certainty, guarantees, foreign-exchange solutions, new investment structures and additional equity capital among the areas that can help mobilise private investment. The underlying issue is straightforward: capital is more willing to commit for longer periods when investors can understand the rules, identify the risks and assess how those risks can be managed.

For Hungary, this creates an opportunity as well as a responsibility.

The opportunity is to move beyond competing primarily for individual projects and strengthen the conditions that encourage companies already operating in the country to deepen their commitments. A new factory may create jobs and exports, but the larger economic value can come when that factory becomes the anchor for suppliers, research, logistics, training, business services and further investment.

The responsibility is to recognise that long-term investors are not only evaluating today’s conditions. They are evaluating the conditions they expect to face five, ten or twenty years from now.

That changes the way investment policy should be viewed.

Instead of asking only, “How much capital can Hungary attract this year?” policymakers and business leaders can also ask, “What makes an investor want to reinvest here after the first project is complete?”

The second question is harder, but it is also more revealing.

A company that builds a plant and later adds a research centre, service operation or additional production line is making a different statement from a company that completes one project and looks elsewhere for its next investment. Reinvestment can therefore be viewed as a practical indicator of how investors experience the business environment over time.

The same logic applies to infrastructure. A logistics terminal is valuable not only because of its own capacity, but because it can reduce friction for manufacturers and connect them more efficiently to markets. A skilled workforce is valuable not only because it fills today’s vacancies, but because it gives companies greater confidence that they can expand tomorrow. Institutional clarity works in the same way: its value is not always visible in a single transaction, but it can influence whether companies are prepared to make the next one.

Hungary’s recent investment activity shows that the country can attract substantial international capital across manufacturing, automotive, electronics and business services. The next stage is therefore less about proving that Hungary can attract capital and more about strengthening the conditions under which capital can become embedded in the economy.

That requires looking at investment as a long-term relationship rather than a single transaction.

For investors, the question is not simply where money can be placed. It is where money can continue to operate effectively as markets, technologies and supply chains change.

For Hungary, the strategic question is correspondingly clear: can the country make today’s investment decisions become tomorrow’s reinvestment decisions?

What’s next? Who gets the house? Property inheritance in Hungary for international owners

The answer will depend not on one incentive, one factory or one announcement, but on the continued performance of the system surrounding every investment.

Capital may arrive because of an opportunity. It stays when the environment continues to make expansion, adaptation and long-term planning possible.

That is the difference between attracting investment and building an investment ecosystem.

World.title: 22 WWII shells in Hungary discovered during construction work – PHOTOS
World.content:
A total of 22 WWII shells in Hungary have been discovered during construction work in the southern city of Baja, prompting a bomb disposal operation and temporary road closures.

The suspected explosive devices were found at the junction of Bokodi Road and Keleti Boulevard, according to Honvédelem, the official news portal of the Hungarian Defence Forces. Police subsequently alerted the military’s bomb disposal service.

22 WWII shells in Hungary removed by bomb disposal experts

Specialists from the Hungarian Defence Forces’ 1st Explosive Ordnance Disposal and Riverine Guard Regiment were sent to the site.

During the operation, roads within a 150-metre radius of the excavation site were closed. The restrictions affected part of a nearby public cemetery, an industrial facility and approximately 50 people.

Bomb disposal experts eventually identified 22 unfired Hungarian artillery shells dating from the Second World War.

The military removed all of the explosive devices and transported them to a central collection facility, where they will later be destroyed under controlled conditions. No injuries were reported.

If you missed it: Hungarian Gripens alerted as man steals aircraft and flies toward Paks nuclear plant

Baja, a city on the Danube in southern Hungary, was affected by military operations during the closing stages of the Second World War. Explosive remnants from the conflict continue to be uncovered across Hungary during construction, excavation and infrastructure projects.

The Hungarian Defence Forces also published a photo gallery showing the shells and the bomb disposal operation in Baja.

World.title: Orbán era faces harsh public verdict as majority choose ‘mafia state’ label, poll finds
World.content:
A new opinion poll paints a strikingly negative picture of how Hungarian voters now view Viktor Orbán’s 16 years in power, with a majority selecting “mafia state” among the two terms they believe best describe his former political system. Seven in ten respondents also said they believed corruption under the Orbán governments had been organised systematically from the top.

The findings come from a survey by Hungarian pollster Medián, reported by HVG. The figures measure voters’ perceptions of the former government and should not be interpreted as legal findings concerning Orbán or individual former officials.

Majority associate Orbán system with ‘mafia state’

Respondents were asked which expressions best described the political system established under Orbán.

Of seven possible descriptions, 37% chose “mafia state” as their first answer. “Civic democracy” was selected by 15%, “autocracy” by 14%, while 13% chose the government’s own term, the System of National Cooperation, commonly known by its Hungarian abbreviation NER.

Photo: www.facebook.com/MészárosLőrinc-vállalkozó

When respondents’ first and second choices were combined, 53% selected “mafia state” as one of their two preferred descriptions.

That represents a marked change from 2023, when the corresponding figure stood at 34% – an increase of 19 percentage points in three years. The proportion choosing descriptions linked to autocracy remained broadly unchanged, while references to dictatorship and civic democracy declined slightly.

The result suggests that perceptions of corruption and the relationship between political and economic power have become increasingly central to how many voters remember the Orbán period.

Another perspective – Viktor Orbán on the past 16 years: everything was lawful and appropriate, all else is political propaganda

Seven in ten see corruption as systemic

The poll also asked respondents about alleged financial abuses during the Orbán governments.

Three quarters of voting-age Hungarians said such abuses had characterised the government to a large extent: 60% described their extent as “very large”, while another 15% selected the next-highest category. Seven in ten said they believed corruption during the NER period had been centrally organised and systemic.

Age produced a substantial difference.

Among voters younger than 30, 82% described the scale of abuses as very large. Among respondents aged 65 and above, the figure fell to 46%.

Political affiliation produced an even sharper divide. Some 89% of supporters of Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s Tisza Party selected the “very large” category, compared with just 1% of Fidesz–KDNP supporters.

The enormous gap underlines how differently the Orbán era continues to be interpreted by Hungary’s competing political camps.

What Hungarians think about Orbán-linked businessmen

Another notable finding concerned businessmen who became exceptionally successful during the former Fidesz government.

According to the poll, 56% of respondents considered it very likely that some of these entrepreneurs had acted as frontmen, or “straw men”, for Orbán. A further 29% considered the possibility conceivable.

Taken together, 85% of respondents did not rule out such an arrangement, although this again represents public perception rather than proof of specific financial or criminal conduct.

Orbán and Fidesz have for years rejected opposition allegations that politically connected businessmen accumulated wealth on behalf of the former prime minister, and have frequently characterised corruption accusations against their governments as politically motivated.

Orbán’s legacy remains deeply polarising

Orbán served as Hungary’s prime minister from 2010 until the change of government in April 2026, after previously holding the post between 1998 and 2002. His governments reshaped Hungary’s constitutional system, media landscape and economy while repeatedly clashing with EU institutions over rule-of-law and corruption concerns.

The latest Medián figures do not show a uniform national view: attitudes remain strongly divided along party, age and education lines.

They do, however, indicate a significant change in the language many Hungarians use when assessing the former Orbán governments. Three years ago, roughly one third placed the “mafia state” description among their top choices. Today, according to Medián, more than half do so – making perceptions of corruption and concentrated economic power an increasingly prominent part of Orbán’s political legacy.

World.title: Hungarian forint slides past 366 per euro: what is driving the sell-off?
World.content:
The Hungarian forint weakened beyond 366 against the euro on Thursday morning and approached 322 against the US dollar, extending a sharp sell-off from the previous session. Although the move looks dramatic after months of relative currency stability, the immediate pressure appears to be coming largely from abroad: a stronger dollar, surging US bond yields and renewed concerns over high oil prices are creating an increasingly difficult environment for the Hungarian currency.

The euro was trading at around HUF 366.7 shortly before 9 am on Thursday, while the dollar had risen to approximately HUF 322.1. The Budapest Stock Exchange also opened slightly lower, with the BUX index initially down around 0.2%.

The moves followed a difficult Wednesday for the Hungarian currency. By comparison, the Hungarian National Bank’s official exchange rate for Wednesday was HUF 363.43 to the euro and HUF 318.30 to the dollar, although the forint weakened considerably later in the trading session.

Why is the Hungarian forint weakening?

The most important factor is the sharp repricing taking place in global bond and currency markets.

Inflation concerns have returned to the centre of attention in the United States, increasing expectations that monetary policy could remain restrictive or even tighten further. St Louis Federal Reserve President Alberto Musalem said this week that further interest-rate increases were likely to be necessary to contain persistent inflation. US inflation pressures have remained elevated despite the Federal Reserve’s attempts to bring price growth back towards its target.

Higher expected US interest rates tend to push Treasury yields upwards and make dollar-denominated investments more attractive. That can strengthen the dollar while putting pressure on currencies such as the forint, particularly when investors reduce exposure to smaller or more volatile markets.

This mechanism helps explain why the forint’s decline against the dollar has been even more pronounced than its fall against the euro. On Wednesday evening, the Hungarian currency briefly weakened beyond HUF 322 per dollar, while the euro-dollar exchange rate was itself moving in favour of the US currency.

If you missed it – Hungary sets 2030 euro target: Government reveals when budget deficit could fall below 3%

Oil above USD 100 adds another layer of pressure

Energy prices are the second major concern.

Világgazdaság reported that Brent crude rose to around USD 103.8 per barrel on Thursday morning, while US WTI crude traded near USD 92.7. Hungary is a major net energy importer, meaning persistently expensive oil and gas can worsen the country’s external balance and increase inflationary risks.

Higher energy prices can therefore affect the forint through several channels at once. They raise import costs, complicate the inflation outlook and can reduce investors’ willingness to hold currencies from energy-dependent economies.

The Hungarian National Bank itself highlighted energy prices and the uncertain global financial environment as important risks when its Monetary Council met on Tuesday.

MNB rates provide a buffer – but global markets can overwhelm it

The central bank left its base rate unchanged at 5.50% on 22 September. The MNB said maintaining current interest-rate conditions remained necessary to achieve price stability sustainably, while explicitly stressing the importance of foreign-exchange market stability.

Relatively high Hungarian interest rates can support the forint because they increase the potential return available on forint-denominated assets. However, that advantage becomes less powerful when US yields rise rapidly.

The central bank is therefore facing a delicate balance. Hungary’s inflation outlook has improved significantly, but cutting rates too quickly could reduce the yield advantage supporting the currency. Keeping monetary conditions tight for longer, meanwhile, may weigh on domestic borrowing and economic activity.

The MNB’s latest communication suggests caution rather than urgency: policymakers kept rates unchanged and said future decisions would depend on inflation, global developments and Hungary’s risk premium.

Is 366 a turning point for the forint?

The level itself is psychologically noticeable, but it does not automatically signal the beginning of a lasting depreciation trend.

Indeed, the forint has traded at significantly weaker levels in previous years. What matters more now is whether the forces behind the latest movement persist. If US bond yields remain elevated, the dollar continues to strengthen and oil stays above USD 100, the external environment could remain hostile to the Hungarian currency.

Conversely, easing energy prices or a retreat in US yields could quickly remove part of the pressure.

Regional currencies provide another useful clue. Világgazdaság reported only small movements in the Czech koruna and Polish zloty against the forint on Thursday morning. This suggests that while global factors dominate the current market narrative, investors are not abandoning Hungarian assets in isolation.

For travellers and foreign residents in Hungary, a weaker Hungarian forint makes euros and dollars more valuable locally. For the Hungarian economy, however, the equation is more complicated: exporters may benefit from a weaker currency, while imported goods, fuel and other foreign-currency costs become more expensive.

The next direction of the forint may therefore depend less on Budapest than on Washington and global energy markets. For now, the combination of higher US yields, a stronger dollar and expensive oil represents precisely the kind of external environment in which the Hungarian currency traditionally faces its toughest test.
