The floor exercise final turned into a family affair for Yulo as his younger brother Eldrew also qualified and ended up seventh with 12.233 points.

More medals are expected from the older Yulo, who will also take part in the vault and parallel bars finals on Friday, September 25.

The younger Yulo, meanwhile, will get another medal opportunity in the horizontal bar final also set on Friday. – Rappler.com

World.title: Kayla Sanchez denied Asian Games medal anew, takes 4th in 50m freestyle
World.content:
BEST BET. Swimmer Kayla Sanchez in action for the Philippines in the 2026 Asian Games.

Kayla Sanchez falls short of ending the Philippines’ 28-year wait for an Asian Games swimming medal, finishing fourth in the women’s 50m freestyle final

MANILA, Philippines – An Asian Games medal remained elusive for Kayla Sanchez.

Sanchez once again fell short of a podium finish as she placed fourth in the women’s 50m freestyle final at the Tokyo Aquatics Centre in Japan on Thursday, September 24.

Logging 24.75 seconds, Sanchez narrowly missed the bronze medal by a 0.29 seconds, with China’s Cheng Yujie beating the Filipina for it with a time of 24.46 seconds.

China completed a 1-3 finish as Wu Qingfeng struck gold with a new Asian Games record of 23.98 seconds, preventing Hong Kong’s Siobhan Haughey from capturing a third freestyle title in this edition of the continental showpiece.

Haughey, who ruled the 100m and 200m events, settled for silver with 24.32 seconds.

The result denied Sanchez from becoming the first Filipino to win a swimming medal in the Asian Games since Raymond Papa bagged bronzes in the men’s 100m and 200m backstroke in the 1998 edition in Thailand.

It was a disappointing outcome for the Filipina-Canadian, considering that she skipped the women’s 100m backstroke on Wednesday, September 23, to preserve her energy for the 50m freestyle.

Sanchez also came oh so close to a medal in the women’s 100m freestyle, where she ended up fourth as well on Tuesday, September 22.

An Olympic silver and bronze medalist back when she still represented Canada, Sanchez led the Philippines’ campaign in the 2025 Southeast Asian Games in Thailand, where she emerged as the most bemedalled Filipino athlete with three golds and five silvers. – Rappler.com

World.title: ADB Forecasts Resilient Growth in Asia-Pacific, Kazakhstan’s Outlook Unchanged
World.content:
ASTANA — Economic growth across developing Asia and the Pacific is expected to moderate to 5% in 2026 from 5.5% in 2025 before rising slightly to 5.1% in 2027, according to the Asian Development Bank’s latest outlook.

The ADB’s September 2026 outlook revised its 2026 regional growth forecast upward by 0.1 percentage points compared with its July projection. Strong investment, government support and growing technology exports linked to global artificial intelligence investment are expected to continue supporting economic activity. At the same time, geopolitical tensions and climate-related risks are putting pressure on food and energy prices.

The bank lowered its regional inflation forecast for 2026 to 4.2%, from 4.3% in July, citing price stabilization measures. However, the forecast for 2027 was raised slightly to 3.5%, compared with 3.4% previously in July. Both projections remain above the 3% inflation rate recorded in 2025.

ADB identified escalating conflicts and a strong El Niño as the main risks to the regional outlook. A prolonged or broader conflict in the Middle East, as well as an intensifying war in Ukraine, could keep global energy prices high and volatile. Meanwhile, El Niño, the periodic warming of sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, is expected to continue through the first quarter of 2027, potentially increasing energy demand and reducing agricultural production.

Kazakhstan growth forecast remains unchanged

Kazakhstan’s economic outlook remains unchanged from the ADB’s July forecast. The bank expects the country’s economy to grow by 4.8% in 2026 and 4.5% in 2027.

This projection is consistent with the ADB’s earlier assessment of Kazakhstan’s economic trajectory, which also forecast growth of 4.8% in 2026 and 4.5% in 2027 amid moderating oil production and continued government investment.

According to the report, growth will be supported by non-oil sectors and continued public investment. Manufacturing, construction and services are expected to contribute to economic activity despite disruptions in the oil sector. Off-budget financing and infrastructure spending are also projected to provide additional support.

The focus on non-oil sectors comes as Kazakhstan seeks to maintain economic momentum while reducing its reliance on hydrocarbons. Recent developments in construction, manufacturing, transport, trade and agriculture have also been highlighted as potential drivers of growth.

Inflation in Kazakhstan is forecast to gradually decline to 10.4% in 2026 and 9.5% in 2027, supported by earlier monetary tightening and prudential measures.

Across Central and West Asia, the ADB revised its growth forecasts downward by 0.1 percentage points for both 2026 and 2027, to 3.7% and 4.1%, respectively. The revision was attributed mainly to weaker-than-expected external demand, particularly in Türkiye.

Earlier ADB forecasts have likewise pointed to inflation and external economic conditions as key factors shaping Kazakhstan’s outlook. In July 2025, the bank raised its regional growth forecast while warning of increasing inflationary pressures in Kazakhstan and other Central Asian economies.

The ADB said developing Asia and the Pacific remain resilient despite growing economic and geopolitical risks. The bank emphasized the importance of measures to protect vulnerable populations from higher food and energy costs as governments navigate continued uncertainty.

World.title: Nine Servicemen Die in Incident During Caspian Sea Military Exercise
World.content:
ASTANA – Nine servicemen have died after 19 Kazakhstan Armed Forces personnel were swept into the Caspian Sea during a naval exercise in the Mangystau Region on Sept. 24 amid a sharp deterioration in weather conditions and strong winds, the Ministry of Defense reported.

Rescuers rescued three servicemen, including one who was hospitalized. Search operations for the remaining servicemen are underway.

The Government has established a commission to investigate the deaths, chaired by Deputy Prime Minister Kanat Bozumbayev. The commission includes the defense minister, Mangystau Region Akim Nurdaulet Kilybay and representatives of relevant ministries and agencies.

Units of the Naval Forces, the Ministry of Emergency Situations, aviation and other relevant services have been deployed to conduct search and rescue operations.

A commission from the Ministry of Defense, headed by Defense Minister Lieutenant General of Aviation Dauren Kossanov, has been urgently dispatched to establish the circumstances of the incident and coordinate the search and rescue efforts.

The Defense Ministry expressed its deep condolences to the families and relatives of the servicemen who died. The families will receive all necessary assistance and support.

The Prosecutor General’s Office has opened a criminal case into the deaths of the servicemen. An investigative team has been established, with officers from the Ministry of Internal Affairs, the Ministry of Emergency Situations and the Prosecutor’s Office working at the site. Authorities have ordered necessary forensic examinations, and the investigation is under special control.

The Khazar Korgany-2026 exercise began on Sept. 22 in Kazakhstan’s sector of the Caspian Sea, involving more than 500 servicemen, Naval Forces vessels and boats, hydrographic vessels, Border Guard Service units and Air Defense Forces aviation.

World.title: Tokayev: Kazakhstan People’s Council to Strengthen State-Society Dialogue
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has called on the newly established Kazakhstan People’s Council to become a practical platform for dialogue between the state and society, saying its constitutional status opens new opportunities to address national and regional problems.

New platform for public dialogue

Speaking at the first session of the Kazakhstan People’s Council, Tokayev described its establishment as an important step in Kazakhstan’s ongoing political transformation. He said the new institution brings together representatives of different groups of society and is designed to strengthen public participation in state decision-making.

According to the President, the council is not an alternative to the Kurultai, Kazakhstan’s new legislative body, and must not interfere with its powers. Instead, the two institutions should maintain regular dialogue and coordinate their work, particularly when developing legislation that affects citizens’ interests, reported Akorda on Sept. 24.

The council includes representatives of ethnic and cultural associations, regional maslikhats and public councils, and civil society organizations. Tokayev said this composition would allow regional issues to be raised at the national level and establish a new system of interaction between the state and society.

He urged council members to avoid formalism and bureaucracy, maintain direct contact with citizens and address complex and pressing issues.

Economic and social progress

Tokayev highlighted Kazakhstan’s economic and social progress over the past seven years. GDP grew by 29% to $306 billion, while foreign exchange reserves and National Fund assets exceeded $138 billion. Kazakhstan attracted more than $162 billion in investment during this period, while small and medium-sized businesses accounted for more than 40% of the economy.

More than 20 million square meters of housing are built annually. Since 2019, 1,342 schools with capacity for more than one million students have been constructed. Life expectancy has reached 76 years, while more than 1,200 healthcare facilities have been opened.

More than 35,000 kilometers of roads have been built and repaired. Tokayev described these as record indicators in Kazakhstan’s history and said the country had entered the top 40 most competitive countries in the world.

Regional development and infrastructure

At the same time, Tokayev called for stronger public oversight of infrastructure projects and higher construction standards, citing concerns about the quality of some housing and roads.

He instructed the authorities to strengthen control over road construction, improve quality-assessment mechanisms and increase public oversight of infrastructure projects.

Tokayev also stressed the need to address Kazakhstan’s future workforce needs. By 2035, the country is expected to require 2.9 million specialists, including 1.8 million in skilled trades, notably in industry, construction, agriculture and IT.

Kazakhstan’s international role

Tokayev said Kazakhstan would continue to deepen international cooperation and attract investment, while promoting the country’s interests, history and culture internationally.

He said his goal was to position Kazakhstan on the global stage as a middle power and promote the country’s opportunities.

Concluding his address, Tokayev urged the People’s Council to remain closely connected with citizens and ensure that its work produces practical solutions to issues affecting the country and its people.

World.title: Astana Brings in Singapore’s Changi for New Airport Development
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is stepping up efforts to develop Astana as an international aviation hub and strengthen its transit potential through a new partnership with Singapore-based Changi Airports International (CAI), a global airport investor, manager and consultant.

The Astana akimat (administration), Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Transport and CAI, a subsidiary of Changi Airport Group (CAG), have signed a framework agreement to cooperate on the long-term development of Astana’s airport infrastructure, including the construction of a new airport and the further development of the existing international airport.

The agreement covers two main areas of cooperation. The first involves constructing a new airport in Astana, while the second focuses on developing Astana International Airport, including potential CAI participation in management, operations and maintenance (O&M), as well as other areas of its development, the Astana Akimat reported on Sept. 23.

The parties are currently working to agree on the partnership structure, project implementation terms and the necessary documentation.

Astana Deputy Akim (Mayor) Yevgeny Glotov, Deputy Minister of Transport Talgat Lastayev, and Changi Airports International Chief Executive Officer Eugene Gan signed the agreement.

About Changi Airport Group

Changi Airport Group is a Singaporean state-owned company that manages and develops the country’s airport infrastructure, including Singapore Changi Airport. CAG oversees airport operations, passenger and cargo traffic, commercial infrastructure, services and digital solutions.

In 2025, Changi Airport handled around 70 million passengers and more than 2 million tons of cargo, connecting Singapore with more than 170 cities worldwide. The airport has been named the World’s Best Airport 14 times at the Skytrax World Airport Awards, including in 2025 and 2026.

CAG conducts its international airport business through Changi Airports International, which has experience across more than 90 airports in over 35 countries.

The agreement comes amid a broader expansion of Kazakhstan-Singapore cooperation. During Singapore Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong’s visit to Kazakhstan in August, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev highlighted Singapore’s airport-development experience, while the two countries have also been strengthening ties in transport, investment, digitalization and technology.

The partnership has gained momentum in recent months, including the launch of a quantum technology center in Almaty and expanded air links between Kazakhstan and Singapore. The new airport agreement adds aviation infrastructure to the growing areas of bilateral cooperation.

World.title: Kazakhstan, China Push for Greater Middle Corridor Connectivity
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and China reaffirmed their commitment to expanding the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR), or Middle Corridor, as a safe, efficient and competitive link between Asia and Europe during a high-level meeting in Beijing.

First Deputy Prime Minister Nurlybek Nalibayev made the remarks while participating in the Global Sustainable Transport Forum and a high-level meeting on the TITR during his working visit to Beijing on Sept. 23 at the invitation of Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang.

Nalibayev said Kazakhstan’s strategic goal is to become a major Eurasian transport and logistics hub by developing the East-West and North-South corridors, upgrading border and port infrastructure, and introducing modern multimodal transport services.

He identified the Middle Corridor as a key priority of Kazakhstan’s transport policy. He called for coordinated efforts to make the route safer, more efficient and predictable through competitive tariffs, streamlined procedures and common service standards, according to Kazinform.

China backs greater corridor capacity

China’s Vice Chairman of the Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress Shohrat Zakir said Beijing attaches particular importance to the TITR and is ready to work with partners to increase its capacity and efficiency.

He proposed strengthening infrastructure connectivity, harmonizing cross-border transport and customs procedures, developing a digital platform for multimodal transportation and expanding financing and business opportunities along the route.

Azerbaijan’s Deputy Prime Minister Shahin Mustafayev also stressed the need for coordinated infrastructure development and removing bottlenecks, while Kyrgyz Deputy Chairman of the Cabinet of Ministers Erlist Akunbekov highlighted the importance of improving transport access for landlocked Central Asian countries.

Kazakhstan-China cooperation

During the visit, Nalibayev held his first bilateral meeting with Ding Xuexiang, who co-chairs the Kazakhstan-China Cooperation Committee. The officials discussed expanding trade and economic ties, investment, agriculture, high technologies, interregional cooperation and transboundary rivers.

Nalibayev also met with executives of China Communications Construction Company (CCCC) and CITIC Group to discuss investment in Kazakhstan and joint infrastructure projects, the Prime Minister’s press service reported.

Before the forum, Nalibayev presented CITIC Group Chairman Xi Guohua with Kazakhstan’s Order of Dostyk (Friendship), second degree, on behalf of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev. The award recognized his contribution to strengthening Kazakhstan-China relations and expanding trade and economic cooperation.

The Global Sustainable Transport Forum brought together around 1,000 representatives of governments, international organizations, diplomatic missions, businesses and expert communities.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Foreign Minister Expands Bilateral Ties at UN General Assembly
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has launched an active diplomatic agenda at the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, with Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi holding talks with counterparts from several countries and discussing global peace, security and humanitarian law on Sept. 23 in New York.

Expanding bilateral partnerships

On the first day of the General Assembly’s High-Level Week in New York, Tileuberdi held talks with his counterparts from Hungary, Moldova, Poland, Slovenia, Ukraine and El Salvador, the ministry’s press service reported.

The discussions focused on bilateral cooperation, prospects for expanding political dialogue and trade and economic ties, as well as key international and regional topics.

Tileuberdi also met with UN Under-Secretary-General and UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) Executive Director Rebecca Grynspan, a candidate for UN Secretary-General, and UNESCO Director-General Khaled El-Enany. The meetings addressed ways to strengthen cooperation with UN institutions and improve the effectiveness of multilateral mechanisms.

Focus on peace and security

Tileuberdi also took part in a high-level discussion, Reaffirming the Promise of Peace: Using the Power We Have, which focused on conflict prevention and resolution, preventive diplomacy, mediation and strengthening partnerships within the international system.

Participants exchanged views on strengthening the UN’s role in maintaining international peace and security and using existing mechanisms more effectively to settle disputes peacefully.

New diplomatic relations

An important outcome of the first day was the establishment of diplomatic relations between Kazakhstan and the Central African Republic. The two countries’ foreign ministers signed a joint communiqué confirming their interest in developing bilateral ties and cooperation on international platforms.

Tileuberdi also participated in a working meeting of foreign ministers of the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) member states, where participants discussed priorities for cooperation between the CSTO and the UN.

Kazakhstan promotes compliance with Humanitarian Law

At a separate meeting with foreign ministers of the founding states of the Global Initiative to Strengthen Political Commitment to International Humanitarian Law (IHL) and International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) President Mirjana Spoljaric, Tileuberdi stressed that the effectiveness of international humanitarian law should be measured by its ability to protect civilians and medical and humanitarian personnel, safeguard critical civilian infrastructure and ensure the delivery of humanitarian assistance.

The meeting brought together the founding states – Kazakhstan, Brazil, China, France, Jordan and South Africa – to discuss preparations for the Humanity in War high-level conference, scheduled for Dec. 7 in Jordan.

Tileuberdi emphasized that international humanitarian law must be applied universally, consistently and in good faith, without selectivity or politicization.

Following the meeting, the founding states and the ICRC called on the international community to join the Initiative, strengthen compliance with international humanitarian law and ensure high-level participation at the upcoming conference in Jordan.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Switzerland Open Way For Up to 28 Weekly Passenger Flights
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Switzerland have expanded the legal framework for direct air connectivity, with the two countries signing a memorandum allowing designated airlines to operate up to 28 passenger flights per week, the Kazakh Civil Aviation Committee’s press service reported.

The memorandum was signed following negotiations between the aviation authorities of Kazakhstan and Switzerland in Astana on Sept. 23. The Kazakh delegation was led by Civil Aviation Committee Chair Saltanat Tompiyeva, while the Swiss delegation was headed by Laurent Noel, head of the negotiation division at the Swiss Federal Office of Civil Aviation (FOCA).

Representatives of Air Astana, SCAT, SWISS International Air Lines, Basel Airport, Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Embassy of Switzerland in Kazakhstan also took part in the talks.

The negotiations focused on prospects for developing direct air links and practical issues related to opening new routes between the two countries. The document also establishes a legal framework for cargo services without restrictions on flight frequencies or capacity. The two sides also agreed and initiated a draft air services agreement for subsequent signing. The agreement is expected to provide an updated legal basis for further development of air connectivity between Kazakhstan and Switzerland.

The Swiss side said it sees potential for expanding direct air links and is currently considering the launch of regular flights to Kazakhstan. The development of direct air connectivity is expected to create additional opportunities for tourism, trade and business cooperation between Kazakhstan and Switzerland.

New routes could also increase passenger and business flows between the two countries by providing more direct travel options for tourists, companies and other travelers. The memorandum and draft agreement create the regulatory conditions for airlines to consider new services, while the actual launch of regular routes will depend on decisions by the carriers involved.

World.title: What Kazakhstan Can Unlock With Its First MICHELIN Keys
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan’s first MICHELIN Keys, awarded on Sept. 22, place the country inside a global system of trust familiar to international travelers, potentially unlocking wider recognition for a destination many are still discovering, said Shyryn Mussina, managing director at Kazakh Tourism national company.

She said the recognition can influence not only where travelers stay, but how they perceive the country before arriving.

“When we travel ourselves, we often choose what is familiar to us. Let’s say we trust the Rixos chain and like that format. We choose what we know because a holiday is a point of relaxation, and we do not want to be disappointed in something,” Mussina told The Astana Times.

The same logic applies when travelers consider Kazakhstan.

“A tourist coming to another country may book through a travel agent or tour operator, or individually. They may be there for a week, three days or 10 days. They want to get an experience based on what is familiar or understandable to them, or through a platform they trust. The MICHELIN Guide is very clear in that sense,” said Mussina.

The MICHELIN Guide currently features 14 hotels in Kazakhstan, five of which received One MICHELIN Key.

The hotel distinction has three levels: One Key denotes a “very special stay,” Two Keys an “exceptional stay,” and Three Keys an “extraordinary stay.” Being listed and receiving a key are therefore not the same: the five Kazakh hotels were singled out from the broader selection.

Mussina acknowledged the importance of recognition because awareness of Kazakhstan remains uneven across markets.

“For some countries, we are already understandable and more or less familiar; for others, we are still not. Many people still have questions about how safe it is here,” she said.

For travelers who do not yet know Kazakhstan well, an international guide can reduce that uncertainty and transfer some of its credibility to the destination.

“When a strong international brand enters the market, the perception that its audience has of that brand is automatically transferred to all of its members. Kazakhstan, in this case, becomes the partner country. It immediately gives a certain unspoken message that the country is gradually gaining momentum in terms of standards and in terms of an expected, good experience,” said Mussina.

Why Tenir matters alongside Ritz-Carlton

The selection is also notable for local and nontraditional properties appearing alongside major luxury chains.

“Kazakhstan is still a trendy destination. It is not super popular, but it is now becoming popular among travelers who want a different experience. And here, ‘different’ is the key word because they want an authentic experience,” said Mussina, pointing to Tenir Eco Hotel and The Veil Hotel as properties able to compete through concept and design rather than an international brand name.

“Tenir Eco Hotel received a key alongside the Ritz. Of course, it is very difficult to ignore the Ritz, both in Almaty and Astana. But Tenir and The Veil received recognition because they are exceptional in terms of design,” said Mussina.

Kairat Sadvakassov, strategic adviser at HiSeas International Tourism Group, said the selection reflects the strength of Kazakhstan’s emerging boutique and destination-based accommodation sector.

“Kazakhstan is getting more and more popular with global travelers. Although we are relatively young in terms of culinary specialties and experiences, the hotel side of the hospitality industry is quite remarkable and deserves recognition from MICHELIN Key and other rankings such as Forbes Travel. I am happy that half of the properties presented are local brands and some of them are not traditional hotels,” he told The Astana Times.

For Sadvakassov, that is particularly encouraging for glamping and boutique lodging, where location and concept can become part of the travel experience.

Six years to get Kazakhstan noticed

Mussina said the recognition follows a years-long effort to bring Kazakhstan to the attention of international media, industry experts and global guides. Kazakh Tourism first began communicating with MICHELIN in March 2020, but contacts slowed during the COVID-19 pandemic and resumed more actively in 2023.

“The most difficult part was actually getting attention for Kazakhstan and accumulating enough of that effect. We worked for a very long time, persistently and carefully so that Kazakhstan would be chosen as a travel destination. This work with international media, international journalists and international awards all comes together because, in the end, it is the same experts and the same professional circles. Together, it creates a cumulative effect that allows the entire industry to grow,” said Mussina.

Mussina compared the process to building a reputation at university.

“In the first year, you work for your grades, and later your grades work for you. (…) Now people are beginning to look into the country itself,” she said.

The regional picture gives the recognition wider significance. MICHELIN lists three hotels in Uzbekistan, with one receiving a key, compared with Kazakhstan’s five key-awarded properties among 14 listed hotels.

“The very fact that Central Asia is represented there is already a very good development for everyone,” said Mussina.

The next layer of MICHELIN recognition

She also emphasized that individual hotels and restaurants do not pay inspectors to receive an assessment. Where destination partnerships with international guides exist, agreements can instead be concluded with public authorities or other third parties that are not themselves being evaluated.

“The important thing to understand is that MICHELIN and Gault & Millau do not take money from an individual business for the assessment of restaurants. Restaurants do not pay for the inspection, hotels do not pay for the inspection,” she said.

Mussina said she would eventually seek Kazakhstan’s engagement with MICHELIN to extend to its restaurant guide, although expansion ultimately depends on whether the destination meets MICHELIN’s own criteria. Such a project, she said, could take roughly one and a half to two years from signing a contract to an awards ceremony.

Sadvakassov said Kazakhstan can make greater use of the recognition it has already secured, including through familiarization, or FAM, trips that bring journalists and travel professionals to experience a destination firsthand.

“Part of the promotion is already done. The hotels and the country got their names out through MICHELIN. The tourism authorities should now use these properties for future press and blog tours and FAM trips,” said Sadvakassov.

World.title: Georgia joins joint statement in support of Ukraine at UN
World.content:
51 UN member states, including Georgia, have signed a joint statement in support of Ukraine, calling on Russia to agree to a full ceasefire and begin peace talks. EU High Representative Kaja Kallas read out the statement in New York during the 81st session of the UN General Assembly.

According to Ukrainian media, the United States did not join the statement.

The signatories expressed solidarity with Ukraine and reaffirmed their support for Kyiv’s efforts to achieve peace amid the ongoing war with Russia.

“Ukraine wants peace. We want peace. Russia must end its aggression, agree to a ceasefire and engage meaningfully in negotiations to achieve a comprehensive, just and lasting peace in accordance with international law,” the statement said.

The countries also called for freedom of navigation and commercial shipping in the Black Sea, the protection of critical infrastructure and the unimpeded export of Ukrainian grain. They said these measures were important for maintaining global food security.

The signatories also urged Russia to immediately return all Ukrainian civilians who had been unlawfully detained, forcibly transferred or deported, including children. The call also covered prisoners of war and internees.

Georgia’s Foreign Minister Maka Bochorishvili also took part in events on Ukraine held in New York. She attended the sixth summit of the International Crimea Platform, titled “Unity under pressure, a call to action”, which took place on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

Bochorishvili said Ukraine was particularly important to Georgia because the country itself was experiencing the consequences of violations of its territorial integrity.

“For Georgia, Ukraine is not just another item on the international agenda. We know very well what it means when a state’s sovereignty and territorial integrity are violated,” the minister said.

According to Bochorishvili, Russia’s occupation of two regions of Georgia continues and remains one of the country’s main security challenges.

“We know very well how devastating occupation can be for individuals, families and society. Based on this experience, Georgia attaches particular importance to solidarity, respect for international law and an unwavering commitment to the principles on which a peaceful and secure international order should be built,” Bochorishvili said.

She also discussed the role of the International Crimea Platform, describing it as an important mechanism for keeping international attention focused on Ukraine and turning political support into concrete action.

Bochorishvili said Georgia supported efforts to end the war and achieve a lasting peace based on the UN Charter and the principles of international law.

“Georgia stands firmly with the Ukrainian people and once again reaffirms its unwavering support for Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders,” she said.

The Crimea Platform is a high-level international forum held annually to provide political support for Ukraine.

UN adopts statement in support of Ukraine

World.title: “Four members of my family are fighting: my mother, two brothers and me” – story of Ukrainian Olha Bihari, known by call sign “Witch”
World.content:
Olha Bihari, Ukraine’s drone commander

Hromadske

Thirty-four-year-old Olha Bihari, who goes by the call sign “Witch,” heads the Unmanned Systems Directorate of Ukraine’s 20th Army Corps. Before joining the military, she studied neuroscience, later earned a law degree and worked in human rights advocacy.

After Russia’s full-scale invasion, Bihari went to the recruitment office with her mother and younger brother. Her other brother has been fighting since 2015. Today, four members of the family are at war.

In an interview with the Ukrainian publication Hromadske, Bihari spoke about her family, commanding troops, losses, unmanned systems and why a modern military must rely on technology and data analysis.

Based on a report by Hromadske

Kramatorsk, family and war

Olha was born in Kramatorsk. She says Ukrainian identity was an important part of her family history.

Her paternal grandfather was an engineer and a dissident from the Prykarpattia region of western Ukraine. His family had ties to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) and the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN). He was monitored by the KGB, never joined the Communist Party and continued to speak Ukrainian.

In the 1990s, her grandfather joined the People’s Movement of Ukraine and campaigned for the country’s independence. He later became involved in public life in Kramatorsk.

Her maternal grandmother came from a Cossack family in the Poltava region. The family maintained Ukrainian traditions at home, sang folk songs and celebrated traditional holidays.

Olha wanted to become a scientist and studied neuroscience. But after the Maidan, she decided not to leave the country to pursue a scientific career abroad. She earned a law degree and, starting in 2019, worked in human rights advocacy.

After Russia launched its full-scale invasion, on Feb. 25, 2022, Olha, her mother and her younger brother went to a military recruitment office. By then, her other brother had already been fighting since 2015.

▇ “No one even considered not serving. How could we? You are either a victim or a defender.”

Before the war, Olha’s mother worked as a journalist. She later trained as a military psychologist and now serves in Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces.

Her younger brother was studying law and went to war at 18. Olha suggested that he finish his studies first.

“Olya, what’s the point of studying to defend people’s rights? If the Muscovites come for us, it won’t help,” he replied.

“We knew very well what occupation was like and, in general, what that whole romance of Russian unity among peoples smelled like,” Bihari said. Photo courtesy of Hromadske.

When the whole family is at the front

According to Bihari, serving together helps the family understand one another. They have a family group chat where they share photos and news every day.

Once, Olha ran into her younger brother in a village near the front. Knowing that his sister barely slept and sometimes did not have time to buy food, he came to cook her dinner and leave enough food for several days.

But when family members are in danger, professional composure cannot keep fear at bay.

During the fighting for Bakhmut, one of Bihari’s brothers found himself surrounded.

“I thought I was going to lose my mind. In those days, I lived on coffee. I had no right to show my emotions, because I could demoralize my troops.”

She did not call her brother. Instead, she called his commander, trying to find out what was happening and whether there was a way to evacuate him.

Bihari generally does not tell her family about her own dangerous missions. If a guided aerial bomb lands nearby or an FPV drone strikes her vehicle, she tells them about it only after she returns.

“When my brother was trapped in Bakhmut and couldn’t get out, I thought I was going to lose my mind,” Bihari said. Photo courtesy of Hromadske.



From neuroscience and law to command

In the spring of 2022, Bihari began serving in the territorial defense infantry near Kyiv. She had no military experience.

According to her, much of what happened in those first weeks was driven by initiative. About 200 people joined the unit, most of them civilians. There was not even a complete personnel roster.

Bihari began gathering data, establishing communication with the command and learning how to navigate military documentation.

▇ “Whoever was willing to take responsibility did so.”

That was how she gradually found herself in a command role.

In 2023, Bihari went to Bakhmut as the acting commander of an infantry platoon. It was there, she said, that she fully understood the importance of planning.

“Casualties are not a matter of chance. They are the result of how well you planned the logistics, scheduled the time of deployment and organized the actions of your units.”

She later completed leadership courses at the Ukrainian Ground Forces Academy.

Bihari has served in infantry, artillery and unmanned systems. She considers organizing units and training personnel her greatest achievements.

“In civilian life, I was criticized for my blunt, tough personality. In the military, it is seen as normal,” Bihari said. Photo courtesy of Hromadske.

“Most casualties are the result of poor planning”

Bihari believes one of a commander’s main responsibilities is to understand each person’s capabilities.

She recalls a serviceman who was afraid to go out to positions. After talking to him, she realized the problem was not that he was unwilling to serve. In her view, he had simply been assigned to the wrong role.

Bihari transferred him to electronic intelligence, where he became a successful specialist.

“Everyone has their strengths. If a commander has problems with personnel, I always step in.”

She connects her approach to command with her scientific background: analysis, methodology and forecasting.

▇ “Most casualties in the military are either the result of emotions taking over and you acting reactively rather than proactively, or a failure in planning.”

“Most casualties in the military are either the result of emotions taking over or a failure in planning,” Bihari said. Photo courtesy of Hromadske.

“We can no longer fight a war in excel”

These days, Bihari’s day begins at around 5 a.m. with a briefing to her senior commander on the situation at the positions.

After that, she always sets aside 10 minutes for coffee and planning. From the many tasks before her, she chooses one priority that she intends to devote most of her resources to.

Bihari describes unmanned systems as a “delivery service.” Drones can carry out strikes, remotely mine areas, deliver ammunition, food, fuel and water, and robotic systems are also used to evacuate the wounded.

A significant part of her work involves data analysis.

Bihari says she digitized military management processes because it is impossible to handle such a volume of information manually.

▇ “We can no longer fight a war in Excel. We have to see earlier, understand faster and act ahead of events, because the enemy has the advantage in numbers, while we have to rely on intelligence and technology.”

She analyzes thousands of strike, logistical and other tasks, identifies weak points and then works with specific units.

She receives around 300 phone calls a day. The fewest she can remember having in a day is 128. On top of that come video conferences and meetings.

Bihari does not use artificial intelligence to analyze military data. She says much of the information is classified or intended for official use only, making it impossible to upload it to external systems.

Three hours of sleep, a son and a manicure

Bihari says she is not very emotional. When a problem arises, her principle is simple: find a solution first, reflect later.

During an especially difficult period, she slept an average of three hours and 40 minutes a day for three months.

“I went to the car, closed the doors, screamed it out, came back — and that was it. I was fine. I could keep working.”

She has no days off and has not taken a vacation in more than a year. She unwinds by reading books on military leadership and planning, and by driving and riding her motorcycle.

She barely sees her son now. When they do meet, they speak to each other in English.

At the same time, Bihari has kept a habit instilled by her grandmother in childhood — taking care of her nails. She does her own manicures, sometimes sacrificing two hours of sleep to do it.

“Nails are actually very useful. I’ve used them to fix a car and even to pull a fragment out of my leg.”

“I barely see my child these days,” Bihari said. Photo courtesy of Hromadske.

Injuries and attitudes toward sexism

Bihari has not officially reported her injuries. She says she feels uncomfortable going to a military hospital with a minor shrapnel wound when there are soldiers there who have undergone amputations.

She also says her hearing has deteriorated following concussions.

Asked about sexism in the military, Bihari says she tries to analyze not the comments themselves but the reasons behind a person’s behavior.

She responds to flirting and inappropriate compliments with a direct question.

“What do you want? Why did you say that? Are you trying to build some kind of relationship with me, or do you just want to chat?”

She says such conversations usually stop after that.

Bihari also uses her public profile to raise money. One charitable campaign raised six million hryvnias for winter uniforms for female service members.

She considers financial independence essential. She started working at the age of 12.

“If you want to see people around you rather than resources, you need to be able to stand on your own. And that is the principle I live by.”

Exchange

World.title: Experts warn of pesticides in Armenian food, inspectors see no issues
World.content:
Pesticides in Armenian food

Pesticides in fruit and vegetables, antibiotics in farmed fish and nitrates in melons and watermelons. These are just some of the problems highlighted in a report by Armenia‘s Food Safety Inspection Body.

Opposition Strong Armenia faction MP Harutyun Mnatsakanyan raised the issue from the National Assembly rostrum, citing the report itself. However, the Food Safety Inspection Body responded by accusing the MP of spreading false information:

“In 2024, it was not 192 but 179 samples that were tested for pesticides. Pesticides were detected in 91 of them, but in only six did pesticide levels exceed the permitted limit established by the relevant EAEU regulations [the economic union of which Armenia is a member].”

The agency also said pesticides could have been found not just in every second sample but in all the fruit and vegetable samples tested. It explained that “these substances are used during cultivation, and it is impossible to produce a healthy crop without them”.

Meanwhile, experts described the data contained in the agency’s report as “appalling and shameful”.

“We are literally living on an experimental testing ground where all kinds of chemicals are being tested on us,” food safety expert David Pipoyan said.

What hazardous substances were detected?

As part of its 2024 report, the Food Safety Inspection Body tested 179 food products for pesticide residues in products of plant origin. A further 19 products were tested for genetically modified organisms (GMOs).

The products tested included apples, peaches, strawberries, plums, grapes, potatoes, tomatoes, cucumbers, peppers, aubergines, watermelons, melons and corn.

Nitrates were detected in samples of melon, watermelon and potatoes.

GMOs accounted for 5.2% of one corn sample brought from Lori Region.

The highest pesticide levels exceeding permitted limits were recorded in products from Ararat, Armavir, Aragatsotn and Kotayk regions.

Of 696 samples tested, heavy metals were detected in nine — including potatoes, tomatoes, cucumbers, peppers and aubergines.

According to the inspection body’s report, unacceptably high levels of antibiotic contamination were found in honey from Vayots Dzor, Gegharkunik and Lori regions.

The report also says that consuming fish farmed in artificial ponds may pose health risks:

“The antibiotics detected in the samples, particularly compounds from the nitrofuran and metronidazole groups, have a cumulative effect and may have carcinogenic and mutagenic effects.”

‘We are putting our children at risk’

MP Harutyun Mnatsakanyan highlighted the presence of nitrates in potatoes, watermelons and melons:

“Our children are the most vulnerable to nitrates. In other words, by consuming products made in Armenia, we are putting the health of our children and our parents at enormous risk. I am not even talking about ourselves.”

He said farmers should not be blamed, as they cannot establish clear standards for pesticide use themselves. Mnatsakanyan said strict controls were needed:

“Controls must extend all the way to the market. The inspection body is proposing legislative amendments to establish pesticide controls throughout the supply chain. This needs to be done now, not after the next round of monitoring.”

The MP proposed taking the following steps urgently:

publishing all of the inspection body’s 2024 monitoring results;

holding parliamentary hearings involving representatives of the inspection body and the Economy Ministry, as well as scientists and MPs.

Inspection body: ‘No banned pesticides detected’

The inspection body said it was unacceptable to “mislead the public with unfounded and panic-inducing headlines”.

It also responded to the opposition MP’s claim that “what is banned in Brussels and Washington ends up on the plates of our elderly parents and children”. The body’s experts said some pesticides may be banned in one country while being permitted in another:

“Armenia is a party to the Rotterdam and Stockholm conventions and, in accordance with its international obligations, prohibits the registration, import and use of pesticides covered by these conventions. No banned pesticides were detected in the products tested in our country.”

Expert commentary

Food safety expert David Pipoyan recalled that industry experts had raised concerns about food quality a year earlier, but the Food Safety Inspection Body had dismissed their claims as defamatory.

“Last year, this same body denied everything at a news conference, saying there had been no violations. This year, it published — effectively hid — this appalling report on a little-known platform,” he said.

According to Pipoyan, if 47 out of every 100 samples tested were contaminated, this would mean that roughly every second purchase could potentially involve a contaminated product. In other words, he said, consumers would face a 47% chance of buying fruit or vegetables contaminated with pesticides.

Pipoyan said the problems went beyond the risk of consuming products containing carcinogenic substances:

“If you look at the range of pesticides being used, you can find neurotoxic substances, as well as pesticides that affect children’s health.”

He stressed that the report’s findings pointed to an ongoing risk for all consumers. In Pipoyan’s view, the publication of such a report in other countries would inevitably have led to those responsible for quality control being held accountable.

Social media reaction

Social media users also expressed outrage over the situation. Here are some of their comments:

“Every day you pay money to eat poison. And then you wonder why Armenia has ranked among the world’s leaders in cancer cases for decades.”

“This shows complete disregard for the health of the country’s own people.”

“We are demanding not token legislative ‘initiatives’ and justifications, but strict, genuine laboratory controls — from the fields to the shops.”

“Agricultural producers, are you happy with what you are doing? Let’s say there are no controls. But what about your conscience? Don’t you understand that you are committing a crime by poisoning people?“

“I’ve been saying it: we eat poison every day. Meanwhile, environmentalists are only concerned with shutting down mining operations. Environmentalists, what do you have to say now?“

“Whatever you feel like eating, pray first and then eat.”

“Everyone who doesn’t care about people’s health should be held accountable.”

World.title: Abkhaz experts discuss Georgian opposition’s proposals, EU stance on conflict resolution
World.content:
The EU on Abkhazia

Statements by Western officials and initiatives of the Georgian opposition surrounding the status of Abkhazia are once again drawing attention to the region. Abkhaz analysts commented on attempts to intensify Abkhazia’s isolation and evaluated the roles of the EU, Russia, and internal Georgian forces in this process.

Key arguments:

The Abkhazian question is being used by the Georgian opposition as a tool in their struggle against the ruling Georgian Dream party. Attempts to harden their stance and achieve the withdrawal of recognitions, as seen in the case of Nauru, are aimed at accusing the current government of a lack of patriotism and of making concessions to Moscow.

The European Union leadership’s focus on the issue of Syria revoking its recognition of Abkhazia is driven not so much by concern for peace as by a desire to weaken Russian influence and maintain levers of influence over Georgia amid a crisis in bilateral relations.

A peaceful or forceful “return” of Abkhazia to Georgia is an unacceptable paradigm for Abkhaz society. Pressure from the EU and Georgia only destroys trust and narrows the possibilities for a diplomatic settlement.

Here are the questions posed to the experts and their responses.

Why would the Georgian opposition, which already faces plenty of problems in its relations with the authorities, choose at this moment to step up efforts toward the further isolation of Abkhazia, following the successful outcome with Nauru?

Respondent 1

It is difficult to judge the motivation of the Georgian opposition in this matter. I can only assume that, as always, the issue of Abkhazia and the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict serves as a bargaining chip in domestic political processes. Regarding Abkhazia, Georgian Dream behaves with more restraint than previous Georgian authorities, at least at the level of public statements. In contrast to it, and as if to demonstrate greater patriotism, the opposition—which lacks broad support among the population outside of Tbilisi—speaks out much more harshly. Apparently, in its largely ineffective struggle against the current government, the Georgian opposition has decided to weaponize the issue of the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict, or as they call it, the “Abkhazian question”.

At the same time, other voices are also being heard within the Georgian opposition. For example, Nika Gvaramia recently gave an interview in which he called on Georgian society to move past the traumatic memories of the past. In his view, conflicts should not act as weights tied to Georgia’s feet on its path toward the European Union.

Thus, within opposition circles, there are proponents of both a forceful “return” of Abkhazia and those who advocate for its “peaceful return”. Another matter entirely is that few in Georgia understand that for the Abkhaz people, peace and a “peaceful return” are by no means the same thing. In Abkhazia, such an approach is perceived as achieving the same end by hook or by crook.

Instead of trying to turn back the clock and forgetting everything we went through in the recent past, we ought to accept reality and seek common ground on issues of mutual interest. And such issues do exist, considering that we are neighbors.

To speak of returning Abkhazia, whether by peaceful or violent means, belongs to an entirely different paradigm. The Abkhaz people will resist either of these two options. However, at least a mindset focused on peaceful solutions makes it possible to maintain stability. Unfortunately, if circumstances develop in a way that favors Georgia, those parties advocating a forceful solution will gain the upper hand.

Respondent 2

I believe that the situation surrounding the revocation of recognition by Nauru undoubtedly emboldened Georgian super-patriots. But it also seems to me, paradoxical as it may sound, that the more liberal, pro-democratic forces in Georgia—meaning the current opposition, parts of which were once in the Georgian leadership—have always been and remain more hardline, nationalistic, and hawkish regarding frozen conflicts.

We have always paid attention to this hawkish rhetoric, which was heard back during Mikheil Saakashvili’s rule. On the one hand, he seemed to democratize Georgia’s governance system, but on the other, he approached conflict resolution in a way that was entirely unliberal and disregarded human rights. The current demands of the opposition appear to be a continuation of that policy.

Another factor relates to the fact that relations between the European Union and Georgia—specifically the ruling Georgian Dream party—have deteriorated so sharply that the European Union has no remaining levers of influence over processes taking place inside Georgia. Since the EU is deprived of the ability to affect Georgia’s internal political matters, it compensates by responding to this narrative to cater to the Georgian opposition, which Europe views as pro-democratic and liberal.

Respondent 3

The Georgian opposition raises this issue with a tactical objective: to demonstrate that the current government lacks principle regarding the problem of Georgia’s territorial integrity and is willing to compromise on it. In doing so, it heightens the level of friction between Western countries and Ivanishvili’s government by framing the latter as conduits for Moscow’s global agenda.

In reality, the approach across the entire political spectrum in Georgia toward relations with the former autonomous entities is identical: restoring the territory of the Georgian SSR either by force or through diplomacy.

Respondent 4

In my view, the Georgian opposition has quite a few problems not only in its relations with the government, but also in internal relations within itself; there is no single, clearly defined leader there, and it appears to me to be fragmented and non-united.

The “Coalition for Change” consists of several parties and is headed by a council of four leaders. That is to say, the Georgian opposition has problems with the authorities, within itself, and with the European Union as well.

To both questions, I would answer the same way: the appeal to Ursula von der Leyen lies within the perspective of Georgia’s domestic political problems and its relations with the European Union.

We see that the Georgian opposition has been protesting for a very long time, people are taking to the streets, but these protests yield no visible results; in my view, Georgia’s tilt away from the European Union towards Russia is growing, public support for the Georgian opposition is falling, and its ratings are falling too.

We often hear that the Abkhazian issue currently sits on the periphery of the international agenda and is virtually invisible against the backdrop of other crises. Why, then, do we see such active support from the European Union for the initiative demanding that Syria revoke its recognition of Abkhazia?

Respondent 1

There are two factors here. One is that Abkhazia is indeed at the very bottom of their agenda, if present at all. Russia and Georgia, however, are present. Therefore, the issue of revoking recognition represents, on the one hand, a policy of countering Russia, and on the other, a step toward trying to regain Georgia’s loyalty. Ursula von der Leyen’s support for the Georgian opposition’s demand on such a sensitive, patriotic issue also serves to bolster the position of opposition forces within Georgian society.

On the whole, the fact that against the backdrop of highly acute global and regional problems, the President of the European Commission finds time for the issue of Syria revoking its recognition of Abkhazia reflects political bias and the double standards associated with such bias, which, unfortunately, have always been displayed toward us by Europe and the international community at large.

It would be appropriate here to ask von der Leyen a question: if EU representatives claim to be committed to a peaceful resolution of the conflict, what does revoking Syria’s recognition have to do with it? How does it bring us any closer to peace? If anything, it does the opposite. Such steps certainly do not help the negotiation process, the building of trust, or any of the other goals declared by the Europeans. What they certainly do is call into question the EU’s role as a mediator, further shrinking its already dramatically reduced presence in the region.

Respondent 2

It is true that in words we often hear that amid the major wars taking place around the EU, the Georgian-Abkhaz context is irrelevant. In practice, however, whenever decisions are made that restrict the rights of Abkhazia’s residents, EU officials quickly spring into action.

Interestingly, Ursula von der Leyen herself, who intends to address the revocation of Syria’s recognition of the Republic of Abkhazia, appears to be going through a difficult period within the European Union. From news sources, we can see how European Parliament sessions unfold, with MEPs from various countries harshly criticizing von der Leyen’s actions, raising many grievances and questions.

In this situation, it is remarkable that despite serious internal problems and challenges, she finds the time to attend to the requests of certain political forces in a non-EU country, Georgia, regarding pressure on another non-EU country, Syria. We have always noted the European Union’s special attitude toward Georgia—an attitude I would describe as unrequited love.

The European Union contributed greatly to the development of the modern Georgian state and supported the reform of its state institutions. It seems to me that Georgia was forgiven for things that were never forgiven in other countries. What is happening now appears to be the lingering, phantom feelings toward Georgia at a time when its official representatives have ceased to reciprocate.

Of course, the factor of relations between the European Union and Russia also plays a role that cannot be ignored. Here, the EU operates on the principle of “the friend of my enemy is my enemy”. Perhaps that is why they show little concern for how EU decisions will be received by the government and civil society in Abkhazia, how these decisions impact the protection of Abkhazia residents’ rights, or how they might ultimately affect the state of the conflict.

Respondent 3

I think it is premature to speak of overly active support for this issue on the part of the European Commission. Although, on the whole, a moderate level of activity aimed at having Syria revoke its recognition of Abkhazia’s sovereignty would not surprise me. First and foremost, it is an effort to undo political acts of the Assad era and further weaken Russian influence in the Eastern Mediterranean.

The complaints of the Georgian opposition are of minor importance in this context. What is interesting, however, is whether it is truly in the West’s own interest to indulge Georgia, given the country’s systematic and deliberate drift toward the East. That remains an open question, and I doubt I am the only one considering it.

Respondent 4

Against the backdrop of these problems in relations between the Georgian opposition and the European Union, a certain reboot is required. Running slightly ahead and trying to answer the second question about why the European Union needs this, I think that such a reboot is needed for the European Union as well.

The chosen tactic and strategy of the European Union—not to engage in contacts with the Georgian government, but rather to cooperate more actively and closely with the Georgian opposition on the assumption that it will sooner or later manage to take power in Georgia—seems to me not to be working or to be working poorly, and it requires a new impetus. Yet no visible tracks on which success could be achieved are in sight.

By success, I mean the need to boost the rating of the opposition itself among the Georgian population and to raise its status. After the regime change in Syria, the new leadership of that country needs some assistance from the European Union, and the EU holds certain leverage over it.

If, at the request of the Georgian opposition, it manages to achieve some progress on the issue of Syria revoking its recognition of Abkhazia, this could sharply boost the rating of the opposition in general and of this opposition bloc in particular. The exact same thing, in my opinion, is required for the European Union itself, since the previous tactic is not working and the opposition forces in Georgia are not gaining, but on the contrary are losing strength and influence.

The European Union put forward eight or nine conditions to the Georgian government so that it could return to the previous course of relations with the EU; Georgia is not fulfilling these conditions, and what is more, the tilt towards Russia has already turned into a stable trend toward rapprochement between these countries against the backdrop of the war with Ukraine and in the Persian Gulf, where Europe has a great deal of problems.

Naturally, the European Union needs to restore relations with Georgia, especially since Georgia is located in that region and used to be a partner of the EU, but is no longer one now.

In this context, I allow that the appeal of the opposition bloc to Ursula von der Leyen is necessary for all the purposes I have mentioned.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website

World.title: Baku-Paris-Moscow: What links French national’s release in Azerbaijan to Russian billionaire’s sanctions relief?
World.content:
Aliyev pardons French citizen

On 23 September, Ilham Aliyev pardoned French citizen Martin Ryan, who had been sentenced to 10 years in prison for espionage.

A day earlier, the European Union agreed, at France’s request, to remove Russian-Uzbek billionaire Alisher Usmanov from its sanctions list. According to the Financial Times, citing diplomatic sources, the two decisions form part of an agreement between Baku and Paris on the release of prisoners.

After years of confrontation over issues involving Armenia, Nagorno-Karabakh and France’s overseas territories, Baku and Paris reached an agreement on specific issues: France secured the release of its citizen, while Azerbaijan secured the lifting of European sanctions against the billionaire it had supported.

From a 10-year prison sentence to a pardon

The French citizen, identified in the pardon decree as Ryan Martin Richard, has been released from serving the remainder of his sentence. Authorities detained him on 4 December 2023, and on 16 March 2026 the Baku Court of Serious Crimes sentenced him to 10 years in prison.

According to the Azerbaijani side, Ryan, the head of Merkorama, was supposed to collect military and other information for France’s Directorate-General for External Security. Paris rejected the allegations. On 30 July, France’s Foreign Ministry condemned the appellate court’s decision to uphold the sentence, called the conviction arbitrary and demanded Ryan’s immediate release.

The 10-year sentence, which the court upheld in July, was therefore brought to an end in September by a presidential decision. Ryan’s fate took a decisive turn not in the courtroom, but as part of diplomatic negotiations over sanctions.

What did Paris do for Usmanov?

On 14 September, the Financial Times reported that France was seeking to have Usmanov removed from the EU sanctions list in exchange for the release of French citizens detained in Azerbaijan. Paris and Bratislava called for his sanctions to be lifted and vetoed the extension of the restrictions for another 12 months. The EU initially granted a one-week delay to allow negotiations to continue.

On 22 September, the sides reached a compromise: Mikhail Fridman was also removed from the sanctions list alongside Usmanov, while the remaining individual sanctions were extended for 36 months instead of the previous six. For Usmanov, this means the lifting of the asset freeze and EU travel ban.

The mechanism allowed Baku’s demand to reach the level of European policy. Azerbaijan, as a non-EU country, could not take part in the sanctions decision-making process. However, France’s interest in securing the return of its citizens allowed Paris to pursue this concession within the European Union.

Why is Usmanov important to Baku?

Azerbaijan’s support for Usmanov did not begin in recent days.

On 18 September, a senior Azerbaijani diplomat told Reuters that between November 2023 and March 2025, Baku and other members of the Organisation of Turkic States had sent letters supporting Usmanov to the leaders of the United States and European countries. The diplomat described him as a philanthropist who helps strengthen ties between the West, Central Asia and the Turkic world.

The same diplomat denied reports that Azerbaijan had pressured France. A French Foreign Ministry representative, meanwhile, declined to disclose details, saying the matter concerned national security.

On 21 September, Euronews also reported that Uzbekistan had played a role in reaching the agreement. According to the report, the proposed deal involved releasing two French citizens detained in Azerbaijan in exchange for removing Usmanov from the sanctions list, with Aliyev expected to sign a pardon decree. The EU made its sanctions decision the following day, after which Ryan received a presidential pardon. The events unfolded in the same sequence that Euronews had previously described.

Confrontation from Nagorno-Karabakh to New Caledonia

The political significance of the agreement becomes clearer against the backdrop of relations between Baku and Paris in recent years. France criticised Azerbaijan’s military actions in Nagorno-Karabakh and expanded defence cooperation with Armenia. Baku, in turn, viewed Paris’s military support for Yerevan as interference in the regional balance of power.

Azerbaijan also extended the confrontation to issues sensitive for France itself. The Baku Initiative Group, established in 2023, held events involving supporters of independence for New Caledonia, French Polynesia, Martinique and other territories. Links were established between these movements and Azerbaijani political structures.

When unrest broke out in New Caledonia in May 2024, France accused Baku of interference. Azerbaijan rejected the allegations. Changes to electoral rules and fears among the indigenous Kanak people of losing political influence lay at the heart of the domestic crisis. At the same time, the crisis became a new source of mutual accusations between Baku and Paris.

The current agreement points not so much to a resolution of these disputes as to the sides’ willingness to set them aside in order to achieve specific results. For Paris, the priority was securing the release of its citizen; for Baku, it was securing a decision on Usmanov, whom Azerbaijan had supported for years.

The cost of the concession for Europe

France is not the only party to face political costs from the agreement. Ukraine’s leadership opposed removing oligarchs from the sanctions list. Within the EU, there were also concerns that making exceptions to the bloc’s common sanctions policy for national interests could set a dangerous precedent.

The political outcome of these events is that the release of a prisoner in Baku became part of negotiations over European sanctions against Russia. France secured the release of its citizen, while Azerbaijan brought one of the EU’s most influential members into supporting a billionaire backed by Baku. This points more to diplomacy based on mutual concessions under pressure than to a restoration of trust between the two countries.

Aliyev pardons French citizen

World.title: Formula 1 Azerbaijan Grand Prix: Race time is set, but getting home is anyone’s guess
World.content:
Formula 1 Azerbaijan Grand Prix

Sports journalist Anar Khanlarov left his home in Sumgayit half an hour earlier than usual on 21 September to make it to Baku in time for a TV programme. But even that was not enough.

He planned to take the metro from 20 January station to Nizami, then a bus to 28 May, followed by bus No 5 towards State Flag Square. As the İdman TV studio was undergoing renovation, filming was taking place at the Rowing Federation building on the boulevard.

His bus became stuck in traffic near Winter Park. Khanlarov continued on foot towards the Puppet Theatre, hoping to catch another bus from there or, failing that, take a taxi. When he reached the theatre at 20:40, he found that the road towards Bayil was closed. The programme began at 21:00, but Khanlarov did not reach the filming location until 21:25, alternating between walking and running. By then he was sweating heavily, and the production team decided he was not in a suitable condition to appear on air. As a result, Khanlarov did not take part in the programme at all that day.

The main events of the Formula 1 Azerbaijan Grand Prix will take place on 24–26 September. But even before the racing begins, road closures and changes to bus routes have brought life in the city to a standstill.

26 bus routes changed, leaving passengers with no real alternative

According to a plan by the Azerbaijan Land Transport Agency (AYNA), 26 bus routes have been changed between 21 and 26 September.

Route No 5, which Khanlarov had planned to take, is among those affected. On one section, the bus runs between Nariman Narimanov metro station and Suleyman Rahimov Street, while on another it runs along a route covering the Salyan Highway, Bibi-Heybat Mosque and the Baku Funicular. Under the new arrangements, it is no longer possible to use the bus to travel from the city centre to Bayil via the usual route. Some stops on this and other routes are inside the restricted race zone. There is no alternative public transport available.

The changes have also affected people travelling into the city from the suburbs. Buses No 149 and 149E from the settlement of Sahil and No 195E from Alat now run only as far as the Lokbatan transport hub near the Bina shopping centre. Passengers travelling to the city centre have to change to another form of transport. Bus No 125 reaches the centre via the ring road through Badamdar.

The transit corridors announced by the organisers are also not an alternative for bus passengers. On 21–22 September, they are open from 07:00 to 09:00 and from 18:00 to 20:00. However, these arrangements do not apply to public transport. Except in emergencies, picking up and dropping off passengers is also prohibited within the transit corridors. By the time Khanlarov reached the Puppet Theatre at 20:40, he says, the evening transit window had already closed.

‘We haven’t moved for an hour and 40 minutes’

Former transport officials have also complained about the traffic jams. Mais Aghayev, former head of the Baku Transport Agency’s press service, wrote on Facebook:

“We haven’t moved for an hour and 40 minutes on the stretch from the Mikayil Aliyev roundabout towards Heydar Aliyev Avenue.”

The congestion has also been acknowledged by the authorities. On the evening of 22 September, the Intelligent Transport Management Centre reported traffic jams on 28 May Street, as well as on the section of Shamsi Badalbeyli Street running from Winter Park towards the Central Bank. These streets are also part of the routes affected by AYNA’s changes to bus services.

Seven schools and universities switch to remote learning

Measures related to the race are not limited to changes to transport. According to the Baku City Education Department, seven schools are holding classes online from 22 to 26 September: Public Schools No 6, 7, 8 and 23, Classical Gymnasium No 160, Lyceum No 132–134 and the Ilyas Efendiyev Elite Gymnasium.

Under an order issued by the Ministry of Science and Education, universities in Baku have also switched to remote learning from 23 to 25 September. The ministry says the measure is intended to ensure continuity of the education process.

The move may reduce the number of daily journeys to schools and universities. However, remote learning creates additional difficulties for working parents: who will look after younger children, and how will families ensure they have the devices and internet access needed for online classes? The switch to remote learning does not mean parents no longer have to go to work. So while it may ease pressure on the transport system, it does not necessarily ease the everyday burden on families.

No indication of how much longer journeys will take

Natig Jafarli, an economist and chairman of the Republican Alternative party, linked the problem to Baku’s fragmented system of governance in a Facebook post on 14 September. In his view, the key factors are the availability of public transport and journey times. He also argues that any changes to working hours should take into account the school schedules of employees’ children.

Economist Akif Nasirli told Radio Azadliq that the race should be held outside the city centre. In his view, the economic benefits of the event should not be used to justify restrictions on residents’ freedom of movement:

“People have the right to move freely in their own country, in their own capital.”

AYNA’s traffic management plan for the race, published on 19 September, lists alternative streets that drivers can use. However, it provides no information on actual bus frequencies along the altered routes, how much additional time journeys will take, or how much time passengers may lose when changing between separate sections of disrupted routes.

For residents, it is not enough simply to know which street a bus will take. They need to know when to leave home, where they will have to change and whether they can get to work on time. Without this information, the burden of adapting to the route changes — and the consequences of any resulting delays — falls on passengers themselves.

World.title: Why Georgia closed 10 schools days into new academic year
World.content:
School closure in Georgia

Ten state schools in Georgia were closed during the first three days of the new academic year. Some of the buildings are due to be demolished and rebuilt, while others will undergo repairs.

The decision followed assessments by the National Forensics Bureau, which found that the school buildings were in a state of disrepair and unsafe for use.

One of the schools is in Tbilisi, while the others are located in different regions across the country.

For the first week after the closures, the schools switched to remote learning. During this period, the Education Ministry and school administrations are expected to urgently find alternative premises.

All 10 schools are likely to be temporarily accommodated in neighbouring schools, with classes held in two or three shifts and lesson times shortened. If any of the alternative schools are too far away, school buses will be provided.

More than 4,000 pupils and around 400 teachers are now waiting for the ministry to decide where they will be relocated and which shifts they will study and work in.

his is not unprecedented. In recent years, thousands of pupils across Georgia have been studying in temporary, “borrowed” premises, while schools that were demolished have yet to be rebuilt.

How events unfolded and what the decisions were based on

The closure of all 10 schools followed the same pattern. The start of the new academic year on 15 September was celebrated as usual, with balloons, flags and flowers in school courtyards and classrooms.

Three days later, on the evening of 17 September, parents received messages informing them that the schools were being closed.

Number of pupils and teachers at the closed schools. Source: JAMnews, based on data from the official schools portal.

In all 10 cases, the decisions to close the schools were based on assessments by the National Forensics Bureau dated 10 September 2026. The education minister says the ministry did not receive the documents until 17 September, explaining why the closures were announced at such short notice.

Some parents do not believe that the school buildings are unsafe. They suspect that some of the decisions may be linked to corrupt deals and investors’ interests.

JAMnews examined publicly available documents relating to all 10 schools, including decisions by the Authorisation Council, expert assessments, public procurement records, renovation plans and municipal reports.

We sought answers to several questions: Why were these schools allowed to begin the academic year as normal on 15 September if their buildings had to be vacated just days later? When did the responsible authorities learn about the condition of the schools? And if the buildings were already destined for demolition, why was money allocated for their renovation year after year?

Renovating schools only to abandon them

The documents examined by JAMnews show that concerns about the poor condition of some of the schools had been known for years. In other cases, however, there had previously appeared to be no need even for repairs, let alone demolition.

Some of the schools underwent minor renovation work in recent years, with substantial sums spent on the projects.

For example, according to public procurement records, Public School No 16 in Kutaisi underwent various repairs in 2015, 2017 and 2022. The largest amount was spent in 2015 — around 190,000 lari [about $70,300].

The Kutaisi school made its most recent purchase just three weeks before the start of the current academic year. On 24 August, the administration signed a 2,500-lari [about $925] contract for maintenance of the school grounds, including mowing and removing grass.

Public School No 16 in Kutaisi. The start of the academic year was celebrated with invited entertainers. Photo: school’s official Facebook page.

The public school in the village of Misaktsieli underwent major renovations in 2008, while its heating system was completely upgraded last winter.

This is also confirmed by the Mtskheta municipality’s 2025 budget. According to the document, several schools were due to undergo renovation work funded through a targeted transfer from the state budget. The school in Misaktsieli was among them.
