Magistrate Mykytowycz said while Nation's mental health was in a "parlous" state, he was currently well supported by family and had been accessing professional help in the community.

Nation wept in court as the magistrate outlined how his mental health declined after the IBAC investigation, which did not result in him being charged.

"It is often the case the fall from grace for those in the public arena is accompanied by increased media attention," the magistrate said.

Nation departed the courtroom with three security guards by his side. His jacket was confiscated and he was provided with a plain white T-shirt to wear.

In 2024, Nation stunned fellow Mooney Valley councillors, when he attended a meeting via video link and abruptly resigned, telling them "Ciao".

Three years earlier, he avoided a criminal conviction after pleading guilty to falsifying claims for two community swim grants.

Earlier on Thursday, Premier Ben Carroll was asked whether the ex-mayor's bid to keep his name suppressed met community standards.

"Simple answer: no," he said.

Opposition Leader Jess Wilson agreed.

"We've had serious concerns about suppression orders for some time," she said.

Both the major parties have pledged to update the state's Open Courts Act, after cases of people charged with serious sex crimes applying to keep their names suppressed.

World.title: Australia calls for 'absolute consensus' on Pacific military group
World.content:
Pacific defence ministers have signalled they will not rush to expand the remit of a new military response group, with Australia's defence chief saying there must be "absolute consensus" about how it evolves.

The South Pacific Defence Ministers' Meeting (SPDMM) — which draws in Australia, Chile, Fiji, France, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea and Tonga — has wrapped up in Fiji.

On top of the agenda was the Pacific Response Group (PRG), which was formed in 2024 as part of a push from Australia and several other governments to develop a more coordinated response to natural disasters in the region.

AFP to push Australia's policing model to UN The AFP commissioner will promote Pacific police training as a model for the UN when she addresses police delegates this week.

Last year, the ministers endorsed a move to broaden the mandate of the PRG so it can also conduct "stabilisation operations" for Pacific nations that request military help to deal with civil unrest.

And in May this year, senior Pacific military officers endorsed a push for a new regional treaty that would govern how deployments take place, recommending Pacific leaders kickstart negotiations on a framework that would make it easier to rapidly send personnel to countries grappling with crises.

But while there is enthusiasm for the idea, it is also politically sensitive.

That is partly because the PRG can easily be seen as part of a broader push by Australia and its allies to block China from the security space, and partly because it will have to grapple with fraught questions around what legal immunity is offered to personnel deployed to other countries.

A review of Fiji's constitution has recommended sweeping changes to the country's supreme law. (AFP)

Some Pacific nations are also dealing with internal political issues — for example, Fiji is embroiled in an intense domestic debate on constitutional reform, and is likely to go to the polls before February next year.

On top of that, Pacific bureaucracies have also struggled to keep pace with the push for rapid change within the PRG just a couple of years after it was established.

When Pacific leaders met in Palau, they did not agree to kickstart negotiations on the treaty, signalling that they wanted to move more slowly on the issue.

And this afternoon, SPDMM defence ministers released a communique saying they had told senior military officers that the framework had to "consider the privileges and immunities relevant to HADR [humanitarian and disaster relief] and any future PRG stabilisation function".

Pacific ministers pose during the South Pacific Defence Ministers' Meeting (SPDMM). (Supplied: Fiji Ministry of Defence & Veterans Affairs)

The ministers also said they had agreed to take a "phased approach" to expanding the PRG's mandate, "recognising the importance of first consolidating and enhancing the PRG's humanitarian assistance and disaster relief [HADR] capabilities" before working to "include stabilisation operations".

Australian Defence Force chief Admiral Mark Hammond, who represented Australia at the meeting along with Assistant Defence Minister Peter Khalil, told the ABC that the group "must pay due respect to sovereign constitutional processes" and there had to be an "absolute consensus of an overlap with respect to national interest".

"We still need some time to work things through their constitutional processes and some of the nations at the table are on the cusp of national elections, some have only recently elected them or had a cabinet reshuffle, so these take time to bed down," Mr Hammond said.

Admiral Mark Hammond speaking at an AUKUS conference in Washington. (Supplied)

But Admiral Hammond told the ABC there was still rock-solid support for the PRG at a "macro level" because it embodied the idea of Pacific-led security.

"When you look at the Pacific Response Group and the number of nations that are present in that, and you see that arriving as an initial response force to one of our Pacific Island nations, there will be representatives from that nation, in the PRG, that will be able to speak to the local issues, to help us cut through bureaucracy and to interpret their national interest into individual language that enables us to get on, deliver and support," he said.

One Pacific government representative, who requested anonymity to speak frankly, said there was not any "opposition" to the PRG, which they said was largely seen as a "great idea."

But they said some of the questions around immunity and sovereignty, as well as the geopolitical backdrop, could be "a little bit sensitive".

Pacific defence ministers dance at the South Pacific Defence Ministers' Meeting (SPDMM). (Supplied: Fiji Ministry of Defence & Veterans Affairs)

"Everyone wants to take this slowly and carefully and get this right," they said.

Pacific security expert Anna Powles from Massey University said it was "not surprising that securing regional consensus is proving challenging".

"Some countries are suggesting the process has been rushed and have questions about where the agreement will sit within the regional security architecture," she said.

"It could be useful to locate the framework under the Biketawa Declaration, which has the credibility and the tested mechanisms to support regionally led responses."

The seven countries represented at SPDMM also expressed "grave concern" over China's ballistic missile test earlier this year, using much stronger language than was adopted at the Pacific Island Forum (PIF) leaders' meeting in Palau earlier this month.

"Ministers highlighted that the manner in which this activity was conducted risked undermining PIF leaders' declaration of the Blue Pacific Continent as an Ocean of Peace," they said.

"It also undermined leaders' call to engage with the Blue Pacific Continent in a manner that honours the Pacific Way, respects national sovereignty and supports national and Pacific-led approaches."

World.title: Second child dies after Blue Mountains stabbing, third child still critical
World.content:
A second child has died after a mother allegedly stabbed her three children in the Blue Mountains on the weekend.

NSW Police said the child, aged one, died on Thursday in hospital after the children were attacked at Valley Heights near Springwood on Sunday.

It comes after one of the child's siblings, a five-year-old boy, was found dead inside the vehicle police responded to on Waratah Road.

The mother was also found at the scene with self-inflicted stab wounds, police have previously said.

Police were told members of the public performed first aid on the children before emergency services arrived.

A third sibling, a three-year-old who also sustained stab wounds, remains in a critical condition in hospital.

The woman has been charged with a second count of murder and is due in court in November. (ABC News)

The woman was charged with murder and police said the mother has now been charged with an additional count of murder.

She is due to face Penrith Local Court in November.

World.title: Brethren members campaigned across NT during 2025 election, inquiry hears
World.content:
A former Northern Territory chief minister has claimed members of a conservative Christian sect engaged in "intimidating" behaviour at NT polling booths while campaigning ahead of the last federal election.

Former Territory Labor leader Eva Lawler gave evidence at a parliamentary inquiry into the 2025 federal election when it sat in Darwin yesterday, saying members of the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church (PBCC) had campaigned across vast areas of the NT.

Mrs Lawler lost her seat in the Territory parliament in 2024, but said while supporting Labor at the following year's federal election, she came across a group of "intimidating men" at booths in Greater Darwin.

Eva Lawler told the inquiry members of the PBCC made comments "derogatory to Anthony Albanese" during the campaign. (ABC News: Jayden O'Neill)

NT-based federal Labor MP Marion Scrymgour has previously alleged members of the church — also known as the Exclusive Brethren — engaged in "aggressive and intimidating" behaviour during the election campaign at a Katherine polling booth.

Mrs Lawler told the inquiry that while she could not say "100 per cent" that the men were members of the PBCC, "they weren't locals".

Brethren Church denies election harassment The Plymouth Brethren Christian Church says it did not pay or coordinate far-right influencers to harass and intimidate candidates during last year's federal election

"[They] were there to push the conservative side of politics," she said.

"I felt they were intimidating people at the booth that I was at.

"[Their comments were] derogatory to Labor, derogatory to Anthony Albanese."

Mrs Lawler said one person "was basically handing out how to vote [cards] for the Country Liberal Party" (CLP).

"But at times you would also see him talking to the One Nation people as well, so definitely on that conservative, right side of politics," she said.

The PBCC this week denied allegations it secretly paid people to disrupt Labor's 2025 federal election campaign, following reports of unusually large numbers of Liberal volunteers manning pre-polling booths in marginal seats.

'Actions of individuals'

During yesterday's hearing, Mrs Lawler also claimed members of the church flew to remote polling booths in Indigenous communities, including Wadeye and Groote Eylandt.

"Particularly in the remote communities there was probably eight or nine [men campaigning] at different times," she said.

Former NT deputy Labor leader Lynne Walker told the inquiry that while she was campaigning in the remote community of Galiwin'ku, a group of men she claimed were "part of the Brethren" flew in from Queensland to campaign for the CLP.

Lynne Walker said it was the first time she'd seen "people come in from interstate" to campaign for the CLP. (ABC News)

"[In previous elections] more often we would see known Country Liberal Party people from Darwin who had travelled out to some of the remote communities to [campaign], so it was the first time I'd seen people come in from interstate," she said.

In response to questions from the ABC, a spokesperson for the PBCC denied the church had played any role in the federal election.

"So we cannot comment on the actions of individuals who did — whether they are speculated to be members of our church or not," they said.

" It is clear that some people who share our faith did get involved, but it is completely wrong to conflate the actions of private individual citizens as being reflective of, or orchestrated by, their faith. "

CLP president Nathan Land said he had "no knowledge of the CLP requesting any particular religious group, including the Exclusive Brethren, to campaign during the 2025 federal election".

Eva Lawler campaigned for federal labor in 2025 after losing her seat in the NT parliament the previous year. (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

"I have read the vague claims made by members of Territory Labor and find some humour in their concern about groups of people coming in to influence an election result," he said.

"Labor's union mates have been doing exactly that for as long as I can remember."

Hancock rejects staffer's claim

Former Territory Labor staffer and volunteer, Kerry Gardiner, also gave evidence at the inquiry, alleging members of the PBCC were flown in and out of Wadeye in a private jet owned by Australia's richest person, Gina Rinehart.

When asked if he could substantiate that claim, Mr Gardiner said he did not have a photo, but the tail of the jet was labelled with the letter H.

"H on he tail — Hancock Prospecting — that's her company," he said.

"I saw the plane."

A spokesperson for Gina Rinehart's company Hancock Prospecting said Mr Gardiner's claims were "wrong and defamatory". (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

In response to the claim, Hancock Prospecting spokesperson James Radford said it was "wrong and defamatory to suggest or report that this Labor volunteer/staffer’s claims are true".

"I understand one Labor volunteer/staffer made these false claims on the basis that he saw the letter H in a multi-character registration number of a random aircraft at an airport somewhere in the NT at some point last year," he said.

One of Darwin's main charter flight companies, Hardy Aviation, also has the letter H on its aircraft.

World.title: Flawed reasons for a just outcome: Why Neale playing in the grand final is the right thing
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion Flawed reasons for a just outcome: Why Neale playing in the grand final is the right thing Jake Niall Chief football writer, The Age September 24, 2026 — 9:55pm

September 24, 2026 — 9:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

From Wharfie Time to Country Roads, this is your one-stop shop for all things Fremantle and Brisbane in the lead-up to the grand final. See all stories . Loading

Lachie Neale did not deserve to miss the grand final for his less-than-forceful gut punch on Jack Ginnivan. The final outcome, which must rank among the most stunning and contentious in the annals of AFL judicial hearings, was just. Fremantle fans will not agree, and conspiracy theorists will enjoy speculating about the tendency for high-profile players to be cleared for grand finals, as though the overturning of the original verdict was preordained. Lachie Neale spoke to the media on Thursday night after having his one-match ban overturned on appeal. Nine News This is a case of questionable reasoning by the appeals tribunal that, nonetheless, has arrived at a fair outcome. Neale’s minor swinging punch on Ginnivan – call it a jog-by – was not an action that warranted the player missing the grand final. A flawed argument – based on improvisational application of elastic AFL rules – can, and did, arrive at the fair outcome.



The appeals board, comprised of three ex-player/lawyers and headed by Richard Loveridge, invoked the rule that allows for exceptional circumstances, in this case Neale’s record of zero suspensions over 320 games; the panel argued that the AFL tribunal, which upheld the match review officer’s original decision to suspend Neale for one match, had not given Neale’s record sufficient weight. Loading Downgrading the ban to a $10,000 fine was an unusual call, too. The player’s advocate, Adrian Anderson, had floated the notion that the suspension be served next year (when Neale will be a Collingwood player, we think). Those with memories of past grand final judicial cases will note that good players who are on the borderline of suspension are usually acquitted, one way or another. Andrew Dunkley had his three-match ban for belting James Hird (who sported a cut eye in his joint Brownlow Medal victory with Michael Voss) postponed three decades ago and won the chance to man Wayne Carey in the grand final. This was a flat out travesty – Dunkley should not have played via a court injunction.



Loading Another critical Swan, Barry Hall, had his match review verdict for a punch to Matt Maguire’s midriff – much more of a gut-wrenching blow than Neale’s – overturned in 2005 via the convenient argument that the punch had been “in play”, rather than off the ball. Hall was seen as lucky, and “big Bazza” did not have an unblemished record to fall back on. Related Article AFL grand final AFL grand final teams, expert tips: Is this Freo’s first premiership side, or will Lions get their three-peat? Carlton’s Aaron Hamill had his two-match suspension for kneeing Bomber Dean Wallis in that extraordinary 1999 preliminary final overturned via the appeals board. The biomechanics expert witness had worked his magic. Richmond skipper Trent Cotchin’s high bump on Dylan Shiel was given the all-clear by the match review panel (of three members then) in a judgment that players would have little hope of gaining in today’s more concussion-conscious times. Shiel was off for the remainder of the game. As with Hall, there was considerable sentiment around the team the skipper represented, and who were about to break lengthy premiership droughts.



The players who were not cleared in grand final week, such as Jason McCartney (1999) and Anthony Rocca (2003), were too far over the line to get leniency. Related Article Brisbane Lions Appeals board stunner: Neale free to play in the grand final, cops fine instead The original verdict of the MRO and upholding of the ban by the AFL tribunal were instances in which those bodies followed the rules that the league has outlined. The AFL, at the direction of football boss and immediate ex-Lions CEO Greg Swann, had instituted crackdown on punches to the body, such as Neale’s. The practical test – would you want someone to miss a grand final for that? – was conducted, and answered in the affirmative by the MRO (which consults the AFL bosses) and then the tribunal. The issue, thus, was not that the MRO or tribunal erred. They applied the rules at their disposal.



The underlying wrinkle was that the match review system leaves little room for shades of grey in the grading of offences. Neale’s advocate, Adrian Anderson, contended that there must be exceptions to the grading grid, the ex-AFL football boss so ironically having been the architect of the grading system back in the 2000s. Neale’s was deemed “medium force” and intentional, when the force was not at the level that deserved suspension, in round 15, let alone a grand final. Loading The appeals panel took a different stance. In effect, they viewed it with fresh eyes, as if it was a de novo case. The difference they found to the tribunal seems to derive from a view that Neale did not deserve to miss the grand final. A reason and rule were invoked to that end.



I had thought on Monday that Neale would be cleared by dint of his record, believing that the tribunal would not so strictly apply Swann’s handiwork and would find an exception for lucky Lachie. He was cleared, eventually. The footy gods smiled on the Lions, at least until Saturday. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Boy dies after being shot inside Sydney apartment
World.content:
An 11-year-old boy accidentally shot in the face inside a Sydney apartment has died in hospital. Detectives are working to establish the circumstances surrounding how the boy was shot at the Moda complex in Norwest on Monday afternoon. An 11-year-old boy has died after being shot in the face inside a Sydney apartment. Instagram Investigators believe the boy, who cannot be legally identified, may have accidentally shot himself while handling an illegal gun inside the apartment, but they have not ruled out the possibility that someone else in the apartment accidentally fired the gun. He is not believed to have been intentionally shot. The boy’s mother and several 18-year-old men were inside the apartment at the time but were not injured.



Paramedics treated the boy, who suffered wounds to his face and neck, before rushing him to The Children’s Hospital at Westmead in a critical condition. His family on Thursday night switched off his life support, police said. The boy’s father, a convicted cocaine dealer, paid tribute to his son in a social media post on Thursday afternoon. The boy’s father, a convicted cocaine dealer, paid tribute to his son on social media. Instagram Police swarmed the Norwest complex on Monday night after the boy was shot. Wolter Peeters “Rip my baby,” he wrote alongside a photo of the pair. Other members of the boy’s extended family are linked to organised crime and known to police.



The boy’s school said its community was deeply saddened by the 11-year-old’s death. Related Article Updated

Crime ‘Absolutely tragic situation’: Boy may have accidentally shot himself while handling gun “Our thoughts and prayers are with his family, friends, classmates and all those affected by this tragic loss,” the school said in a statement on Thursday night. None of the occupants inside the apartment have cooperated with investigators, who as a result have been unable to establish how the boy was shot. The boy’s family has cooperated with police. Homicide squad commander Detective Superintendent Joe Doueihi on Thursday said that investigators had spoken to all but one of the people inside the apartment at the time of the shooting.



Police are yet to locate the gun involved in the shooting, and believe one of the men inside the apartment fled with the weapon before emergency services arrived. Police said no firearms were registered to the apartment. The circumstances of how the gun came to be in the home are under investigation. Police do not believe the shooting is linked to ongoing conflicts between Sydney organised crime networks. “It’s evident that one of the occupants or one of the persons present at the unit has taken the firearm away shortly after the shooting and got rid of the evidence,” Doueihi said. An 18-year-old man, Isaac Bechara, remains in custody charged with concealing a serious indictable offence. Bechara was arrested at the apartment alongside two other 18-year-old men, who were released without charge. He did not apply for bail when he appeared in Bankstown Local Court on Tuesday. No arrests have been made over the 11-year-old’s death. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: The flow-on effect of stardom
World.content:
Peter B Buckley of New Ulm, Minnesota, USA, lords it over us with this celebrity encounter (C8): “In 1961, my father and I were staying at the Savoy in London when there was a knock on the door. It was the hotel manager who informed him that our bath had overflowed and flooded the suite below. After finding out the room where the affected people had been moved to, we went down to apologise and present a bottle of champagne as a peace offering, as it were. My father knocked on the door, and as it opened, he said, ‘Why, hello Larry.’ It was Sir Laurence Olivier. It was then that I learnt they had met back in 1941, ironically at the Savoy, during World War II.”

Not to be outdone, Lance Dover of Pretty Beach was browsing one lunchtime in the tiny RM Williams city store. “I thought I was the only customer, until the change room door opened, and I came face to face with Lauren Bacall. I was, unusually, left speechless as we just nodded to each other. She was appearing in Sweet Bird of Youth at the time. The Rolls-Royce outside was nice looking too.”

“Sorry Tom Meakin, no offence meant, but to your mother’s claim that she was playing hide and seek with Profumo, I can only repeat the famous Mandy Rice-Davies reply: ‘Well she would say that, wouldn’t she?’” With thanks to Jeremy Parsons of Milton.

“If Pauline Hanson would let the back of her hair grow a bit, we would have the first sighting of a red mullet in Canberra,” notes John Elder of Annerley (Qld). “Until then we’ll have to put up with the plain old red snapper.”

Jack Dikian of Mosman observes that “Trump declared the US would officially refer to AI as ‘Super Intelligence’. I’m surprised he didn’t land on ‘American Intelligence’.”

World.title: Keep Miley weird! But maybe not this kind of weird, this is bad weird
World.content:
CultureMusicReview Keep Miley weird! But maybe not this kind of weird, this is bad weird Robert Moran and John Shand September 24, 2026 — 8:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

On Bass Persuades, Miley dips a toe into grimy club music, and worse. Miley, Bass Persuades ★★ It’s about time Miley Cyrus was recognised as pop’s prevailing kook. A veteran at 33, whose career peaked by the time she was 20, she’s a cultural figure of the psychedelic ’60s kind, the kind of pop star who definitely would’ve written a song with Charles Manson. One day she’s out here hosting a tacky TV special in Solid Gold sequins, the next she’s inviting outré weirdos like Wayne Coyne or Ariel Pink or Harmony Korine into the studio to collaborate. With those bona fides, you’d imagine you could play her albums backwards and summon Satan, but somehow they always just sound like ABBA cast-offs or Bruno Mars-style AM-soul. I don’t get it.



On Bass Persuades, she’s dropped the last name and gone full club mode, enlisting indie provocateur Cole Haden of Model/Actriz as a partner-in-crime. His queer carnality and penchant for grinding distortion brings a daring touch to the (potentially) blasphemous Different Religion, Orbit and Innocent Ways. But in typical Miley fashion, it’s mostly a wreck. The titular single, with its faux-Gaga disco stomp, is an odd attempt at spurring a generation from its apathetic malaise, a sort of Kids in America for the post-monoculture era. But its limping melody and confounding lyrics (“Ghosts went to Bermuda ’cause there’s no one to haunt”) inspire less abandon and more furrowed brow. And then there’s Neon Signs, which might actually be the worst song ever, a bizarre tilt at Serge Gainsbourg and Jane Birkin’s orgasmic Je T’aime... Moi Non Plus, recorded with Oscar-winning Miike Snow singer-songwriter Andrew Wyatt, who is 22 years Miley’s senior. It is simply grotesque. Miley Cyrus, pop’s prevailing weirdo, follows her own muse – for better or worse – on her new album.



And yet, somehow, it could be worse. At a time when Slovak breakout Adela is crafting chart-toppers with Cyrus’ peak sound, you’ve gotta admire Miley for sticking to her own weirdo wavelength. Someday, something good will come of it, surely? Robert Moran Mike Nock & Leah Berry, The Gift ★★★★ An exquisite dichotomy exists between the sweetness of Leah Berry’s voice and the worldliness of her words. “I move slow,” she tells us, “since the last time I found warmth in your embrace.” Yet, at the end, she’s affirming, “You’ll stay in my dreams.”



This complex love song about clinging to passionate memories is called The Gift, and the music was penned by pianist Mike Nock as a wistful instrumental. Berry sent her lyrics to Nock, and a collaboration was born. She set words to eight more tunes, and they also used Jo Lawry’s lyrics to Nock’s exotic Nata Lagal. Mike Nock and Leah Berry find a natural collaboration on The Gift. Embracing You is a variation on The Gift’s lyrical content, this time about a glance, a smile, an affair, and another love that will live on post-fling, like a soul that’s left its body. The terminated affair in Sunshowers sparks more overt bitterness, Dawn Bird is a poetic account of awakening in New Zealand’s Haast Pass, and Thinking of You is a reverie about a parent. Nock, revelling in having words set to his music, responds with some of his most lavish lyricism, superbly supported by bassist Jonathan Zwartz and drummer Laurence Pike. John Shand

World.title: How sons of Lions royalty forged their own legacies, and can go even further
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 How sons of Lions royalty forged their own legacies, and can go even further Nick Wright September 24, 2026 — 7:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

From Wharfie Time to Country Roads, this is your one-stop shop for all things Fremantle and Brisbane in the lead-up to the grand final. See all stories .

Their fathers are some of the most famous names in Lions’ history, but this modern-day trio are on the cusp of succeeding their legacies. After Adrian Fletcher cemented his reputation as one of the old Brisbane Bears’ toughest competitors, before featuring in the Lions’ maiden campaign, Marcus Ashcroft etched his name into the record books within the famed triple premiership-winning sides of the early 2000s. Now their sons – Jaspa Fletcher and Will Ashcroft – are a win over Fremantle on Saturday away from equalling those three-straight titles. But more remarkably, given Ashcroft senior retired after hoisting the trophy in 2003, they are still in the fledgling stages of their AFL careers. Jaspa Fletcher and Will Ashcroft joined the Lions at the same time as father-son draftees. Getty Images At just 22, Will has announced himself as one of the code’s leading players in big moments – evidenced by his back-to-back Norm Smith Medals. Another medallion would draw him level with Richmond great Dustin Martin, but make him the first to achieve the feat in consecutive seasons.



His exploits in the preliminary final thriller against Hawthorn – finishing with a goal, 28 disposals, eight clearances, 10 inside 50s and two goal assists – thrust him to the top of the leaderboard in the race for the Gary Ayres Award for the finals series’ most dominant player. As Fletcher – who joined Will in Brisbane as a father-son draftee in 2023 – declared his close mate “sets his sight on September” from the first rep of preseason, younger brother Levi Ashcroft said his ability to raise his standard in big games stemmed from their childhood. “It is widely known all the things he does during the week – preparation, nutrition, all the stuff that goes on – he’s doing all the extras the top guys do,” Levi, whose debut season finished with the 2025 premiership, said. “All that stuff definitely helps him be ready and be prepared for big moments, and it just feels like he elevates himself and his game when those big moments come.



“I feel like that’s the narrative; we’re born to play in these moments, but I feel like with all the hard work we’ve done behind the scenes for 15 years to be ready and feel like we’re prepared for big moments, we really like to attack them and want to make an impact.” While the Ashcroft siblings have captured headlines, Fletcher’s quieter demeanour and defensive nous has meant his own piece of history has flown under the radar. Levi Ashcroft has become a star in his own right out of his family shadows. AFL Photos via Getty Images On Saturday, the 22-year-old will become the first player of the AFL era to reach the last Saturday of September in each of his first four seasons. It is ironic, Fletcher laughed, given his junior career included a solitary grand final; one he lost by 100 points. While his first for the Lions ended in defeat to the Magpies in 2023, he believed it proved the catalyst for the club’s back-to-back titles.



Related Article AFL 2026 ‘I owe them’: The heartbreaking setbacks fuelling Lions’ comeback warriors “I remember after the game, [coach Chris Fagan’s] first message was ‘sometimes to win a grand final, you have to lose one’. I know at the time that’s not what people wanted to hear, but at the end of the day, I think it’s probably true,” Fletcher said. “You learn a lot of lessons about how to go about the day and the week leading in, so I think that 2023 loss – as much as you want to win – probably set us up the last couple of years knowing how to go about grand final week, and how different the day is compared to a regular game.” After a year in which the halfback concedes he has not lived up to his own lofty standards – his average disposals (18.92), rebound 50s (3.08) and inside 50s (2.08) all down from last season, after enduring a slow start from off-season shoulder surgery – Fletcher vowed to cast his frustrations behind him on the biggest stage. “I’ve been pretty honest with my form this year and haven’t been overly proud with how I’ve gone about it. I think I could’ve gotten a little bit more out of myself,” he admitted.



“I had my shoulder done in the off season, and you don’t really do much of a preseason, everything’s a bit delayed, and it’s a 20-week injury. But at the same time I don’t really like to use that as an excuse – that’s just part of footy.” Loading The Ashcrofts and Fletcher had been poised to have even more demanded of them against the Dockers, after Lachie Neale had faced being banned for a gut punch on Hawthorn’s Jack Ginnivan. However, the two-time Brownlow Medal winner sensationally won his appeal on Thursday evening, with his punishment downgraded to a $10,000 fine. It will likely be his last game in Lions’ colours, with 33-year-old tipped to join Collingwood from 2027.



“He’s probably one of the toughest players I’ve seen and played with. He’s left such a great legacy at the club,” Fletcher said. Related Article AFL grand final Why Conor McKenna’s magic acts are no luck of the Irish “He’s got to do what’s right for him, but at the same time I’d love to still have him. As a mate and [my] mentor, I can’t thank him enough for what he’s done for me.” Levi – who was drafted as an inside midfielder, before being used on the wing and in the forward line for Brisbane – declared before the verdict he was ready to take on greater duties, on grand final day and beyond. And he vowed to help ensure Brisbane would not fall in the same manner they did when last reaching four-straight deciders – reaching just one finals series from their 2004 grand final defeat to 2019.



“I feel like I’m ready to do that and step up. As an under-ager I played more inside midfield, so to be able to play these positions, I’ve learnt heaps over the last two years,” the 19-year-old said. “But I’m ready to go if that happens. Obviously, he’s a huge part of our team ... but I feel like we’ve got a really good midfield that surrounds him. “We’ve got some really good youth coming through, so hopefully we can continue to bring in youth and still stay young while we have some older veterans playing good footy.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

Carlton’s Aaron Hamill had his two-match suspension for kneeing Bomber Dean Wallis in that extraordinary 1999 preliminary final overturned via the appeals board. Richmond skipper Trent Cotchin’s high bump on Dylan Shiel was given the all-clear by the match review panel (of three members then) in a judgment that players would have little hope of gaining in today’s more concussion-conscious times. Shiel was off for the remainder of the game. As with Hall, there was considerable sentiment around the team the skipper represented, and who were about to break lengthy premiership droughts.



The players who were not cleared in grand final week, such as Jason McCartney (1999) and Anthony Rocca (2003), were too far over the line to get leniency. Related Article Brisbane Lions Appeals board stunner: Neale free to play in the grand final, cops fine instead The original verdict of the MRO and upholding of the ban by the AFL tribunal were instances in which those bodies followed the rules that the league has outlined. The AFL, at the direction of football boss and immediate ex-Lions CEO Greg Swann, had instituted crackdown on punches to the body, such as Neale’s. The practical test – would you want someone to miss a grand final for that? – was conducted, and answered in the affirmative by the MRO (which consults the AFL bosses) and then the tribunal. The issue, thus, was not that the MRO or tribunal erred. They applied the rules at their disposal.



The underlying wrinkle was that the match review system leaves little room for shades of grey in the grading of offences. Neale’s advocate, Adrian Anderson, contended that there must be exceptions to the grading grid, the ex-AFL football boss so ironically having been the architect of the grading system back in the 2000s. Neale’s was deemed “medium force” and intentional, when the force was not at the level that deserved suspension, in round 15, let alone a grand final. Loading The appeals panel took a different stance. In effect, they viewed it with fresh eyes, as if it was a de novo case. The difference they found to the tribunal seems to derive from a view that Neale did not deserve to miss the grand final. A reason and rule were invoked to that end.



I had thought on Monday that Neale would be cleared by dint of his record, believing that the tribunal would not so strictly apply Swann’s handiwork and would find an exception for lucky Lachie. He was cleared, eventually. The footy gods smiled on the Lions, at least until Saturday. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Boy dies after being shot inside Sydney apartment
World.content:
An 11-year-old boy accidentally shot in the face inside a Sydney apartment has died in hospital. Detectives are working to establish the circumstances surrounding how the boy was shot at the Moda complex in Norwest on Monday afternoon. An 11-year-old boy has died after being shot in the face inside a Sydney apartment. Instagram Investigators believe the boy, who cannot be legally identified, may have accidentally shot himself while handling an illegal gun inside the apartment, but they have not ruled out the possibility that someone else in the apartment accidentally fired the gun. He is not believed to have been intentionally shot. The boy’s mother and several 18-year-old men were inside the apartment at the time but were not injured.



Paramedics treated the boy, who suffered wounds to his face and neck, before rushing him to The Children’s Hospital at Westmead in a critical condition. His family on Thursday night switched off his life support, police said. The boy’s father, a convicted cocaine dealer, paid tribute to his son in a social media post on Thursday afternoon. The boy’s father, a convicted cocaine dealer, paid tribute to his son on social media. Instagram Police swarmed the Norwest complex on Monday night after the boy was shot. Wolter Peeters “Rip my baby,” he wrote alongside a photo of the pair. Other members of the boy’s extended family are linked to organised crime and known to police.



The boy’s school said its community was deeply saddened by the 11-year-old’s death. Related Article Updated

Crime ‘Absolutely tragic situation’: Boy may have accidentally shot himself while handling gun “Our thoughts and prayers are with his family, friends, classmates and all those affected by this tragic loss,” the school said in a statement on Thursday night. None of the occupants inside the apartment have cooperated with investigators, who as a result have been unable to establish how the boy was shot. The boy’s family has cooperated with police. Homicide squad commander Detective Superintendent Joe Doueihi on Thursday said that investigators had spoken to all but one of the people inside the apartment at the time of the shooting.



Police are yet to locate the gun involved in the shooting, and believe one of the men inside the apartment fled with the weapon before emergency services arrived. Police said no firearms were registered to the apartment. The circumstances of how the gun came to be in the home are under investigation. Police do not believe the shooting is linked to ongoing conflicts between Sydney organised crime networks. “It’s evident that one of the occupants or one of the persons present at the unit has taken the firearm away shortly after the shooting and got rid of the evidence,” Doueihi said. An 18-year-old man, Isaac Bechara, remains in custody charged with concealing a serious indictable offence. Bechara was arrested at the apartment alongside two other 18-year-old men, who were released without charge. He did not apply for bail when he appeared in Bankstown Local Court on Tuesday. No arrests have been made over the 11-year-old’s death. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: The flow-on effect of stardom
World.content:
Peter B Buckley of New Ulm, Minnesota, USA, lords it over us with this celebrity encounter (C8): “In 1961, my father and I were staying at the Savoy in London when there was a knock on the door. It was the hotel manager who informed him that our bath had overflowed and flooded the suite below. After finding out the room where the affected people had been moved to, we went down to apologise and present a bottle of champagne as a peace offering, as it were. My father knocked on the door, and as it opened, he said, ‘Why, hello Larry.’ It was Sir Laurence Olivier. It was then that I learnt they had met back in 1941, ironically at the Savoy, during World War II.”

Not to be outdone, Lance Dover of Pretty Beach was browsing one lunchtime in the tiny RM Williams city store. “I thought I was the only customer, until the change room door opened, and I came face to face with Lauren Bacall. I was, unusually, left speechless as we just nodded to each other. She was appearing in Sweet Bird of Youth at the time. The Rolls-Royce outside was nice looking too.”

“Sorry Tom Meakin, no offence meant, but to your mother’s claim that she was playing hide and seek with Profumo, I can only repeat the famous Mandy Rice-Davies reply: ‘Well she would say that, wouldn’t she?’” With thanks to Jeremy Parsons of Milton.

“If Pauline Hanson would let the back of her hair grow a bit, we would have the first sighting of a red mullet in Canberra,” notes John Elder of Annerley (Qld). “Until then we’ll have to put up with the plain old red snapper.”

Jack Dikian of Mosman observes that “Trump declared the US would officially refer to AI as ‘Super Intelligence’. I’m surprised he didn’t land on ‘American Intelligence’.”

World.title: Keep Miley weird! But maybe not this kind of weird, this is bad weird
World.content:
CultureMusicReview Keep Miley weird! But maybe not this kind of weird, this is bad weird Robert Moran and John Shand September 24, 2026 — 8:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

On Bass Persuades, Miley dips a toe into grimy club music, and worse. Miley, Bass Persuades ★★ It’s about time Miley Cyrus was recognised as pop’s prevailing kook. A veteran at 33, whose career peaked by the time she was 20, she’s a cultural figure of the psychedelic ’60s kind, the kind of pop star who definitely would’ve written a song with Charles Manson. One day she’s out here hosting a tacky TV special in Solid Gold sequins, the next she’s inviting outré weirdos like Wayne Coyne or Ariel Pink or Harmony Korine into the studio to collaborate. With those bona fides, you’d imagine you could play her albums backwards and summon Satan, but somehow they always just sound like ABBA cast-offs or Bruno Mars-style AM-soul. I don’t get it.



On Bass Persuades, she’s dropped the last name and gone full club mode, enlisting indie provocateur Cole Haden of Model/Actriz as a partner-in-crime. His queer carnality and penchant for grinding distortion brings a daring touch to the (potentially) blasphemous Different Religion, Orbit and Innocent Ways. But in typical Miley fashion, it’s mostly a wreck. The titular single, with its faux-Gaga disco stomp, is an odd attempt at spurring a generation from its apathetic malaise, a sort of Kids in America for the post-monoculture era. But its limping melody and confounding lyrics (“Ghosts went to Bermuda ’cause there’s no one to haunt”) inspire less abandon and more furrowed brow. And then there’s Neon Signs, which might actually be the worst song ever, a bizarre tilt at Serge Gainsbourg and Jane Birkin’s orgasmic Je T’aime... Moi Non Plus, recorded with Oscar-winning Miike Snow singer-songwriter Andrew Wyatt, who is 22 years Miley’s senior. It is simply grotesque. Miley Cyrus, pop’s prevailing weirdo, follows her own muse – for better or worse – on her new album.



And yet, somehow, it could be worse. At a time when Slovak breakout Adela is crafting chart-toppers with Cyrus’ peak sound, you’ve gotta admire Miley for sticking to her own weirdo wavelength. Someday, something good will come of it, surely? Robert Moran Mike Nock & Leah Berry, The Gift ★★★★ An exquisite dichotomy exists between the sweetness of Leah Berry’s voice and the worldliness of her words. “I move slow,” she tells us, “since the last time I found warmth in your embrace.” Yet, at the end, she’s affirming, “You’ll stay in my dreams.”



This complex love song about clinging to passionate memories is called The Gift, and the music was penned by pianist Mike Nock as a wistful instrumental. Berry sent her lyrics to Nock, and a collaboration was born. She set words to eight more tunes, and they also used Jo Lawry’s lyrics to Nock’s exotic Nata Lagal. Mike Nock and Leah Berry find a natural collaboration on The Gift. Embracing You is a variation on The Gift’s lyrical content, this time about a glance, a smile, an affair, and another love that will live on post-fling, like a soul that’s left its body. The terminated affair in Sunshowers sparks more overt bitterness, Dawn Bird is a poetic account of awakening in New Zealand’s Haast Pass, and Thinking of You is a reverie about a parent. Nock, revelling in having words set to his music, responds with some of his most lavish lyricism, superbly supported by bassist Jonathan Zwartz and drummer Laurence Pike. John Shand

World.title: PM needs to stand up for more that’s in our interests
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters PM needs to stand up for more that’s in our interests September 24, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Photo: Matt Davidson To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. Good to see the Prime Minister, Anthony Albanese, being prominent at the United Nations General Assembly (“Albanese says the old world order ‘not fit for purpose’ ″⁣, 24/9). He has meaningful insights into middle nations developing new partners for trade and security.

He is being recognised for “his role in strengthening Australia’s alliances … across the Indo-Pacific”. He admits “for our Pacific neighbours climate change is the most immediate security threat”. Not just for them.

It would be appropriate then, for Australia to be more of a leader in climate change amelioration, and Albanese’s seat at the UN would be a great opportunity for promoting such action.

If he can stand up to the president of the United States, why can’t he stand up to mining interests in Australia and cease extending and opening new fossil fuel mines here? Why can’t we phase down our exports of these products, and have some input into reducing world carbon emissions?

The answer, of course, is that money and power speak loudly.

This underlines the importance of coalitions and working together on these complex and potentially deadly problems.

Jan Marshall, Brighton Society must be rebuilt, from bottom up

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is right about the old order of the world. The COVID-19 pandemic changed it and now there is Donald Trump. Some of the assumptions including eternal growth must be ditched.

My concern is that one in seven of us are living in poverty after 40 years of the old order, call it trickle-down economics or whatever. We need to rebuild our society from the bottom up, not the top down.

No more tax cuts, which inevitably lead to higher-income earners getting the advantages.

John Rome, Mt Lawley, WA The UN has to be remodelled

Everybody knows the international order is broken (“Albanese says the world order ‘not fit for purpose’ “, 24/9), but no one seems to want to do anything about it.

When the United Nations was formed, most of the world lived under totalitarian communism, dictatorships, absolute monarchies or colonial occupation, so no world organisation could avoid the participation of those groups. That is no longer the case.

The UN is a hypocritical talkfest. It’s time to ditch it and form a new international organisation of democracies with an elected general assembly and a security council with permanent membership of the world’s largest democratic economies from every continent not of only the five World War II victors, two of which are dictatorships. More democratic than the US, you’re in; less democratic, you’re out.

Democracy is under threat, while peace has gone, and democracies need to stick together to stop everything getting even worse.

Chris Curtis, Hurstbridge



Hanson not a star turn

The article on the prime minister’s major foreign policy speech in New York highlights Australia’s rise as an influential middle power working to shape the global geopolitical future at a time of tremendous international uncertainty.

In similar circumstances, what would One Nation leader Pauline Hanson say if she were the PM? Something that would go down about as well as Nikki Osborne’s performance at the Carbine Club as reported in CBD.

James Young, Mt Eliza That selfie, Albanese, sullied your trip

Oh Anthony Albanese, what were you thinking? Yes, you had to go to the US and yes I guess a meeting with the president was inevitable, but was it really necessary to make us all cringe with that selfie with Donald Trump? That’s about as tacky as the redecorated Oval Office.

Ross Bardin, Williamstown THE FORUM Toss graduate package

In New York, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese pushes for regulation of social media. At home, Education Minister Jason Clare is unable to say whether the Job-ready Graduates Package introduced by the Morrison government will be repealed before the 2028 election. The article, ″⁣Flat fee push to end $50,000 arts degrees″⁣ (24/9), notes distaste for this package is almost universal. An increasing number of educators and other professionals are alarmed at the effect of AI on brain development and skills.

The Morrison government deliberately steered students away from the humanities that help develop those skills. Change should be an urgent priority.

The long-term costs of failure to act could be even more substantial than other potential Morrison catastrophes such as AUKUS.

Norman Huon, Port Melbourne Tax incentives

Federal Treasurer Jim Chalmers has recently talked about income tax relief, which would surely negate the Reserve Bank’s increasing of interest rates.

What if the government increased income tax and used that extra money to reduce government debt with the required result of reducing money in circulation and bringing down inflation? Then the Reserve Bank could leave interest rates where they are. The cost burden would be more fairly spread and, in the longer term, there would be more money to pay for services we all need.

Judy Kevill, Ringwood



Parkland woes

Re the article, ″⁣No happy median in clamp on roadway drinking″⁣ (22/9): On the contrary, that people are having to resort to drinking in grassed central medians in Carlton, or elsewhere, only proves the giant deficit in parkland per capita that Melbourne has suffered for the sake of all its high-density development.

And lest we forget, whenever Indigenous Australians have done the same thing, they’ve swiftly been told to move on, or locked up, often with catastrophic consequences.

Bernadette George, Mildura A letter home

As an avid letter writer to The Age, now in my 60s, I know the demographic I’m reaching. I have a son in his 20s and one in his 30s. I was a high school teacher for 37 years. I know for certain it is most certainly not these age groups who are reading newspapers.

It worries me that the people who are going to change the world are not being so influenced by us – the ones who created the problems – but are relying on themselves to experience the issues and self-reliantly act to counter them.

Still, I will keep having a say. Perhaps you never really know who reads these words.

Frank Flynn, Cape Paterson Slaughterhouse dive

Those who worry about AI are right. When asked for information on the Australian short story, The Sleeping Doll, it insisted there was no such story. I insisted and eventually, it conceded it was wrong.

The story is about a farm worker during the Depression who worked in an abattoir. He was told to butcher some sheep. How many? Never mind how many, the owner said, just keep going until I get back. Needless to say, when he got back, every sheep had been killed.

The point? The worker had followed his instructions to the letter. The analogy becomes clear

if you substitute “humanity” for “sheep”.

As for the chatbot, it blamed its programmer, saying it had just followed the instructions it had been given. It apologised profusely, saying it was “mortified”, which was quite weird.

If not treated with respect, AI is something of which to be scared.

Claude Miller, Castlemaine What a choice

Barnaby Joyce has let the catastrophe out of the bag by revealing the demands that One Nation would make upon a Coalition minority government if given the chance (“Joyce names price of One Nation backing Angus Taylor”, 24/9).

One Nation’s retrograde policies are, however, only marginally more strident and ridiculous than the Coalition’s own policies on energy and climate, education, and immigration.

It matters not what weak assurances Coalition leaders may make; an anachronistic alliance between the Coalition government and One Nation is an absolute certainty if the Coalition has a chance to govern and needs the support of One Nation to do so.

Graeme Henchel, Yarra Glen Think before you vote

Many people are looking towards One Nation as a viable alternative at the next Victorian election. The information they are presenting online appears to be merely a lot of motherhood statements which may sound good, but there isn’t an action plan associated with the delivering of those policies, particularly one that has a timeframe and any economic costing associated with it.

It is important that people don’t vote based solely on a brand name, hoping that a change will produce results. Until you know what that change will be, its implications, and its effects on you, be wary. Ask questions, get definitive answers.

At election time, all sorts of promises will be made beforehand. It is better to know whether they are just ambit claims designed only to lure your vote, or they are ones that can, and will actually be delivered.

A vote in an election is valuable and is a privilege. It also gives you a chance to have your say. Do your research and find out what you are likely to get from all candidates and their parties.

Greg Tuck, Warragul



Tilting at windmills

With climate change denial in vogue in the Coalition, the policy it has announced this week on energy and net zero is no surprise in one sense, yet its failure to heed the economics is breathtaking.

While Quixotic tilting at off-shore wind farms may have a certain romantic appeal, Don Quixote was delusional. So, too, is the latest crusade against renewables when they are integral to lowering electricity prices.

It is astonishing that the Liberals, once the party of private enterprise, would abandon the pragmatism of letting the private sector choose whether power is generated using a particular resource or not based on cost.

The evidence suggests opting for nuclear power and investing in aged coal-fired power plants, drawing heavily on public money while blocking or frustrating private investment in renewables, will cost Australians far more than staying the course with an energy transition that several state conservative governments (though not all of them now) have backed in the past.

Jim Allen, Panorama, SA A muddle of policies

More than 450,000 people are projected to die from heat brought about by the super El Nino in the next six months, according to estimates prepared by climate scientists associated with the University of Chicago.

This sobering news comes as the Coalition wants to cancel the net zero emissions bill, offshore wind zones, and climate laws for heavy industry and car makers.

Further, the life of coal-powered electricity generators would be extended.

Former prime minister Malcolm Turnbull was quick to condemn the idiocy of this new Coalition energy plan.

It appears that the Coalition is either dominated by climate-change deniers or that they have a callous indifference to the future of humanity and especially today’s young people.

Ian Bayly, Upwey Sober reflection

In a world fraught with cynicism about politicians, it was refreshing to read Chip Le Grand’s column on Greens MP Tim Read (“Some of the best work is done quietly”, 24/9). The tributes to Read from colleagues – from all sides of politics – in Parliament House this week were enlightening.

Not only for the commentary on Read and his sense of “intelligence, curiosity and decency”, but because of the impact the man had on those he met. What a legacy to leave behind when politicians laud another because he “made us want to be better”.

And Le Grand reminds us what we often forget: behind the mask are many individuals who genuinely care about

making a difference.

Sally Davis, Malvern East The tram to Santa ...

Your correspondent (Letters, 23/9) reminded me of Santa’s tram in Bendigo during the 1970s. For the four weekends before Christmas, Santa’s tram left the Chinese Joss House tram stop full of excited children with their bags of lollies on their way to Myer. The tram was “controlled” by Santa (a young university student, yours truly).

On reaching Myer, Santa stopped the traffic and led the children up the Myer escalator to Santa’s throne for a photo and a confidential chat. Very commercial, but a lot of fun.

Wayne Rice, East Melbourne ... and to the din

Last year, we boarded the Bendigo tourist tram but unfortunately, we couldn’t hear any of the information broadcast due to the noise of the tram itself. We were left in the dark as to the significance of the edifices we passed. It was pleasant viewing but not, sadly, an informative experience.

Margaret Collings, Anglesea



AI is out of control

AI clearly can’t be controlled. And yet, the government has been conned into allowing for the exploitation of land, water and energy – with pie in the sky returns for this ″⁣investment″⁣.

Martin Field, Healesville Repeat after me

Brisbane won a premiership in 2024 then repeated in 2025. It seeks to repeat a second time on Saturday. This should be called a “twopeat” because they would be repeating the original premiership a second time not a third.

Pete Hickey, Albert Park On your bike

I agree with your correspondent (Letters, 24/9), questions over One Nation’s missing plane provides an excellent opportunity for Pauline Hanson to get on her bike.

Karen Campbell, Geelong AND ANOTHER THING Politics

Barnaby Joyce and One Nation have given the Coalition their conditions of support to form a federal government (“Joyce names price of One Nation backing Angus Taylor”, 24/9). Are they all drunk on anticipated power?

Patrick Alilovic, Pascoe Vale South



The Coalition and One Nation competing to see who can be first to abandon net zero emissions – what planet are they on?

Greg Curtin, Nunawading So, Dan Tehan promises to “take a chainsaw to Labor’s ideologically driven, energy-restrictive approach to energy”. I wonder if we can take a chainsaw to the Liberals’ ideologically driven, energy-restrictive approach to energy?

Bob Zanker, Leopold Prime minister, getting the gambling issue right can simply be achieved by adopting all the recommendations of the Murphy report.

Warren Thomas, Ivanhoe Trump

So US President Donald Trump prefers super intelligence to artificial intelligence. At least, he didn’t call it God.

Bruce Prosser, North Balwyn Donald Trump commits an act of stupid intelligence.

Jenny Bone, Surrey Hills



How about renaming AI as American intelligence?

Tim Durbridge, Brunswick Donald Trump’s repeated bleating about annihilating Iran sounds more and more like the boy who cried wolf. I can’t imagine that the Iranians are quivering in their boots.

John Walsh, Watsonia Furthermore

Ex-ADF members should definitely be unleashed on unruly preppies who lack discipline.

Colleen Heatley, Drouin West Remember when we thought all our data was in ″⁣the cloud″⁣? Turns out, it is in huge power- and water-hungry noisy buildings.

Bronwen Murdoch, South Melbourne Your correspondent (Letters, 23/9) has broken my heart by saying St Kilda will still be looking for its second premiership in 40 years. I will be about 110 by then and crestfallen.

Phil Labrum, Trentham

World.title: Allegations of favouritism, 'unsustainable' workloads at Education Ministry's curriculum division
World.content:
A damning review has found serious problems including allegations of favouritism and lack of public sector values in the Education Ministry's curriculum division.

The division is responsible for the government's curriculum rewrite and has been under scrutiny this week after multiple whistleblowers alleged attempts to subvert the Official Information Act.

The ministry commissioned the review in response to concerns raised through confidential channels and 107 provided information.

It found:

Widespread concern about favouritism by senior leaders, especially in relation to the many temporary appointments in Te Poutāhū | Curriculum Centre

Widespread concern regarding the application of public sector values and principles including fair and transparent appointment processes, conflict of interest management and concerns about the obligation to give free and frank advice to the minister not being met

Unreasonable or unprofessional workplace behaviours exhibited or tolerated by leaders

Strategy, work planning and commissioning

Organisational design and resourcing, particularly the extensive use of contractors or other temporary arrangements

Deeply held concerns about speaking up. This included fear of negative career consequences, which it was considered others had experienced, and because of

A small number of other examples of concerns relating to diversity, inclusion or equity, and sexual harassment.

The review report said some staff made positive comments, others described the workplace as toxic, and many were in the middle.

"The strongest concerns of almost all participants relate to workload and well-being. Feedback consistently described workloads as unsustainable, characterised by constant urgency and short deadlines. It was considered that more could be done to manage workloads and timeframes," the review report said.

The report said many participants were not convinced senior leaders were giving the government free and frank advice, especially with regard to the time required for implementing changes.

Some participants said some former employees left because they had difficulty being politically neutral, the report said.

"Some people spoken to were extremely passionate about their work, and the reviewer could see how this could give rise to an interpretation that they may not be willing to serve the government of the day if they disagreed with the decisions," the report said.

"However, in many cases participants described a desire for further explanation of the context or rationale of an instruction they received, or clarity about where certain instructions were coming from.

"Many referred to the opaqueness of instructions, in that they were not always sure whether an instruction was coming from the minister's office or whether it was a decision of senior leadership."

Many participants said the curriculum centre's leadership was outdated and authoritarian, the report stated.

Examples included unreasonable and intimidating behaviours, a general prevalence of swearing - though not at people, and rudeness.

Some participants said they had seen bullying, others said they had not but gave examples of less-than-ideal leadership practices.

"However, in the course of other parts of their interviews they would describe behaviours that may amount to 'indirect' examples of unreasonable behaviours (such as exclusion from work, gaslighting, threats about job security, and retaliation for voicing work-related concerns)," the report said.

World.title: Glimmer of hope in fight against kauri dieback
World.content:
Audio player for " Kauri seedlings planted with hope they are resistant to kauri dieback " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/environment/1558052%2Fglimmer-of-hope-in-fight-against-kauri-dieback

Kauri seedlings planted with hope they are resistant to kauri dieback Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

Before vast numbers were felled to build the villas of Ponsonby and Grey Lynn for early European settlers, Auckland's Waitakere Ranges were covered in ancient kauri forests.

This century they've faced another existential threat - this time in the form of kauri dieback, a fungus-like organism spread by just a pinhead of mud or soil that attacks the tree's fragile roots.

There is no known cure.

But a collaboration between mana whenua, scientists, Auckland Council and volunteers is providing a glimmer of hope.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6405516408112

On Wednesday the last some 2000 kauri seedlings were planted in the ranges and it is hoped that the young trees will have some resistance to the disease.

The scientific name for the kauri dieback, phytophthora agathidicida, translates to "plant destroyer; kauri killer".

Kauri dieback has taken out some the last of the Waitakere's giants, including the thousand-year-old Aunt Agatha.

"Unfortunately that's since succumbed to kauri dieback, " Stuart Leighton said, lead ranger for west Auckland iwi Te Kawerau ā Maki.

"She's still there as a sort of dead skeleton tree now, but we did take seeds from that tree."

Stuart Leighton and Sarah Killick. Nick Monro

He hoped the project would see Aunt Agatha's offspring thrive in the ranges.

Seeds were taken from some 650 mother kauri trees, identified by scientists and iwi as being healthy and, hopefully, resistant to kauri dieback.

Kauri dieback made it clear that something was very wrong with the overall health of the forest, Leighton said.

"When your biggest, oldest thing starts to die, then that's a real sign that we need to really start to focus our attentions on looking after this place."

A Kauri seedling. Nick Monro

Auckland Council's principal biosecurity advisor Dr Sarah Killick said they had learned a lot about kauri dieback through the project, and continue to discover more.

"We've discovered how the pathogen works - what it looks like, where it lives. We know it's a soil-borne pathogen and that's really important for us, so we know that because it lives in the dirt, the best thing we can do for kauri protection is to stop the dirt from moving between forests."

Selwyn Insley. Nick Monro

Selwyn Insley is the Māori Partnership lead for the Bioeconomy Science Institute, which collected the seeds and raised them at their Rotorua nursery.

"Specialist teams went up and collected the cones. The cones were then taken back to our nursery, dried and put into pots to grow up into the kauri trees that we see in the regional park today."

He was very excited to see the young kauri trees return to their ancestral home.

Some 2000 kauri seedlings are ready to repopulate the Waitakere Ranges. Nick Monro

"The team that looked after these trees from seed to small seedlings, I'm just wrapped that they're here," he said.

"Seeing them in the environment, at the regional park at Te Kawerau ā Maki, Tāmaki Makaurau, I'm very excited."

World.title: Former Kamo Wildlife Sanctuary lion Cleo dies, animal rescue group says
World.content:
One of four lions who faced being put down at a Whangārei animal park has died in her sleep, an animal rescue group says.

In a post on Facebook, HUHANZ said Cleo - a lion based at Kamo Wildlife Park in Northland - had severe non-regenerative anaemia and there was a high suspicion she had internal cancer.

"Before any further intervention was needed, Cleo quietly slipped away in her sleep," the post read.

"Our team have gathered around her, surrounding Cleo with the love, tenderness and respect she deserves. And perhaps there is some comfort in knowing that when Cleo showed us something was wrong, we acted immediately.

"We got her the veterinary care she needed and, importantly, we now understand that there was an underlying illness that we could not have fixed."

Cleo was born at Kamo Wildlife Park and spent her 20 years there.

Cleo is suspected to have had cancer. HUHANZ

Last November, the the directors of Kamo Wildlife Sanctuary announced the sanctuary would close and the five remaining elderly lions would be euthanised.

Operator Janette Vallance said the park's owners, Bolton Equities, made the difficult decision to euthanise the cats, which were aged between 18 and 21.

"There were no real options left. The staff and I are devastated."

HUHA stepped in and the park was purchased by ethical investors and the Lionhearts Project Trust was set up to provide for the animals' going forward, the NZ Herald reported.

At its peak in the early 2000s the park was home to 33 big cats, including lions, white tigers, leopards and cheetahs.

At that time it was called Zion Wildlife Gardens and run by Craig Busch, better known as "The Lion Man", and his mother Patricia Busch.

Busch became a national celebrity in 2004 thanks to the TV series Lion Man, and the park put Whangārei on the domestic tourism map.

However, the park ran into financial difficulties in 2006, and was bailed out by Patricia Busch, who became the sole director.

In 2009, after senior keeper Dalu Mncube was killed by a tiger, the then Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry (MAF) ordered the temporary closure of the park for safety and management improvements.

Another closure was ordered in 2014 for enclosure upgrades, this time by MAF's successor, the Ministry for Primary Industries.

Bolton Equities, which is owned by businessman Murray Bolton, bought Zion Wildlife Gardens in 2014 and reopened it as Kamo Wildlife Sanctuary in 2021.

World.title: Auckland Transport explores changes to level crossing after student's death
World.content:
Audio player for " AT explores changes to level crossing after student death " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/community/1558816%2Fauckland-transport-explores-changes-to-level-crossing-after-student-s-death

AT explores changes to level crossing after student death Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Two weeks on from a tragedy at a level crossing in Mount Albert, Auckland Transport officials have met with residents to get their views on changes to level crossings in the area.

Intended to improve safety and traffic flow, the changes will be expensive and disruptive.

Auckland Transport is talking to residents about six level crossings from Kingsland to Mount Albert.

Local residents Rob and Merla were among those who went to find out more about the level crossing changes at the Mount Albert Community Centre on Wednesday evening.

"They're not ideal the way they are, and we're keen to see the trains increase in frequency, so something has to be done. Otherwise, the traffic will be banking up into the neighbourhoods more and more, the more they close for a train to come through," Rob said.

Merla was concerned about the risk of more fatalities.

"There's been a recent one here in this neighbourhood, so it's quite prescient at the moment."

Flowers laid at Baldwin Ave train station where a Mount Albert Grammar student was fatally hit by a train. Caitlin McGee

Options for improving the crossings include raising roads, lowering the rail line, building road bridges or underpasses, and even removing homes to make new road connections.

Partial or full closure is an option for some crossings.

Rob said it's frustrating the best options are always the most expensive.

"I'm in favour of doing the right thing rather than the cheap thing. Hopefully they'll take some of that on board and give us the best solution."

Safety was also on the radar for local resident, Mark, after the recent death at Baldwin Ave Station

"When something happens, and my understanding is that's not the first time we've had something happen there, it raises (safety) closer to the top of the list."

Any changes needed to maintain connectivity through the area, he said.

"We've taken the kids through to primary school using the walking buses, and now they're up to high school level we use the public transport as well, so we love the trains. We're glad that we've got the new connections, but ...we don't want to do this at the cost of the liveability of our local areas either."

Ailsa Barr wanted to know how options for the busy Morningside Drive level crossing could impact her property which was affected by the 2023 storms.

"...because of the fact that we were impacted by the flood and everything gets put on hold for a long time, we're now potentially facing that again. I see that as a problem," Barr said.

Jenny Rasch has also been through flooding and the ensuing repairs. She worried about what could happen if the changes go ahead.

Rasch said local businesses had been trying to rebuild after COVID which had a "huge impact".

"Eden Park are now opening up to more concerts and more games and more things like that. So you want the area to become more vibrant and more people in it, but (if) you're going to start getting rid of dwellings and rerouting the roads that's going to impact everybody."

Auckland Transport head of level crossings Tom Willetts said safety improvements had been made to all level crossings in Auckland, including gates at all pedestrian level crossings.

"The next stage from that, as we look to increase train frequencies in future years, is to look to remove or replace level crossings further because that really does mitigate the risk."

Willetts said people are naturally concerned about disruptions from construction tied up with removing or replacing the crossings.

"We're working very hard to better understand the communities so that we can mitigate those impacts both in the design of the final outcome of the removal or the replacement, but also so we can build into our thinking around how the replacements or removals will be constructed."

He said each site had its own challenges.

"We have to consider impacts on the local community, but we also have to consider engineering technicalities such as ground conditions and topography, slopes and such like."

Willetts said once AT has the community feedback, they'll review the options and make a final decision with Auckland Council.
