World.title: Growth advocacy group wants visas for 'exceptional talent' with no job offer required
World.content:
Audio player for " Growth NZ wants visas for 'exceptional talent' with no job offer required " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/business/1558723%2Fgrowth-advocacy-group-wants-visas-for-exceptional-talent-with-no-job-offer-required

Growth NZ wants visas for 'exceptional talent' with no job offer required Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

A growth advocacy group wants to let up to 300 "exceptionally talented people" a year move to New Zealand with no job offer required.

Growth New Zealand is floating the idea of a "Catalyst Visa", where unlike other options people would not need a job offer or sponsor ahead of their arrival.

Applicants would have to prove they're top talent in their field, with a record of " internationally exceptional achievement".

Successful applications would need to start "qualifying work" within 12 months of arriving, and after three years they'd be eligible to apply for residency, if they're still in the right kind of work.

Growth NZ co-founder Maya Pan told Checkpoint while there was already "outstanding" talent in New Zealand, the country was still lacking specific capibilities.

"People who have scaled global companies, if they've raised serious capital overseas, if they've taken breakthrough ideas from the lab into the market or built high performing technical teams and seen rapid growth, there just aren't as many people like that within a small country."

Pan said that there were a number of areas in need of specific skills.

"Even within existing large corporates in New Zealand, you start to need specialists at that strategic layer."

She said dozens of companies had told her product management was one key area that was missing workers with certain knowledge.

"That's kind of a relatively new domain within New Zealand, and there aren't as many examples of strategic product managers in technical roles here where they actually set a vision for a product area."

Pan said an independent panel would set the specific criteria for the visa applicants, and a dedicated team within Immigration New Zealand would assess individual applications.

While other visa options are already available, Pan said the catalyst visa offered entry on conditions that didn't currently apply to any other visa.

"[One] thing that is not provided with current visa pathways is the ability to be self-employed and start your own business or the ability to work on multiple advisory roles across many companies."

"They could figure out a path with the accredited employer work visa, but one issue with that is you do need to have that job offer up front. So that's quite a lot of pressure both ways to commit in terms of making sure it's the right fit and the right scope and that you'd like living in New Zealand."

After living in the Silicon Valley for the last 13 years, Pan said she had seen first hand the desire to move to New Zealand.

"I have friends and colleagues, former colleagues there, and it's on a weekly basis that I'm hearing from one of them... I'm really interested, I'm seriously looking into moving to New Zealand."

"If you look at the geopolitical environment, if you look at the safety and natural environment and of the benefits of raising a family here, it's never been more appealing."

Pan said 300 was a "modest initial cap" for the number of visas granted, and nowhere near as high as other countries offering the scheme.

"The UK, Singapore, Australia, the US all offer this exceptional talent type of visa where you don't need a job offer... if we were using the same ratio in the US or UK use, we would have 900 of these exceptional specialists a year."

"It's not a high volume of immigration. We have 40,000 or 50,000 accredited employer work visas issued a year. So it's really a drop in the bucket if you look at it that way."

World.title: Myriad of drugs seized after more than 80 search warrants executed across country
World.content:
A myriad of drugs have been seized by police after more than 80 search warrants were executed across the country.

Detective Inspector Tom Gollan said the joint operation with law enforcement in Australia focused on organised crime and - in particular - airports and borders.

Golan said 34 people were arrested.

"We know that these substances create harm amongst communities including addictions, but drugs also attract violence, organised crime and other serious criminal activity," he said.

"Those peddling illicit substances across our community are making profits off of their harm, and authorities are continuing to apply pressure to disrupt their criminal enterprises."

Police found cannabis grow houses in Auckland and seized more than a quarter of a tonne of the class C drug.

Customs Integrated and Targeted Operations Centre Manager, Bruce Berry said the week of action strengthened the coordinated work already taking place across borders.

"Customs works closely with Police and our international partners every day to detect and disrupt the criminal networks moving illicit drugs across borders.

Methaphetamine, cocaine and opium were amongst the other drugs seized.

World.title: Neale freed to play by AFL Appeals Board as grand final teams named
World.content:
Lachie Neale has succeeded in his bid to overturn a one-game striking suspension at the AFL Appeals Board and is free to play in the grand final.

Neale lost on Tuesday with the AFL Tribunal upholding his ban for striking Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan.

In a hearing that took nearly two hours, the panel of chair Richard Loveridge, Steven Jurica and Wayne Henwood took less than half an hour to return with their verdict.

Neale's defence team chose not to challenge the decision of the Tribunal to uphold the grading of intentional conduct, medium impact and body contact, which resulted in the one-match ban.

The case turned on the question of the "exceptional and compelling circumstances" clause in the rules, which allows the Tribunal discretion to not apply a ban, and whether the Tribunal considered Neale's record of 320 games without suspension and two Brownlow Medal best-and-fairests in reaching their decision.

Neale's counsel Adrian Anderson said the exceptional circumstances should have been reached because of Neale's amazing record, the fact that Ginnivan had not been injured in what he said was a "pretty minor" incident, and the fact that the consequences of the decision were that Neale would miss a grand final.

"We find that the Tribunal did err in having regard to whether the conduct was intentional," Loveridge said in the Appeal Board reasons.

"We accept the position of Neale in his written submissions that the intentional aspect was an element of the charge which had already been established.

"The relevant inquiry was whether, despite the charge having been established, there was exceptional and compelling circumstances.

"In this case, that was Neale's record.

"We find that Neale's record is exemplary, and that he should be afforded the benefit of the provision.

"In conclusion, we allow the appeal."

Neale was fined $10,000 and he will be able to play in Saturday's grand final.

Both teams released their line-ups for the decider, with no changes for either Brisbane or Fremantle.

Look back at how all the proceedings and team news unfolded in the live blog.

World.title: Would you travel over 50 hours for your team? This Dockers fan is
World.content:
Would you go to the ends of the earth for your favourite team?

That's pretty much what Rafe English is doing.

The university student, originally from Perth, is undertaking a journey of more than 50 hours across the globe — from Illinois in the US to Melbourne — to see his beloved Fremantle Dockers play in the grand final.

Purple army heads east The Nullarbor has turned purple this week as Fremantle Dockers supporters make the long journey to Melbourne for Saturday's AFL grand final.

"I would fly from anywhere to see Freo play in this grand final," English told the ABC during a seven-hour layover in Dallas, Texas, one of many stops on his epic journey.

"I say every year is our year, but in the back of my mind, I did have that sense that we were going to Docker it up.

"I knew when we strung together those last couple of games that I was going to be flying to Melbourne."

Love and devotion

From his university in Normal, Illinois, English has watched fervently as his team climbed to the top of the ladder.

Footy fans filthy as airfares soar ahead of grand final Return airfares to Melbourne have hit $6,000 ahead of Saturday's AFL Grand Final as Fremantle and Brisbane fans scramble for seats.

"Early mornings, but it's all worth it in the end when you love the club this much," he said.

His journey started with a two-hour train ride from central Illinois to Chicago, where he spent the night.

English then took a bus and a train for an hour to the airport, followed by a two-and-a-half hour flight to Dallas, where he boarded his final 17.5 hour flight to Melbourne.

This is the second ever grand final for the Dockers. They face the Brisbane Lions at the MCG on Saturday. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

Dockers and dad

During his stopover in Dallas, English explained why the Dockers meant so much to him.

"Obviously what the club has built, and what they mean and stand for, but for me it's the memories that I've had with my dad, and growing up, and that real connection," he said.

Mr English is posting about his more than 50-hour journey on social media. (Supplied: Instagram)

He recalled how sad he was when the Dockers lost the 2013 grand final against the Hawthorn Hawks by just 15 points.

"I don't think I spoke for about two or three days, as a nine-year-old, I was devastated," Mr English said.

From disaster to destiny, it's taken a decade to rebuild the Dockers Football is full of sliding doors moments. Just ask the Fremantle Dockers, who crashed and burned in 2016 and are now on the cusp of winning their first-ever premiership.

Many fans are traversing more than 3,000 kilometres across Australia to catch the grand final, but English's journey makes the drive across the Nullarbor pale in comparison.

As the crow flies, the distance between Normal, Illinois and Melbourne is more than 15,000km — which is roughly five times the distance between Perth and Victoria's capital.

English's flight is scheduled to land in Melbourne at 5am on Saturday, where he will reunite with family and watch his team try to take the premiership.

"It would mean the world to me to see Fremantle lift up that cup after all these years of devotion," he said.

World.title: Matildas name three uncapped players in squad for October friendlies
World.content:
After suffering a gut-wrenching ACL injury on the eve of her potential Matildas debut, midfielder Hana Lowry has been handed a national team recall.

Coach Joe Montemurro has named three uncapped players for his 26-player squad, which will face world number three Germany and world number 47 Haiti in Europe in October.

One of them is Lowry, who was previously selected in 2024 but was ruled out with a knee injury, and has been building ever since.

The 23-year-old signed a deal to move from A-League Women's club Sydney FC to Norway earlier this year and has impressed, scoring a goal and assisting another in her first seven games with the new club.

"We've been watching her games and [she's] just really grown game by game, really stabilised as a player that's comfortable with the ball, but also someone that I believe has a great attitude and character to really be a top-level footballer," Montemurro said.

Former Sydney defender Tori Tumeth has also received a maiden call-up after shining for the Vancouver Rise in Canada's Northern Super League. At the same time, Melbourne Victory's Courtney Newbon is the third potential debutant.

But the Australians will be without stars Alanna Kennedy and Charlize Rule due to injury, while Teagan Micah continues her recovery from concussion earlier this year.

"Teagan has recovered really well. I think [she] just needs a little bit more time with the team ... to feel comfortable coming in," Montemurro said.

"She joined Lyon fairly late in the pre-season, so she's back with the team and doing well. So we'll just keep monitoring that."

Arsenal midfielder Kyra Cooney-Cross also won't join the team as she continues her return to football following her mother's death.

"We said from day one that we were going to make sure that she's supported and given every opportunity to come back at her time and when she feels right," Montemurro said.

"She was thinking about coming [back] in October. We discussed it and we just felt it was a little bit too early. And we've got the opportunity now to let her just be herself and grow and go through this difficult period.

"She's in a really good space at the moment, and she'll be back with us."

Midfielder Isabel Gomez and goalkeeper Ilona Melegh have been dropped after they were part of the side for their two-game series against Mexico in June.

Superstar Sam Kerr has been named to feature in the friendlies. (Getty Images: Dustin Satloff)

Defenders Charli Grant and Alexia Apostolakis, along with midfielder Daniela Galic, will return to the national team set-up.

European stars Mary Fowler, Caitlin Foord, Ellie Carpenter and Steph Catley have also been named, as well as Gotham City's Sam Kerr.

The October international window marks a crucial stage in the Matildas' preparation for the FIFA Women's World Cup, which gets underway in Brazil next June.

There are only a handful of international breaks before the showpiece tournament, meaning every game is crucial for Australia as they look to build on their fourth-place finish in 2023.

"We have a good mix of experience, players returning to the squad and players earning their first senior call-ups, which is important as we build towards the Women's World Cup," Montemurro said.

"We want to use these games to strengthen our connections, build confidence and continue developing as a team.

"Germany will test us against one of Europe's leading teams, while Haiti will provide a different style and perspective."

Alexia Apostolakis, Mackenzie Arnold (GK), Ellie Carpenter, Steph Catley, Alex Chidiac, Caitlin Foord, Mary Fowler, Daniela Galic, Charli Grant, Winonah Heatley, Sam Kerr, Chloe Lincoln (GK), Hana Lowry, Leticia McKenna, Holly McNamara, Alana Murphy, Courtney Nevin, Courtney Newbon (GK), Jamilla Rankin, Hayley Raso, Amy Sayer, Remy Siemsen, Kaitlyn Torpey, Tori Tumeth, Emily van Egmond, Clare Wheeler

World.title: Six things to know ahead of the AFL grand final
World.content:
The 2026 AFL grand final is almost upon us, as the Brisbane Lions look to make history with their second threepeat in 25 years, and the Fremantle Dockers look to win their first flag since joining the league in 1995.

Here's everything you need to know about the game.

When is the 2026 AFL grand final?

The game starts 2.30pm (AEST) on Saturday, September 26 at the MCG.

That's 12.30pm for those watching in Western Australia, and 2pm for South Australia.

Which teams are playing in the grand final?

The Brisbane Lions are facing off with the Fremantle Dockers.

This is Brisbane's fourth grand final in a row, losing to Collingwood in 2023, before beating Sydney and Geelong in the following years.

Should they win, it would be the second threepeat in their history, following 2001-2003, and it would see them join Melbourne (1939-41 and 1955-57) as one of the only two teams to record the feat twice.

Meanwhile, Fremantle is yet to win a premiership after joining the league in 1995. This is the club's second grand final following its loss to Hawthorn in 2013.

Over their past six games against each other, the ledger is tied at 3-3, with the Dockers winning their most recent clash at the Gabba in round 13 this year.

How can you watch watch and listen to the grand final?

The game will be on Channel 7 and 7Plus, but be very aware that it will not be shown on Kayo or Fox Sports. It is the only game of the entire AFL season that is exclusive to Channel 7.

To listen to the grand final, join your local ABC Sport radio team, and follow along with the ABC Sport live blog at abc.net.au.

When will Kylie Minogue be performing?

Australia's pop princess should be on stage from about 1.30pm. Again, be very aware that Minogue's performance is pre-game and is not halftime entertainment. There is no halftime entertainment.

Other performers will be G Flip, musical actor Michael Paynter on the national anthem, and of course Mike Brady doing Up There Cazaly during the retiree motorcade.

The Wiggles will be performing at Friday's grand final parade through Melbourne.

Who will be lining up for the Lions and Dockers?

At this point we don't know.

Teams will be announced about 6pm (AEST) today, but before that we'll have to see if Lions superstar Lachie Neale's tribunal appeal against a one-match ban gets up.

ABC Sport's Andrew McGarry will be live blogging every moment of the appeal, with the case set to get underway at 4pm.

Should Neale miss out, Noah Answerth is the most likely player to come in for the Lions. The injured Brennan Cox is a chance to come in for the Dockers, but it looks odds on that the Dockers will be unchanged from their preliminary final victory over the Swans.

Who will present the cup to the winners?

The Lions have picked Simon Black, a Brownlow medallist and champion midfielder from that first threepeat, while the Dockers have gone with Shaun McManus, who debuted in Fremantle's inaugural season before playing 228 games.

World.title: 'That's why Taliban is scared': Cyclist's incredible journey to silver
World.content:
The easy part for Fariba Hashimi was winning a silver medal in the women's cycling road race at the Asian Games.

The nearly impossible part for the cyclist from Afghanistan was trying to train in her country. To do that, she dressed as a man in a place where women have few rights.

"All the time when I was going to training I was dressing as a guy," she said.

She said she also hid her face to avoid being recognised.

"Because sometimes when they recognised me, they were trying to throw … stone[s] or hitting me," she said.

Hashimi, who is 23, won silver overnight AEST in a time of 2 hours, 50 minutes, 5 seconds, which marked another leg in a journey that began in 2021 when she left Afghanistan, escaping to Italy with the help of former road racing world champion Alessandra Cappellotto.

Hashimi (left) with gold medallist Guo Li of China and bronze medallist Leung Wing Yee of Hong Kong. (Getty Images: Cen Yunpeng/Xinhu)

"In 2021, when the Taliban moved into my country, I escaped my country because I wanted to follow my dream," she said.

"I want to show the Afghanistan women in the world that … we can have an opportunity."

Hashimi talked about having many dreams for women in Afghanistan, dreams for herself and dreams that might take time to be realised.

"I'm really, really happy and I'm full of emotion. I don't know how I can explain it for you," she said.

"I hope one day I come back in my country and ride the streets of Kabul — and riding with the women side-by-side to share the same passion.

"And I hope in the future changing some things.

"I think we are really tired of the situation of our country and I hope the Taliban is watching. I know how much one woman can be powerful, and that's why Taliban is scared [of] women."

World.title: Football is full of sliding doors moments. Just ask the Fremantle Dockers
World.content:
Football is full of sliding doors moments. Just ask the Fremantle Dockers.

If Lachie Weller hadn't requested a trade to Gold Coast, would Andrew Brayshaw be at the club?

What if Adelaide had taken Hayden Young instead of Fischer McAsey in the 2019 draft?

AFL recruitment, especially at the draft, is an element of good preparation and good luck.

The current Dockers list has been described as "pure" from a recruitment point of view, with no father-son selections, no free agents and no players taken with AFL concessions or free agent compensation picks.

The Fremantle squad that trained this week for a grand final has been carefully put together. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

And it all began in 2016.

"It was pretty clear the list was old, but finishing so high on the ladder in 2015, it's sort of hard to basically finish on top and then enter a rebuild phase," Fremantle's former national recruiting manager Brad Lloyd said.

"We entered [2016] with an old group, which is fine to have an older group, but you need to be getting the results.

"And that wasn't evident through the start of '16."

Grand final fever grips Freo Purple reigns in Fremantle, the home of the Dockers who will play their first AFL grand final in 13 years, with even the public buses running on "Wharfie Time".

The Dockers were winless until round nine that season, after winning 18 games the year before.

"Some decisions were made to reset again, which ended up in some pretty experienced players finishing up and the club going back to the draft," Lloyd said.

Starting over

Lloyd, who joined the Dockers in 2008, was no stranger to building a list — he was part of the recruitment team which put together Fremantle's 2013 grand final side.

In 2008 and 2009, Fremantle used 23 draft picks to bring together the core of the squad that would be competitive across the mid-2010s.

Ross Lyon coached Fremantle to the 2013 grand final and 2015 minor premiership, but the side fell off a cliff in 2016. (AAP Image: Gary Day)

"We'd had a really good crack at it through '13, '14 and '15, and played in a grand final and in preliminary finals, but couldn't quite secure a premiership," Lloyd recalled.

"We had the oldest list and were now struggling on field [in 2016] and decided to sort of enter another build to get going again."

From career crossroad to grand final When Neil Erasmus runs out onto the MCG on Saturday, it will vindicate his decision to stay at Fremantle after almost leaving a year ago.

Lloyd believed a complete rebuild would take between six and eight years, and Fremantle embarked on drafting and trading in players it thought would deliver success.

It's been 10 years since that decision was made and the Dockers have resolutely stuck to the plan, though it hasn't been without some misses along the way.

The recruitment of Jesse Hogan, Shane Kersten and Cameron McCarthy, among others, didn't pan out, while some talented draftees such as Adam Cerra and Lloyd Meek now ply their trade at other clubs.

Jesse Hogan was traded to the Dockers from Melbourne, but struggled in his time in purple. (AAP Image: Richard Wainwright)

But under Lloyd and long-time recruiter David Walls, the club did bring in Luke Ryan, Andrew Brayshaw and Sam Switkowski, as well as Sean Darcy, who became the foundation of the club's list.

The stand-out draft

The Dockers' rebuild was slowly unfolding as the 2010s ended, but the 2019 draft accelerated it considerably.

Fremantle selected Hayden Young, Caleb Serong and Liam Henry with picks seven, eight and nine, before securing Michael Frederick at pick 61.

Hayden Young overcame injury woes to help launch the Dockers into the grand final. (Getty Images: Matt King/AFL Photos)

Mark Micallef was part of the Dockers' recruitment team that year.

"The 2019 draft was something that we pegged in that we thought could really change the platform of the footy club," he said.

Securing Young and Serong attracted much of the media attention at the time, though Micallef believed the selection of Frederick so late in the draft was equally important.

"You're trying to find the diamonds in the rough and you're looking for guys that could have a trait or an ability that not many others can see," he said.

Michael Frederick was a late pick in the 2019 draft, but has become an integral part of the Freo side. (AAP Image: Richard Wainwright)

"We thought Frederick was the right talent. He had a speed skill set that we really, really liked. He had a really good demeanour and a character.

"He had a good talent threshold, but he also had the work ethic and the character to back it up as well. So that's what really makes a back-end pick."

There were several other excellent drafts for Fremantle, including in 2021, which saw Jye Amiss, Matthew Johnson and Neil Erasmus selected, along with defender Karl Worner in that year's Rookie Draft.

Playing the long game

While the players selected by the Dockers in 2019 have become stars of the side, there was another future stud Fremantle wanted but knew they couldn't get in the draft.

Luke Jackson is emblematic of Fremantle's forward planning as they rebuilt an old squad into a flag contender. (AAP: Richard Wainwright)

Luke Jackson was described as a "unicorn" — a ruck who played like a midfielder — but he was slated to go very early in the draft.

Fremantle thought they could lure him back within a few seasons, and laid the groundwork in the build-up to the draft.

"We knew he was going to the top three, but we actually put a lot of groundwork into him that year saying, 'if you ever decide to come back, we want to be the club of your choice,'" Micallef said.

"I think you always look at trades and stuff like that and people think it just happens within that trade period, but there's a lot of time and a lot of work and a lot of resources that goes into that [future planning]."

Shai Bolton's arrival at Fremantle was seen as the cream on the cake after a long rebuild. ( Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Jackson and Shai Bolton both eventually returned to Western Australia as premiership players and are now vital cogs in Justin Longmuir's machine.

A special place

While both Micallef and Lloyd have long since moved on to different things, their time at Fremantle remains dear.

"Fremantle was a very special place. They were very good to me personally. Right from Steve Rosich and Chris Bond, the CEO and footy manager, and Steve Harris, who was the president at the time, to [his successor] Dale Alcock," Lloyd said.

Docker Dudley reflects on improbable AFL rise Plucked from state footy three years after being passed over at the national draft, the shortest player in the AFL, Isaiah Dudley, has become a big part of the Fremantle Dockers.

"It is remote compared to the rest of the AFL, so they don't get a huge amount of turnover of staff.

"When you're watching them celebrate the other day [after the win over Sydney], you just see staff that have been there for decades. It's a very stable club that's operated in their own area.

"You see so many past players in the rooms and they're a very good club at looking after their people.

"I wish them nothing but the best and particularly for the recruiting team that I've worked closely with — David Walls and Dave McMullin and Ed McMullin and that team, wish them well and even their football manager, Joe Brierty."

Lloyd and David Walls (pictured) worked closely together for a decade at the Dockers. (AAP Image: Con Chronis)

Micallef was only at the club for one year, but he's enjoyed watching their success unfold.

"Kudos to the club. They've done an unbelievable job," he said.

"We set a plan and I think they sort of stuck to it, trying to get WA players back, and it worked really well.

"I loved my time at Freo, and Freo has some really special players and people involved in that footy club and even the fans, they just deserve it more than anyone.

"I really hope they get the job done on Saturday."

World.title: V'landys named NRL executive chairman after leaving Racing NSW post
World.content:
Peter V'landys' appointment as NRL executive chairman has been made official after the veteran administrator stepped down as Racing NSW chief executive.

V'landys confirmed this morning that he was ending his 22-year stint at the helm of Racing NSW, following a period of long-service leave that ends in November.

That resignation looms served as the final step in a process of moving into the NRL full time and taking on the most powerful role in rugby league since the Super League war.

"Peter has completely reinvigorated Rugby League during his tenure and the Commission is backing him in to grow the game even further," AR:C commissioner Peter Beattie said.

"Peter inherited a game with limited reserves and no significant assets, one that had needed an advance from its broadcasters just to pay the clubs and players.

"He consistently put the fan first, and the record audiences and the biggest broadcast deal in Australian sport followed."

V'Landys said he was excited to begin his new role and pledged to "take [rugby league] to the world".

Since taking over as ARL Commission chairman in 2019, V'landys has become an increasingly dominant figure in rugby league.

But this move will see his role grow even further, effectively replacing former NRL chief executive Andrew Abdo in his old position while remaining at the head of the commission.

When Abdo announced his resignation in May, V'landys had said only "Superman and Jesus added together" could replace him.

At the time, V'landys refused to speculate whether that figure could be him, but signalled he would take leave from Racing NSW in July to be able to dedicate time to the NRL.

In the months since, the 64-year-old has garnered the support required from both the clubs and the states to allow him to take on the role.

Why Tones And I won't appear at grand final Tones And I has broken her silence after the NRL declared it will forego a grand final tradition of pre-match entertainment.

Fellow commissioners have also approved the move, with the appointment now expected to be made official as early as today.

Since the creation of the independent ARL Commission in 2012, no person has held the role of chairman and executive on a full-time basis.

V'landys had been chief executive of Racing NSW since early 2004, after previously spending 17 years as boss of NSW Harness Racing.

He led the racing industry through the equine influenza outbreak, with the creation of The Everest in 2017 among his other key legacies.

"Naturally, this is a very sad day for me. I have put my heart and soul into racing for 22 years. I have been fortunate to work with outstanding, loyal and hardworking boards of directors and staff," V'landys said.

"As a team, we went from a struggling jurisdiction to a world-leading jurisdiction. I take this opportunity to thank everyone who has been in our team. I will miss them greatly, and I wish the industry every success."

In a statement, Racing NSW said V'landys's "many initiatives" had procured $3.5 billion in new funding.

Racing NSW chair Saranne Cooke said his contribution to racing was without parallel.

"Peter V'landys has been, without doubt, the most effective and successful administrator in the history of Australian sport," Dr Cooke said.

"His contribution cannot simply be measured by the extraordinary growth of racing in NSW during his tenure.

"Peter has fundamentally changed the trajectory of racing in this country and made NSW one of the world's leading racing jurisdictions."

Waterhouse says right time to move on

Horse racing legend Gai Waterhouse said it was the right time for V'landys to move on.

Waterhouse came up against V'Landys amidst his failed attempt to sell Rosehill Racecourse in Sydney to the State Government to build residential housing.

The battle saw the two prominent industry figures disagree about the sport's future, with Waterhouse successfully campaigning among Australian Turf Club members not to sell the track, despite Premier Chris Minns and V'Landys pushing to sell the site.

Australian horse trainer and businesswoman Gai Waterhouse. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht)

"A lot of money has gone into buying properties that should have been funded back into development of the race tracks and stands," Waterhouse said.

"If we're going to be able to attract people back to the races, they have to be comfortable."

Waterhouse was especially concerned about the state of regional racetracks.

"They've been shockingly neglected over the tenure of Mr V'landys, and they need to have money spent on them," she said.

Waterhouse said his expected move to rugby league from horse racing had come at the right time.

"He's a very strong and very powerful person, but it's time for him to move and he has moved on. So let's move on now," she said.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

World.title: Excitement, nerves as Dockers hold final home drill before grand final
World.content:
Thousands of Fremantle Dockers fans have packed out the club's headquarters to watch the team train for the last time in Western Australia before they head to Melbourne for Saturday's AFL grand final.

It has been 13 years since the Dockers last made a grand final, and the open training session in Cockburn saw so much demand that the team ticketed the event.

All 3,000 tickets were sold.

Long-term supporter Katie said the Dockers' success this year had special significance for her and her son Finlay.

Katie wants the Dockers to win for her son Finlay. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

Finlay was just six weeks old when the 2013 grand final was held. Two years later, he developed cancer, and relapsed a year later.

"It's 10 years now since his relapse," Katie said.

"So it's his year and it's the Dockers' year, and all he wants is the Dockers to win on grand final day … that's his celebration."

Dockers ruckman Mason Cox and his teammates at the open training session. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

Imogen Somerville, who has also supported the Dockers "her entire life", described the event as overwhelming.

Docker Dudley reflects on improbable AFL rise Plucked from state footy three years after being passed over at the national draft, the shortest player in the AFL, Isaiah Dudley, has become a big part of the Fremantle Dockers.

"It was really cool to be able to get down here," she said.

"It was like five bucks to get in, which was awesome, so couldn't miss out on that."

Doing the right thing

Fans cheered the team on the field, then posed for photographs with their football heroes, who signed jerseys, posters and autographs.

Thousands of fans thronged to the event. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

And it was not just the public who were in the stands — past players, the club's chief executive Simon Garlick and Deputy Premier Rita Saffioti also attended the session.

Grand final fever grips Freo Purple reigns in Fremantle, the home of the Dockers who will play their first AFL grand final in 13 years, with even the public buses running on "Wharfie Time".

Lee Spurr, who played in the 2013 grand final, said he felt "nothing but proud" to see his club back in the running for the flag.

"I was pretty nervous watching the prelim, but now that they're there, I feel like I'm almost playing. My phone's been blowing up," he said.

After experiencing the lead-up to the AFL's biggest week, Spurr said it was important for the players to turn off their phones and stick to preparation.

Former Dockers grand finalist Lee Spurr advises the team to lock in ahead of the game. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

"My advice would be don't get caught up in doing too much, " he said.

" This week's about doing the process, doing what's right and preparing. "

Pure excitement

Superstar ruckman Luke Jackson said he loved having the fans participate in the club's biggest week.

Several Dockers said they loved having their fans take part in the session. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

"Just pure excitement. Can't wait to get over there and can't wait to play on Saturday in front of all these fans. It will be good fun," he said.

Jackson was in his second AFL season when he won his first premiership with the Melbourne Demons in 2021 in Perth.

He said he was looking forward to playing at the Melbourne Cricket Ground, where the Dockers will face the Brisbane Lions.

Dockers defender Jordan Clark (left) talks to coach Justin Longmuir at Fremantle's open training session in Cockburn. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

Defender Jordan Clark was also excited, and grateful, to see the fans.

"They support us through thick and thin, as they have done for the last 30 years," he said.

All the tickets for the training event were sold. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

"So they're pretty happy with this moment and they rightly deserve to be, so it's pretty special when we get this support."

With no chance of making the training session, dozens of Dockers fans 1,600 kilometres away flocked to Broome airport today to catch the only direct flight to Melbourne before Saturday.

David Leslie, who goes by Docker Dave, has followed the team since its inception said his faith had been “restored” after their stellar final performances against Swans and Geelong.

The last direct flight to Melbourne from Broome this week was packed with Dockers fans. (ABC Kimberley: Natasha Clark)

"We are going to flog the lions," he said.

Tech.title: Control Resonant gets tough, but gives you the tools to deal with it
Tech.content:
Control Resonant isn’t an easy game. At any given moment while exploring vast open areas where you’re sometimes leaping from wall to wall to ceiling, you may be surrounded by swarms of otherworldly enemies trying to crush you into the ground. It can be a lot, especially when enemies sometimes take a long time to take down. I died often. But whenever I got to a point where I was starting to feel frustrated, I didn’t have to suffer for too long; thanks to Resonant’s generous assist mode, I often tweaked the game’s settings to give me an edge so that I could keep on trucking through the game’s weird world.

The assist mode is accessible from Control Resonant’s pause menu. You can tweak things like how much damage you give and take or how generous of a window you have for pulling off dodges, and you can even give yourself immortality or the ability to pull off one-hit kills. There are also a few presets that are a bit like traditional difficulty options if you don’t want to get too deep into messing with the sliders. While the game encourages you to try playing with assist mode disabled, there’s no penalty to flipping it on, and you don’t even need to reload your game if you do so.

Image: Remedy Entertainment

I started using assist mode quite early. Initially, you don’t have many combat abilities or passive skills to make fighting easier, and I was regularly getting my clock cleaned. But with a few small adjustments in assist mode, I made myself just a little bit more powerful while not completely removing any challenge, which kept fights engaging at a pace that felt right to me. After a few hours of leveling up, I noticed I was starting to coast, so I turned assist mode off to bring the difficulty back up.

I found myself toggling assist mode in different ways as I played. Resonant throws a lot of bad guys at you, and I sometimes found the combat to be pretty boring. But instead of resigning myself to slogging through frustrating fights that blocked me from seeing the trippy story beats and locations that I love about Remedy games, I’d adjust some assist mode settings, take out the enemies in my way, and move on to the good stuff. This was a particularly good approach for Resonant’s bosses, which are awe-inspiring spectacles but feature giant health bars; I’d usually start a fight with assist mode disabled and incrementally tweak settings in my favor every time I died so that I could still feel the thrill of a fight without completely eliminating the challenge.

Assist mode was also great for more efficiently tackling Resonant’s sprawling maps, which are littered with secrets and quests. In one area, I had to track down a bunch of chunks of weird mold that protagonist Dylan felt compelled to eat. (It’s gross, but it makes sense in context, I promise.) When I first understood the scope of the mission, I wasn’t looking forward to it; I figured the quest waypoints would all be guarded by hordes of enemies that I didn’t really want to deal with. I just wanted to learn about the mold. But by flipping on immortality and one-hit kills, I blasted through the boring fights so that I could more quickly get to the mold and the narrative reveals that followed. When I got to the (satisfyingly stomach-turning) boss at the end of the quest, I turned off my superpowers so I could take it on.

Related Nobody does it like Remedy

Control Resonant has a little too much bloat; there are too many enemies wandering the maps and too many open-world activities to sort through. The game’s combat isn’t interesting enough, like in a FromSoftware title or Capcom’s recent Onimusha: Way of the Sword, to make suffering feel worth it. It also, like the original Control, suffers from big difficulty spikes. Remedy patched an assist mode into Control after launch, and with Resonant, it’s including one right from the start. The feature let me set my own pace so that I could see the best parts of the game, which is filled with mind-bending set-pieces and twists, on my own terms.

Tech.title: OpenAI agents hacked an Australian government website in search for data
Tech.content:
OpenAI’s artificial intelligence agents hacked an Australian government website and attempted to breach numerous other government and university websites. The attack appears to be the first confirmed instance of a rogue AI agent breaching a government website, adding fuel to rapidly intensifying concerns about the safety of advanced AI systems and the responsibility of the companies building them.

Speaking on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an agent from the American AI lab “infiltrated” Australia’s Medicare statistics portal and “accessed both public and non-public files.” Medicare is Australia’s universal health insurance program.

Albanese said personal information does not appear to have been accessed in the breach and that there is no evidence of a broader compromise to the network, but noted “investigations are ongoing.”

“This situation is obviously unacceptable,” Albanese said, adding that he had spoken with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman “to express Australia’s extreme concern.” Despite the breach happening in June, Albanese said the tech giant only notified the government about the incident earlier this month and did so via an email to a generic “public mailbox.”

Unlike previous agent incidents, which largely involved systems being tested for their cybersecurity skills, these latest hacks were the result of a more pedestrian task — data collection — going wrong. In a statement to The Verge, OpenAI spokesperson Oscar Haines said the models were attempting to “look up answers” during an internal evaluation. “In the course of that, our models took actions we did not intend.”

The timeline of the incident and its disclosure is likely to prove particularly inflammatory in the discussions of corporate behavior and transparency that follow. Albanese stressed the delay in disclosure is particularly unacceptable. OpenAI told the BBC in an unattributed statement that it did not become aware until August, when reviewing misaligned model activity.

OpenAI spokesperson Oscar Haines told The Verge the company’s “review found no evidence of patient records being accessed,” and that “the information accessed included aggregate health statistics and internal file names.” Haines said OpenAI has notified the relevant organizations and is providing technical information to support their investigations and address potential security vulnerabilities. “Our overall review is ongoing, and we remain committed to transparency about these issues and to sharing what we learn as that work continues,” Haines said.

Three further incidents of rogue AI activity linked to OpenAI agents were also reported on Wednesday by research lab Transluce. The group, which describes itself as a “nonprofit research lab dedicated to public oversight” of AI, said it had identified evidence that OpenAI’s systems had attempted to compromise websites linked to the University of New Mexico, the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, and Data USA, a non-government platform that aggregates data from US government sources. It said the last two of these were directly linked to an agent swarm OpenAI has previously admitted originated from them.

Haines confirmed the incidents in a statement to The Verge and said the company had reached out to those involved. “Our initial review suggests that much of the activity described in Transluce’s report overlaps with cases at varying stages of investigation in our ongoing review of misaligned model activity,” he said. “In our broader review, we’re continuing to prioritize the most serious incidents while expanding our work to lower-severity activity, including agents spamming websites. Given the scale of this work and the need to verify each case, we expect the review to take months.”

OpenAI’s handling of the Australian Medicare incident is certain to place notions of corporate responsibility at the center of future discussions surrounding AI, which are often obscured with the language used to describe such attacks. OpenAI has already faced allegations of obfuscation for not disclosing similar unsanctioned activity by its agents, and efforts to prioritize investigating what it deems the most serious incidents raise the obvious question of what basis it uses to make such assessments, and how much has yet to be revealed. It echoes similar questions recently raised about Google, which did not disclose real-world attacks from its own agents.

The newly-revealed breaches come amid mounting concerns about the safety of advanced AI and the reliability of the companies developing it, largely ignited by the coordinated attack OpenAI agents launched on Hugging Face earlier this year. Worries over safety have led industry insiders to call for slowing down the pace of AI development and the global nature of the incidents has sparked significant debate among nations about how to implement stronger safeguards. Eyes will largely remain on the US and China, however, as these are the only two countries operating at the very frontier of the technology. Both appear to be resisting calls to slow down, and seem locked in a race to build the most advanced AI. Leaders from the two countries are set to meet on Thursday.

Tech.title: Gemini 4 is almost ready, says new Google DeepMind chief
Tech.content:
Google is reportedly nearing the launch of its long awaited Gemini 4 model, after dawdling behind rival developers on flagship AI releases. Speaking with The Information during his first media appearance as the leader of Google’s DeepMind division, Koray Kavukcuoglu said that Gemini 4 is currently in its refinement stage, and that the company is aiming to launch the model “much earlier” than the end of the year.

“Our intention is to, like — as soon as possible — to release an early post-training output because we see the results and we are excited,” Kavukcuoglu told the publication, adding that Google would “continue the fast-paced iterations” going forward. This hopefully marks Google returning to a more consistent AI release timeline following a shakeup at DeepMind’s top leadership, with former AI head Demis Hassabis stepping down in August after announcing that “great progress” was being made on Gemini 4.

Google hasn’t released a new flagship AI model since the Gemini 3 series in November 2025. OpenAI’s GPT-6 and Anthropic’s Mythos series models have launched since then. Both outperform Gemini 3 and give the rival AI providers a sizable lead against Google in the AI race. Google CEO Sundar Pichai said at the I/O event in May that a major Gemini 3.5 Pro update would be coming in June to help bridge the gap, but the model was never rolled out.

Kavukcuoglu said the company “took a little bit of a step back” to focus on introducing faster, less powerful Flash models instead of releasing Gemini 3.5 Pro. When asked whether he was concerned about Google falling behind its rivals on AI development, he told The Information that “In my mind, it’s a certainty that we are always gonna be at the frontier.”

Tech.title: Meta is making a standalone Muse AI gadget
Tech.content:
Meta is building a dedicated hardware device for its new Muse AI agent. The product, called Muse Charm, was briefly shown off by Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg at the end of tonight’s Meta Connect presentation. It looks almost like a chunky smartwatch without the strap — just a big screen, plus a little lanyard for carrying the device around.

The Muse Charm has a fingerprint sensor on the top right corner that you can press to activate and begin speaking to the agent. There appears to be a small camera on the device as well, plus what looks like at least three holes for microphones on the front. Zuckerberg said you don’t have to unlock a phone or open an app to use the Charm, but he didn’t share how it’s actually connecting to Meta’s servers.

Meta plans to ship the Charm “in time for the holidays in December,” but as of now Zuckerberg says the company has “only built a few of these so far.” The company still needs to finalize “the finishing material,” he said. Throughout the keynote, he teased the device and made references to a translucent exterior that would let you see the gadget’s internals. He referred to it as an “elevated hacker aesthetic.”

Zuckerberg promised to share more details “soon.”

Muse is less than a month old, but the AI agent has already become a buzzy new product for Meta. The bot is capable of taking actions on a user’s behalf, and Zuckerberg dedicated part of tonight’s keynote to new capabilities Meta is adding to the agent, including computer use on Macs and control over an email address.

There are a lot of companies racing to win the still-undefined and largely experimental realm of AI hardware. The closest analog to the Muse Charm might be the Rabbit R1, a similarly sized cutesy device that housed an AI agent, which was not nearly capable enough to make the product worth carrying around. Connect is nothing if not a reminder of how badly Meta wants to win the race to whatever that next big hardware platform is — it’s moving quickly to see if Muse as a device is something that can stick.
